reading.title: The career-change generation
reading.text: For our parents, a career was often a single straight line: one company, one profession, a gold watch at retirement. Today, it looks more like a zigzag. Surveys suggest that many young professionals expect to change careers — not just jobs — several times in their lives. Take Rodrigo, 38. He worked as a lawyer for ten years, but he'd been feeling unhappy for a long time. Three years ago, he started a coding bootcamp at night. "I've been working as a software developer for two years now, and I've never been happier," he says. Experts say the key skills for this new world are adaptability and continuous learning. In other words, the question is no longer "What do you want to be when you grow up?" but "What have you been learning lately?"

grammar.title: Can / could / be able to
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Can** = habilidade **presente** (saber, conseguir, poder):
"I **can** speak three languages." / "**Can** you swim?"

**Could** = habilidade **geral no passado**:
"I **could** read when I was five." / "I **couldn't** sleep last night."

**Be able to** = o mesmo sentido de can, mas funciona em **todos os tempos**, onde can não pode ir:
- futuro: "I**'ll be able to** come tomorrow." (❌ "I'll can")
- present perfect: "I**'ve never been able to** whistle." (❌ "I've could")
- depois de outro verbo: "I'd like **to be able to** play the piano."

**Sucesso numa situação específica do passado:** use **was able to** ou **managed to** (não could):
"The fire was huge, but everyone **was able to** escape." / "I **managed to** finish on time."
Na negativa, **couldn't** funciona sempre: "I **couldn't** find my keys."

**Perguntas com How:** How **fast** can you run? How **long** can you hold your breath? How **well** can you cook? How **far** can you swim?

reading.title: It's never too late
reading.text: Many adults believe that they can't learn new skills after a certain age. "I couldn't learn a language now — my brain is too old," they say. Neuroscience says otherwise. Thanks to neuroplasticity, our brains can create new connections throughout our lives. Children may learn some things faster, but adults have advantages too: they can organize their study, understand grammar rules and connect new information to what they already know. Consider Dona Neusa from Minas Gerais: she couldn't read until she was 70. She went back to school, and two years later she was able to read her first novel. "I've been able to do things I never imagined," she says. Her secret? "I never gave up."

grammar.title: Pedidos e How could you...?
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Escala de educação dos pedidos:**
1. **Can you** + verbo? → informal, amigos e família
2. **Could you** + verbo? → educado, o mais versátil
3. **Would you** + verbo? → educado
4. **Would you mind** + verbo-**ing**? → muito educado (bom para favores grandes)
5. **I was wondering if you could** + verbo → muito indireto e formal

Para pedidos grandes, **prepare o terreno**: "Could you do me a **big** favor?" / "I hate to ask, but..."

**Respostas:**
- Sim: Sure! / Of course. / No problem. / I'd be happy to.

reading.title: The Ben Franklin effect
reading.text: Do you want someone to like you more? Ask them for a favor. It sounds strange, but it's a well-known psychological phenomenon called the Ben Franklin effect. In the 18th century, Benjamin Franklin had a political rival who didn't like him. Instead of being extra nice to him, Franklin wrote a polite letter asking if he could borrow a rare book from the man's library. The rival lent it, Franklin returned it with a warm thank-you note, and the two became friends. Psychologists explain that when we do someone a favor, our brain looks for a reason: "I helped this person, so I must like them." The lesson? Small favors — "Could you recommend a good restaurant?" — can build relationships. Just don't ask for too many!

grammar.title: Conselhos: should, ought to, had better
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Should / shouldn't** + verbo base → conselho, opinião (o mais comum):
"You **should** see a doctor." / "You **shouldn't** work so late." / "**Should** I call him?"

**Ought to** + verbo base → mesmo sentido de should, um pouco mais formal e menos comum em perguntas e negativas:
"You **ought to** apologize."

**Had better ('d better)** + verbo base → conselho **forte, com aviso** de consequência negativa (é presente/futuro, apesar do "had"):
"You**'d better** leave now, **or** you'll miss your flight."
Negativa: "You**'d better not** tell her."

**Outras formas de aconselhar:**
- **If I were you, I'd** + verbo → "If I were you, I'd take the job." (note: **were** para todas as pessoas)
- **Why don't you** + verbo? → "Why don't you try yoga?"
- **Have you tried** + -ing? → "Have you tried meditating?"
- **I'd recommend** + -ing → "I'd recommend talking to HR."

Lembre-se: **advice** é incontável → "some advice", "a piece of advice" (❌ "an advice", "advices").

reading.title: Advice from 100-year-olds
reading.text: What can we learn from people who have lived for a century? Journalists and researchers who have interviewed centenarians around the world have noticed some common advice. "You shouldn't worry so much about money — you can't take it with you," said a 102-year-old woman from Okinawa, Japan. A former farmer from Sardinia, Italy, recommended: "Walk every day, and eat with your family." Many said that people ought to forgive more easily, because holding grudges only hurts yourself. And almost all of them mentioned relationships: "If I were you, I'd call my friends more often. In the end, people are what matter." Interestingly, very few of them talked about work or success. Maybe we'd better listen to them before it's too late.

grammar.title: must / have to / mustn't / don't have to + might / may
grammar.explanation_pt:
**OBRIGAÇÃO**
- **Must** + verbo → obrigação forte, regras escritas, ou algo que **você** acha necessário: "Passengers **must** wear seatbelts." / "I **must** call my mom."
- **Have to** + verbo → obrigação externa, do dia a dia (regras, circunstâncias). É mais comum na fala e funciona em todos os tempos: "I **have to** work on Saturday." / "She **has to** wear a uniform." / "I **had to** wait for an hour." / "You'll **have to** pay a fine."

**⚠️ A grande pegadinha das negativas:**
- **mustn't** = **proibido** (não pode!): "You **mustn't** use your phone while driving."
- **don't have to** = **não precisa** (é opcional): "You **don't have to** wear a tie. It's casual Friday."

**POSSIBILIDADE (talvez)**
- **might / may / could** + verbo = pode ser que, talvez: "It **might** rain." / "She **may** be late." / "That **could** be a problem."
- Negativa: **might not / may not** (não could not): "I **might not** go."

**DEDUÇÃO (tenho quase certeza)**
- **must be** = deve ser (certeza positiva): "You worked 12 hours? You **must be** exhausted!"
- **can't be** = não pode ser (certeza negativa): "That **can't be** Ana — she's in Paris."

reading.title: Strange laws around the world
reading.text: Every country has its rules, but some laws might surprise you. In Singapore, you mustn't chew gum in most situations — selling it has been illegal since 1992 to keep the streets clean. In Switzerland, some apartment buildings have rules saying residents mustn't flush the toilet late at night because of the noise. In Japan, companies with employees aged 40 to 74 have to measure their waists during health checks — a policy to fight obesity. In Denmark, parents must choose their babies' names from an official list of approved names, or ask for special permission. These laws might seem strange, but each one tells us something about the culture that created it.

grammar.title: Causative: get / have + objeto + particípio
grammar.explanation_pt:
Quando **outra pessoa** faz algo **para você** (geralmente um serviço pago), use o **causative**:

**get / have + objeto + particípio passado**
- I **got my hair cut**. (o cabeleireiro cortou — não eu)
- She **had her car washed**.
- We need to **get the roof repaired**.

Compare:
- "I **cut my hair**." = eu mesmo cortei (com tesoura em casa! ✂️)
- "I **got my hair cut**." = cortei no salão

**Get** é mais informal e comum na fala; **have** é um pouco mais formal. O sentido é o mesmo.

O causative funciona em **todos os tempos** — só muda o get/have:
- presente: I **get** my nails done every two weeks.
- passado: I **had** my eyes tested yesterday.
- futuro: I**'m going to get** my car fixed.
- present perfect: Have you **had** your passport renewed?
- modal: Where **can** I **get** this printed?

**Perguntas:** "Where **did** you **get** your hair **cut**?" / "Where can I **have** my shoes **repaired**?"

I'm going to get my hair cut.

examples.pt: Vamos pintar o apartamento semana que vem, então vamos ficar com meus pais.

grammar.tip_pt: Expressões fixas muito úteis: **get your nails done** (fazer as unhas), **get a tattoo** (fazer uma tatuagem), **get your eyes tested** (fazer exame de vista), **get your teeth cleaned** (fazer limpeza nos dentes).

common_mistakes.why_pt: Se outra pessoa cortou, use o causative.

common_mistakes.why_pt: O mecânico conserta: causative + at the mechanic's.

common_mistakes.why_pt: O verbo vai no particípio (fixed).

pronunciation.tip_pt: No causative, o particípio fica no fim e é bem audível. Lembre os três sons: **fixed** ("fikst"), **cleaned** ("klínd"), **painted** ("pêintid"). E **cut**, **done**, **made** são irregulares.

reading.title: The right to repair
reading.text: Have you ever had a phone repaired, only to be told that it's cheaper to buy a new one? You're not alone. For years, many manufacturers have made it difficult for customers to get their devices fixed: special screws, glued batteries, and parts that only official stores can buy. Now, a global movement called "Right to Repair" is fighting back. The European Union and several US states have passed laws requiring companies to sell spare parts and repair manuals for many products. Supporters say this will reduce electronic waste — one of the fastest-growing types of waste in the world — and save consumers money. In Brazil, small repair shops have always been part of the culture: we get our shoes resoled, our clothes altered and our appliances fixed. Maybe the rest of the world is finally catching up.

grammar.title: prefer / would prefer / would rather
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Prefer** → preferência **geral** (sempre):
- prefer + **substantivo** + **to** + substantivo: "I prefer **tea to** coffee."
- prefer + **-ing** + **to** + -ing: "I prefer **walking to** driving."

**Would prefer ('d prefer)** → preferência **específica** (agora, nesta situação):
- 'd prefer + **to** + verbo: "I'd prefer **to stay** home tonight."
- 'd prefer + substantivo: "I'd prefer a window seat."

**Would rather ('d rather)** → preferência **específica**, muito comum na fala:
- 'd rather + verbo **base** (sem to!): "I'd rather **stay** home."
- comparação com **than**: "I'd rather **walk than take** the bus."
- negativa: "I'd rather **not** go."
- pergunta: "**Would you rather** watch a movie **or** go out?"

Resumo das estruturas:
- prefer A **to** B
- would prefer **to** do A (**rather than** do B)
- would rather do A **than** do B

grammar.tip_pt: **I'd rather not** é uma ótima forma educada de recusar sem dar explicações: "How much do you earn?" — "**I'd rather not say.**"

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I'd rather** soa "**áid réder**" (americano) ou "**áid ráde**" (britânico). O 'd é curto mas importante — sem ele, "I rather" está errado. **Either** e **neither** têm duas pronúncias: "íder / áider".

reading.title: Introverts and extroverts at work
reading.text: Some people would rather work in a quiet room alone; others prefer a busy open office full of conversation. Psychologists often describe this difference using the terms introvert and extrovert. Introverts usually prefer deep one-on-one conversations to big group meetings, and many would rather write an email than make a phone call. Extroverts, on the other hand, often get energy from people and prefer brainstorming out loud. Most people, however, are somewhere in the middle — sometimes called ambiverts. The problem is that many workplaces are designed for extroverts: open-plan offices, constant meetings and team-building events. Smart companies now offer options: quiet zones, "no-meeting" days and flexible work. After all, people do their best work when they can choose how they work.

questions.q: What are ambiverts?

grammar.title: Verb + -ing / verb + to
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Verbos + -ing (gerúndio):**
enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, keep, give up, consider, suggest, miss, practice, can't stand, don't mind
"I **enjoy reading**." / "She **gave up smoking**." / "Do you **mind waiting**?"

**2. Verbos + to + verbo (infinitivo):**
want, need, decide, hope, plan, expect, agree, refuse, promise, learn, afford, manage, offer, would like
"I **want to travel**." / "They **decided to move**." / "I can't **afford to buy** a car."

**3. Preposição + -ing (sempre!):**
"I'm interested **in learning**." / "She's good **at drawing**." / "Thanks **for coming**." / "I'm thinking **of moving**." / "**Before leaving**, check the windows."
Atenção: **look forward to** e **be used to** terminam em preposição **to**, então pedem **-ing**: "I look forward to **meeting** you."

**4. Verbos que mudam de sentido:**
- **stop + -ing** = parar de fazer: "I **stopped smoking**." · **stop + to** = parar para fazer: "I **stopped to buy** water."
- **remember + to** = lembrar de fazer (antes): "**Remember to lock** the door!" · **remember + -ing** = lembrar de ter feito: "I **remember meeting** him in 2010."
- **try + to** = tentar (esforço): "I **tried to open** the jar." · **try + -ing** = experimentar: "**Try drinking** tea with ginger."

**5. Like, love, hate, start, begin, continue** → aceitam os dois com pouca diferença: "I like **swimming** / **to swim**."

examples.en: I've been considering moving abroad, but I can't afford to leave my job yet.

examples.en: Remember to send the report! — Don't worry, I remember sending it yesterday.

examples.en: I'm really looking forward to seeing you next week.

grammar.tip_pt: Aprenda esses verbos **em chunks**, não em listas: "enjoy doing", "want to do", "good at doing", "look forward to doing". Repetir os blocos é mais eficiente que decorar regras.

reading.title: Why we procrastinate
reading.text: We all know the feeling: you need to finish a report, but you keep checking your phone, cleaning your desk, or watching "just one more" video. Most people think procrastination is about being lazy, but psychologists disagree. Research suggests that procrastination is mainly about avoiding negative emotions — boredom, anxiety, fear of failure. When a task makes us feel bad, our brain decides to look for something more pleasant. So how can we stop procrastinating? Experts suggest breaking big tasks into tiny steps ("open the document" instead of "write the report"), using a timer to work for just 25 minutes, and forgiving yourself for procrastinating in the past. Interestingly, people who forgive themselves are less likely to procrastinate again. Now, stop reading and go do that thing you've been avoiding!

grammar.title: Subject x object questions
grammar.explanation_pt:
Quando a pergunta é sobre o **objeto** (quem **recebe** a ação), use o auxiliar normal (do/does/did):
- "**Who did** you **call**?" → "I called **my mom**." (você ligou para alguém — quem?)
- "**What did** she **buy**?" → "She bought **a car**."

Quando a pergunta é sobre o **sujeito** (quem **faz** a ação), **não use auxiliar** — a question word **é** o sujeito e o verbo fica na forma afirmativa:
- "**Who called** you?" → "**My mom** called me." (alguém ligou — quem?)
- "**What happened**?" (❌ "What did happen?")
- "**Which** app **works** best?"
- "**How many people came** to the party?"

Compare:
- **Who loves** Ana? (alguém ama a Ana — quem?) → Pedro loves Ana.
- **Who does** Ana **love**? (a Ana ama alguém — quem?) → Ana loves Pedro.

**Perguntas indiretas** (mais educadas): depois de "Do you know...?" / "Can you tell me...?", use a ordem de **afirmativa**:
- "Where **is** the bank?" → "Do you know where **the bank is**?"
- "Who **did** you **call**?" → "Can you tell me who **you called**?"

reading.title: The power of word of mouth
reading.text: Who do you trust more: an advertisement or a friend? For most people, the answer is obvious. Marketing studies have repeatedly shown that personal recommendations are among the most trusted forms of advertising. That's why so many businesses invest in referral programs: "Recommend a friend and you both get 20% off." Online reviews have become a digital version of word of mouth — but they have a problem. Who writes them? Some companies pay for fake five-star reviews, and some competitors post fake negative ones. How can you tell what's real? Experts suggest reading the three-star reviews, which are often the most honest, looking for specific details, and checking whether the same reviewer has written many similar reviews. And, of course, asking someone you actually know.

grammar.title: Passive voice: be + past participle
grammar.explanation_pt:
Na **voz ativa**, o foco está em **quem faz**: "Oscar Niemeyer **designed** Brasília."
Na **voz passiva**, o foco está **no que aconteceu** ou **no objeto**: "Brasília **was designed** by Oscar Niemeyer."

**Estrutura:** sujeito + **be** (no tempo certo) + **particípio passado** (+ by + agente)

- **Present simple passive:** am / is / are + particípio → "Coffee **is grown** in Brazil." / "These phones **are made** in China."
- **Past simple passive:** was / were + particípio → "The Eiffel Tower **was built** in 1889." / "The windows **were broken**."

**Negativa e pergunta:** mexa só no **be**: "It **wasn't made** in Italy." / "**Where was** it **made**?" / "**When were** the pyramids **built**?"

**Quando usar a passiva?**
1. Quando **não sabemos** quem fez: "My bike **was stolen**."
2. Quando **não importa** quem fez: "The office **is cleaned** every night."
3. Quando o **óbvio**: "He **was arrested**." (pela polícia, claro)
4. Em textos **formais, científicos e notícias**.

**By + agente** só quando a informação é importante: "*Dom Casmurro* **was written by** Machado de Assis."

grammar.tip_pt: Para a passiva funcionar, você precisa dominar os **particípios** (built, made, written, sold, spoken, grown, stolen, chosen). Revise a lista de verbos irregulares!

reading.title: The story of coffee
reading.text: Coffee is drunk by billions of people every day, but where did it come from? According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia, when a goat herder noticed that his goats became very energetic after eating some red berries. The plant was later taken to Yemen, where coffee was first prepared as a drink. In the 18th century, coffee seeds were brought to Brazil — legend says they were secretly given to a Portuguese officer in French Guiana. Today, Brazil is the world's largest coffee producer: around a third of the world's coffee is grown here, mainly in Minas Gerais, São Paulo and Espírito Santo. The beans are harvested between May and September and are exported to more than 100 countries.

source_refs: Top Notch 3A – Unit 5 (past perfect)

objectives: Formar o past perfect (had + particípio)
Mostrar que uma ação aconteceu antes de outra no passado
Usar by the time, when, already, before, after com past perfect
Entender notícias com sequências de eventos

warmup.text_pt: "Quando cheguei ao cinema, o filme **já tinha começado**." Esse "já tinha começado" é o **past perfect**: uma ação passada que aconteceu **antes** de outra ação passada.
questions: Have you ever arrived somewhere and something had already happened?
Had you studied English before this course?

vocabulary.pt: quando, até o momento em que

chunks.en: When I arrived, the movie had already started.
chunks.pt: Quando cheguei, o filme já tinha começado.

chunks.pt: Eu nunca tinha visto nada parecido.

grammar.title: Past perfect
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Estrutura:** **had** + particípio passado (igual para todas as pessoas)
- Afirmativa: I **had** (I'd) **finished**. / She'd **left**.
- Negativa: They **hadn't seen** it.
- Pergunta: **Had** you **been** there before?

**Uso:** mostrar que uma ação aconteceu **antes** de outra ação **no passado**. É o "tinha feito".

Linha do tempo:
[ação 1 — past perfect] → [ação 2 — simple past] → agora
"When I **got** to the station, the train **had left**." (o trem saiu primeiro; depois eu cheguei)

Compare:
- "When I arrived, the train **left**." = cheguei e então o trem saiu (vi saindo)
- "When I arrived, the train **had left**." = o trem saiu antes de eu chegar (perdi!)

**Palavras frequentes:** **by the time**, **when**, **already**, **just**, **never... before**, **before**, **after**, **because**.

**Já com before e after**, a ordem fica clara e o past perfect é opcional: "After I (had) finished, I went home."

💡 Em notícias e histórias, o past perfect volta no tempo para explicar o contexto: "The firefighters rescued a man who **had been** trapped for six hours."

examples.en: By the time the firefighters arrived, the neighbors had already rescued the dog.
examples.pt: Quando os bombeiros chegaram, os vizinhos já tinham resgatado o cachorro.

examples.en: I'd never seen snow before I moved to Canada.
examples.pt: Eu nunca tinha visto neve antes de me mudar para o Canadá.

examples.en: It turned out that the man had lost his memory after the accident.
examples.pt: Descobriu-se que o homem tinha perdido a memória depois do acidente.

grammar.tip_pt: Cuidado com a contração **'d**: pode ser **had** ("I'd finished") ou **would** ("I'd go"). Se vem particípio depois, é **had**; se vem verbo base, é **would**.

common_mistakes.wrong: When I arrived, the party already finished.
common_mistakes.right: When I arrived, the party had already finished.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A festa terminou antes da chegada: past perfect.

common_mistakes.wrong: I had saw that movie before.
common_mistakes.right: I had seen that movie before.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Past perfect usa o particípio (seen).

common_mistakes.wrong: I had went to bed when you called.
common_mistakes.right: I had gone to bed when you called.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Particípio de go = gone.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala, **had** quase sempre vira **'d**, que é muito curto: "I'd left" = "áid léft", "she'd gone" = "shíd gón". Às vezes o 'd é quase inaudível — o particípio é o que mostra que é past perfect.
practice: By the time we arrived, they'd gone.

reading.text: Last month, a taxi driver in Belo Horizonte made headlines for an act of honesty. Carlos Mendes, 54, had just finished his shift when he noticed a wallet on the back seat. A passenger had dropped it earlier that day. Inside, there was 3,000 reais in cash, credit cards and a plane ticket to Lisbon for the next morning. Carlos didn't have the owner's phone number, but he found a business card in the wallet. He called the number, and it turned out that it belonged to the passenger's daughter. By the time Carlos reached the passenger's house, the man had already canceled his cards and had almost given up on his trip. "I'd never felt so relieved," said the passenger. When he tried to give Carlos a reward, the driver refused. "I only did what anyone should do," he said.

grammar.title: Tempos narrativos combinados
grammar.explanation_pt:
Para contar um evento passado de forma completa, combine **quatro** estruturas:

1. **Past continuous** → o **cenário**, o que estava acontecendo:
"It **was raining** heavily, and most people **were sleeping**."

2. **Past perfect** → o que tinha acontecido **antes** (contexto, causas):
"It **had been raining** for three days, and the river **had risen** two meters." (had been + -ing = past perfect continuous, para duração antes de um ponto do passado)

3. **Simple past** → os **eventos principais**, em sequência:
"At 3 a.m., the water **reached** the houses. Families **climbed** onto their roofs."

4. **Past passive** → o que **aconteceu com** pessoas e coisas:
"Thousands of people **were evacuated**, and two bridges **were destroyed**."

**Ordem típica de uma reportagem:** o que aconteceu (simple past/passive) → contexto e causas (past perfect) → detalhes do momento (past continuous) → consequências (passive) → situação atual (present / present perfect).

grammar.tip_pt: **Past perfect continuous** (had been + -ing) é o "primo" do present perfect continuous, só que no passado: "It **had been raining** for days **when** the dam broke." (Estava chovendo havia dias quando a barragem rompeu.)

reading.title: Climate change and extreme weather
reading.text: Scientists have been warning us for decades: as the planet gets warmer, extreme weather events become more frequent and more intense. In recent years, the world has seen record-breaking heatwaves in Europe, devastating wildfires in Canada and Australia, and severe floods in Pakistan and southern Brazil. Warmer air can hold more water, which means heavier rain when storms happen. At the same time, some regions are suffering from longer droughts. In 2023 and 2024, parts of the Amazon experienced one of the worst droughts on record: rivers dropped to historic lows, and entire communities were left isolated because boats couldn't travel. Experts say that we need two kinds of action: reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting our cities — with better drainage, early-warning systems and protected green areas.

questions.q: What two kinds of action do experts recommend?

grammar.title: Certeza, dúvida e a passiva de relato
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Expressar graus de certeza:**
- Certeza alta: "I'm **sure / certain** that..." / "It's **definitely** true." / "There's **no doubt** that..."
- Probabilidade: "It's **likely / probably** true." / "It **seems / appears that**..."
- Dúvida: "I **doubt** (that)..." / "I'm **not sure / not convinced** that..." / "It's **unlikely** that..."
- Ceticismo: "I find that **hard to believe**." / "That **sounds** too good to be true."

**Passiva de relato (reporting passive)** — muito usada em notícias quando a informação **não é confirmada** ou a fonte é geral:
- **It is said that** + frase → "It is said that the city was founded by pirates."
- **It is believed that** + frase → "It is believed that 30% of online reviews are fake."
- **It is reported / thought / estimated that**...

Outra forma: **sujeito + is said / believed + to + verbo** → "The singer **is said to be** very shy." / "The painting **is believed to be** worth millions."

**Atribuir a fonte:** **According to** + fonte ("According to the WHO...") / "**The report says / claims that**..."

💡 **Claim** = afirmar (sem prova) — sinal de cautela: "The post **claims** that coffee cures cancer."

listening.title: How to spot fake news
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista dá dicas para identificar notícias falsas em um vídeo educativo.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Here are five quick ways to spot fake news. One: check the source. Is it a website you know? Two: read beyond the headline — clickbait headlines are designed to make you angry or scared. Three: check the date — old stories are often shared as if they were new. Four: look for evidence. Are there names, data, links to studies? Five: if it seems too good, or too terrible, to be true, it probably is. And remember: it's believed that people are more likely to share news that confirms what they already think. So be extra careful with stories you love!

reading.title: Lies travel fast
reading.text: "A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." This famous quote — which, ironically, is often wrongly attributed to Mark Twain — describes a real phenomenon. A well-known study by researchers at MIT analyzed more than 100,000 stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017. It was found that false stories were much more likely to be retweeted than true ones and reached people significantly faster. Why? The researchers believe that fake news is usually more surprising and emotional, and people love sharing things that are new and shocking. Interestingly, the study suggested that humans, not bots, were mainly responsible for the spread. With AI tools now able to create realistic fake images and videos, experts say media literacy — the ability to evaluate information critically — is one of the most important skills of the 21st century.

grammar.title: Zero and first conditional
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Zero conditional** → fatos, verdades gerais, coisas que **sempre** acontecem:
**If + present simple, present simple**
- "If you **heat** water to 100°C, it **boils**."
- "If I **drink** coffee after 6 p.m., I **can't** sleep."
(Aqui, **if** = **when**: sempre que.)

**First conditional** → situações **reais e possíveis no futuro** e suas consequências:
**If + present simple, will + verbo**
- "If it **rains** tomorrow, we**'ll stay** home."
- "If you **don't hurry**, you**'ll miss** the bus."
- "What **will** you **do** if you **don't get** the job?"

⚠️ **Regra de ouro:** depois de **if**, **nunca** use will: ❌ "If it will rain..." ✅ "If it **rains**..." (em português usamos o futuro do subjuntivo — "se chover" — mas em inglês é presente simples).

A ordem pode inverter (sem vírgula): "We'll stay home **if** it rains."

**Variações comuns na segunda parte:**
- modal: "If you finish early, you **can** go home." / "If it's sunny, we **might** go to the beach."
- imperativo: "If you see Ana, **tell** her to call me."
- going to: "If he's late again, I**'m going to** talk to him."

reading.title: Small habits, big results
reading.text: If you read ten pages a day, you'll read about a dozen books a year. If you save ten reais a day, you'll have more than 3,600 reais in twelve months. This is the logic behind "small habits", an idea popularized by writers like James Clear. The concept is simple: small actions, repeated consistently, produce big results over time. It works the other way too: if you sleep one hour less every night, you'll lose more than 300 hours of sleep in a year — and your health will suffer. Experts suggest using "if-then" plans to build new habits: "If it's 7 a.m., I'll drink a glass of water." "If I feel like checking social media, I'll do five push-ups first." Studies show that people who make if-then plans are much more likely to achieve their goals.

grammar.title: Second conditional + I wish
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Second conditional** → situações **imaginárias, hipotéticas ou improváveis** (no presente ou futuro):
**If + past simple, would + verbo**
- "If I **won** the lottery, I**'d buy** a house in the mountains."
- "If I **had** more time, I**'d learn** to play the guitar."
- "What **would** you **do** if you **lost** your job?"

O passado aqui **não fala do passado** — ele mostra **distância da realidade** (como o "se eu ganhasse" do português).

**If I were...** → com o verbo to be, use **were** para todas as pessoas (formal e recomendado): "If I **were** rich..." / "If she **were** here..." (Na fala informal, "if I was" também aparece.)

**Could / might** também funcionam: "If I had a car, I **could** visit you more often."

**First x second:**
- "If it **rains** tomorrow, I**'ll** stay home." → possível, realista
- "If it **snowed** in Rio, I**'d** build a snowman." → imaginário, improvável

**I wish + past simple** → desejo de que o **presente** fosse diferente:
- "I **wish** I **lived** near the beach." (mas não moro)
- "I **wish** I **were** taller."
- "I **wish** I **could** speak Japanese." (habilidade → could)

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I'd** = "áid", **you'd** = "iúd", **we'd** = "uíd" — o D é curto, mas não pode sumir ("I travel" ≠ "I'd travel"). **Wouldn't** = "uúdent" (L mudo, T leve).

reading.title: Would money make you happier?
reading.text: If you suddenly became a millionaire, would you be happier? Most people say yes immediately. But research on lottery winners shows a more complicated picture. In a famous study from the 1970s, psychologists compared lottery winners with ordinary people and found that, after some time, the winners weren't much happier — they had adapted to their new lives. More recent research suggests that money does increase happiness, especially when it removes financial stress. But how you use it matters. People who spend money on experiences, on other people, or on buying time — like paying someone to do the chores they hate — tend to report more satisfaction than those who buy expensive things. So, if you won the lottery tomorrow, what would make you happier: a sports car, or more time with the people you love?

grammar.title: Unless e time clauses no futuro
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Unless** = **if... not** (a menos que):
- "**Unless** you study, you'll fail." = "**If** you **don't** study, you'll fail."
- ⚠️ Unless já é negativo: ❌ "Unless you don't study..."

**Time clauses no futuro** — a mesma regra do if: depois de **when, as soon as, before, after, until**, use o **presente simples**, mesmo falando do futuro:
- "I'll call you **when** I **arrive**." (❌ when I will arrive)
- "**As soon as** I **get** the results, I'll let you know."
- "We'll wait **until** the rain **stops**."
- "**Before** you **leave**, turn off the lights."
- "**After** I **finish** this course, I'm going to take the TOEFL."

Também dá para usar o **present perfect** para enfatizar que a ação estará completa: "I'll call you **as soon as** I**'ve finished**."

**In case** = por precaução (caso aconteça):
- "Take an umbrella **in case** it rains." (leve — talvez chova)
- Compare: "Take an umbrella **if** it rains." (só leve se estiver chovendo)

**As long as / provided that** = desde que (condição):
- "You can use my car **as long as** you **drive** carefully."

reading.title: SMART goals
reading.text: "I want to improve my English" is a wish, not a goal. Unless a goal is specific, it's very hard to achieve. That's why many coaches recommend SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Compare "I'll study more" with "I'll study English for 30 minutes a day, five days a week, until I reach B2 by December." The second one tells you exactly what to do, how to measure it and when the deadline is. Experts also suggest breaking big goals into milestones. As soon as you reach one, celebrate — and then move to the next. Keep track of your progress in a notebook or app, in case you lose motivation on difficult days: looking back at how far you've come is one of the best ways to keep going.

grammar.title: Revisão do B1 + estratégias de conversação
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Mapa do B1 — o que você já sabe:**
- **Tag questions:** It's nice, isn't it?
- **Present perfect:** experiências (Have you ever...?), duração (for/since), recentes (already/yet/just), continuous (I've been working...)
- **Modais:** can/could/be able to, could you...?, should/had better, must/have to/mustn't/don't have to, might/must be
- **Causative:** I got my hair cut.
- **Preferências:** I'd rather... / I prefer A to B
- **Verb patterns:** enjoy doing, decide to do, good at doing
- **Perguntas:** Who called? / Who did you call? / Do you know where...?
- **Passiva:** It was built in... / It is said that...
- **Narrativa:** past continuous + simple past + past perfect
- **Condicionais:** zero, first, second + unless, as soon as, I wish

**Estratégias de fluência** (o que nativos fazem o tempo todo):
1. **Ganhar tempo:** "Well...", "Let me think...", "That's a good question."
2. **Contornar palavras que faltam (paraphrasing):** "It's a kind of... / It's something you use to... / It's like..."
3. **Pedir esclarecimento:** "What do you mean by...?", "Could you rephrase that?"
4. **Desenvolver respostas** com a fórmula **A-R-E**: **A**nswer (resposta) → **R**eason (motivo) → **E**xample (exemplo).
   "Would you live abroad? — **Yes, I would.** **Because I love learning about other cultures.** **For example, when I visited Chile, I...**"
5. **Devolver a pergunta:** "What about you?"

rows: Well... / Let me think... / That's a good question.
It's a kind of... / It's something you use to... / It's like...
What do you mean by...? / Could you rephrase that?
For example... / For instance... / Like when I...
On the one hand... on the other hand... / However...
So, to sum up... / Anyway, that's what I think.

grammar.tip_pt: Na conversa, **fluência** (continuar falando) é mais importante que **precisão** (não errar nada). Nativos também erram, hesitam e se corrigem. Se travar, use uma estratégia em vez de parar ou mudar para o português!

pronunciation.tip_pt: Falar rápido não é falar bem. Use **pausas** curtas entre ideias e **enfatize** as palavras-chave. Hesitações naturais em inglês são "um", "uh", "well", "you know" — não "é...", "tipo..." em português!

reading.title: The intermediate plateau
reading.text: Many English learners feel fast progress at the beginning: every week, they can say new things. Then, around B1, something strange happens: progress seems to stop. This is known as the intermediate plateau. It happens because you can already communicate in most everyday situations, so you're no longer forced to learn new language. You keep using the same words and structures that "work". How can you break the plateau? Teachers suggest three things. First, consume more authentic content — podcasts, series, YouTube channels and articles about topics you love. Second, push yourself to use new vocabulary on purpose, even if you make mistakes. Third, get feedback: record yourself, write texts and ask someone to correct them. The plateau isn't a sign that you've stopped learning. It's a sign that you're ready for the next level.

questions.q: What is the intermediate plateau?
questions.answer: A period around B1 when progress seems to stop.

questions.q: Why does it happen?
questions.answer: You can already communicate, so you keep using the same words and structures.

questions.q: What are the three suggestions?
questions.answer: Consume authentic content, use new vocabulary on purpose, get feedback.

questions.q: What is the plateau a sign of, according to the text?
questions.answer: That you're ready for the next level.

writing.model: When I started learning English, I couldn't understand a single song, and I was terrified of speaking. I had tried to learn several times before, but I had always given up after a few months. This time was different. I've been studying for almost two years now, and I've learned much more than grammar. I've learned to stop translating everything in my head and to keep talking even when I make mistakes. The most difficult part was the present perfect — I still sometimes say "I live here since..."! Last month, I had a video call with a client from Canada, and I didn't need my boss to help me. That was the moment I realized how far I'd come. I wish I had more time to study, but I'm proud of my progress. As soon as I finish this level, I'm going to start B1+. If everything goes well, I'll take an international exam next year. grammar.title: Present simple x continuous: além do básico
grammar.explanation_pt:
Você já sabe o básico: simple = rotina/fatos; continuous = agora/temporário. No B1+, acrescente:

**Present continuous para tendências e mudanças em andamento:**
"More people **are working** from home." / "Salaries **are rising**." / "The job market **is changing** fast."

**Present simple para estados permanentes e opiniões:**
"I **believe** that work should have purpose." / "This job **requires** patience."

**Verbos com dois sentidos** — são stative num sentido e de ação em outro:
- **think**: "I **think** it's a good idea" (opinião = simple) x "I**'m thinking** about quitting" (processo de pensar = continuous)
- **have**: "She **has** two jobs" (posse) x "She**'s having** a hard time" (experiência)
- **see**: "I **see** what you mean" (entender) x "I**'m seeing** a client at 3" (encontrar)
- **feel**: "I **feel** that..." (opinião) x "I**'m feeling** tired today" (sensação agora — ambos possíveis)
- **be**: "He **is** rude" (característica) x "He**'s being** rude" (comportamento temporário, agora)

**Always + continuous** = hábito irritante: "My boss **is always changing** deadlines!"

rows: I think remote work is better.
I'm thinking of applying for the job.

examples.pt: Cada vez mais empresas estão oferecendo semanas de quatro dias.

reading.title: The meaning of work
reading.text: For decades, the typical career path was simple: study, get a stable job, climb the career ladder and retire. Today, many workers are questioning that model. Surveys in several countries suggest that a large number of employees — especially younger ones — are prepared to leave a job that doesn't match their values. Researchers who study job satisfaction say that money matters, but only up to a point. Once people earn enough to live comfortably, other factors become more important: autonomy (control over how you work), mastery (the feeling that you're improving) and purpose (the sense that your work matters to others). Interestingly, purpose doesn't require a "heroic" job. Hospital cleaners who see their role as helping patients recover often report high satisfaction. In other words, meaning doesn't only come from what we do, but from how we think about what we do.

grammar.title: Verb + object + infinitive / make & let
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1 você viu **verbo + -ing** e **verbo + to**. Agora, o padrão com **objeto** (a pessoa que recebe a ação):

**verbo + objeto + to + verbo**
want, ask, tell, expect, encourage, allow, persuade, remind, advise, teach, need, would like
- "My manager **wants me to lead** the project."
- "She **asked us to arrive** early."
- "My teacher **encouraged me to apply**."
- "They don't **allow employees to use** their phones."

⚠️ Em português dizemos "quero **que você** venha"; em inglês **nunca** use "that" aqui: ❌ "I want that you come" ✅ "I want **you to come**."

**make / let + objeto + verbo base (sem to):**
- **make** = obrigar, fazer com que: "My first boss **made me redo** the report three times."
- **let** = deixar, permitir: "My company **lets us work** from anywhere."
- (allow = let, mas com to: "They **allow us to work**...")

**Adjetivo + preposição + -ing:**
good **at**, capable **of**, keen **on**, interested **in**, used **to**, committed **to**, responsible **for**, tired **of**
- "She's **capable of managing** a big team." / "I'm **committed to improving** my English."

reading.title: Grit: the secret ingredient?
reading.text: Why do some people succeed while others with the same talent give up? Psychologist Angela Duckworth spent years studying this question with groups as different as military cadets, salespeople and children in spelling competitions. Her answer was a quality she called "grit": a combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals. According to her research, grit was often a better predictor of success than talent or IQ. Gritty people aren't necessarily the most intelligent; they're the ones who keep going after failure. The good news is that grit can be developed. Parents and teachers can encourage children to finish what they start, let them experience small failures, and teach them to see mistakes as part of learning. Some critics argue that the concept is too similar to older ideas like conscientiousness, but the message remains popular: talent is important, but effort counts twice.

grammar.title: Used to / would / be & get used to
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Used to + verbo base** → hábitos ou estados do passado que **não são mais verdade**:
- "I **used to** play video games every night." (não jogo mais)
- "There **used to** be a cinema here."
- Negativa: "I **didn't use to** like coffee." (sem -d!) · Pergunta: "**Did** you **use to** live here?"

**Would + verbo base** → **ações** repetidas no passado (estilo nostálgico, narrativo). **Não** funciona com estados:
- "Every summer, we **would** go to the beach and **would** stay for weeks." ✅
- "I would have long hair." ❌ (estado → "I **used to** have long hair")

**Be used to + -ing / substantivo** → **estar acostumado**:
- "I**'m used to** wak**ing** up early." / "She **isn't used to** the cold."

**Get used to + -ing / substantivo** → **acostumar-se** (processo):
- "I**'m getting used to** speak**ing** English at work." / "You'll **get used to** it."

**Narrar a origem de algo:** past continuous (cenário) + simple past (eventos) + used to (como era antes):

reading.title: From fad to mainstream
reading.text: Why do some ideas disappear after a few months while others change the world? Sociologist Everett Rogers studied this question in the 1960s and developed a theory called the "diffusion of innovations". According to Rogers, new ideas spread through a population in stages. First come the innovators, a tiny group who love taking risks. Next, the early adopters try the idea and, crucially, tell others about it. Only after that does the majority follow — first the "early majority", then the more skeptical "late majority". Finally, the "laggards" accept the change, often reluctantly. Smartphones followed this pattern: in 2007 they were expensive gadgets for tech fans; a decade later, even grandparents were sending voice messages. Fads, on the other hand, usually never get past the early adopters. The difference? Real innovations solve a problem people actually have.

grammar.title: Indirect questions
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Perguntas indiretas** soam mais **educadas e profissionais**. Começam com uma expressão introdutória e usam a **ordem de afirmativa** (sujeito + verbo), **sem do/does/did**:

**Expressões introdutórias:**
- Could you tell me...? / Can you tell me...?
- Do you know...? / Do you have any idea...?
- I was wondering... / I'd like to know...
- Would you mind telling me...?

**Transformação:**
- "What **does the job involve**?" → "Could you tell me what **the job involves**?"
- "When **will I hear** from you?" → "Do you know when **I'll hear** from you?"
- "Why **did she leave**?" → "I was wondering why **she left**."

**Perguntas de sim/não** usam **if** ou **whether**:
- "**Is** remote work possible?" → "Could you tell me **if/whether** remote work **is** possible?"

Repare na pontuação: se a frase introdutória é uma afirmação ("I was wondering..."), termina com **ponto**, não interrogação.

**No contexto de entrevista**, perguntas indiretas são ótimas para fazer perguntas sensíveis com elegância: "I was wondering **what the salary range is** for this position."

reading.title: The questions behind the questions
reading.text: Most interview questions aren't really about what they seem to ask. "Tell me about yourself" isn't an invitation to share your life story; the interviewer wants a short, relevant summary that explains why you're right for the job. "Why do you want to leave your current job?" is testing your professionalism: criticizing your current boss is a red flag, even if your boss is terrible. "Where do you see yourself in five years?" checks whether your goals match what the company can offer — and whether you're likely to stay. And the famous "What's your biggest weakness?" is about self-awareness: the worst answers are "I don't have any" or the cliché "I'm a perfectionist" without any example. Experts suggest preparing three or four short stories about your experience that you can adapt to different questions. When you understand the question behind the question, you can answer what the interviewer really wants to know.

grammar.title: Quantifiers
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Grande quantidade:**
- **a lot of / lots of** + contável e incontável (principalmente afirmativas): a lot of money, lots of bills
- **many** + contável · **much** + incontável → principalmente em **perguntas e negativas**: How much debt? / not many options
- **plenty of** = mais que suficiente: "Don't worry, we have **plenty of** time."

**Pequena quantidade — a diferença sutil:**
- **a few** (contável) / **a little** (incontável) = **alguns, um pouco** → sentido **positivo** (é suficiente)
  "I have **a little** money saved. Let's go out!"
- **few** / **little** (sem "a") = **poucos, pouco** → sentido **negativo** (quase nada)
  "**Few** people save enough for retirement." / "There's **little** hope."

**Excesso e falta:**
- **too much** + incontável / **too many** + contável = demais (problema): "I spend **too much** money on apps." / "I have **too many** subscriptions."
- **(not) enough** + substantivo = (não) suficiente: "I don't have **enough** savings."

**Nenhum:**
- **no** + substantivo = "There's **no** money left." (= not any)
- **none (of)** sozinho: "How much is left? **None**."

lines.speaker: Educator
lines.en: Here are a few rules I teach everyone. One: before you buy something that isn't essential, wait 48 hours. Most impulse purchases don't survive the wait. Two: try the 50-30-20 rule — 50% of your income for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings or paying debt. Three: build an emergency fund. Ideally, you should have enough to cover three to six months of expenses. And four: be careful with credit card debt. In some countries, the interest rates are extremely high — few loans are more expensive. If you can't pay the full bill, cut back on something else before you pay only the minimum.

reading.title: Cashless societies
reading.text: In just a few years, the way people pay for things has changed dramatically. In Sweden, very few shops still accept cash, and some banks no longer handle coins and notes at all. In Brazil, Pix — the instant payment system launched by the Central Bank in 2020 — became one of the most widely used payment methods in the country in a remarkably short time. Street vendors, taxi drivers and even beggars now display QR codes. The advantages are clear: payments are fast, free for individuals and convenient. But there are concerns too. Digital payments make it easier to spend without noticing — paying with a phone doesn't "hurt" as much as handing over a banknote. Fraud and scams have also increased. And not everyone has a smartphone or a bank account, so a fully cashless society could leave the most vulnerable people behind. The question is not whether cash will disappear, but how quickly — and who will pay the price.

grammar.title: Present perfect x past simple (nível B1+)
grammar.explanation_pt:
Você já conhece a regra básica (tempo terminado x aberto). No B1+, veja como os dois tempos **trabalham juntos** em textos de não ficção e notícias:

**1. Present perfect para apresentar o tema ou resultado atual → past simple para os detalhes:**
"Scientists **have studied** self-control for decades. The first famous experiment **took place** at Stanford in the 1960s."

**2. Present perfect com `since` + past simple na outra parte:**
"**Since** the study **was published**, many researchers **have tried** to replicate it."

**3. Superlativo + present perfect (ever):**
"It's **the most famous** psychology experiment I**'ve ever read** about."

**4. `It's the first time` + present perfect:**
"**It's the first time** I**'ve saved** money for a whole year."

**5. Expressões de período aberto (present perfect):** recently, lately, so far, up to now, over the past few years, in the last decade
"**Over the past few years**, researchers **have questioned** the original conclusions."

**Expressões de tempo fechado (past simple):** in the 1960s, at that time, back then, when I was..., years ago, at first
"**At that time**, nobody **questioned** the results."

reading.title: What the marshmallow test really tells us
reading.text: The marshmallow test is one of the most famous experiments in psychology. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, researchers at Stanford University offered preschool children a choice: eat one treat now, or wait alone for about fifteen minutes and get two. Years later, follow-up studies suggested that the children who had waited tended to have better school results and other positive outcomes. The idea spread quickly: self-control, it seemed, was a key to success. Since then, however, the story has become more complicated. The original groups were small and mostly came from families connected to the university. In 2018, a larger study with a more diverse group of children found a much weaker connection, and much of it seemed to be explained by factors like family income and education. Other researchers have shown that children wait longer when they trust the adult who made the promise. So the test may measure not only willpower, but also experience: if promises in your life have often been broken, eating the marshmallow now is a rational choice.

grammar.title: Present perfect simple x continuous
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing)** → foco no **processo**, na **duração**, na **atividade** (que pode ainda não ter terminado):
- "I**'ve been writing** my thesis **for** two years." (processo em andamento)
- "She**'s been training** every day." (esforço repetido)
- "Why are you so tired? — I**'ve been studying** all night." (atividade recente com efeito visível)

**Present perfect simple (have + particípio)** → foco no **resultado**, na **quantidade**, no que foi **concluído**:
- "I**'ve written** three chapters." (quantidade concluída)
- "She**'s won** two medals."
- "I**'ve finished** my thesis!" (completo)

**Pergunta-chave:**
- **How long** have you been...? → duração (continuous)
- **How many / How much** have you...? → quantidade (simple)

**Stative verbs** (know, believe, have [posse], want, own) → sempre simple: "I**'ve known** her for years."

**Live, work, study, teach** → com for/since, os dois são possíveis com pouca diferença; o continuous sugere algo mais **temporário**: "I've lived here all my life" (permanente) x "I've been living here since March" (temporário).

reading.title: The myth of talent
reading.text: When we see a brilliant musician, athlete or entrepreneur, we often assume they were simply born with a special talent. But researchers who study expertise tell a different story. In a famous study in the 1990s, psychologist Anders Ericsson looked at violin students at a music academy in Berlin. He found that the best students had practiced significantly more hours than the others — and, crucially, that they had practiced in a specific way. Ericsson called it "deliberate practice": working on your weaknesses, getting regular feedback and constantly pushing beyond your comfort zone. Writer Malcolm Gladwell later popularized the idea as the "10,000-hour rule", although Ericsson himself said that the number was not a magic rule. Since then, other scientists have argued that factors like genes, starting age and opportunity also matter. Still, the main lesson remains: behind most "overnight successes" there are years of invisible, focused work.

grammar.title: Should have / shouldn't have + particípio
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Should have + particípio** → algo que **deveria ter acontecido, mas não aconteceu** (arrependimento ou crítica sobre o passado):
- "I **should have checked** the numbers." (não conferi — me arrependo)
- "You **should have told** me earlier!" (você não me contou — crítica)

**Shouldn't have + particípio** → algo que **aconteceu, mas não deveria**:
- "I **shouldn't have sent** that email." (mandei — erro)
- "You **shouldn't have spent** so much money!" (às vezes é carinho, ao receber um presente!)

Na fala: **should have** = "**shúdav**" ou até "**shúda**".

**Estrutura de um bom pedido de desculpas profissional:**
1. **Reconheça:** "I'm sorry for / I apologize for + -ing / substantivo": "I apologize for **missing** the deadline."
2. **Assuma a responsabilidade** (sem culpar outros): "It was my fault. I **should have** asked for help earlier."
3. **Explique** brevemente (sem desculpas longas): "I underestimated how long it would take."
4. **Ofereça solução:** "I'll send it by 10 tomorrow."
5. **Prevenção:** "In future, I'll make sure to..."

⚠️ **Sorry for** + -ing/substantivo (sobre algo que você fez) · **sorry to** + verbo (algo que você está fazendo agora): "Sorry **to bother** you." / "Sorry **for being** late."

reading.title: The anatomy of a good apology
reading.text: Why do some apologies make things better while others make them worse? Researchers who study communication have identified several elements that make an apology effective. The most important one, according to some studies, is acknowledging responsibility: saying clearly "It was my fault" or "I made a mistake". The second is offering to repair the damage. Expressing regret ("I'm sorry") matters too, but on its own it often isn't enough. Interestingly, long explanations can backfire: if you spend too much time explaining why something happened, people may hear it as an excuse. The worst apologies are "non-apologies" — phrases like "I'm sorry if you were offended" or "Mistakes were made", which avoid taking real responsibility. Public figures and companies use them all the time, and audiences usually notice. The lesson? A good apology is short, specific and focused on the other person, not on yourself.

questions.answer: Acknowledging responsibility.

grammar.title: Articles
grammar.explanation_pt:
Artigos são um dos maiores desafios para brasileiros, porque em português usamos "o/a" muito mais.

**A / an** → algo **não específico** ou mencionado pela **primeira vez**; profissões:
- "They launched **a** new campaign." / "She's **an** influencer."

**The** → algo **específico**, **já mencionado**, **único** ou que todos sabem qual é:
- "They launched a new campaign. **The** campaign was a disaster." (já mencionada)
- "**The** CEO of the company..." (só há um)
- "**The** internet / **the** environment / **the** world"
- superlativos: "**the** best brand"; ordinais: "**the** first ad"
- instrumentos musicais: "play **the** guitar"
- países com plural/União: **the** USA, **the** UK, **the** Netherlands

**Zero article (sem artigo)** → **generalizações** com plurais e incontáveis — aqui o português usa artigo, o inglês **não**:
- "**Customers** trust **reviews**." (os clientes em geral) ❌ "The customers trust the reviews"
- "**Marketing** is changing." / "**Social media** is powerful." / "I love **coffee**."
- nomes de pessoas, cidades, a maioria dos países, idiomas, refeições, esportes: "**Brazil**", "**English**", "have **lunch**", "play **soccer**"
- go to **work / school / bed / church** (função), at **home**

**Teste rápido:** a frase fala de **algo em geral** ou de **algo específico**? Geral → sem artigo. Específico → the.

reading.title: From influencers to "de-influencers"
reading.text: For more than a decade, influencer marketing has been one of the fastest-growing areas of advertising. Brands pay creators — from celebrities with millions of followers to "micro-influencers" with just a few thousand — to recommend their products. The logic is simple: people trust people more than they trust ads. But audiences have become more skeptical. Many followers now know that a glowing review may be a paid partnership, and regulators in several countries require influencers to label sponsored posts clearly. In this context, a new trend has appeared: "de-influencing". Creators post videos explaining which popular products are not worth the money and suggesting cheaper alternatives. Ironically, de-influencing has itself become a marketing strategy, as some brands now position themselves as the honest alternative. The lesson for marketers is clear: in a world full of advertising, authenticity is the most valuable — and the most difficult — thing to sell.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Relative clauses** adicionam informação sobre um substantivo:

- **who** → pessoas: "The woman **who** designed this app is Brazilian."
- **which** → coisas e animais: "The phone **which** I bought last year is already slow."
- **that** → pessoas ou coisas (informal, muito comum nas defining clauses): "It's a gadget **that** everyone wants."
- **whose** → posse (cujo/cuja): "I have a friend **whose** brother works at Apple."
- **where** → lugares: "This is the shop **where** I bought my laptop."
- **when** → tempo: "I remember the day **when** I got my first phone."

**1. Defining relative clauses** (sem vírgulas) → informação **essencial** para saber de quem/do que falamos:
"The app **that** I use for running is free."
➡ Quando o pronome é **objeto** do verbo seguinte, pode ser **omitido**: "The app (that) **I use**..." / "The man (who) **we met**..."
➡ Quando é **sujeito**, não pode: "The app **that helps** you..." (❌ "The app helps you...")

**2. Non-defining relative clauses** (com vírgulas) → informação **extra**, não essencial. Use **who/which** (nunca **that**) e nunca omita:
"My laptop, **which** I bought in 2020, still works perfectly."
"Melissa Marshall, **who** teaches communication, gave a great talk."

**Which** também pode se referir à frase inteira: "The battery lasts two days, **which** is amazing."

reading.title: The products that changed everyday life
reading.text: Some products are so ordinary that we forget they were once revolutionary. Take the ballpoint pen, which was patented in 1938 by László Bíró, a Hungarian journalist who was tired of smudged ink. Or the shopping cart, which was invented in the 1930s by a supermarket owner in Oklahoma whose customers stopped shopping when their baskets got too heavy. At first, shoppers refused to use carts — men thought they looked weak and women thought they looked like baby strollers — so the owner hired actors to push them around the store. In Brazil, an example of a product that changed daily life is the flip-flop. Havaianas, which were created in 1962, were inspired by Japanese zori sandals, and for decades they were seen as cheap shoes for poor people. A clever marketing strategy in the 1990s transformed them into a fashion item that celebrities wear all over the world. The lesson? A good product is important, but the story that people tell about it can matter just as much.

grammar.title: Future forms (revisão avançada)
grammar.explanation_pt:
No A2 você conheceu as formas de futuro. No B1+, use-as com precisão — especialmente em apresentações e no trabalho:

**will + verbo:**
- **previsão / opinião** (sem evidência concreta): "I think AI **will** change medicine." / "Scientists probably **won't** find a cure soon."
- **decisão no momento**: "The projector isn't working. — I**'ll** call IT."
- **promessa / oferta**: "I**'ll** send you the slides after the talk."

**be going to + verbo:**
- **plano / intenção** já decidido: "In this talk, I**'m going to** explain three ideas."
- **previsão com evidência** visível agora: "Look at the data — the temperature **is going to** rise."

**Present continuous:** **compromisso marcado** (agenda): "I**'m presenting** at the conference on Friday."

**Present simple:** **horários fixos** e programações: "The talk **starts** at 10 and **finishes** at 11."

**Expressões úteis para graduar certeza:** will **definitely** / will **probably** / **might** / probably **won't** / definitely **won't**.

**Na estrutura de uma apresentação:**
- Abertura (plano): "Today **I'm going to** talk about..."
- Transição: "Now **I'm going to** show you..." / "Let's move on to..."
- Previsão: "In ten years, this technology **will** probably..."
- Encerramento (oferta): "**I'll** be happy to answer your questions."

reading.title: Why explaining matters
reading.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, millions of people suddenly needed to understand complex scientific ideas: how viruses spread, how vaccines work, what an "R number" is. Scientists who could explain these ideas clearly became incredibly influential, while those who used technical language often failed to reach the public — and misinformation filled the gap. Experts in science communication say there are a few simple rules. First, start with why it matters to the audience, not with the method. Second, use analogies: comparing the immune system to a security team or DNA to a recipe book helps people make sense of abstract ideas. Third, avoid jargon, or explain it the first time you use it. Fourth, tell stories: people remember narratives far better than statistics. Finally, be honest about uncertainty. Saying "we don't know yet, but we're going to find out" builds more trust than pretending to have all the answers. In the future, many experts believe these communication skills will be as important for scientists as research itself.

writing.model:
Good evening, everyone. Have you ever wondered why you feel so tired after a night of bad sleep, even if you've spent eight hours in bed? Today I'm going to talk about something that happens in your brain every night while you sleep.

Think of your brain like a busy city. During the day, the city produces a lot of garbage. At night, while you're sleeping, a cleaning team comes out and washes the streets. Scientists have discovered that during deep sleep, a fluid in your brain does exactly that: it removes waste that builds up during the day.

In other words, sleep isn't just rest — it's maintenance. And when we don't sleep enough, the garbage stays in the streets.

In the next few minutes, I'm going to show you three simple habits that help your brain's cleaning team do its job. I'm sure that by the end of this talk, you'll never think of sleep in the same way. And of course, I'll be happy to answer your questions at the end.

grammar.title: Linguagem funcional de networking
grammar.explanation_pt:
Networking usa estruturas que você já conhece, combinadas em **funções**:

**1. Abrir a conversa (comentário + pergunta):**
- Comentário sobre o contexto + tag question ou pergunta: "Great talk, **wasn't it**?" / "Is it your first time **at this conference**?"
- Pedir para se juntar: "**Mind if I join you?**" / "**Do you mind if** I sit here?"

**2. Apresentar-se e apresentar outros:**
- "I don't think we've met. I'm Ana, **I work for**... / **I'm in charge of**..."
- "**Have you met** Pedro? Pedro, **this is** Laura. **She's the one who** organized the event." (relative clause!)

**3. Manter a conversa — perguntas abertas** (What / How / Why), não sim/não:
- "**What brings you** here?" / "**How did you get into** marketing?" / "**What are you working on** at the moment?"
- **Comentários de interesse:** "Oh, that sounds fascinating!" / "Really? How interesting."
- **Encontrar algo em comum:** "**So do I!**" / "**Me too** — I've been working in tech for five years."

**4. Encerrar com elegância** (nunca sair sem dizer nada):
- "**I'll let you** go and mingle." / "**I should** go and say hi to my colleague."
- "**It's been** great talking to you." (present perfect!)
- "**Let's** connect on LinkedIn." / "**I'll** send you an email next week." (will = promessa)

listening.title: Networking tips from an expert
listening.context_pt: Uma especialista em carreira dá dicas de networking num webinar.

lines.speaker: Coach
lines.en: Many people hate networking because they think it's about selling themselves. It isn't. Good networking is about being curious. Here are my top tips. First, arrive early — it's much easier to start conversations when the room is half empty. Second, prepare three open questions, like "What are you working on at the moment?" Third, listen more than you talk; people remember how you made them feel, not your job title. Fourth, don't stay with the same person all night — after ten minutes, politely move on. And finally, follow up within 48 hours. Send a short message mentioning something specific you talked about. That's how a five-minute conversation becomes a long-term relationship.

reading.title: The strength of weak ties
reading.text: Who is most likely to help you find your next job: your best friend, or someone you met once at a conference? Surprisingly, research suggests it's often the second. In a classic 1973 study, sociologist Mark Granovetter interviewed people who had recently changed jobs and found that many of them had heard about the opportunity through acquaintances — people they saw only occasionally — rather than close friends. He called this "the strength of weak ties". The explanation is simple: your close friends usually know the same people and hear about the same opportunities as you. Acquaintances, on the other hand, move in different circles, so they bring new information. A large study published in 2022, which analyzed data from millions of LinkedIn users, found further support for the idea, showing that moderately weak connections were the most useful for job mobility. So the next time you're at an event and feel tempted to talk only to your colleagues, remember: the stranger by the coffee machine might be the key to your next opportunity.

questions.q: What did Granovetter find?
questions.answer: Many people heard about new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.

questions.q: Why are acquaintances useful?
questions.answer: They move in different circles and bring new information.

questions.q: What did the 2022 LinkedIn study show?
questions.answer: Moderately weak connections were the most useful for job mobility.

questions.q: What's the advice at the end?
questions.answer: Talk to people you don't know at events, not only your colleagues.

grammar.title: Superlativos + present perfect · the first time
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Superlativo + present perfect + ever** → a maior/melhor/pior experiência **até agora**:
- "It's **the most inspiring** talk I**'ve ever seen**."
- "She's **the kindest** person I**'ve ever met**."
- "That's **the hardest** thing I**'ve ever done**."
(o **that/who** antes do sujeito pode ser omitido: "the best book (that) I've ever read")

**It's the first/second/only time + present perfect** → experiência vivida agora:
- "**It's the first time** I**'ve spoken** in public."
- "**This is the third time** I**'ve visited** Lisbon."

⚠️ No **passado**, a estrutura muda para **past perfect**: "**It was the first time** I**'d ever seen** snow." (No A2/B1 você viu o past perfect — aqui ele volta!)

**Never... before** → também expressa primeira vez: "I**'ve never** worked with such a diverse team **before**."

**Expressões de aprendizado:**
- "I**'ve learned** (how) **to** + verbo": "I've learned to listen more."
- "I**'ve learned that** + frase": "I've learned that everyone communicates differently."
- "X **has taught me to/that**...": "My brother has taught me to be patient."

It's the first time + present perfect
It's the first time I've tried this.
It was the first time + past perfect

grammar.tip_pt: Ao falar de deficiência, prefira linguagem que a própria comunidade usa. Muitos preferem **"person with a disability"** (person-first) e muitos autistas preferem **"autistic person"** (identity-first). Na dúvida, pergunte ou siga como a pessoa se descreve.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Superlativo + experiência até agora = present perfect (padrão britânico e de provas).

common_mistakes.wrong: It's the first time I come here.
common_mistakes.right: It's the first time I've come here.
common_mistakes.why_pt: It's the first time + present perfect.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was the first time I've seen snow.
common_mistakes.right: It was the first time I'd seen snow.
common_mistakes.why_pt: No passado (It was), use past perfect.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I've ever** se junta: "**áivéver**". Na frase, a força vai no superlativo e no particípio: "the **BEST** book I've ever **READ**". **Eye-opening** = "ÁI-ôupenin".

listening.title: Inclusive workplaces
listening.context_pt: Uma gerente de RH fala sobre o programa de inclusão da empresa.

lines.speaker: HR Manager
lines.en: Three years ago, we started a program to hire more neurodivergent people — for example, autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia. It's been the best decision we've ever made. We changed our interviews: instead of asking abstract questions, we let candidates show their skills with practical tasks. We created quiet rooms and allowed flexible hours. The results? Our data team, which now includes several neurodivergent analysts, has found errors that nobody had noticed for years. But the biggest change has been cultural. Everyone has learned to communicate more clearly — and that has helped all of us.

reading.title: Different minds at work
reading.text: For a long time, many workplaces were designed for one type of brain. Job interviews rewarded people who were good at small talk and eye contact, open-plan offices were full of noise, and instructions were often vague. As a result, many talented neurodivergent people — including autistic people and people with ADHD or dyslexia — struggled to find or keep jobs. In recent years, some large companies have started neurodiversity hiring programs. Instead of traditional interviews, candidates might spend a few days solving real problems, and managers receive training on how to give clear, direct feedback. Several of these companies report that neurodivergent employees bring valuable strengths, such as pattern recognition, attention to detail, creative problem-solving and deep focus. Advocates point out, however, that the goal shouldn't only be productivity. "Inclusion isn't about finding hidden superpowers," one autistic activist explains. "It's about accepting that people think differently — and that's normal."

questions.q: Why did many neurodivergent people struggle at work?
questions.answer: Workplaces were designed for one type of brain (small talk, noise, vague instructions).

questions.q: How are some hiring programs different?
questions.answer: Candidates solve real problems for a few days; managers learn to give clear feedback.

questions.q: What strengths are mentioned?
questions.answer: Pattern recognition, attention to detail, creative problem-solving and deep focus.

questions.q: What do advocates say the goal should be?
questions.answer: Accepting that people think differently, not only productivity.

writing.model: The person who has changed the way I see the world the most is my grandfather, Seu João. He grew up on a farm in Bahia and left school when he was ten, but he's the wisest person I've ever met. When I was a teenager, I thought success meant money and a big title. My grandfather taught me a different lesson. Every morning, he would share his coffee with the street sweepers and ask about their families. "Everyone has something to teach you," he used to say. The turning point for me was at his 80th birthday party. It was the first time I'd seen so many different people in one room — doctors, farmers, children, neighbors — all there because he had been kind to them. grammar.title: Previsões com graus de certeza
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1+, em vez de usar só **will**, mostre **o quanto você tem certeza**:

**100% →** will definitely / be bound to (com certeza vai) / certainly will
"Electric cars **will definitely** become cheaper." / "There**'s bound to** be traffic."

**~80% →** will probably / be likely to + verbo
"Most new cars **will probably** be electric by 2035." / "Prices **are likely to** fall."

**~50% →** may / might / could + verbo (talvez)
"Flying taxis **might** be available in some cities." / "It **could** take decades."

**~20% →** probably won't / be unlikely to / I doubt (that)...
"People **probably won't** stop driving completely." / "It's **unlikely to** happen soon."

**0% →** definitely won't / there's no way...
"Cars **definitely won't** disappear by 2030."

**Posição dos advérbios:**
- afirmativa: **will + advérbio** → "It **will probably** rain."
- negativa: **advérbio + won't** → "It **probably won't** rain." (❌ "It won't probably")

**Futuro contínuo e perfeito (reconhecimento):**
- "In 2040, we**'ll be traveling** in autonomous cars." (ação em andamento num momento futuro)
- "By 2035, many countries **will have banned** new gasoline cars." (concluído até um ponto futuro)

rows: EVs are likely to get cheaper.

examples.en: Electric buses are likely to replace diesel buses in most big cities.
examples.pt: Ônibus elétricos provavelmente vão substituir os ônibus a diesel na maioria das cidades grandes.

examples.en: Self-driving cars might be safer, but people probably won't trust them for a while.

examples.en: By 2040, many cities will have closed their centers to private cars.
examples.pt: Até 2040, muitas cidades terão fechado seus centros para carros particulares.

grammar.tip_pt: **Be likely to** é muito usado em notícias e relatórios: "The new law **is likely to** affect millions of drivers." É uma ótima forma de soar mais sofisticado do que "will probably".

common_mistakes.wrong: It won't probably happen.
common_mistakes.right: It probably won't happen.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Na negativa, o advérbio vem antes de won't.

common_mistakes.wrong: Prices are likely to falling.
common_mistakes.right: Prices are likely to fall.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Be likely to + verbo base.

common_mistakes.wrong: Maybe flying cars will might exist.
common_mistakes.right: Flying cars might exist. / Maybe flying cars will exist.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Não combine dois modais (will + might).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala rápida, **probably** vira "**PRÓB-li**" (quase duas sílabas) e **definitely** vira "**DÉF-net-li**". **Likely** = "LÁIK-li". A força está sempre no começo dessas palavras.

dialogue.title: Debate: cars in the city center
dialogue.context_pt: Num debate da associação de moradores, dois vizinhos discutem a proposta de fechar o centro para carros.

lines.speaker: Moderator
lines.en: The proposal is to close the city center to private cars by 2030. What do you think will happen?

listening.title: Transport predictions
listening.context_pt: Uma especialista em mobilidade urbana faz previsões para os próximos 20 anos.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.en: Let me make a few predictions. First, electric vehicles will definitely dominate new car sales in many countries — that's already happening. Second, cities are likely to invest more in bikes, e-scooters and public transport, because they're cheaper and take up less space. Third, self-driving cars might become common on highways, but I doubt we'll see many in chaotic city centers soon — the technology still struggles with unpredictable situations. And flying taxis? They could appear in a few rich cities, but they're unlikely to become a normal way to commute. Most people will still be taking the bus in 2045 — just a cleaner, quieter bus.

reading.title: The 15-minute city
reading.text: What if everything you needed — work, school, shops, a doctor, a park — was within a 15-minute walk or bike ride from your home? That's the idea behind the "15-minute city", a concept developed by the urbanist Carlos Moreno and adopted by Paris and other cities around the world. Supporters argue that it's likely to reduce traffic, pollution and stress, while making neighborhoods more lively and social. In Paris, the city has created hundreds of kilometers of new bike lanes and turned some streets around schools into car-free zones. Critics, however, say the idea may not work in places with low population density, where shops and jobs are far apart. Others worry that it could increase housing prices in well-designed neighborhoods, pushing poorer residents out. Some online conspiracy theories have even claimed, without evidence, that 15-minute cities are a plan to restrict people's freedom of movement. The debate is bound to continue — but as cities grow and the climate crisis worsens, many planners believe that shorter, greener journeys are the future.

questions.q: Where might the idea not work?
