writing.model:
Transport in Curitiba in 2045

Curitiba has always been a pioneer in public transport, so its future is likely to be exciting. First, the city's famous bus rapid transit system will definitely continue, but the buses are bound to be fully electric and much quieter. Second, the number of bike lanes is likely to double, because more young people prefer cycling to driving. Self-driving cars might become common on highways around the city, but I doubt they will be popular in the busy center, where pedestrians and cyclists make traffic unpredictable. Flying taxis could appear for business travelers, but they're unlikely to be affordable for most people. On the other hand, private cars probably won't disappear completely, especially for families in the suburbs. In my opinion, the biggest change will be cultural: by 2045, many residents will have stopped seeing the car as a symbol of status, and the city will probably be greener, quieter and more pleasant to live in.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction: present and past
grammar.explanation_pt:
Usamos **modais de dedução** para dizer o que achamos que **é verdade** com base em evidências.

**PRESENTE — modal + verbo base (ou be + -ing):**
- **must** = tenho quase certeza que **sim**: "You've been working for 12 hours. You **must be** tired."
- **might / may / could** = **talvez**: "He's not answering. He **might be** in a meeting."
- **can't** = tenho quase certeza que **não**: "That **can't be** Ana. She's in Japan."
⚠️ O oposto de **must** (dedução) é **can't**, não "mustn't" (mustn't = proibição).

**PASSADO — modal + have + particípio:**
- **must have** + particípio = com certeza aconteceu: "The streets are wet. It **must have rained**."
- **might / may / could have** + particípio = talvez tenha acontecido: "She's late. She **might have missed** the bus."
- **can't / couldn't have** + particípio = com certeza **não** aconteceu: "He **can't have stolen** the money — he was with me all night."

**Para ação em andamento:**
- presente: "She **must be working** late."
- passado: "They **must have been sleeping** when the alarm went off."

Na fala, **must have** = "**mâstav**", **might have** = "**máitav**", **can't have** = "**kéntav**".

rows: must have been / must have worked

grammar.tip_pt: Não confunda **must have** (dedução: deve ter) com **should have** (crítica/arrependimento: deveria ter). "He **must have** forgotten" (tenho quase certeza que esqueceu) x "He **should have** remembered" (era para ter lembrado).

reading.title: The mystery of the Voynich manuscript
reading.text: In 1912, a book dealer named Wilfrid Voynich bought a strange manuscript from a collection in Italy. The book, which is now kept at Yale University, has about 240 pages full of drawings of unknown plants, astronomical diagrams and women bathing in green pools. But the strangest thing is the text: it's written in an alphabet that nobody has ever been able to read. Carbon dating has shown that the parchment must have been made in the early 15th century. So who wrote it, and why? Some researchers believe it might be written in a lost natural language. Others think it could be a code designed to hide secret medical or alchemical knowledge. Some skeptics argue that it can't contain real meaning at all: it might have been a clever hoax, created to sell to a rich collector. Over the years, linguists, cryptographers and even AI programs have tried to decode it, and several people have claimed to have solved the mystery — but none of their solutions has been widely accepted. For now, the Voynich manuscript remains one of the most famous unsolved puzzles in the world.

Case report: The empty office

On Monday morning, employees at a design studio in Belo Horizonte found something strange. All the plants in the office had been moved to the meeting room, every chair was facing the window, and there was a birthday cake on the table with no name on it. Nobody remembered ordering it.

There are several possible explanations. First, the cleaning team might have moved the plants to clean the floor, but this can't explain the cake. grammar.title: Linguagem de telefone e mensagens
grammar.explanation_pt:
Ao telefone, a linguagem é bem **fixa** — aprenda em **blocos**:

**1. Identificar-se:** em inglês, diga **"This is..."** (não "I am..."): "Hello, **this is** Pedro from Alfa Bank." / Para perguntar quem fala: "**Who's calling, please?**" / "**May I ask who's calling?**"

**2. Pedir para falar com alguém:** "**Could I speak to**...?" / "**I'm calling about**..." / "**I'm returning** Ms. Lee's **call**."

**3. Pedidos educados:** **will / would / could** — "**Could you** ask her to call me back?" / "**Would you** mind spelling that?"

**4. Ofertas com will (decisão na hora):** "**I'll** put you through." / "**I'll** tell him you called." / "**I'll** call back later."

**5. Passar recados (reported requests — introdução):**
- Ela disse: "Call me back." → **She asked you to call her back.**
- Ele disse: "I'll be late." → **He said (that) he'd be late.**
(Você vai aprofundar o reported speech no Módulo 6!)

**6. Estrutura de uma boa mensagem de voz:**
1. Cumprimento + **quem é** (nome + empresa)
2. **Hora/data** da ligação
3. **Motivo** da ligação
4. **Ação** pedida ("Could you call me back...?")
5. **Número** — falado **devagar**, de preferência **duas vezes**
6. Despedida

reading.title: Why we hate phone calls
reading.text: For many young professionals, an unexpected phone call feels almost like an emergency. Surveys in the UK and the US have found that a large number of people under 35 avoid answering calls from unknown numbers, and many feel anxious when they have to make a call. Some even rehearse what they're going to say before dialing. Why? Researchers point to several reasons. Text messages and emails give us time to think and edit; phone calls happen in real time, with no chance to delete a mistake. Calls can also feel intrusive: they interrupt whatever you're doing. And for people speaking a second language, the lack of facial expressions and gestures makes understanding much harder. However, many managers say that phone calls are still the fastest way to solve complex problems and build relationships. A five-minute call can save twenty emails. The solution? Practice. Experts suggest preparing a few key phrases, keeping a notepad ready and remembering that it's completely normal to say: "Sorry, could you repeat that?"

grammar.title: Instruções: imperativos + condicionais + time clauses
grammar.explanation_pt:
Instruções claras em inglês combinam três estruturas:

**1. Imperativos** (verbo base, sem sujeito):
- "**Hold** the lace in your right hand." / "**Don't pull** too hard." / "**Be careful not to** cut yourself."
- Com **sequenciadores**: First, ... / Then, ... / Next, ... / After that, ... / Finally, ...

**2. Zero conditional** → resultados sempre verdadeiros (como funciona):
- "If you **pull** both ends, the knot **gets** tighter."
- "When the water **boils**, the light **turns** off."

**3. First conditional** → consequências e avisos:
- "If you **tie** it this way, it **won't** come undone."
- "If you **don't** save the file, you**'ll lose** everything."

**Imperativo + if** (dicas): "**If** the app freezes, **restart** your phone." / "**If** in doubt, **ask**."

**Time clauses** (presente simples, mesmo falando do futuro):
- "**Once** you**'ve tied** the first knot, **make** a loop." (once + present perfect = depois que você tiver feito)
- "**As soon as** the light **turns** green, **press** start."
- "**Unless** the instructions **say** otherwise, **use** cold water."

rows: Don't + verbo / Be careful not to
If you press here, it opens.
If you skip this step, it won't work.

examples.en: First, cross the laces. Then, make a loop with the right lace. Be careful not to pull too hard.
examples.pt: Primeiro, cruze os cadarços. Depois, faça um laço com o cadarço direito. Cuidado para não puxar demais.

reading.title: Small changes, big results
reading.text: Most of us want to be more productive, but we often look for big solutions: a new job, a new app, a complete change of routine. Productivity experts suggest the opposite. If you make small, specific changes, they'll add up over time. Here are some research-backed ideas. If you check your email first thing in the morning, you'll spend the day reacting to other people's priorities — so start with your most important task instead. When you work on a difficult task, turn off notifications: some studies suggest that it can take a long time to fully refocus after an interruption. Use the "two-minute rule": if something takes less than two minutes, do it immediately. And unless you have a very good reason, don't multitask. Our brains don't really do two things at once; they switch quickly between them, and every switch costs energy. As the saying goes, "If you chase two rabbits, you'll catch neither."

How to make the perfect Brazilian rice

First of all, rinse one cup of rice in cold water until the water runs clear. If you skip this step, the rice will be sticky.

Then, heat two tablespoons of oil in a pan and add half a chopped onion and one clove of garlic. Be careful not to burn the garlic — if it turns dark, it'll taste bitter.

Next, add two cups of hot water and a teaspoon of salt. As soon as the water boils, turn the heat down to low and cover the pan.

grammar.title: Obligation and advice: nuances
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1 você aprendeu must/have to/mustn't/don't have to. No B1+, as **nuances**:

**Must x have to (afirmativa):**
- **must** → obrigação que **o falante** sente ou impõe (interna, pessoal) e regras **escritas** formais: "I **must** call my mother — I promised." / "Passengers **must** wear seatbelts." (aviso oficial)
- **have to** → obrigação **externa** (regras, circunstâncias), mais comum na fala: "I **have to** wear a uniform at work." (a empresa exige)

**Need to / don't need to / needn't:**
- **need to** = é necessário: "We **need to** fix this bug before the launch."
- **don't need to / needn't** = não é necessário (= don't have to): "You **don't need to** bring anything." / "You **needn't** worry." (needn't é mais britânico/formal)

**Mustn't x don't have to (revisão — o erro mais comum):**
- **mustn't** = proibido: "You **mustn't** share your password."
- **don't have to / don't need to** = não é necessário: "You **don't have to** reply today."

**Should / ought to** → recomendação (o certo a fazer, mas não obrigatório):
- "You **should** proofread every email before sending it." / "We **ought to** update the checklist."

**Passado:** **had to** (obrigação), **didn't have to / didn't need to** (não era necessário), **should have** (crítica — Módulo 2).

don't have to / don't need to / needn't

grammar.tip_pt: **Need** como verbo comum pede **to** (need to do) e **do/does** nas perguntas (Do I need to...?). **Needn't** (modal) é usado sem to: "You needn't come."

reading.title: The power of checklists
reading.text: In 1935, a new American bomber plane crashed during a test flight, killing two of its crew. The investigation found that the pilots hadn't made a mechanical error — they had simply forgotten one step: they hadn't released a lock on the controls. The plane was considered "too complex for one person to fly". Instead of giving up, test pilots created a simple solution: a checklist. With it, the plane went on to fly safely for millions of miles. Decades later, surgeon and writer Atul Gawande argued in his book The Checklist Manifesto that the same idea could save lives in hospitals. A study coordinated by the World Health Organization in eight hospitals around the world found that a simple surgical safety checklist was associated with a significant reduction in complications and deaths. The checklist didn't teach surgeons anything new; it made sure that the basic steps — confirming the patient's identity, checking allergies, counting instruments — weren't overlooked. The lesson goes beyond medicine: experts don't fail because they lack knowledge, but because even the best people sometimes forget the obvious.

Welcome to the team! Your first month: rules and tips

Rules
• You have to complete the online security training in your first week. It's compulsory for all employees.
• You must wear your ID badge at all times in the building.
• You mustn't share client information on personal devices or social media.
• You don't need to come to the office on Fridays — it's our remote day — but you do need to be online between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.

Tips
• You should ask questions. Nobody expects you to know everything, and it's much better to ask than to guess.
• You ought to introduce yourself to people in other departments. Coffee breaks are a great opportunity.
• Before you send anything to a client, double-check the details: names, dates and numbers. A small typo can cause big problems.
• Finally, you don't have to be perfect. Everyone makes mistakes in their first month — the important thing is to learn from them.

grammar.title: Passive voice: all tenses
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1 você aprendeu a passiva no presente e no passado simples. A regra é sempre a mesma: **be (no tempo certo) + particípio**. Só muda o **be**:

- **Present simple:** am/is/are + particípio → "Plastic **is recycled** here."
- **Present continuous:** am/is/are **being** + particípio → "A new park **is being built**." (está sendo construído)
- **Past simple:** was/were + particípio → "The garden **was created** in 2015."
- **Past continuous:** was/were **being** + particípio → "The river **was being cleaned** when I visited."
- **Present perfect:** has/have **been** + particípio → "More than 1,000 trees **have been planted**."
- **Future (will):** will **be** + particípio → "The results **will be published** next year."
- **Going to:** am/is/are going to **be** + particípio → "The old factory **is going to be turned** into a park."
- **Modais:** can / should / must / might **be** + particípio → "Glass **can be recycled** forever." / "Food waste **should be composted**."

**Para descrever processos**, a passiva é a forma mais natural, com sequenciadores:
"First, the bottles **are collected**. Then they**'re washed** and **cut** into small pieces. After that, the pieces **are melted** and **turned** into new products."

**Get + particípio** (informal) às vezes substitui be: "My bike **got stolen**." / "The project **got cancelled**."

Batteries must be disposed of safely.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **Being** = "BÍ-in" (duas sílabas). **Been** = "bin" (EUA) / "bín" (UK) — uma sílaba, fraca. Confundir os dois muda o tempo verbal: "is **being** built" (agora) x "has **been** built" (concluído).

lines.speaker: Guide
lines.en: Welcome to our cooperative. Let me show you how plastic bottles are recycled. First, the bottles are collected from homes and businesses by our members. Then they're sorted by color and type — this step is still done by hand. After that, the labels and caps are removed, and the bottles are washed. Next, they're cut into small flakes, which are melted and turned into pellets. Finally, these pellets are sold to factories, where they're used to make new products — clothes, carpets, even new bottles. Last year, more than 500 tons of plastic were processed here, and our cooperative has been recognized as one of the most efficient in the state.

reading.title: Brazil's recyclers
reading.text: In Brazil, a large part of the waste that gets recycled is collected not by machines or big companies, but by people: the catadores, or waste pickers. Estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of Brazilians work in this activity, many of them in cooperatives. For decades, their work was largely invisible and badly paid. In recent years, however, their role has been increasingly recognized. A national policy on solid waste, approved in 2010, encouraged cities to include waste picker cooperatives in their recycling systems, and in many places their work is now being formally contracted by local governments. Aluminum cans are a famous success story: Brazil has recycled a very high proportion of its aluminum cans for many years, largely thanks to the work of catadores. Challenges remain — many waste pickers still work in difficult and unsafe conditions — but their story shows that environmental solutions can't be separated from social justice.

grammar.title: Linguagem de esclarecimento
grammar.explanation_pt:
Esclarecer envolve três movimentos — e usa estruturas que você já domina (perguntas indiretas, modais, reformulação):

**1. PEDIR esclarecimento:**
- Não ouviu: "Sorry, I **didn't (quite) catch** that." / "Could you **say that again**, please?"
- Não entendeu uma palavra: "What **exactly do you mean by** 'scalable'?" / "What does '...' **mean**?"
- Quer mais detalhes: "Could you **elaborate** on that?" / "Could you **give me an example**?"
- Perguntas indiretas (mais educadas): "**I'm not sure I understand what** you mean." / "**Could you explain how** that works?"

**2. CHECAR o que você entendeu (parafrasear):**
- "**So, if I understand correctly**, you want us to...?"
- "**So what you're saying is**...?" / "**Do you mean that**...?"
- "**In other words**, ...?"

**3. DAR esclarecimento / reformular:**
- "**Let me put it another way.**" / "**What I mean is**..." / "**In plain English**, ..."
- "**To give you an example**, ..." / "**Basically**, ..." / "**The bottom line is**..."
- Checar se o outro entendeu (sem parecer arrogante): "**Does that make sense?**" / "**Is that clear?**" (cuidado: "Do you understand?" pode soar condescendente)

**Corrigir um mal-entendido com educação:**
"**Sorry, I think there's been a misunderstanding.** What I meant was..." / "**That's not quite what I meant.**"

reading.title: Lost in translation
reading.text: Misunderstandings between cultures are rarely about grammar. More often, they come from different expectations about how directly people should speak. Researchers on intercultural communication describe some cultures — like the Netherlands, Germany or Israel — as "low-context": people tend to say exactly what they mean, and the words carry most of the message. Other cultures — like Japan, China or much of Latin America, including Brazil — are often described as "high-context": a lot of the meaning comes from tone, relationships and what is not said. This can cause confusion. When a British colleague says "That's an interesting idea", they may actually mean "I don't agree". When a Brazilian says "Let's meet up sometime!", it may be a friendly expression rather than a real plan. Experts suggest a simple strategy for international teams: when in doubt, check. Paraphrase what you understood ("So you'd like me to...?"), ask for concrete details (dates, numbers, next steps) and never assume that silence means agreement.

grammar.title: Reported speech
grammar.explanation_pt:
Para relatar o que alguém disse, usamos **say** e **tell** e geralmente **voltamos um tempo** no passado (backshift):

**Say x tell:**
- **say** (something) (**to someone**): "She **said** (that) she was busy." / "She **said to me** that..."
- **tell + pessoa** (sempre com objeto!): "She **told me** (that) she was busy." (❌ "She said me" / ❌ "She told that...")

**Backshift (quando o verbo introdutório está no passado):**
- present simple → past simple: "I **work** here." → She said she **worked** there.
- present continuous → past continuous: "I'**m leaving**." → He said he **was leaving**.
- present perfect / past simple → past perfect: "I'**ve finished**." / "I **finished**." → She said she **had finished**.
- will → would: "I'**ll help**." → He said he **would help**.
- can → could: "I **can** come." → She said she **could** come.
- must → had to: "You **must** go." → He said I **had to** go.

Também mudam **pronomes** e **referências de tempo/lugar**: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

💡 Se a informação **ainda é verdade**, o backshift é opcional: "He said he **lives** in Rio." (ainda mora)

**Perguntas relatadas** — ordem de **afirmativa**, sem do/does/did:
- sim/não → **if / whether**: "Are you ready?" → She asked **if I was** ready.
- wh- → "Where **do you live**?" → He asked **where I lived**.

**Pedidos e ordens:** **ask / tell + pessoa + (not) to + verbo**: "Please sit down." → She **asked me to sit** down. / "Don't be late!" → He **told us not to be** late.

grammar.tip_pt: Além de say e tell, use **reporting verbs** mais precisos para soar mais natural: **explained** (explicou), **admitted** (admitiu), **claimed** (afirmou), **warned** (alertou), **promised** (prometeu), **suggested** (sugeriu), **reminded** (lembrou).

pronunciation.tip_pt: **Said** = "séd" (não "sêid"!). **Told** = "tôuld". **Asked** = "ésk(t)" — o -ed vira um T leve e quase some: "She ask(t) me...".

reading.title: Quotes that weren't
reading.text: "Be the change you wish to see in the world," said Gandhi. Or did he? This famous quote appears on posters, mugs and social media posts, but researchers who have studied Gandhi's writings say he never wrote or said those exact words. He did write something with a similar idea, but in a much longer and more complex sentence. The same thing has happened to many other famous people. Einstein is often quoted as saying that doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results is "the definition of insanity" — but there's no evidence he ever said it. And Marie Antoinette almost certainly never told hungry French peasants to "eat cake". Why do fake quotes spread so easily? Psychologists suggest that a sentence seems more true and more wise when it's attached to a famous name. So the next time someone tells you that a celebrity said something brilliant, you might want to ask a simple question: "Where exactly did they say it?"

The conversation that changed my career

Five years ago, I was unhappy in my job and didn't know what to do. One evening, I had coffee with my former university professor, Dr. Helena Ramos. She asked me what I really enjoyed doing. When I said I didn't know, she smiled and told me that was the most honest answer I could give.

She explained that most people waited for clarity before taking action, but that clarity usually came after action. She admitted that she had changed careers three times before becoming a professor. Then she suggested that I try one small project outside my job every month.

Before we said goodbye, she warned me that the first few months would feel uncomfortable. She also reminded me that failing at a small project was the cheapest lesson I would ever get.

I followed her advice. A year later, one of those small projects became my new career in UX design. I still remember everything she told me that day.

grammar.title: Past perfect simple x continuous
grammar.explanation_pt:
Os dois olham para **antes de um ponto do passado**:

**Past perfect simple (had + particípio)** → ação **concluída** antes de outro momento passado; foco no **resultado** ou na **quantidade**:
- "By the time she was 25, she **had written** three books."
- "When I arrived, the meeting **had** already **started**."
- "He **had never seen** the sea before that trip."

**Past perfect continuous (had been + -ing)** → atividade **em andamento por um período** até um momento do passado; foco na **duração** ou na **causa** de algo:
- "She **had been working** as a nurse **for ten years** when she decided to study medicine."
- "His eyes were red because he **had been crying**."
- "They **had been trying** to have a baby for years before their daughter was born."

Mesma lógica do present perfect simple x continuous — só que **um passo para trás**.

**Conectores úteis:**
- **by the time** + past simple, ... past perfect: "By the time we arrived, they **had left**."
- **before / after / when / once / until**
- **already, just, never... before, for, since**

**Estrutura de uma biografia:** past simple para a linha principal dos fatos; past perfect para voltar no tempo e explicar o contexto; past continuous para cenas: "In 2008, she **launched** her app. She **had been developing** it for three years, and she **had been rejected** by fifteen investors. On the day of the launch, she **was** still **sleeping** on her friend's sofa."

reading.title: Late bloomers
reading.text: We often celebrate young geniuses: the teenage tech founder, the 20-year-old Olympic champion. But many remarkable people achieved success much later. Before she published the first Harry Potter book at 32, J.K. Rowling had been rejected by numerous publishers and had been living as a single mother on very little money. The fashion designer Vera Wang had worked as a journalist and figure skater before she designed her first dress at 40. Colonel Sanders had tried many careers — and failed at several — before he started franchising his fried chicken in his sixties. In Brazil, the writer Cora Coralina had been writing poetry for most of her life, but her first book wasn't published until she was 75. Researchers who study creativity suggest that there are different types of creators: some make their breakthroughs early through bold experiments, while others need decades of accumulated experience. The lesson? If you haven't found your path by 30 — or 50 — you're in very good company.

Ana Lins dos Guimarães Peixoto Bretas, known as Cora Coralina, was born in 1889 in the city of Goiás. She had only four years of formal education, but she had been writing poems and short stories since she was a teenager.

For most of her life, however, few people read her work. She got married, moved to the state of São Paulo and raised her children. To support her family, she sold books and, later, she made and sold sweets. All this time, she had been writing in secret.

grammar.title: Second conditional (avançado) + I wish / If only
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Second conditional** = **If + past simple, would / could / might + verbo** → situações **hipotéticas**, imaginárias ou **diferentes da realidade atual**:
- "If I **slept** more, I**'d be** less stressed." (realidade: não durmo o suficiente)
- "If we **walked** to work, we **could save** money." (could = seria possível)
- "If she **took** a break, she **might feel** better." (might = talvez)

**First x second — a escolha depende de quão real você acha a situação:**
- "If I **get** a promotion, I**'ll** buy a car." → possível, realista
- "If I **got** a promotion, I**'d** buy a car." → menos provável, hipotético

**If I were you...** → conselho (were para todas as pessoas): "If I **were** you, I**'d** see a doctor."

**Wh- questions:** "What **would** you **do** if you **had** a month off?"

**I wish / If only + past simple** → desejo de que o **presente** fosse diferente:
- "I **wish** I **had** more free time." (mas não tenho)
- "**If only** I **didn't have** to work on Saturdays!" (If only = mais enfático)
- com habilidade: "I wish I **could** sleep better."
- com be: "I wish I **were** more relaxed."

**I wish + would** → reclamação sobre o comportamento de **outra pessoa**: "I wish my neighbor **would** stop playing loud music."

rows: If I exercised, I'd feel better.
If I had a bike, I could cycle to work.
If you meditated, you might sleep better.
If I were you, I'd take a holiday.
I wish I lived near the beach.
I wish he would stop smoking.

examples.pt: Queria conseguir me desligar depois do trabalho, mas fico checando os e-mails.

grammar.tip_pt: Na fala, **I would** quase sempre vira **I'd**, e **would not** vira **wouldn't**. E nunca use would na oração com **if**: ❌ "If I would have time..." ✅ "If I **had** time..."

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would sleep more, I would feel better.
common_mistakes.right: If I slept more, I would feel better.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Na oração com if, use o past simple (não would).

common_mistakes.wrong: I wish I have more time.

common_mistakes.why_pt: I wish (presente) + past simple.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I was you, I'd rest. (em contexto formal)
common_mistakes.right: If I were you, I'd rest.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A forma padrão é If I were.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I'd** = "áid", **you'd** = "iúd", **she'd** = "shíd" — o D é curto, mas essencial (sem ele, a frase vira presente). **Wouldn't** = "uúdent". **I wish** = "ái uísh".

reading.title: The Blue Zones
reading.text: Why do people in some parts of the world live much longer than others? Journalist Dan Buettner, working with researchers and demographers, identified five regions with unusually high numbers of centenarians and called them the "Blue Zones": Okinawa (Japan), Sardinia (Italy), Nicoya (Costa Rica), Ikaria (Greece) and Loma Linda (California, USA). In these places, people don't go to the gym or follow strict diets. Instead, they share some simple habits. They move naturally throughout the day — walking, gardening, doing housework. They eat mostly plants, especially beans, and they stop eating before they feel completely full. They have a strong sense of purpose and close family and community ties. If we all lived like this, would we live to 100? Not necessarily — genes and healthcare also matter, and some researchers have questioned parts of the data. But the main message is hard to argue with: if our daily lives included more movement, better food and stronger relationships, most of us would probably be healthier and happier.

writing.model:
I strongly agree that companies would be more successful if they cared more about their employees' well-being.

First, if employees slept better and worked fewer extra hours, they would make fewer mistakes and have better ideas. Tired people are rarely creative. Second, if companies offered flexible hours, many workers could exercise, take their children to school and still be productive. People who feel trusted usually work harder, not less. Third, if managers paid attention to mental health, fewer employees would burn out and leave. Replacing a good employee is expensive, so investing in well-being also saves money.

Some people argue that well-being programs are just a trend and that results are what matter. However, in my experience, results and well-being are connected. In my previous job, I worked twelve hours a day, and I wish someone had told me to stop earlier — I burned out after two years.

In conclusion, if more leaders saw well-being as an investment rather than a cost, both companies and people would be healthier.

grammar.title: Linguagem de decisão + estrutura de apresentação
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Apresentar opções:** "We have **three options**. **The first one is**... **Alternatively**, we could... **Another possibility would be**..."

**2. Avaliar prós e contras** (comparativos + condicionais):
- "**The main advantage of** option A **is that** it's **cheaper than** B."
- "**The drawback is that** it would take **longer**."
- "**If we chose** option B, we**'d save** time, **but** we**'d have to** hire more people." (second conditional = hipótese)
- "**It's worth considering**..." / "**There's a trade-off between** cost **and** quality."

**3. Discutir em grupo** (concordar, discordar, sugerir — revisão do curso):
- "**I see your point, but**..." / "**That's a good idea, although**..."
- "**What if we**...?" / "**How about**...?" / "**Why don't we**...?"
- "**Could we compromise**? **What if** we tried A **for three months** and then reviewed it?"

**4. Decidir:**
- "**On balance**, I think we **should go for**..."
- "**So, have we agreed that**...?" / "**Shall we go with that?**"
- "**Let's go for** option B. **We'll** review the results in June." (will = decisão)

**5. Estrutura de uma apresentação estilo TED (5 minutos):**
1. **Gancho** (pergunta, história ou dado surpreendente): "Have you ever wondered...?"
2. **Por que importa** (o problema): "Every year, ..."
3. **Sua história ou experiência** (narrativas no passado, past perfect)
4. **Sua ideia** (present simple, passiva, relative clauses)
5. **Evidências e exemplos** (reported speech: "Researchers have found that...")
6. **Imagine se...** (second conditional: "If every company did this, ...")
7. **Chamada para ação** (imperativos, will): "Tomorrow, try..."

The main advantage is that... / It's worth...
The drawback is that... / There's a trade-off between...
If we chose A, we would...
What if we tried...? / Could we compromise?
On balance, we should go for... / Shall we go with that?

grammar.tip_pt: Pesquisas sobre decisão mostram que, para escolhas importantes, **escrever prós e contras** e **dormir sobre o assunto** (sleep on it) ajudam a evitar decisões impulsivas. E às vezes vale ouvir o **gut feeling** — mas explique-o com argumentos!

pronunciation.tip_pt: Para uma apresentação marcante: **pause** antes da ideia principal, **enfatize** números e palavras-chave, **varie o ritmo** (devagar para o importante, mais rápido para contexto) e **olhe para o público**. Grave-se e ouça: você soa convencido(a) da sua ideia?

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Have you ever pretended to understand something in English just because you were too embarrassed to ask? I have. Hundreds of times. Five years ago, I was in a meeting with clients from Canada, and I nodded at everything they said. I hadn't understood half of it. Two weeks later, we delivered the wrong project. That day, I made a decision: I would never pretend again. Today, I'm going to share three simple strategies that changed the way I speak English — and the way I work. reading.title: The paradox of choice
reading.text: In a supermarket in California, researchers once set up a table with samples of jam. On some days, the table offered 24 flavors; on other days, only 6. The large display attracted more visitors, but when only 6 flavors were offered, a much higher percentage of people actually bought a jar. This famous experiment, published in 2000, helped popularize an idea that psychologist Barry Schwartz called "the paradox of choice": having too many options can make it harder to decide and less satisfying once we have decided. When we have many alternatives, we worry that we might have chosen badly, and we imagine how much better the other options might have been. Later studies have shown that the effect doesn't always appear — it depends on how complex the options are and how much we know about them. Still, many experts suggest a practical strategy for everyday decisions: reduce your options to two or three, decide what really matters to you, and remember that "good enough" is often better than "perfect". As Schwartz has argued, people who look for the absolute best option are often less happy with their choices than people who are satisfied with a good one.

questions.answer: More people visited the table, but a lower percentage bought jam.

questions.q: What is "the paradox of choice"?
questions.answer: Too many options make it harder to decide and less satisfying afterward.

questions.q: Does the effect always appear?
questions.answer: No — it depends on how complex the options are and how much we know.

questions.q: What practical strategy do experts suggest?
questions.answer: Reduce options to two or three, decide what matters and accept "good enough".

writing.model:
The power of asking "What do you mean?"

Have you ever pretended to understand something just to avoid looking stupid? I'm sure you have. We all have.

Every day, in offices, classrooms and hospitals around the world, millions of small misunderstandings happen. Some are funny. Some are very expensive.

Five years ago, I was working at a design agency in São Paulo. One morning, a client from Canada asked us for "something clean and bold". I nodded and said I understood. I didn't. I had been studying English for years, but I was afraid to ask. Two weeks later, we presented the design. The client looked at it for a long time and then said, very politely, that it wasn't quite what he had imagined. We had to start again from zero.

That day, I made a promise to myself: I would never pretend to understand again.

Since then, I've learned that asking for clarification is not a weakness — it's a skill. Researchers who study communication have found that people who ask questions are often seen as more competent, not less. A question that takes ten seconds can save weeks of work.

So here's my idea: let's make "What do you mean?" the most normal question in any meeting. Imagine if every team did this. If managers asked their teams to check understanding, and if everyone felt safe to say "I'm not sure I follow", we would have fewer mistakes, better ideas and much more trust.

It must sound simple — and it is. But simple doesn't mean easy.

So tomorrow, try this: in your next conversation, when you're not 100% sure, stop and ask: "What exactly do you mean?" You might feel uncomfortable for a second. But I promise you, it's worth it.

Thank you.

grammar.title: Talking about habits with nuance
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B2, além de **usually** e **used to**, você tem estruturas que mostram **atitude** sobre o hábito:

**1. Will + verbo (presente)** → hábito **característico** de alguém (muitas vezes com carinho ou resignação):
"My grandma **will** always **offer** you food, even if you've just eaten."
**Would + verbo (passado)** → o mesmo, no passado (só ações, não estados):
"When I was a kid, my dad **would** wake us up singing."

**2. Will / would com ênfase** (WILL, WOULD acentuados) → hábito **irritante**:
"He **WILL** leave his shoes in the middle of the room!" / "She **WOULD** say that — she always takes his side."

**3. Always / constantly / forever + present continuous** → hábito irritante ou surpreendente:
"You're **always losing** your keys!" / "He's **constantly checking** his phone."

**4. Keep (on) + -ing** → repetição (frequentemente irritante): "The printer **keeps jamming**." / "She **kept interrupting** me."

**5. Tend to + verbo** → tendência geral (mais neutro, ótimo para generalizar com cuidado):
"Introverts **tend to** prefer small groups." / "I **tend not to** trust first impressions." (negativa: tend not to / don't tend to)

**6. Be prone to / be inclined to** (mais formal): "He's **prone to** exaggerating."

**Come across as** + adjetivo/substantivo = passar a impressão de ser: "She **comes across as** arrogant, but she's just shy."

rows: She WILL leave the lights on!

examples.en: My boss will reply to emails at 2 a.m. — it's just how he is.
examples.pt: Meu chefe é capaz de responder e-mails às 2 da manhã — é o jeito dele.

grammar.tip_pt: **Tend to** é uma das palavras mais úteis do B2: ela **suaviza generalizações**. Em vez de "Brazilians are late" (estereótipo), diga "Brazilians **tend to** be more flexible about time".

common_mistakes.right: He used to be very tall... / He was very tall...
common_mistakes.why_pt: Would não funciona com estados (be, have, know) — só com ações repetidas.

common_mistakes.wrong: She tends to be talking a lot.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Tend to + verbo base.

common_mistakes.wrong: He seems arrogant, but he comes across as shy.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Come across as = a impressão (aparente); depois vem a realidade.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Para mostrar irritação, os nativos **acentuam** will/would, que normalmente são fracos: "He **WILL** leave his socks everywhere!" ("rí UÍL lív..."). Compare com o neutro: "He'll sit for hours reading" ("ríl").

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: Research suggests that we form an impression of someone's face in a fraction of a second — some studies say about a tenth of a second. We tend to judge whether someone is trustworthy, competent or friendly almost instantly. The problem is that these snap judgements are heavily influenced by bias. For example, we tend to see people who look like us as more trustworthy, and we'll often assume that attractive people are also smarter — something psychologists call the halo effect. The good news is that first impressions aren't fixed. If we keep meeting someone and they keep behaving in a way that contradicts our first judgement, we'll eventually update our opinion. The key is to stay curious and to be aware of our own biases.

reading.title: Why we misjudge people
reading.text: Imagine meeting two job candidates. One walks in confidently, makes eye contact and tells a funny story. The other speaks quietly and looks down. Most of us would instinctively prefer the first — even though nothing we've seen tells us who would actually do the job better. Psychologists have identified several reasons why our judgements of other people tend to be unreliable. One is the halo effect: when someone has one attractive quality, we'll tend to assume they have others too. Another is the fundamental attribution error: when other people behave badly, we tend to blame their personality ("He's rude"), but when we behave badly, we blame the situation ("I was tired"). Culture also plays a role. In some cultures, direct eye contact signals honesty; in others, it can come across as disrespectful. What seems confident in one country may seem arrogant in another. None of this means we should ignore our instincts completely. But it does suggest that we should hold our first impressions lightly, look for evidence, and give people the same benefit of the doubt that we would want them to give us.

questions.q: What does the writer recommend?

writing.model:
My Aunt Zélia

At first glance, my Aunt Zélia comes across as a rather serious woman. She's tall, wears her grey hair in a tight bun and tends to look at people over the top of her glasses, as if she were assessing them. Strangers often find her intimidating.

But anyone who spends more than ten minutes with her soon discovers that she's one of the most down-to-earth and generous people you could meet. She'll stop to talk to the man who sells popcorn on her street, and she'll remember the names of all his children. When I was a teenager, she would call me every Sunday just to ask about my week, and she never once judged me, even when I made terrible decisions.

She isn't perfect, of course. She's incredibly stubborn: once she's made up her mind, there's no point arguing. And she WILL insist on giving you a second plate of food, no matter how many times you say you're full. She's forever telling me I look thin!

Still, I can't imagine my life without her. If I've learned anything from Aunt Zélia, it's that the people who seem the toughest on the outside are often the softest inside.

culture_note.title: Diretos x indiretos
culture_note.text_pt: O que é "confiante" ou "educado" muda entre culturas. Nos EUA, autopromoção e contato visual forte costumam ser vistos como confiança; no Japão, modéstia é valorizada; no Reino Unido, o **understatement** (dizer menos do que se sente) é comum: "It's not bad" pode significar "é ótimo!". No B2, perceber essas nuances é parte da fluência.

summary_pt: will / would = hábito característico (would: só ações).
always / forever + continuous e keep + -ing = repetição irritante.
tend to = generalização suave.
come across as = passar a impressão de ser.

objectives: Usar phrasal verbs de relacionamento com naturalidade
Diferenciar phrasal verbs separáveis e inseparáveis
Usar phrasal verbs de três partes (put up with, look up to)
Falar sobre amizades, conflitos e reconciliações

warmup.text_pt: O inglês do dia a dia é cheio de **phrasal verbs** — verbo + partícula com sentido próprio. Nativos dizem "we fell out" muito mais do que "we had a disagreement". No B2, dominar os mais comuns faz você soar natural.

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs: tipos e posição do objeto
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Intransitivos (sem objeto):** fall out, make up, break up, drift apart, grow up
"We **fell out** last year, but we've **made up** now."

**2. Separáveis (transitivos)** — o objeto pode ficar **no meio ou no fim**; mas se for **pronome**, **tem que ficar no meio**:
- "She **let her friends down**." / "She **let down her friends**." ✅
- "She **let them down**." ✅ / ❌ "She let down them."
- Outros: bring up (criar), turn down (recusar), cheer up (animar), talk into (convencer), ask out (convidar para sair)

**3. Inseparáveis** — o objeto vem sempre **depois** da partícula:
- "I can always **count on her**." (❌ count her on) / "She **takes after her mother**." (puxou à mãe) / "I **ran into** an old friend." (encontrei por acaso)

**4. Três partes** (verbo + advérbio + preposição) — sempre inseparáveis:
- **put up with** (tolerar), **look up to** (admirar), **look down on** (menosprezar), **get on with** (dar-se bem), **catch up with** (colocar o papo em dia), **come up with** (ter uma ideia), **stand up for** (defender), **fall out with** (brigar com)
- "I **look up to** my grandmother." / "How do you **put up with** the noise?"

💡 **Dica de registro:** phrasal verbs são mais **informais**; em textos formais, muitas vezes existe um verbo latino equivalente: put up with → **tolerate**; fall out → **argue**; look up to → **admire**; bring up → **raise**.

rows: She brought up three kids. / She brought three kids up.
I look up to my mom.

examples.en: My parents brought me up to stand up for what I believe in.
examples.pt: Meus pais me criaram para defender aquilo em que acredito.

examples.en: We used to be inseparable, but we drifted apart when she moved abroad.
examples.pt: Éramos inseparáveis, mas nos afastamos quando ela se mudou para o exterior.

examples.en: I ran into my ex at the supermarket — awkward! But we caught up and it was fine.
examples.pt: Encontrei meu ex no supermercado por acaso — constrangedor! Mas colocamos o papo em dia e foi tranquilo.

grammar.tip_pt: Aprenda phrasal verbs **em contexto e por tema** (relacionamentos, trabalho, viagens), nunca em listas alfabéticas. E use um bom dicionário (Cambridge, Oxford Learner's) para saber se são separáveis.

common_mistakes.wrong: He let down me.
common_mistakes.right: He let me down.

common_mistakes.wrong: I can't put up this noise.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Put up with tem três partes.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Sem objeto, use as formas intransitivas (fall out, make up).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em phrasal verbs, a **partícula** costuma ser a sílaba mais forte: "We fell **OUT**", "They broke **UP**", "Don't let me **DOWN**". Em verbos de três partes, a força fica no meio: "put **UP** with", "look **UP** to".

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: Not really. We drifted apart after she moved to Recife. And then we fell out over something silly.

lines.speaker: Lia
lines.en: What happened?

lines.speaker: Jade

lines.speaker: Lia
lines.en: That must have hurt. Did you ever talk about it?
lines.pt: Deve ter doído. Vocês chegaram a conversar sobre isso?

lines.speaker: Jade
lines.en: No. I didn't want to bring it up, and she never explained. But last month I ran into her mum, who told me Carol had been going through a really hard time back then.

listening.title: Radio: what makes friendships last?
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre amizades na vida adulta.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: One of the most common things people tell us is that they've drifted apart from friends without any real conflict. Life just gets in the way: people move, have children, change jobs. Research suggests that adult friendships need regular contact to survive — not necessarily long conversations, but small gestures, like sending a message or catching up over coffee. Another key factor is how people deal with conflict. Friends who fall out but then talk openly and make up often end up closer than before. On the other hand, friendships where people keep putting up with things they don't like, without saying anything, tend to fade. So my advice is simple: reach out, and if something bothers you, bring it up — kindly.

questions.q: Why do many adults drift apart from friends?
questions.answer: Life gets in the way: moving, having children, changing jobs.

questions.q: What do adult friendships need to survive?
questions.answer: Regular contact — small gestures like messages or coffee.

questions.q: What happens to friends who fall out and then make up openly?
questions.answer: They often end up closer than before.

questions.q: What's the researcher's advice?
questions.answer: Reach out, and if something bothers you, bring it up kindly.

reading.title: The friendship recession
reading.text: In recent years, several surveys in the United States and other countries have suggested that adults have fewer close friends than they used to. Some commentators have even started talking about a "friendship recession". The reasons are complex. People work longer hours, move more often for jobs and spend more time online. Many say they simply don't have time to catch up with friends, and that friendships slowly fade without anyone falling out. Researchers also point out that making new friends as an adult is harder than at school or university, where we meet the same people every day without trying. One frequently quoted study by Jeffrey Hall estimated that it takes around 50 hours of time together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, and more than 200 hours to become close friends. That's a lot of coffees. However, there are reasons for optimism. Many people are deliberately making time for friendship: joining running clubs, book clubs and volunteer groups, where repeated contact happens naturally. As one participant put it, "I used to wait for friendships to happen. Now I put the effort in — and I've never felt less lonely."

questions.q: What is the "friendship recession"?
questions.answer: The idea that adults have fewer close friends than they used to.

questions.q: Why is making friends harder as an adult?
questions.answer: We don't meet the same people every day without trying, as at school or university.

questions.q: How many hours does it take to become close friends, according to the study?
questions.answer: More than 200 hours.

questions.q: What are some people doing about it?
questions.answer: Joining clubs and groups where repeated contact happens naturally.

writing.model:
Hi Carol,

I know it's been ages since we last spoke, and I'm really sorry I haven't been in touch. After the wedding, life just got in the way — new job, new apartment, and suddenly two years had gone by. I've thought about you so many times.

The other day I ran into your mum at the bakery near my old house. She told me you'd been going through a really tough time around the time of my wedding. I had no idea, and I feel awful that I didn't reach out. I think I was hurt that you couldn't come, and instead of bringing it up, I just stayed quiet. That wasn't fair to either of us.

Anyway, I'd love to catch up properly. I've got loads of news (yes, I finally gave up my terrible job at the bank!), and I want to hear everything about your life in Recife. I'm actually going to be there for a conference next month. Could we meet up for lunch?

You've always been someone I looked up to, and I don't want us to drift apart for good. You can always count on me — I hope I can still count on you too.

Lots of love,
Jade

E um **frenemy** é aquela pessoa que finge ser amiga, mas compete com você. Em inglês britânico, "**Cheers, mate!**" serve para agradecer quase tudo.

summary_pt: Intransitivos: fall out, make up, drift apart.

lessons.title: Generation gaps
lessons.subtitle_pt: Comparações avançadas: the more... the more, far / slightly / nowhere near, as... as

TopNotch 3B Teacher's Book – Unit 9 (controversial issues)
objectives: Modificar comparativos com far, much, slightly, a bit, considerably
Usar not nearly as / nowhere near as / just as / twice as

warmup.text_pt: Boomers, Geração X, Millennials, Geração Z, Alpha... Cada geração acha que a outra "não entende nada". Existem diferenças reais ou são só estereótipos? Hoje vamos comparar com **precisão** — e com cuidado.
questions: Which generation do you belong to? Do you identify with its stereotypes?
What's the biggest difference between you and your parents?

grammar.title: Advanced comparisons
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Modificar comparativos** (o quanto maior/menor):
- grande diferença: **much / far / a lot / considerably / significantly** + comparativo → "Rent is **far higher** than it was in 2010."
- pequena diferença: **slightly / a bit / a little / marginally** → "Gen Z is **slightly more** likely to..."
- também com superlativos: "**by far the** biggest change" / "**easily the** best"

**2. As... as (com modificadores):**
- **just as** (exatamente tão): "Young people are **just as** hard-working **as** their parents."
- **not quite as / not nearly as / nowhere near as** (não tão / nem de longe tão): "Buying a house is **nowhere near as** easy **as** it was."
- **twice / three times as... as** (o dobro / o triplo): "Houses cost **three times as much as** they did."
- **the same as / similar to / different from**

**3. Comparativos duplos (mudança progressiva / correlação):**
- **-er and -er / more and more** (cada vez mais): "Life is getting **more and more** expensive." / "Phones are getting **smaller and smaller**."
- **The + comparativo..., the + comparativo** (quanto mais..., mais...): "**The more** you read, **the better** you write." / "**The older** I get, **the less** I care about what people think." / "**The sooner, the better.**"

**4. Linguagem para evitar estereótipos:** use **tend to**, **on average**, **many / some (but not all)**, **compared with**: "**On average**, Gen Z **tends to** change jobs more often **than** previous generations."

rows: We're just as worried as they were.
It's nowhere near as cheap as before.
The more I learn, the less I know.

examples.en: On average, young people today are far more likely to rent than to own a home.
examples.pt: Em média, os jovens hoje têm muito mais chance de alugar do que de ter casa própria.

examples.en: My grandparents' generation had nowhere near as many choices as we do.
examples.pt: A geração dos meus avós não tinha nem de longe tantas opções quanto nós.

examples.en: The more time I spend with my grandmother, the more I realize how much she's been through.
examples.pt: Quanto mais tempo passo com minha avó, mais percebo o quanto ela passou.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português dizemos "**cada vez mais caro**"; em inglês, **more and more expensive** ou, para adjetivos curtos, **cheaper and cheaper**. Nunca "each time more" ❌.

common_mistakes.wrong: It's each time more difficult.
common_mistakes.right: It's getting more and more difficult.
common_mistakes.why_pt: "Cada vez mais" = more and more / -er and -er.

common_mistakes.wrong: More you study, more you learn.
common_mistakes.right: The more you study, the more you learn.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A estrutura exige the nas duas partes.

common_mistakes.wrong: It's very more expensive.
common_mistakes.right: It's much/far more expensive.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Use much/far (não very) com comparativos.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Nas frases "the more..., the more...", há duas partes com ritmo paralelo e uma pausa no meio: "The **MORE** you **READ** ↗ | the **BET**ter you **WRITE** ↘." A voz sobe na primeira parte e desce na segunda.
practice: The more you read, the better you write.

listening.title: Generations at work
listening.context_pt: Uma consultora de RH fala sobre equipes com várias gerações.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: Today, many workplaces have four or even five generations working side by side. Managers often ask me whether younger employees are really that different. My answer: slightly, but nowhere near as much as the headlines suggest. Surveys show that, on average, younger workers tend to value flexibility and feedback a bit more, while older workers tend to value stability. But when you look at what people want most — fair pay, respect and meaningful work — the generations are remarkably similar. The bigger problem is stereotypes. The more we assume that a 60-year-old can't learn new technology, or that a 25-year-old won't stay in a job, the worse our teams work. The best approach is mentoring in both directions: older employees share experience, younger ones share new tools. The more they learn from each other, the better.

questions.q: How different are the generations, according to the consultant?
questions.answer: Slightly, but nowhere near as much as headlines suggest.

questions.q: What do younger workers tend to value a bit more?
questions.answer: Flexibility and feedback.

questions.q: What do all generations want most?
questions.answer: Fair pay, respect and meaningful work.

questions.q: What approach does she recommend?
questions.answer: Mentoring in both directions.

video.title: The danger of a single story
video.speaker: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
video.task_pt: Assista à palestra (cerca de 18 minutos). Ela fala sobre estereótipos culturais, mas a ideia se aplica também às gerações. Responda:

reading.title: Are young people really so different?
reading.text: Every generation seems to believe that the next one is lazier, more selfish and more addicted to whatever technology is new. Similar complaints about young people can be found in texts from centuries ago. Today, the target is often Generation Z, described in headlines as anxious, glued to their phones and unwilling to work hard. But how much of this is true? The data paint a more complex picture. On the one hand, young people today do spend considerably more time online than previous generations did at the same age, and surveys in several countries suggest that reported levels of anxiety among teenagers have risen. On the other hand, many members of Gen Z drink far less alcohol and smoke much less than their parents did as teenagers, and they're often just as interested in meaningful work. Economic conditions matter too. In many countries, housing has become far more expensive relative to income, making it nowhere near as easy for young people to reach traditional milestones like buying a home. Researchers increasingly argue that differences between generations are often less about character and more about circumstances. Put simply: the more you change the world young people grow up in, the more their choices will change too.

questions.q: What do many generations believe about the next one?
questions.answer: That it's lazier, more selfish and more addicted to new technology.

questions.q: In what ways might Gen Z be different?
questions.answer: They spend more time online and report more anxiety.

questions.q: In what ways might they be "better" than their parents at the same age?
questions.answer: They drink less alcohol and smoke less.

questions.q: What do researchers increasingly argue?
questions.answer: Differences are less about character and more about circumstances.

writing.model:
It is often said that young people today have a far better life than their grandparents did. While there is some truth in this, the picture is much more complex.

On the one hand, in many ways life has become considerably easier. Most young people today have access to far more information, healthcare and opportunities than their grandparents could have imagined. In Brazil, for example, the average life expectancy is significantly higher than it was in the 1960s, and many more people go to university. Technology also allows us to stay in touch with friends and family who live thousands of kilometers away.

On the other hand, some aspects of life have become harder and harder. Housing is nowhere near as affordable as it was, and stable, lifelong jobs are much less common. Many young people also report higher levels of anxiety, partly because of the constant pressure of social media.

In my opinion, it is misleading to say that one generation has it better than another. Each generation faces different challenges. My grandparents had fewer choices, but they had more stability; we have more freedom, but less security. Rather than competing over who suffered more, I believe that the more generations listen to each other, the better we will understand the world we share.

grammar.title: Hedging and softening
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Hedging** é suavizar uma afirmação para soar menos absoluto, mais educado ou mais preciso. É essencial em reuniões, textos acadêmicos e conversas delicadas.

**1. Verbos que suavizam:** **seem / appear / tend / suggest / indicate**
- "The plan **seems to** have some problems." (em vez de "The plan has problems")
- "The data **suggest** that..." / "It **appears that** prices will rise."

**2. Modais de possibilidade:** **might / may / could / would**
- "That **might** not be the best approach." / "I **would** say that..." / "I **would have thought**..."

**3. Advérbios e expressões de grau:** **perhaps, possibly, arguably, presumably, to some extent, in some ways, relatively, fairly, rather, a little, somewhat**
- "It's **arguably** the most important issue." / "I **somewhat** disagree."

**4. Estruturas impessoais:** **It could be argued that... / It is often said that... / There is some evidence that...**

**5. Discordância suave** (nunca "You're wrong"):
- "**I'm not sure I agree.**" / "**I see what you mean, but**..." / "**I'm not entirely convinced.**"
- "**Couldn't it also be argued that**...?" (pergunta negativa = sugestão educada)
- "**With respect**, I see it a bit differently."

**6. Quantificadores cuidadosos:** many (not all), some, most, a significant number of — em vez de **all / everyone / never / always**.

⚠️ Não exagere: hedging demais soa inseguro. Use mais em **opiniões e temas sensíveis**, menos em **fatos claros**.

rows: I'm not entirely sure that idea would work.
This is arguably the best solution.
There seems to be a serious problem with corruption in some areas.
I think we might be seeing this from different angles.

listening.title: Academic hedging
listening.context_pt: Uma professora universitária explica por que a linguagem acadêmica é cheia de "talvez".

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: Students often ask me why academic writing is so full of words like "may", "suggest" and "appear". Isn't it better to be confident? The answer is that good researchers try not to claim more than their evidence shows. If one study finds that coffee drinkers live longer, a careful scientist won't write "Coffee makes you live longer." They'll write something like "The results suggest that moderate coffee consumption may be associated with a lower risk of mortality." It's less exciting, but it's more honest. The study can't prove that coffee is the cause — perhaps coffee drinkers also tend to have other healthy habits. Hedging isn't weakness. It's precision. And in a world full of exaggerated headlines, I'd argue we need much more of it.

questions.answer: Researchers try not to claim more than their evidence shows.

questions.q: What does the professor say hedging is?

reading.title: How to disagree well
reading.text: In 2008, computer scientist and essayist Paul Graham proposed a "hierarchy of disagreement" — a pyramid showing different ways people argue, from the least to the most useful. At the bottom is name-calling: attacking the person rather than the idea ("You're an idiot"). Slightly higher is responding to tone ("Why are you being so aggressive?"), which avoids the actual argument. In the middle is contradiction: simply stating the opposite view without evidence. Near the top is counterargument — giving reasons and evidence for a different position — and at the very top is refutation: identifying exactly where the other person's argument goes wrong and explaining why. Graham's model has been widely shared online, perhaps because many public debates seem to be stuck at the bottom of the pyramid. Social media, which rewards quick and emotional reactions, arguably makes things worse. Psychologists who study conflict suggest a few habits that may help: listen to understand rather than to reply, summarize the other person's view before responding ("So you're saying..."), and look for common ground. Disagreeing well doesn't mean avoiding conflict. It means making conflict productive.

questions.q: What is at the bottom of the hierarchy of disagreement?
questions.answer: Name-calling (attacking the person, not the idea).

questions.q: What is the difference between contradiction and counterargument?
questions.answer: Contradiction states the opposite without evidence; counterargument gives reasons and evidence.

questions.q: Why might social media make things worse?
questions.answer: It rewards quick and emotional reactions.

questions.q: Name two habits that may help.
questions.answer: Listen to understand, summarize the other person's view, look for common ground.

Our productivity data from the last year appear to show that focused tasks, such as writing reports and analyzing data, have actually improved since we became hybrid. grammar.title: Future continuous & future perfect
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Future continuous: will be + -ing** → ação **em andamento** num momento do futuro:
- "This time tomorrow, I**'ll be flying** to Lisbon." (estarei voando)
- "Don't call at 8 — we**'ll be having** dinner."
- **Perguntas educadas** sobre planos (sem pressionar): "**Will you be using** the car tonight?" (soa menos invasivo que "Will you use...?")
- Coisas que vão acontecer **naturalmente / como rotina**: "I**'ll be seeing** Ana at work anyway, so I'll give her the book."

**Future perfect simple: will have + particípio** → ação **concluída até** um ponto do futuro:
- "**By** 2030, I**'ll have finished** my master's." (terei terminado)
- "By the time you arrive, we**'ll have eaten**."
- Negativa: "I **won't have finished** by Friday."
- Com **by**: by then, by the time, by next year, by the end of the month

**Future perfect continuous: will have been + -ing** → **duração** até um ponto do futuro:
- "In June, I**'ll have been working** here **for** five years." (farei cinco anos)
- "By the time she retires, she**'ll have been teaching for** 35 years."

**Lembre:** em time clauses (when, by the time, as soon as), use o **presente**: "By the time you **arrive** (❌ will arrive), we'll have left."

examples.en: This time next year, I'll be working remotely from a small town by the sea.

listening.title: The future of careers
listening.context_pt: Um futurista fala sobre como as carreiras devem mudar até 2035.

lines.speaker: Futurist
lines.en: Let me paint a picture of 2035. By then, many of the jobs we know today will have changed dramatically — and some will have disappeared altogether. Millions of people will be working in roles that don't exist yet. Most of us won't be doing the same job for forty years; instead, we'll be retraining several times throughout our careers. By the time today's teenagers retire, they'll probably have had five or six different careers, not just different jobs. AI tools will be handling many routine tasks, which means humans will be focusing more on creativity, empathy and complex problem-solving. The question isn't whether your job will change. It's whether you'll have learned how to keep learning.

reading.title: The 100-year life
reading.text: In their book The 100-Year Life, Lynda Gratton and Andrew Scott argue that as life expectancy increases, the traditional three-stage life — education, work, retirement — will no longer make sense for many people. If you're likely to live to 90 or 100, you probably won't be able to stop working at 60 and live on your savings for forty years. Instead, the authors predict a multi-stage life. People will be studying, working, taking breaks and retraining in different combinations throughout their lives. Someone might work in finance until 40, take a year off to travel, retrain as a teacher and then set up a small business at 60. By the time they finally retire, they will have had several careers, not one. This has big implications. Governments will need to rethink pensions and education. Companies will have to stop seeing older workers as a cost and start seeing them as an asset. And individuals will need to invest in what the authors call "intangible assets": skills, health, relationships and the ability to adapt. The good news? A longer life means more time to try new things. The challenge is that most of our institutions were designed for a much shorter one.

questions.q: What are "intangible assets"?

grammar.title: Future in the past
grammar.explanation_pt:
Quando contamos uma história no passado, às vezes precisamos falar do que era **futuro naquele momento**. O inglês usa as formas de futuro "no passado":

**1. was/were going to + verbo** → plano ou intenção passada (geralmente **não** aconteceu):
- "I **was going to** call you, but I forgot." (eu ia te ligar)
- "We **were going to** move to Portugal, but then the pandemic happened."

**2. would + verbo** → previsão ou expectativa vista do passado (o "will" do passado):
- "I **knew** you **would** understand." (eu sabia que você entenderia)
- "She **promised** she **would** help." / "Nobody **thought** the company **would** survive."
- Também para narrar o destino: "He moved to London in 1990. He **would** never return to Brazil." (nunca mais voltaria)

**3. was/were about to + verbo** → algo **iminente** no passado (estava prestes a):
- "I **was about to** give up when I got the job offer."
- Mais formal: **was on the point of** + -ing: "She **was on the point of** resigning."

**4. was/were supposed to + verbo** → o que estava **combinado/esperado** (e geralmente não aconteceu):
- "The package **was supposed to** arrive yesterday."

**5. was/were + -ing** (present continuous no passado) → compromisso marcado no passado: "I couldn't meet him because I **was flying** to Recife the next day."

**6. was/were to + verbo** (formal/narrativo) → algo destinado a acontecer: "It was 2005. She **was to become** one of Brazil's greatest athletes."

reading.title: The plans that failed — and the success that followed
reading.text: Many famous success stories begin with a plan that went wrong. In the early 2000s, a small company called Odeo was going to become a major podcasting platform. Then Apple added podcasts to iTunes, and the founders realized their product would never compete. Instead of giving up, they held a brainstorming session, and one employee suggested a simple service for sharing short status updates. That idea became Twitter. Similarly, the founders of Slack were originally building an online game called Glitch. The game failed, but the internal chat tool the team had built to communicate turned out to be far more valuable than the game itself. Nobody at the time thought it would become one of the most widely used workplace tools in the world. Psychologists say that people who handle these moments well tend to share two qualities: they're flexible enough to change direction, and they see failure as information rather than as a final verdict. In other words, the plan you were going to follow might not be the plan you were supposed to follow. Sometimes, the most important skill is knowing when to let go.

The plan that changed my life

In 2020, I had everything planned. I was going to finish my engineering degree, get a job at a big construction company and buy an apartment by the time I was 30. My parents were proud, and I was sure it would all work out perfectly.

Then the pandemic came. The internship I was supposed to start in April was called off, and the company I had dreamed of working for stopped hiring. For months, I stayed at home, applying for jobs that never replied. At one point, I was on the point of giving up on engineering altogether.

To keep myself busy, I started making short videos explaining maths problems for my younger cousin. I posted a few online, never imagining that anyone would watch them. Within six months, my channel had 50,000 subscribers. Students from all over Brazil were writing to thank me.

I didn't know it then, but those videos would become my career. Today, I run an online education company with a team of twelve people. I still use my engineering skills every day — just not in the way I was going to.

Looking back, the cancelled internship turned out to be a blessing in disguise. If you're facing a plan that's fallen through, my advice is simple: stay curious. The plan you were going to follow might not be the best one for you.

grammar.title: Conditionals and language for negotiating
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Condições** (alternativas mais precisas ao if):
- **provided (that) / providing (that)** = desde que (formal) → "We can deliver by Friday, **provided that** you confirm the order today."
- **as long as / so long as** = contanto que → "You can work from home **as long as** you attend the Monday meeting."
- **on condition that** = sob a condição de que (muito formal)
- **unless** = a menos que → "We can't lower the price **unless** you order more units."
⚠️ Depois dessas expressões, use **presente simples** para o futuro (como com if).

**2. Propostas hipotéticas — second conditional** (soa mais flexível e menos ameaçador que o first):
- "**If we ordered** 500 units, **would** you **give** us a 10% discount?"
- "**What if we offered** a two-year contract?"
- "**Suppose** we paid upfront — **could** you deliver earlier?"

**3. Linguagem diplomática** (would, could, might, a bit, slightly, I'm afraid):
- "**We'd** like to propose..." / "**We'd be willing to**..."
- "That's **slightly higher than** our budget." (em vez de "too expensive")
- "**I'm afraid** we **wouldn't be able to** accept that."
- Perguntas negativas como sugestão: "**Wouldn't it make sense to**...?"

**4. Concessão em troca (if... then):**
"**If you could** extend the deadline, **we could** reduce the price by 5%." — nunca dê algo sem pedir algo em troca!

listening.title: Salary negotiation tips
listening.context_pt: Uma recrutadora dá dicas de como negociar salário numa oferta de emprego.

lines.speaker: Recruiter
lines.en: Many people accept the first offer because they're afraid the company will withdraw it. In reality, most employers expect some negotiation, as long as you're polite and realistic. Here's my advice. First, research the market so you know your value. Second, never give the first number if you can avoid it — ask what the budget for the role is. Third, if the salary is lower than you hoped, try negotiating other things: extra vacation days, a training budget, remote work. You might say: "I'm very excited about the role. I was hoping for something closer to X. If the salary isn't flexible, would it be possible to discuss other parts of the package?" And finally, once you've reached an agreement, ask for everything in writing.

reading.title: Getting to Yes
reading.text: In 1981, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project published Getting to Yes, a book that changed how many people think about negotiation. Instead of seeing negotiation as a battle where one side wins and the other loses, they proposed a method called "principled negotiation". It has four main ideas. First, separate the people from the problem: you can be tough on the issue while being respectful to the person. Second, focus on interests, not positions. A position is what someone says they want ("I want a 20% raise"); an interest is why they want it ("I need to pay for my children's school"). When you understand interests, creative solutions often appear — perhaps a smaller raise plus an education allowance. Third, invent options for mutual gain before deciding. Finally, insist on objective criteria, such as market prices or expert standards, rather than pure willpower. The authors also introduced the concept of BATNA — your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. If you know what you'll do if the deal fails, you'll be much less likely to accept a bad one. Decades later, these ideas remain central to negotiation training around the world.

questions.q: How did Getting to Yes change the view of negotiation?

grammar.title: Meeting language by function
grammar.explanation_pt:
A linguagem de reuniões é altamente **funcional**: cada momento tem suas frases. Repare em como elas usam estruturas que você já domina (modais, perguntas indiretas, present perfect).

**ABRIR (chair):** "Shall we get started?" / "The **purpose** of today's meeting is to..." / "We have three **items** on the agenda." / "We've got 30 minutes, so let's keep it brief."

**DAR A PALAVRA:** "Ana, **would you like to** start?" / "**What are your thoughts on** this, Leo?" / "**We haven't heard from** Pedro yet."

**INTERROMPER com educação:**
- "**Sorry to interrupt, but**..." / "**Can I just come in here?**" / "**If I could just add something**..."
- Em reuniões online: "**Sorry, go ahead.**" (quando duas pessoas falam juntas)

**MANTER A PALAVRA:** "**If I could just finish** my point..." / "**Just one more thing**..." / "**Bear with me**..."

**DISCORDAR (com hedging do B2-M1!):** "**I see your point, but**..." / "**I'm not sure that would work because**..." / "**Have we considered**...?"

**CONTROLAR O RUMO E O TEMPO:**
- "**I think we're getting off track.** Let's get back to..."
- "**That's a good point, but maybe we could take it offline.**" / "**Let's park that for now.**"
- "**We're running out of time**, so let's move on."

**RESUMIR E DEFINIR AÇÕES (present perfect + will/going to):**
- "**So, to sum up**, we**'ve agreed** to... / we**'ve decided** that..."
- "**Action points:** Ana **will** send the report by Friday; Leo **is going to** contact the client."
- "**Who's going to** follow up on this?" / "**Let's touch base** next week."

What are your thoughts on this? / We haven't heard from...
Sorry to interrupt, but... / Can I just come in here?
If I could just finish... / Just one more thing...
I think we're getting off track. / Let's park that.
We're running out of time. / Let's move on.

grammar.tip_pt: Em reuniões online com estrangeiros, usar o botão **"raise hand"** e dizer "**Could I add something?**" é uma ótima estratégia para quem tem dificuldade de interromper. E sempre termine com **action points** claros: quem faz o quê até quando.

listening.title: Why meetings fail
listening.context_pt: Um consultor de produtividade explica os erros mais comuns em reuniões.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: Surveys suggest that many professionals feel a large share of their meetings are unproductive. Why? In my experience, there are four main reasons. First, there's no clear purpose — people come without knowing what decision needs to be made. Second, the wrong people are invited: too many people, or not the ones who can actually decide. Third, nobody controls the discussion, so the conversation goes off track and the loudest voices dominate. And fourth — the most common — the meeting ends without clear action points. Everyone leaves thinking someone else will do the work. My rule is simple: no agenda, no meeting. And no meeting should end without three answers: what have we decided, who will do what, and by when.

questions.q: What is the first reason meetings fail?
questions.answer: There's no clear purpose.

questions.q: What problem is there with the people invited?
questions.answer: Too many people, or not the ones who can decide.

questions.q: What happens when nobody controls the discussion?
