reading.title: The silent participants
reading.text: In multinational companies, managers often notice a pattern: some team members — frequently non-native speakers — rarely speak up in meetings, even when they have excellent ideas. Research on international teams points to several reasons. One is language anxiety: the fear of making mistakes in front of colleagues, especially native speakers who talk quickly and use idioms. Another is cultural. In some cultures, interrupting is considered rude, and people wait for a pause that, in a fast-paced meeting, never comes. In others, junior employees are expected not to contradict senior ones publicly. The result is that companies lose valuable perspectives. Some organizations have started to change their meeting culture. Chairs are trained to invite quieter participants directly ("Marta, what's your view?"), agendas are shared in advance so people can prepare, and some meetings use a "round" format where everyone speaks in turn. Native speakers are encouraged to slow down and avoid slang. Non-native speakers, in turn, can benefit from learning a small set of phrases for entering a discussion. Ultimately, the goal is simple: the best idea should win — not the fastest speaker.

questions.q: Who often stays silent in multinational meetings?
questions.answer: Some team members, frequently non-native speakers.

questions.q: What are two reasons for this?
questions.answer: Language anxiety and cultural norms (e.g., interrupting is rude, juniors don't contradict seniors).

questions.q: What changes have some organizations made?
questions.answer: Chairs invite quieter participants, agendas are shared in advance, round formats are used.

questions.q: What is the ultimate goal, according to the text?

grammar.title: Reporting verb patterns
grammar.explanation_pt:
Cada reporting verb tem um (ou mais) **padrão** obrigatório. Aprenda em blocos:

**1. verbo + to + infinitivo:** agree, refuse, offer, promise, threaten, claim, decide
- "The company **refused to comment**." / "He **threatened to resign**."

**2. verbo + objeto + to + infinitivo:** ask, tell, urge, warn, advise, persuade, encourage, remind, invite, beg, order
- "The doctor **advised me to rest**." / "They **persuaded her to stay**." / "Police **warned drivers not to travel**."

**3. verbo + -ing:** deny, admit, suggest, recommend, regret, mention
- "He **denied stealing** the documents." / "She **admitted making** a mistake." / "I **suggest leaving** early."
- Para algo anterior, use **having + particípio**: "He **denied having seen** her."

**4. verbo + (objeto) + preposição + -ing:**
- accuse sb **of**, blame sb **for**, apologize **for**, insist **on**, congratulate sb **on**, thank sb **for**, criticize sb **for**, warn sb **against**
- "They **accused him of lying**." / "She **apologized for being** late." / "He **insisted on paying**."

**5. verbo + that + frase:** say, explain, claim, admit, deny, insist, announce, complain, point out, argue
- "She **insisted that** she was innocent." / "The CEO **announced that** the company would close."

⚠️ **Suggest** e **recommend** NÃO aceitam objeto + to: ❌ "He suggested me to go" → ✅ "He **suggested going**" / "He **suggested that I (should) go**".

O **backshift** do B1+ continua valendo quando o verbo introdutório está no passado.

reading.title: The power of a single verb
reading.text: Journalism students are often taught a simple rule: when in doubt, use "said". The reason is that reporting verbs are never neutral. Imagine a politician who makes a statement about the economy. A newspaper could report that she "said", "claimed", "admitted", "insisted" or "boasted" that unemployment had fallen. Each verb sends a different message to the reader. "Claimed" suggests the statement might not be true; "admitted" suggests she was forced to reveal something; "boasted" implies arrogance. Researchers who study media bias have found that the choice of reporting verbs can influence how readers judge the people being quoted, even when the facts are identical. This is one reason why many style guides, such as those of major news agencies, recommend using neutral verbs like "said" in news reports and saving more expressive verbs for when they're clearly justified. As readers, we can protect ourselves by paying attention not only to what people are reported to have said, but also to the verbs journalists choose to report it. Sometimes, a single word tells you more about the writer than about the person being quoted.

LOCAL CAFÉ ACCUSED OF COPYING RECIPE

A popular café in Florianópolis has been accused of copying a famous recipe from a neighbouring bakery.

grammar.title: Passive reporting structures
grammar.explanation_pt:
Usamos estruturas passivas com verbos como **say, believe, think, report, know, expect, consider, estimate, claim** para relatar informações quando a fonte não é importante, é genérica ("as pessoas") ou a informação **não está confirmada**.

**Estrutura 1: It + is/was + particípio + that + frase**
- "**It is said that** the castle is haunted."
- "**It was believed that** the earth was flat."
- "**It is estimated that** 3 million people live there."

**Estrutura 2: Sujeito + is/was + particípio + to + infinitivo** (mais elegante e comum em notícias)
- "The castle **is said to be** haunted."
- "He **is believed to be** the richest man in the country."

**O infinitivo muda conforme o tempo da informação:**
- **to + verbo** → mesmo tempo (presente): "She is said **to live** in Paris." (Dizem que ela mora em Paris)
- **to be + -ing** → ação em andamento agora: "He is thought **to be hiding** in the forest." (Acredita-se que esteja se escondendo)
- **to have + particípio** → ação **anterior**: "The suspect is believed **to have left** the country." (Acredita-se que tenha deixado)
- **to have been + -ing** → ação contínua anterior: "She is reported **to have been working** on a new album."

**Advérbios equivalentes (mais informais):** **allegedly, reportedly, apparently, supposedly**
- "The singer has **reportedly** signed a new contract." / "He **allegedly** stole the car."

**Em português** esses sentidos são "dizem que", "acredita-se que", "supostamente", "segundo relatos".

reading.title: Urban legends
reading.text: Every culture has its urban legends — stories that are passed from person to person and are widely believed to be true, despite little or no evidence. One well-known example is the idea that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space with the naked eye. It was widely repeated in textbooks for decades, but astronauts have said they could not see it. Another is the claim that we only use 10% of our brains, which is often attributed to early psychologists but has been rejected by neuroscientists: brain scans show activity across virtually all regions. In Brazil, many people grew up hearing that mixing mango and milk could be fatal. The belief is thought to have originated during the colonial period, possibly to stop enslaved workers on plantations from drinking the milk produced on the farms. Today, nutritionists confirm that the combination is perfectly safe. Why do such stories survive? Psychologists suggest that legends spread because they are simple, surprising and emotionally engaging — and because once a belief is shared by many people, questioning it feels strange. The lesson? "Everyone knows" is not the same as "it's true".

questions.q: What is an urban legend?
questions.answer: A story passed from person to person and widely believed, with little or no evidence.

questions.answer: They could not see it from space with the naked eye.

questions.q: Where is the mango-and-milk belief thought to have originated?

questions.q: Why do legends survive, according to psychologists?
questions.answer: They're simple, surprising and emotional, and questioning shared beliefs feels strange.

writing.model:
The legend of the Boto: Amazon's mysterious charmer

If you travel along the rivers of the Amazon, you will almost certainly hear about the Boto, the pink river dolphin. According to local legend, the Boto is said to transform into a handsome young man on nights of celebration, especially during the June festivals.

Dressed in white and always wearing a hat — which is believed to hide the breathing hole on top of his head — he is said to charm the most beautiful women at the party. Before dawn, he allegedly returns to the river, leaving behind broken hearts and, sometimes, a baby.

The legend is thought to have originated among Indigenous communities and is known to have spread widely in the region. Historians suggest that, in the past, the story may have been used to explain pregnancies outside marriage.

Today, the pink dolphins are reported to be endangered, and it is estimated that their population has fallen significantly in recent decades. Conservation groups are urging tourists to observe them only with licensed guides.

So, if a mysterious man in a white hat asks you to dance in Belém, you've been warned!

Por isso, uma notícia que diz "the thief" antes do julgamento pode ser considerada problemática.

grammar.title: Emphasis and rhetoric
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Cleft sentences com What** → destacam uma informação colocando-a no fim:
- Normal: "I love the design." → Ênfase: "**What I love is** the design."
- "**What we need is** more time." / "**What worries me is** the cost."
- Com ações: "**What I did was** (to) call the manager." / "**What you should do is** talk to her."
- Variações: **All I want is**... (tudo o que eu quero é) / **The thing (that) I like is**... / **The reason (why)**... / **The place where**...

**2. Cleft sentences com It** → destacam **quem / o quê / quando / onde**:
- "Ana broke the record." → "**It was Ana who** broke the record." (foi a Ana, não outra pessoa)
- "**It was in 2015 that** everything changed." / "**It's not the price that** bothers me — **it's** the quality."

**3. Do / does / did enfático** → reforça uma afirmação (muitas vezes em contraste):
- "I **do** like your idea — I just think it's expensive."
- "She **did** call you; you just didn't hear the phone."
- Em imperativos (educado e caloroso): "**Do** come in!" / "**Do** let me know."

**4. Recursos retóricos:**
- **Regra de três:** "It's faster, cheaper and greener."
- **Perguntas retóricas:** "Who doesn't want more free time?"
- **Contraste/antítese:** "It's not about working harder; it's about working smarter."
- **Repetição:** "We will try. We will fail. We will try again."
- **Inversão com Never / Not only** (formal, enfática): "**Never have I** seen such talent." / "**Not only is it** cheaper, **but it's** also faster."

rows: What I need is a holiday.
What annoys me is the noise.
My mother taught me to cook.
It was my mother who taught me to cook.
Not only is it cheap, but it's also fast.
I've never seen anything like it.
Never have I seen anything like it.

examples.en: What makes this app different is that it learns from your habits.
examples.pt: O que torna este app diferente é que ele aprende com seus hábitos.

examples.en: It wasn't the money that convinced me — it was the team.
examples.pt: Não foi o dinheiro que me convenceu — foi a equipe.

examples.en: I do appreciate your help; I just need a bit more time to decide.
examples.pt: Eu realmente agradeço sua ajuda; só preciso de um pouco mais de tempo para decidir.

grammar.tip_pt: Cleft sentences são ótimas em **apresentações e entrevistas**: "**What I'd like to talk about today is**..." / "**The reason why** I applied for this job **is**..." / "**What I'm most proud of is**..." Elas dão tempo para pensar e criam expectativa.

common_mistakes.wrong: What I need it's a holiday.
common_mistakes.right: What I need is a holiday.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Não acrescente it: What + sujeito + verbo + is...

common_mistakes.wrong: Was my mother who taught me.
common_mistakes.right: It was my mother who taught me.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A cleft sentence com It precisa do sujeito it.

common_mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen this.
common_mistakes.right: Never have I seen this. / I have never seen this.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Com never no início, há inversão (auxiliar + sujeito).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em cleft sentences, a voz faz uma pequena **pausa depois de "is"** e **acentua** a informação final: "What I **need**... is a **HOLIDAY**." Com o do enfático, o auxiliar é **forte**: "I **DO** like it!" (normalmente seria fraco).
practice: What I need... is a HOLIDAY.

lines.speaker: Mentor

listening.title: Analyzing a famous ad
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de marketing analisa as técnicas de um anúncio inventado de carro elétrico.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: Let's look at this electric car ad. It opens with a rhetorical question: "What if your car could make the world cleaner?" That's an emotional appeal. Then we hear the rule of three: "Silent. Smart. Sustainable." Notice the alliteration too — three words starting with S. Next comes a contrast: "It's not just a car. It's a statement." And finally, the call to action: "The future is waiting. Don't keep it waiting." What makes the ad effective isn't the technical information — there's almost none. It's the feeling. That's the key lesson of persuasion: people decide emotionally and justify their decision logically afterwards.

reading.title: Ethos, pathos, logos
reading.text: More than two thousand years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three ways to persuade an audience. Remarkably, his framework is still taught in business schools, law faculties and marketing courses today. The first is ethos: credibility. We're more likely to be persuaded by someone we trust or respect — which is why advertisers use doctors, athletes and celebrities, and why speakers often begin by explaining their experience. The second is pathos: emotion. Stories, images and music can make an audience feel joy, fear, anger or hope. It is pathos that makes a charity advert with a single child's face so much more powerful than a list of statistics. The third is logos: logic. This includes facts, data, examples and clear reasoning. What effective persuaders do is combine all three. A strong pitch might begin with a personal story (pathos), present data showing the size of the problem (logos), and mention the speaker's expertise or a respected partner (ethos). Of course, the same techniques can be used to manipulate. What distinguishes persuasion from manipulation is honesty: persuasion helps people make a decision with full information, while manipulation tries to hide it. Understanding these techniques, then, is not only useful for persuading others — it's essential for protecting ourselves.

questions.q: What is ethos?
questions.answer: Credibility (trusting or respecting the speaker).

questions.q: Why is a charity advert with a child's face so powerful?
questions.answer: Because of pathos — emotion is more powerful than statistics.

questions.q: How might a strong pitch combine all three?
questions.answer: Personal story (pathos), data (logos), expertise or respected partner (ethos).

questions.q: What distinguishes persuasion from manipulation?
questions.answer: Honesty — persuasion gives full information; manipulation hides it.

writing.model:
Why our city needs more bike lanes

Who here has spent more than an hour in traffic this week? Almost everyone, I imagine. I'm a doctor, and every day I see the consequences of the way we move around this city: stress, back pain, respiratory problems.

What many people don't realize is that the solution is surprisingly simple. Cities that have invested in safe bike lanes — like Bogotá, Copenhagen and, closer to home, Fortaleza — have seen traffic fall, air quality improve and residents become healthier. Not only are bikes cheaper than cars, but they also take up a fraction of the space.

It was a patient of mine who changed my mind about cycling. Five years ago, she was overweight, stressed and taking medication for blood pressure. Then she started cycling to work. Today, she no longer needs the medication. What she told me last month stayed with me: "I don't feel like I'm commuting anymore. I feel free."

I do understand the concerns. Our streets aren't safe for cyclists — yet. But that's exactly the point. What we need isn't more courage from cyclists; it's more courage from our leaders.

So here's my request: sign the petition, come to the council meeting on Thursday, and, if you can, try cycling to work once this month. Healthier people. Cleaner air. A better city. Let's build it together.

warmup.text_pt: Debater bem não é falar mais alto — é **estruturar** argumentos, **reconhecer** o lado do outro e **refutar** com evidências. Hoje você vai juntar tudo deste módulo (reporting verbs, hedging, ênfase) num debate formal em inglês.

What's a topic you've changed your mind about?

chunks.en: Admittedly, there are some risks. However, ...

grammar.title: Language for debating
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Estruturar um argumento (PEEL / PRE):** **P**oint (ponto) → **R**eason (razão) → **E**xample/**E**vidence (exemplo/evidência) → **L**ink (volta ao tema)
"**Firstly**, a four-day week **would** improve productivity. **This is because** rested workers make fewer mistakes. **For instance**, a large trial in the UK found that... **Therefore**, ..."

**2. Sequenciar:** Firstly / First of all → Secondly / Furthermore / Moreover / In addition → Finally / Last but not least

**3. Conceder (reconhecer o outro lado) + contra-argumentar:**
- "**Admittedly**, ... **However**, ..." / "**It's true that**..., **but**..."
- "**While** it's true that..., we **must** also consider..." / "**Granted**, ... **Nevertheless**, ..."
- "**Even if** that were true, ..." (second conditional — hipótese para enfraquecer o argumento)

**4. Refutar com precisão (reporting verbs + hedging!):**
- "**My opponent claims that**..., **but** the evidence suggests otherwise."
- "**That argument overlooks** / **fails to take into account**..."
- "**That's an oversimplification.**" / "**That doesn't necessarily follow.**"
- "**I'd question** the idea that..."

**5. Concluir:** "**To sum up** / **In conclusion** / **All things considered** / **On balance**, we firmly believe that..."

**Falácias comuns para evitar e identificar:** **ad hominem** (atacar a pessoa), **straw man** (distorcer o argumento do outro), **slippery slope** ("se X, então inevitavelmente Z"), **false dilemma** ("ou A ou B", ignorando outras opções).

rows: This is because... / The main reason is...
For instance, ... / A case in point is...
My opponent claims that..., but... / That overlooks...

examples.en: Admittedly, a four-day week might not work for every industry. However, the evidence from several trials is very encouraging.
examples.pt: É verdade que a semana de quatro dias pode não funcionar para todo setor. No entanto, as evidências de vários testes são muito animadoras.

examples.en: My opponent claims that social media connects people, but that argument overlooks the growing evidence of loneliness among teenagers.
examples.pt: Meu oponente alega que as redes sociais conectam as pessoas, mas esse argumento ignora as crescentes evidências de solidão entre adolescentes.

examples.en: Even if online classes were cheaper, they couldn't replace the social experience of school.
examples.pt: Mesmo que as aulas online fossem mais baratas, não poderiam substituir a experiência social da escola.

grammar.tip_pt: Em debates em inglês, **reconhecer** um bom argumento do outro lado ("That's a valid point") **aumenta** sua credibilidade. Quem nunca concede nada parece radical — e perde o público.

common_mistakes.wrong: In the other hand, ...
common_mistakes.right: On the other hand, ...
common_mistakes.why_pt: A expressão é on the other hand.

common_mistakes.wrong: Even if that is true, it would not work.
common_mistakes.right: Even if that were true, it wouldn't work. / Even if that is true, it won't work.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Mantenha a coerência do tipo de condicional.

common_mistakes.wrong: You are stupid if you believe that.
common_mistakes.right: I'd question that idea, because...
common_mistakes.why_pt: Ataque pessoal (ad hominem) é uma falácia e destrói sua credibilidade.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em debates, as palavras de transição (**Firstly**, **However**, **Admittedly**, **In conclusion**) são **seguidas de pausa** e ditas com **ênfase**. Elas funcionam como placas na estrada: ajudam o público e os juízes a acompanhar sua estrutura.
practice: ALL things considered... (pausa) we firmly believe...

dialogue.title: Debate: Should homework be banned?
dialogue.context_pt: Num debate escolar, duas equipes discutem a moção "This house would ban homework in primary schools".

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: The motion is: "This house would ban homework in primary schools." Proposition, you have two minutes.
lines.pt: A moção é: "Esta casa proibiria tarefa de casa no ensino fundamental I." Proposição, vocês têm dois minutos.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: Thank you. Firstly, research suggests that homework has little benefit for young children's learning. Secondly, it takes away time for play, sleep and family. Children need to be children.
lines.pt: Obrigada. Em primeiro lugar, pesquisas sugerem que a tarefa traz pouco benefício para o aprendizado de crianças pequenas. Em segundo lugar, ela tira tempo de brincar, dormir e ficar com a família. Crianças precisam ser crianças.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: Opposition, your response.
lines.pt: Oposição, sua resposta.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.en: Admittedly, too much homework can be stressful. However, banning it completely is an oversimplification. Small amounts of reading at home help build habits and involve parents in their children's education.
lines.pt: É verdade que tarefa demais pode ser estressante. No entanto, proibir completamente é uma simplificação excessiva. Pequenas quantidades de leitura em casa ajudam a criar hábitos e envolvem os pais na educação dos filhos.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: My opponent claims that homework involves parents, but that argument overlooks the fact that many parents work long hours and can't help. Homework actually increases inequality.
lines.pt: Meu oponente alega que a tarefa envolve os pais, mas esse argumento ignora o fato de que muitos pais trabalham muitas horas e não podem ajudar. A tarefa na verdade aumenta a desigualdade.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.en: That's a valid point. But even if some parents can't help, wouldn't it be better to support those families rather than remove the opportunity from everyone?
lines.pt: É um ponto válido. Mas mesmo que alguns pais não possam ajudar, não seria melhor apoiar essas famílias em vez de tirar a oportunidade de todos?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: In conclusion, what young children need most isn't more worksheets — it's time to rest, play and be curious. We urge you to support the motion.
lines.pt: Em conclusão, do que as crianças pequenas mais precisam não é de mais folhas de exercícios — é de tempo para descansar, brincar e ser curiosas. Pedimos que vocês apoiem a moção.

lines.speaker: Theo
lines.en: All things considered, the answer isn't a ban, but better homework: shorter, more meaningful and more flexible. We oppose the motion.
lines.pt: Considerando tudo, a resposta não é uma proibição, mas uma tarefa melhor: mais curta, mais significativa e mais flexível. Somos contra a moção.

listening.title: Debate coach's advice
listening.context_pt: Uma técnica de debate dá conselhos a alunos antes de uma competição.

lines.speaker: Coach
lines.en: Remember three things tomorrow. First, structure. Judges can't give you points for arguments they can't follow, so signpost clearly: "My first point is...", "My second point is...". Second, engage with the other side. The worst thing you can do is read a prepared speech and ignore what your opponents have just said. Listen, take notes, and refute their strongest argument, not their weakest. Third, stay calm and respectful. Attacking your opponent personally is a fallacy, and judges will penalize you for it. And one more thing: it's perfectly fine to concede a point. Saying "Admittedly, that's true, but..." shows confidence, not weakness. The best debaters aren't the loudest — they're the clearest.

reading.title: The four-day week: does it work?
reading.text: In recent years, the idea of a four-day working week — with no reduction in pay — has moved from the fringes to the mainstream. Supporters argue that it improves employees' well-being, reduces burnout and can even increase productivity. They point to a large trial in the United Kingdom in 2022, coordinated by the non-profit 4 Day Week Global with researchers from several universities, in which around 60 companies reduced working hours. According to the organizers, the large majority of participating companies chose to continue with the policy after the trial, and many employees reported lower stress and better sleep. Similar pilots have been carried out in countries such as Iceland, Spain and, more recently, Brazil. Critics, however, raise several concerns. Admittedly, the results look impressive, but the companies that volunteered for trials may not be representative: they were probably already open to flexible work. Furthermore, a four-day week may be much harder to implement in sectors like healthcare, education or retail, where someone must be present at all times. Some economists also question whether productivity gains can be sustained in the long term. On balance, the evidence so far suggests that the four-day week can work well in some contexts — but it is unlikely to be a universal solution.

questions.answer: It improves well-being, reduces burnout and can increase productivity.

questions.q: What is the writer's conclusion?

writing.model:
Should social media be banned for children under 16?

In recent years, several governments have proposed restricting social media for teenagers. While the idea has strong support, it also raises important questions.

Those in favour argue that a ban would protect young people's mental health. Firstly, studies have linked heavy social media use to anxiety, poor sleep and low self-esteem among teenagers. Secondly, platforms are designed to be addictive, and it is unreasonable to expect a 13-year-old to resist techniques created by expert engineers. For instance, endless scrolling and constant notifications make it extremely difficult to stop. Therefore, supporters believe the responsibility should not fall on children alone.

On the other hand, critics point out that a ban may be impossible to enforce. Admittedly, age-verification technology is improving; however, many teenagers would probably find ways around it. Furthermore, social media also has benefits: young people use it to stay in touch with friends, find communities and learn new skills. A complete ban, critics argue, could isolate those who rely on online support, such as LGBTQ+ teenagers in conservative environments.

All things considered, I believe that the risks are serious enough to justify stronger regulation, but that a total ban is an oversimplification. What we need is a combination of measures: stricter rules for platforms, better age verification, and digital education in schools. Even if a ban were possible, it would not teach young people how to use technology wisely — and that is a skill they will need for the rest of their lives.

grammar.title: Third conditional
grammar.explanation_pt:
O **third conditional** fala de situações **imaginárias no passado** — algo que **não aconteceu** e sua consequência também imaginária.

**Estrutura: If + past perfect, would have + particípio**
- "If I **had studied** harder, I **would have passed** the exam." (Não estudei → não passei)
- "If she **hadn't missed** the bus, they **wouldn't have met**." (Ela perdeu → eles se conheceram)

**Contrações na fala (muito importantes):**
- **I'd** = I had (na parte do if) / I would (na consequência): "If **I'd** known, **I'd** have called."
- **would have** → **would've** ("uúdav"); **wouldn't have** → **wouldn't've**

**Outros modais na consequência:**
- **could have + pp** = poderia ter (possibilidade/habilidade): "If we'd left earlier, we **could have caught** the train."
- **might have + pp** = talvez tivesse: "If you'd asked, she **might have said** yes."

**Perguntas:** "What **would** you **have done** if you **had lost** your passport?"

**A ordem pode inverter** (sem vírgula): "I would have helped **if** you'd asked me."

**Inversão formal (sem if):** "**Had I known**, I would have come." (= If I had known) — comum em textos formais e no B2 First.

⚠️ **Nunca** use "would have" na oração com if: ❌ "If I would have known..."

rows: I didn't study, so I failed.
If I had studied, I would have passed.
It rained, so we cancelled the trip.
If it hadn't rained, we wouldn't have cancelled the trip.
I didn't know, so I didn't help.
If I'd known, I could have helped.
She took the job in Lisbon and met her husband.
If she hadn't taken the job, she might not have met him.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português, na fala, muitas vezes dizemos "se eu **soubesse**, eu **tinha** te contado" para o passado. Em inglês, use sempre a estrutura completa: **If I had known, I would have told you.**

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have come.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Na oração com if, use past perfect (had + pp).

common_mistakes.why_pt: Consequência = would have + particípio.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Hipótese sobre o passado = past perfect.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Nativos quase nunca dizem "would have" por extenso: **would've** = "**uúdav**", **could've** = "**kúdav**", **wouldn't have** = "**uúdentav**". E "If I'd known, I'd have..." = "if áid nôun, áidav...". Treine o ouvido — e use na fala.

reading.title: History's great "what ifs"
reading.text: Historians are often cautious about "counterfactual" questions — imagining what would have happened if events had been different — but these questions can help us understand how fragile history really is. Consider the discovery of penicillin. In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mould had contaminated one of his bacterial cultures — and that the bacteria around the mould had died. If he had cleaned his laboratory before leaving, or if the mould had landed on a different plate, he might never have noticed the effect. Penicillin, and the antibiotics that followed, have since saved millions of lives. Or take the Post-it note, which we saw in an earlier unit: if Spencer Silver hadn't "failed" to make a strong glue, one of the world's most famous office products would not have been invented. Of course, history is rarely shaped by a single moment. Had Fleming not noticed the mould, someone else might eventually have discovered penicillin. Still, these stories remind us that chance, curiosity and the ability to notice the unexpected have played a much larger role in human progress than we usually admit.

writing.model:
The email I almost didn't send

In 2019, I was working as an accountant in a job I didn't enjoy. One evening, I saw an online advert for a course in graphic design. The deadline for applications was midnight, and it was already eleven o'clock. I was tired, and I almost closed the laptop.

If I had gone to bed that night, my life would have been completely different. I would probably still be working in accounting, and I might never have discovered how much I love design. I wouldn't have met Lucas, my teacher on the course, who later offered me my first freelance project. And if he hadn't recommended me to his clients, I couldn't have built my own studio, which now has four employees.

Of course, things could have gone wrong. If the course had been terrible, I might have lost money and confidence. Had my family not supported me, I would never have had the courage to quit my stable job.

With hindsight, I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I'd made the change earlier. But I don't really regret the years in accounting: they taught me how to manage a business. Sometimes, the turning point isn't a big event. It's an email you send at 11:57 p.m.

grammar.title: Mixed conditionals
grammar.explanation_pt:
Os condicionais "puros" mantêm o mesmo tempo nas duas partes. Mas a vida real mistura tempos! Os **mixed conditionals** combinam partes do **second** e do **third** conditional.

**Tipo 1: condição no PASSADO → resultado no PRESENTE**
**If + past perfect, would + verbo base (now)**
- "If I **had accepted** the job in Canada, I **would be living** there **now**." (não aceitei → não moro lá hoje)
- "If she **hadn't studied** medicine, she **wouldn't be** a doctor today."
- "If we **had saved** more, we **wouldn't have** these money problems **now**."

**Tipo 2: característica PRESENTE (permanente) → resultado no PASSADO**
**If + past simple, would have + particípio**
- "If I **were** more confident, I **would have spoken** in the meeting yesterday." (não sou confiante → não falei)
- "If he **didn't have** a fear of flying, he **would have come** to the wedding."
- "If I **spoke** French, I **would have understood** the film."

**Como escolher?** Pergunte-se: **quando** é a condição? **Quando** é o resultado?
- passado → passado = **third** (If I'd known, I'd have come)
- presente/geral → presente/futuro = **second** (If I knew, I'd come)
- passado → presente = **mixed tipo 1** (If I'd known, I'd be there now)
- presente → passado = **mixed tipo 2** (If I knew him, I'd have invited him)

**Palavras-pista:** now, today, still (presente) / yesterday, last year, in 2015 (passado).

rows: If I had money, I'd travel.
If I'd had money, I'd have travelled.
If I'd saved money, I'd be travelling now.

examples.en: If she were more organized, she wouldn't have missed the deadline.
examples.pt: Se ela fosse mais organizada, não teria perdido o prazo.

examples.pt: Se tivéssemos comprado aquele apartamento em 2015, ele valeria o dobro agora.

grammar.tip_pt: Mixed conditionals são muito comuns na **fala natural** — muitas vezes até mais que os puros. Ouvir "If I'd known, I wouldn't be here" num filme é muito frequente!

common_mistakes.wrong: If I had taken the job, I would have lived in Lisbon now.
common_mistakes.right: If I had taken the job, I would be living in Lisbon now.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Resultado no presente (now) = would + verbo base.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I was more patient, I wouldn't shout at him yesterday.
common_mistakes.right: If I were more patient, I wouldn't have shouted at him yesterday.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Resultado no passado (yesterday) = would have + particípio.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would have studied, I would be a doctor.
common_mistakes.right: If I had studied, I would be a doctor.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Nunca would na oração com if.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em mixed conditionals, os marcadores de tempo (**now**, **today**, **yesterday**, **back then**) costumam receber ênfase, porque são eles que mostram a mistura: "If I'd taken the job... I'd be living in Lisbon **NOW**."

reading.title: The road not taken
reading.text: "Two roads diverged in a wood, and I — / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." These lines from Robert Frost's 1916 poem "The Road Not Taken" are among the most quoted in American literature, often printed on posters encouraging people to be brave and different. Yet many literary critics argue that the poem is widely misunderstood. Earlier in the poem, Frost actually describes the two roads as being worn "really about the same". The traveller only imagines that, years later, he will tell the story as if his choice had been dramatic and meaningful. In other words, the poem may be less about bravery and more about how we construct stories about our decisions after the fact. Psychologists have found something similar: we tend to justify our choices once they are made, convincing ourselves that the path we took was the right one. If we had chosen differently, we would probably be just as good at explaining why that choice was the best. Perhaps that's not a bad thing. If we didn't have this ability, we might spend our lives tormented by the roads we didn't take.

questions.q: How are Frost's lines usually interpreted?
questions.answer: As encouraging people to be brave and different.

questions.answer: Frost describes the two roads as being about the same; the traveller only imagines telling it as dramatic later.

questions.q: What have psychologists found about our choices?

writing.model:
Is it better to regret what you did, or what you didn't do?

A famous saying claims that we regret the things we didn't do more than the things we did. Research by psychologists has offered some support for this idea: in the short term, people tend to regret their mistakes, but over a lifetime, they regret their missed opportunities more.

My own experience supports this view. When I was 22, I was offered a scholarship to study in Germany, but I turned it down because I was afraid of leaving my family. If I had accepted it, I would probably speak German fluently now, and I might be working in a completely different field. If I weren't so attached to my home, I would have taken that chance without hesitation. Even today, I sometimes wonder what might have been.

On the other hand, my brother took a risk that went wrong. He invested in a restaurant that closed after a year. If he hadn't opened it, he would have saved a lot of money. Yet he insists he has no regrets. If he hadn't tried, he says, he would still be dreaming about it today instead of having learned so much about business. Had he not failed, he wouldn't have started the successful catering company he runs now.

In my opinion, regrets about actions usually teach us something, while regrets about inaction stay with us as unanswered questions. Therefore, I believe it is generally better to take reasonable risks than to play it safe forever.

grammar.title: Wish, if only, it's time, would rather
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Wish / If only + past simple** → desejo sobre o **presente** (revisão):
"I **wish** I **had** more free time." / "**If only** I **were** taller!"

**2. Wish / If only + past perfect** → arrependimento sobre o **passado**:
- "I **wish** I **had studied** harder at school." (não estudei — me arrependo)
- "**If only** I **hadn't said** that!"
- "She **wishes** she **had taken** the job in London."

**3. Wish + would / wouldn't** → **reclamação** sobre o comportamento de **outra pessoa** ou situação que queremos que mude:
- "I **wish** you **would** stop leaving your clothes on the floor!"
- "I **wish** it **would** stop raining."
⚠️ Não use "I wish I would..." (sobre você mesmo, use could: "I wish I **could** stop procrastinating").

**4. It's (high / about) time + sujeito + past simple** → já passou da hora de algo acontecer (crítica/urgência):
- "**It's time** we **went** home." / "**It's high time** the government **did** something about it."
- Também: **It's time to** + verbo (mais neutro): "It's time to go."

**5. Would rather + sujeito + past simple** → preferência sobre o que **outra pessoa** faz:
- "**I'd rather you didn't** smoke here." (prefiro que você não fume — educado!)
- "**I'd rather** we **met** tomorrow."
- Compare com **I'd rather + verbo base** (sobre você mesmo): "I'd rather stay home."

**Resumo do "backshift" para irrealidade:** presente → past simple · passado → past perfect.

rows: I wish I lived by the sea.
I wish I hadn't bought that car.
I wish he would call me.
It's time you got a job.

examples.en: I wish I had started investing when I was in my twenties.

grammar.tip_pt: **I'd rather you didn't** é uma forma muito educada de dizer "não faça isso" em inglês: "Do you mind if I open the window?" — "**I'd rather you didn't**, actually. I'm a bit cold."

common_mistakes.why_pt: Arrependimento sobre o passado = past perfect.

common_mistakes.wrong: I wish I would stop eating sugar.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Sobre você mesmo, use could (não would).

common_mistakes.wrong: It's time we go home.
common_mistakes.right: It's time we went home. / It's time to go home.
common_mistakes.why_pt: It's time + sujeito + past simple.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I wish I'd** soa "ái uísh áid" — o 'd é curto, mas essencial (sem ele, a frase vira presente). **I'd rather** = "áid réder". **If only** tem ênfase forte em **ONLY** e entonação emotiva: "If **ONLY** I'd known!"

listening.title: The top five regrets
listening.context_pt: Uma apresentadora fala sobre o livro de uma enfermeira de cuidados paliativos.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Australian palliative care nurse Bronnie Ware spent years caring for people in the last weeks of their lives, and she wrote about the regrets they shared with her. Her list became famous around the world. Many of her patients said: "I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself, not the life others expected of me." Others said: "I wish I hadn't worked so hard." Some told her: "I wish I'd had the courage to express my feelings," and "I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends." And finally: "I wish I had let myself be happier." What's striking is that none of these regrets is about money or possessions. They're all about courage, relationships and choices — things we can still change today.

reading.title: Learning from regret
reading.text: Regret has a bad reputation. We're often told to "live with no regrets" and to avoid dwelling on the past. But some psychologists argue that regret, when handled well, is one of our most useful emotions. In his book The Power of Regret, Daniel Pink describes a large survey in which thousands of people around the world shared their regrets. He identified four core types: foundation regrets ("If only I'd saved more money / looked after my health"), boldness regrets ("I wish I'd asked her out / started that business"), moral regrets ("I wish I hadn't cheated / been unkind") and connection regrets ("I wish I had kept in touch with my brother"). Interestingly, regrets about inaction — the chances we didn't take — tend to last longer than regrets about actions. Pink suggests a three-step method for using regret productively. First, reframe it: talk about it or write it down, which reduces its emotional power. Second, be kind to yourself — treat your past self as you would treat a friend who made a mistake. Third, extract a lesson for the future: "Next time, I'll speak up." Regret, in this view, isn't something to avoid. It's information about what we value most.

questions.q: What are the four core types of regret Pink identified?
questions.answer: Foundation, boldness, moral and connection regrets.

questions.q: Which regrets tend to last longer?
questions.answer: Regrets about inaction (chances not taken).

questions.q: What is the first step of Pink's method?
questions.answer: Reframe it: talk about it or write it down.

questions.q: What does regret tell us, according to this view?
questions.answer: What we value most.

Dear 17-year-old me,

I know you won't listen to everything I'm about to say — I certainly wouldn't have — but I'll try anyway.

First, I wish you had taken English more seriously at school. You thought you'd never need it. If only you'd known that, fifteen years later, you would be using it in meetings every day! You'll learn it eventually, but the hard way, in evening classes after long days at work.

Secondly, I wish you hadn't worried so much about what other people thought. You spent so much energy trying to fit in. I'd rather you spent that energy on the things you actually love: drawing, music, the friends who accept you exactly as you are.

I also wish you had told Grandpa how much he meant to you. He knew, I think — but I wish you'd said it out loud.

Here's the good news: you turn out fine. Better than fine, actually. You find work you enjoy, and people who love you.

So, it's high time you stopped waiting for the "perfect moment" to start things. It doesn't exist. Sign up for the art course. Call your friends. Say "I love you" more often.

And please — start using sunscreen.

With love,
Your older (and slightly wiser) self

grammar.title: Alternatives to if
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Suppose / Supposing / Imagine / What if** → introduzem **cenários hipotéticos** (no lugar de if). Funcionam com qualquer tipo de condicional:
- "**Suppose** you **won** the lottery — what **would** you do?" (second)
- "**Supposing** the flight **is** cancelled, what **will** we do?" (first)
- "**What if** we **had** missed the train?" (third)

**2. Otherwise / Or else** → "se não" — mostram a **consequência negativa** se algo não acontecer:
- "Save your work, **otherwise** you'll lose it." (= If you don't save it, you'll lose it.)
- "Leave now, **or else** you'll miss the bus."
- Também no passado: "I took a taxi; **otherwise** I would have been late."

**3. But for + substantivo** (formal) = "não fosse por" (if it weren't for / if it hadn't been for):
- "**But for** the rain, the festival would have been perfect."
- "**If it hadn't been for** your help, I would have failed."
- "**If it weren't for** my family, I wouldn't be here."

**4. In case** → **precaução** (fazer algo agora por causa de uma possibilidade futura):
- "Take an umbrella **in case** it rains." (leve agora — talvez chova)
- Compare: "Take an umbrella **if** it rains." (só leve se estiver chovendo)
- **In case of** + substantivo (avisos): "**In case of** fire, use the stairs."

**5. Even if** → mesmo que (a condição não muda o resultado): "**Even if** it rains, we'll go."

**6. Revisão B1+/B2:** **unless** (a menos que), **provided / providing (that)**, **as long as**, **on condition that**.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.en: Suppose a major storm hit your city tonight and you lost electricity and water for three days. Would you be ready? Most people wouldn't. Here's what I recommend. Keep at least three days of water and non-perishable food at home, in case of emergencies. Have a power bank fully charged, otherwise you could lose all communication. Keep copies of important documents in a waterproof bag or in the cloud. And agree on a meeting point with your family, in case you can't reach each other by phone. Even if you think it'll never happen to you, it takes only a few hours to prepare. In my experience, but for these simple steps, many families would have suffered much more during recent floods.

reading.title: Thinking in scenarios
reading.text: In the early 1970s, the oil company Shell began using a technique called scenario planning. Instead of trying to predict a single future, its planners imagined several possible futures and asked: "Suppose this happened — how would we respond?" One of the scenarios they explored was a sudden, dramatic rise in oil prices. Most companies considered this unlikely. When the oil crisis of 1973 arrived, Shell was widely seen as being better prepared than many of its competitors, and the company's approach became famous in business schools. Today, scenario planning is used by governments, cities and businesses around the world. The idea is not to guess correctly, but to become more flexible. A city might ask: "What if sea levels rose faster than expected?" or "Supposing a pandemic closed schools for months, how would children learn?" The process often reveals weaknesses that nobody had noticed. Psychologists point out that individuals can benefit from the same thinking. Imagining a worst-case scenario — and planning how you would cope — can actually reduce anxiety, because the future feels less threatening once you have a plan. As the old saying goes: hope for the best, but prepare for the worst.

questions.q: How can it help individuals?

writing.model:
What if...? Be prepared for your first trip abroad!

Travelling abroad for the first time is exciting, but things don't always go as planned. Here's how to be ready for the most common problems.

Supposing you lose your passport, what would you do? Before you leave, take a photo of it and save a copy in the cloud, in case you need to prove your identity at the embassy. Also, write down your country's embassy phone number — your phone might be stolen too!

What if your bank card stops working? Always carry two different cards and some cash, otherwise you could be stuck without money on your first night. Tell your bank you're travelling, or else your card might be blocked for "suspicious activity".

Travel insurance is essential. Even if you're young and healthy, a hospital bill abroad can be extremely expensive. Many travellers have told me that, but for their insurance, an accident would have ruined them financially.

Finally, plan your first day carefully. Book your first night's accommodation in advance, as long as you can cancel it for free, and know how to get there from the airport.

Of course, you can't predict everything. But if you prepare for the worst-case scenario, you'll be able to relax and enjoy the best parts of your adventure. Bon voyage!

culture_note.title: "Hope for the best, prepare for the worst"
culture_note.text_pt: Culturas variam muito na forma de lidar com incerteza. Em equipes internacionais, combinar planejamento e flexibilidade é uma grande vantagem.

grammar.title: Advanced relative clauses
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Preposição + which / whom (formal)**
Na fala, a preposição vai para o final; em textos formais, ela vem **antes** do pronome:
- Informal: "the city (that) I grew up **in**"
- Formal: "the city **in which** I grew up"
- Informal: "the people I work **with**" → Formal: "the people **with whom** I work"
⚠️ Depois de preposição, use **which** (coisas) ou **whom** (pessoas) — **nunca** that ou who: ❌ "in that", ❌ "with who".

**2. Which para comentar a frase inteira** (= o que)
- "Rents have doubled, **which** means many families have had to move."
- "He didn't apologize, **which** I found rude."
Sempre com **vírgula** e sempre **which** (nunca that, nunca what): ❌ "..., what is a problem".

**3. Quantificador + of which / of whom**
**some / many / most / all / none / both / neither / half / one / a few + of which (coisas) / of whom (pessoas)**
- "The city has 30 parks, **most of which** are in rich areas."
- "I have two brothers, **both of whom** live abroad."
- "We received 200 complaints, **none of which** were answered."

**4. Whose** (posse — pessoas **e** coisas)
- "a neighbourhood **whose** residents are fighting gentrification"
- Formal: "the building, the roof **of which** collapsed" (= whose roof)

**5. Where / when / why** em vez de preposição + which:
- "the area **where** I live" (= in which) · "the year **when** the metro opened" · "the reason **why** I left"

**Lembrete:** relative clause **não restritiva** (informação extra) vem entre vírgulas e **não aceita that**.

lines.en: It's Sunday morning on one of the busiest avenues in the city — except that today, there isn't a single car. Since the avenue started closing to traffic on Sundays, it has become a huge open-air park, which attracts thousands of cyclists, skaters, families and street musicians. Bogotá, in Colombia, is often cited as the pioneer of this idea: its weekly Ciclovía, which began in the 1970s, now opens many kilometres of roads to people instead of cars. Not everyone is happy, of course. Some shop owners, most of whom depend on drivers, complain that they lose customers. But surveys in several cities suggest that most residents support the idea, many of whom say it's the only time they feel the city really belongs to them.

questions.answer: It closes to cars and becomes an open-air park.

reading.title: The 15-minute city
reading.text: Imagine a neighbourhood in which you could reach almost everything you need — work, school, shops, a doctor, a park — within a 15-minute walk or bike ride. This is the idea behind the "15-minute city", a concept popularized by the urbanist Carlos Moreno, whose work influenced the plans of Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo. Supporters argue that cities designed around cars have created long commutes, pollution and lonely suburbs, all of which damage our health and quality of life. By bringing services closer to people, the 15-minute city aims to cut emissions, revive local businesses and give residents more free time. Several cities, among which are Melbourne, Barcelona and Bogotá, have experimented with similar ideas. The concept is not without its critics, however. Some point out that in many cities, including those in Brazil, jobs and good services are concentrated in a few central areas, which means that a 15-minute city could easily become a privilege for the rich. Others fear that improving a neighbourhood will push up rents, forcing out the very people for whom the changes were intended. The challenge, then, is not only to design better neighbourhoods, but to ensure that everyone can afford to live in them.

questions.q: What is a 15-minute city?
questions.answer: A neighbourhood where you can reach most things you need within a 15-minute walk or bike ride.

questions.q: What problems do supporters say car-based cities have created?
questions.answer: Long commutes, pollution and lonely suburbs.

questions.q: Why could it become a privilege for the rich in Brazil?
questions.answer: Jobs and good services are concentrated in a few central areas.

questions.q: What risk do others fear?
questions.answer: Rising rents could force out the people the changes were meant to help.

Proposal: Turning the old market square into a community park

Introduction
The purpose of this proposal is to suggest a new use for the old market square in Jardim Esperança, a neighbourhood in which more than 40,000 people live but where there is not a single public park.

The current situation
The square, whose market closed in 2018, is now used as an informal car park. It is poorly lit, which makes many residents, especially women and older people, feel unsafe at night. Local children, most of whom live in small flats, have nowhere safe to play.

grammar.title: Participle clauses
grammar.explanation_pt:
Participle clauses **encurtam** orações quando o **sujeito é o mesmo**. Há três formas:

**1. Present participle (-ing)** → sentido **ativo** / ações simultâneas
- Relative clause reduzida: "People **who live** in cities..." → "People **living** in cities..."
- Tempo: "**While I was walking** home, I saw..." → "**Walking** home, I saw..."
- Causa: "**Because I didn't know** the answer, I stayed quiet." → "**Not knowing** the answer, I stayed quiet."
- Resultado: "The storm hit the coast, **causing** serious damage."

**2. Past participle (-ed / 3ª forma)** → sentido **passivo**
- "The houses **which were built** in the 1950s..." → "The houses **built** in the 1950s..."
- "**Built** in 1960, Brasília was designed by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer."
- "**Asked** about the problem, the mayor refused to comment."

**3. Perfect participle (having + particípio)** → ação **anterior** à principal
- "**After she had finished** university, she moved to Lisbon." → "**Having finished** university, she moved to Lisbon."
- Passiva: "**Having been** rejected twice, he finally got the job."

**Negativa:** **not** antes do particípio: "**Not having** a car, I take the bus."

⚠️ **Dangling participle (erro clássico):** o sujeito da participle clause **tem que ser** o mesmo da oração principal.
❌ "**Walking** down the street, the rain started." (a chuva estava andando?)
✅ "**Walking** down the street, **I** got caught in the rain."

listening.title: Brazil is getting older
listening.context_pt: Uma demógrafa explica, num podcast, o envelhecimento da população brasileira.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Brazil is undergoing one of the fastest demographic transitions in the world. Having had one of the youngest populations in the 1970s, the country is now ageing rapidly. Two trends explain this. First, the birth rate has fallen dramatically: Brazilian women today have, on average, fewer than two children, compared with around six in the 1960s. Second, life expectancy has increased considerably, thanks to better healthcare and sanitation. The result is a population growing older faster than in many European countries, which took much longer to go through the same change. Faced with this situation, the country will need to rethink its pension system, its healthcare services and even the way its cities are designed. Having said that, an older population also brings opportunities, from new businesses to a more experienced workforce.

reading.title: The remote work revolution
reading.text: Before 2020, remote work was a privilege enjoyed by a small minority of workers. Then, almost overnight, the COVID-19 pandemic forced millions of office employees to work from their kitchens and living rooms. Having been told for years that remote work was impossible, many companies discovered that it worked surprisingly well. Freed from long commutes, employees gained hours of free time each week. Some left expensive capital cities altogether, moving to smaller towns or the coast and taking their salaries with them. Several countries, including Portugal and Costa Rica, began offering special visas designed to attract "digital nomads". Not everyone has benefited equally, however. Jobs requiring physical presence — in hospitals, shops, factories and construction — cannot be done from home, which means that remote work has, in some ways, increased the gap between different groups of workers. Managers, too, have expressed concerns, arguing that teams working only online lose creativity and that young employees miss out on learning from experienced colleagues. Having experimented with every possible model, many organizations have now settled on a hybrid approach. Having said that, the debate is far from over.

writing.model:
How my generation is different

Born in the early 1990s, my parents' generation grew up in a very different Brazil. Having lived through years of high inflation, they learned to save every penny and to value job security above everything else. My father, having worked for the same company for 32 years, still finds it strange that I've had four jobs in eight years.

My generation, raised with the internet, sees the world differently. Connected to people all over the planet, we tend to be more open to new ideas, cultures and ways of living. Many of my friends, not wanting to spend three hours a day in traffic, have chosen jobs that allow them to work remotely. Others, inspired by influencers and entrepreneurs, have started their own businesses.

We also talk more openly about topics that our parents rarely mentioned, such as mental health, gender equality and the environment. Asked about therapy, my mother once told me that "in my time, we just got on with life". My friends, on the other hand, see therapy as something completely normal.

Having said that, our generation has its own problems. Faced with high rents and unstable jobs, many of us still live with our parents well into our thirties. And, having grown up with smartphones, we often find it difficult to switch off.

In the end, every generation is shaped by the world in which it grows up. Perhaps the most important thing is to keep listening to each other.

grammar.title: Contrast and concession linkers
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Although / Even though / Though + oração** (sujeito + verbo)
- "**Although** the city is rich, many people live in poverty."
- **Even though** = mais enfático ("mesmo que, ainda que"): "**Even though** he earns a lot, he never saves."
- **Though** = mais informal; também no fim da frase: "It's expensive. I love it, **though**."

**2. Despite / In spite of + substantivo ou -ing** (sem sujeito + verbo!)
- "**Despite** the rain, we went out." / "**In spite of** being tired, she kept working."
- Para usar uma oração: **despite the fact that** + oração: "**Despite the fact that** it was raining, we went out."
- ⚠️ ❌ "despite **of**" — não existe. ❌ "Despite it was raining".

**3. Whereas / While** → **contraste direto** entre duas coisas (comparação):
- "Rich families have fast internet at home, **whereas** many poor families rely on mobile data."
- "**While** some see AI as a threat, others see it as an opportunity."

**4. However / Nevertheless / On the other hand** → ligam **duas frases** (vêm depois de ponto ou ponto e vírgula, seguidos de vírgula):
- "The internet has created opportunities. **However**, not everyone can access them."
- **Nevertheless / Nonetheless** (formal) = "mesmo assim": "The project was expensive. **Nevertheless**, it was a success."
- **On the other hand** → apresenta o outro lado de um argumento: "On the one hand, ... **On the other hand**, ..."
- **Yet** (formal, = but): "simple **yet** effective"

⚠️ **However não liga duas orações com vírgula** como "but": ❌ "It's cheap, however it's bad." ✅ "It's cheap. However, it's bad." / "It's cheap; however, it's bad."

listening.title: The digital divide

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: When people hear that most Brazilians are now online, they often assume the digital divide has disappeared. However, the reality is more complex. Although the majority of the population uses the internet, many low-income users rely only on a mobile phone with a limited data plan, whereas wealthier families usually have fast broadband and several devices at home. This difference matters. Doing homework, applying for a job or taking an online course on a small phone screen is much harder. During the pandemic, when classes moved online, many children were left behind despite their schools' efforts. Nevertheless, there is some good news: public Wi-Fi programmes and community centres are helping to narrow the gap. Connection is no longer the only issue, though. Digital skills are just as important.

reading.title: Will AI make us more equal?
reading.text: Artificial intelligence has been described as the most important technology of our time. Yet economists disagree sharply about whether it will reduce or increase inequality. On the one hand, optimists argue that AI tools could empower people who have traditionally been left behind. A small farmer can now get advice about crops in her own language, while a student without access to private tutors can ask a chatbot to explain a difficult maths problem. Although these tools are not perfect, they are often free or cheap. On the other hand, pessimists point out that previous waves of technology tended to benefit those who already had capital and education. Despite creating new jobs, automation has often replaced routine tasks performed by lower-paid workers, whereas highly skilled professionals have seen their productivity — and salaries — increase. There is also the question of who owns the technology: a handful of large companies, most of which are based in the United States and China. In spite of these concerns, most experts agree on one point: the outcome is not inevitable. Whether AI narrows or widens the gap will depend largely on political choices, including investment in education, regulation and public access to digital tools.

writing.model:
Has technology reduced inequality?

On the one hand, technology has opened doors for millions of people. Although many Brazilians still cannot afford a computer, most now have a smartphone, which gives them access to free courses, banking apps and job opportunities. Instant payment systems, for instance, have made it much easier for small businesses and informal workers to receive money, whereas in the past many of them had no bank account at all. Despite its limitations, a phone with an internet connection can be a powerful tool for learning and earning.

On the other hand, technology has also created new forms of inequality. While wealthy families have fast broadband and several devices, many poor families share one phone with a limited data plan. During the pandemic, this difference meant that some children kept learning, whereas others were left behind. Furthermore, automation is replacing routine jobs, yet the new jobs being created usually require skills that low-income workers have had little opportunity to develop.

In my opinion, technology itself is neither good nor bad; it is a double-edged sword. It has certainly reduced some inequalities. Nevertheless, without public investment in internet access and digital education, it may end up widening the gap rather than narrowing it.

warmup.text_pt: Na prova **B2 First (Cambridge)**, a Parte 1 da escrita é sempre um **essay** de 140–190 palavras. No IELTS, é a Task 2 (mínimo de 250). Em qualquer caso, a nota depende não só da gramática, mas da **organização** e dos **conectores**. Hoje você aprende a estrutura que funciona.

grammar.title: Essay structure and formal linkers
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Estrutura clássica (4 parágrafos):**

**1. Introdução** — apresente o tema com uma frase geral e mostre do que o texto vai tratar. Não dê sua opinião completa ainda (ou dê de forma breve, se a pergunta pedir).
"It is often said that university should be free for everyone. This essay will examine both sides of this question."

**2. Parágrafo 1** — **topic sentence** + argumento + exemplo/explicação.
"**Firstly**, free education would increase social mobility. **For instance**, ..."

**3. Parágrafo 2** — outro argumento **ou** o lado oposto.
"**On the other hand**, it could be argued that... **As a result**, ..."

**4. Conclusão** — resuma e dê sua opinião clara. Não traga ideias novas.
"**In conclusion**, **all things considered**, I believe that..."

**Linking words por função:**
- **Adicionar:** furthermore, moreover, in addition, what is more, not only... but also
- **Exemplificar:** for example, for instance, such as, a good example of this is
- **Causa:** because of, due to, owing to, since, as
- **Efeito:** as a result, consequently, therefore, thus, which means that
- **Contraste:** however, nevertheless, on the other hand, although, despite
- **Opinião:** in my view, from my point of view, I firmly believe that, it seems to me that
- **Concluir:** in conclusion, to sum up, all things considered, overall

**Linguagem impessoal** (soa acadêmica e objetiva):
- **It is often argued / claimed / believed that...**
- **There is no doubt that...** / **It is undeniable that...**
- Evite contrações (don't → do not), gírias e frases muito curtas em sequência.

**Dica de ouro:** **não exagere** nos conectores! Um por frase, no máximo — e use variedade.

For instance, For example, such as
due to, owing to, because of, since

In conclusion, To sum up, All things considered

dialogue.title: Essay feedback
dialogue.context_pt: Uma professora dá feedback para um aluno sobre a redação dele.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Your ideas are really good, Lucas. The problem is the organization. Your introduction is half a page long!
lines.pt: Suas ideias são muito boas, Lucas. O problema é a organização. Sua introdução tem meia página!

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.en: I wanted to explain the whole context first.
lines.pt: Eu quis explicar todo o contexto primeiro.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: I understand, but in a B2 essay, the introduction should be just two or three sentences: introduce the topic and say what you'll discuss.
lines.pt: Entendo, mas num essay B2, a introdução deve ter só duas ou três frases: apresentar o tema e dizer o que você vai discutir.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.en: OK. What about the main paragraphs?
lines.pt: OK. E os parágrafos principais?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Start each one with a clear topic sentence. Here, for instance, you start with an example, so the reader doesn't know what your argument is until the end.
lines.pt: Comece cada um com uma topic sentence clara. Aqui, por exemplo, você começa com um exemplo, então o leitor só entende seu argumento no final.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.en: Right. And the linking words? I used "moreover" a lot.
lines.pt: Certo. E os conectores? Usei muito "moreover".

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Six times, actually! Try to vary them: in addition, what is more, furthermore. And avoid contractions — it's a formal text.
lines.pt: Seis vezes, na verdade! Tente variar: in addition, what is more, furthermore. E evite contrações — é um texto formal.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.en: Got it. So: short introduction, topic sentences, varied linkers, no contractions, and a clear conclusion.
lines.pt: Entendi. Então: introdução curta, topic sentences, conectores variados, sem contrações e uma conclusão clara.

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Exactly. All things considered, it's a very promising essay.
lines.pt: Exatamente. Considerando tudo, é uma redação muito promissora.

listening.title: How examiners mark your essay
listening.context_pt: Uma examinadora explica os critérios de correção de redação em provas de nível B2.

lines.speaker: Examiner
lines.en: Many students think the most important thing in an essay is grammar. In fact, in the Cambridge B2 First, your writing is assessed on four criteria. First, content: have you answered the question and included all the required points? Second, communicative achievement: is the style appropriate — formal, in the case of an essay — and does your text hold the reader's attention? Third, organization: are your ideas logically connected, with clear paragraphs and a good variety of linking words? And finally, language: how wide and accurate is your vocabulary and grammar? So, as you can see, grammar is only one part. A text with a few small mistakes but excellent organization will often score better than a perfect text that doesn't answer the question. My advice? Spend five minutes planning before you write. It makes a huge difference.

questions.q: How many criteria are used to assess writing in B2 First?
questions.answer: Four.

questions.q: What does "content" mean?
questions.answer: Answering the question and including all required points.

questions.q: What does "organization" include?
questions.answer: Logical connection, clear paragraphs and varied linking words.

questions.q: What is the examiner's advice?
questions.answer: Spend five minutes planning before you write.

reading.title: Model essay: Should university education be free?
reading.text:
In many countries, including Brazil, the cost of higher education is a controversial issue. While public universities offer free courses, places are limited and highly competitive. This essay will consider whether university education should be free for everyone.

There are strong arguments in favour of free higher education. Firstly, it can increase social mobility. When students do not have to pay fees, talented young people from low-income families have a real chance of entering professions such as medicine or engineering. Furthermore, a more educated population tends to benefit the whole economy, as graduates generally earn more and contribute more in taxes.

On the other hand, it could be argued that free education is not truly free, since it is paid for by all taxpayers, including those who never go to university. In addition, if universities receive too little funding, the quality of teaching may suffer. As a result, some experts suggest alternatives, such as income-based loans, where graduates repay their fees only when they earn above a certain salary.

In conclusion, all things considered, I believe that higher education should remain free at public universities, as it is one of the most effective ways of reducing inequality. However, governments must ensure that it is adequately funded and that access is fair for students from all backgrounds.

questions.q: What does the introduction do?
questions.answer: Introduces the topic and says what the essay will consider.

questions.q: What are the two arguments in favour?
questions.answer: It increases social mobility and benefits the economy.

questions.q: What alternative do some experts suggest?
questions.answer: Income-based loans, repaid only above a certain salary.

questions.q: What is the writer's final opinion?
questions.answer: Public university education should remain free but be adequately funded and fair.

writing.task: Write a B2 First–style essay (140–190 words) answering this question: "Some people think that all students should learn to code at school. Do you agree?" writing.model:
Should all students learn to code at school?

Technology plays a central role in almost every area of modern life. As a result, many people believe that coding should be a compulsory subject at school. This essay will consider whether this is a good idea.

Firstly, digital skills are increasingly valued in the job market. Even professions that are not directly related to technology, such as marketing or medicine, now require people who understand how software works. Furthermore, learning to code develops problem-solving skills, as students must break complex problems into smaller steps and test different solutions.

On the other hand, it could be argued that the school timetable is already full. If coding is added, other important subjects, such as art or physical education, may be reduced. In addition, many schools lack computers and trained teachers.

In conclusion, I believe that all students should have the opportunity to learn basic coding. However, it should be introduced gradually and combined with other subjects rather than replacing them.

Os textos em inglês também costumam ser mais **diretos**: frases mais curtas e uma ideia por parágrafo.

grammar.title: Past modals
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Needn't have + pp** x **didn't need to + verbo**
- **needn't have done** = você **fez**, mas **não era necessário** (esforço desperdiçado):
"You **needn't have brought** a cake — we already had three!" (você trouxe, mas não precisava)
- **didn't need to do** = **não era necessário** (geralmente a pessoa **não fez**):
"I **didn't need to** take a taxi because Ana gave me a lift."

**2. Should have / Ought to have + pp** → crítica ou arrependimento (o certo não aconteceu)
- "You **should have told** me!" / "I **ought to have checked** the date."
- Negativa: "I **shouldn't have eaten** so much."

**3. Could have + pp** → possibilidade que **não aconteceu**, ou crítica
- "You **could have been** killed!" (podia ter acontecido)
- "You **could have called**!" (crítica: você podia ter ligado — e não ligou)
- **Couldn't have + pp** = impossível no passado: "I **couldn't have done** it without you."

**4. Might have / May have + pp** → especulação sobre o passado (talvez)
- "She **might have missed** the bus." / "It **may have been** a mistake."
- "It **might have been** worse." (poderia ter sido pior)

**5. Would have + pp** → disposição/vontade no passado (ligado a condições)
- "I **would have helped** you, but you didn't ask."
- "I **wouldn't have** done that." (eu, no seu lugar, não teria feito)

**6. Revisão B1+:** **must have** (dedução: certeza) · **can't have** (impossível).

**Na fala:** should've = "**shúdav**", could've = "**kúdav**", needn't have = "**nídentav**".

rows: You needn't have cooked — we ate out.
I didn't need to wait; the bus came.
I would have come, but I was ill.
She must have left. / He can't have known.

examples.en: I spent the whole night preparing for the interview, but I needn't have worried — they offered me the job in ten minutes.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português, "podia ter" serve para tudo. Em inglês, escolha: **could have** (era possível), **should have** (era o certo), **might have** (talvez tenha acontecido).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Nativos reduzem o **have** a um "av" fraco, colado no modal: **should've** "shúdav", **could've** "kúdav", **might've** "máitav", **needn't have** "nídentav". ⚠️ Na escrita, nunca escreva "should of" — é um erro comum até entre nativos, por causa da pronúncia.

listening.title: The worry experiment
listening.context_pt: Um psicólogo fala num podcast sobre preocupações que nunca se concretizam.

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: Here's an exercise I often suggest. For two weeks, write down every worry you have — "I might lose my job", "My presentation will be a disaster" — and then check later whether it actually happened. In a small study at Penn State University, researchers asked people with generalized anxiety to do something similar. They found that most of the participants' worries did not come true, and when something negative did happen, people often coped better than they had expected. In other words, they needn't have worried so much. Of course, this doesn't mean all worry is useless. Some concern helps us prepare. But if you look back at your list and see that you spent hours worrying about things that never happened, it can be a real wake-up call. You might decide to save your energy for the problems that actually appear.

questions.answer: Writing down every worry for two weeks and checking later whether it happened.

reading.title: Lucky breaks
reading.text: History is full of people whose failures turned out to be blessings in disguise. Take the author J.K. Rowling, who has said in interviews that her manuscript for the first Harry Potter book was rejected by many publishers before Bloomsbury accepted it. Any one of those editors could have changed literary history; they simply didn't. Steve Jobs, forced out of Apple in 1985, later described being fired as one of the best things that could have happened to him, because it freed him to start again. Of course, survivor stories like these can be misleading. For every person whose rejection led to success, there are many others who might have been equally talented but never got a second chance. Psychologist Richard Wiseman, who studied people who considered themselves lucky or unlucky, suggested that "lucky" people tend to notice opportunities, listen to their intuition and recover quickly from bad experiences. In one of his well-known experiments, participants were asked to count the photographs in a newspaper. Many of the "unlucky" ones missed a large message inside it telling them they needn't have kept counting. Perhaps luck is partly a matter of where we choose to look.

writing.model:
The best mistake I ever made

Three years ago, I sent an email that I definitely shouldn't have sent. I was working in a marketing agency, and after a terrible meeting I wrote a long message complaining about our biggest client. I meant to send it to my best friend. Instead, I sent it to my boss.

I should have read the address twice. I could have waited until I was calmer. I certainly needn't have used so many capital letters! My heart stopped when I realized what I'd done. I was sure I would be fired — and honestly, many bosses would have fired me on the spot.

But my boss called me into her office and, to my surprise, she said she agreed with most of my points. She'd been thinking the same about that client for months. She might have been annoyed by my tone, but she said I'd shown that I really cared about the quality of our work.

Two weeks later, she asked me to lead a new project to improve how we managed difficult clients. Within a year, I'd been promoted.

Looking back, it could have ended very badly. I was lucky, and I don't recommend sending angry emails! But the mistake taught me something important: sometimes being honest — in the right way — can open doors. These days, though, I always check the address.

culture_note.title: "Should of"?

Se você escrever "should have", estará escrevendo melhor que muitos nativos!
