warmup.text_pt: "Eu odeio **ser interrompido**." "Ela parece **ter esquecido**." "Ele nega **ter dito** isso." Para expressar ideias mais complexas, o inglês usa gerúndios e infinitivos **passivos** e **perfeitos**. Hoje você vai usá-los para falar sobre comunicação e como queremos ser tratados.

grammar.title: Advanced gerunds and infinitives
grammar.explanation_pt:
Você já sabe quais verbos pedem **-ing** (enjoy, avoid, deny, mind...) e quais pedem **to** (want, decide, seem, expect...). Agora vamos às formas **passivas** e **perfeitas**:

| | Gerúndio | Infinitivo |
|---|---|---|
| simples | doing | to do |
| **passivo** | **being done** | **to be done** |
| **perfeito** | **having done** | **to have done** |
| **perfeito passivo** | having been done | to have been done |

**1. Passivo** → o sujeito **recebe** a ação:
- "I hate **being interrupted**." (eu sou interrompido)
- "Nobody likes **being criticized** in public."
- "Everyone wants **to be taken** seriously."
- "The report needs **to be finished** today."

**2. Perfeito** → ação **anterior** ao verbo principal:
- "He denied **having taken** the money." (negou ter pegado)
- "She seems **to have forgotten** our meeting." (parece ter esquecido)
- "I regret **not having studied** more." (= I regret not studying more — também correto)
- "He's thought **to have left** the country." (formal)

**3. Verbos que mudam de sentido:**
- **remember / forget + -ing** = lembrar/esquecer de algo que **aconteceu** ("I remember **meeting** her.")
- **remember / forget + to** = lembrar/esquecer de **fazer** algo ("Remember **to call** her.")
- **stop + -ing** = parar uma atividade · **stop + to** = parar **para** fazer outra coisa
- **try + -ing** = experimentar ("Try **turning** it off and on.") · **try + to** = tentar com esforço ("I tried **to open** it, but I couldn't.")
- **regret + -ing** = arrepender-se · **regret + to** = lamentar informar (formal: "We regret **to inform** you...")

rows: Lembro de ter trancado a porta.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português usamos "ter + particípio" ("negou **ter dito**") — em inglês, o paralelo é **having said** (depois de verbos com -ing) ou **to have said** (depois de verbos com to).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Não confunda: **being** = "BÍ-in" (duas sílabas) e **been** = "bín" (uma sílaba; no americano às vezes "bin"). "I hate **being** interrupted" x "I've **been** interrupted".

listening.title: The art of listening
listening.context_pt: Uma especialista em comunicação explica a escuta ativa.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Most of us think we're good listeners. But research on communication suggests that we often listen in order to reply, not to understand. While the other person is talking, we're planning what to say next. Active listening is different. It means giving the person your full attention, avoiding being distracted by your phone, and trying not to interrupt. It also means checking that you've understood: "So what you're saying is..." People who are listened to in this way feel respected. They're more likely to trust you, and less likely to feel misunderstood. A simple exercise: in your next conversation, try waiting two seconds before you reply. You'll be surprised how much more you notice — including what's said between the lines.

reading.title: Why we want to be understood
reading.text: Being understood is one of our deepest psychological needs. Researchers studying relationships have found that people who feel understood by their partners tend to report higher satisfaction, and in some studies even smaller increases in stress during conflict. Interestingly, it seems that what matters most is not having our ideas accepted, but being listened to. In one line of research, participants who were allowed to explain their point of view — even when the other person disagreed — reported feeling more respected than those who were simply agreed with quickly. Feeling misunderstood, on the other hand, can be painful. Many people describe being left out or not being taken seriously at work as one of the most frustrating experiences of their professional lives. Psychologists suggest a few habits for helping others feel understood: asking open questions, repeating key points in your own words and avoiding being too quick to give advice. Admitting to having made assumptions also helps: "I think I misunderstood you — can you explain again?" Sometimes, the most powerful thing we can do is not to have the right answer, but to have truly listened.

writing.model:
How to make your colleagues feel heard

In our last staff survey, many of you said that you wanted to be listened to more in meetings. Nobody likes being interrupted or having their ideas ignored. Here are four simple habits that can help.

1. Stop multitasking. When a colleague is speaking, try putting your phone face down. Being given someone's full attention is rare these days — and people notice it.

2. Let people finish. Many of us interrupt without realizing it. If you remember interrupting someone, go back to them: "Sorry, I cut you off — please continue."

3. Give credit. Nothing is more frustrating than seeing your idea presented by someone else. If you build on a colleague's idea, mention them. Everyone deserves to be recognized for their contributions.

4. Check your understanding. Before you reply, try repeating the main point in your own words. If you realize you've misunderstood, admit having made an assumption. It shows respect.

These habits take practice. Several team leaders who tested them last month said they were surprised to have noticed so many changes in their meetings. One said: "People seem to have become more confident about sharing ideas."

Next time you're in a meeting, remember to listen as carefully as you'd like to be listened to.

culture_note.title: Comunicação direta x indireta
culture_note.text_pt: Culturas variam no nível de **franqueza**. Holandeses e alemães são conhecidos por feedback direto; britânicos, por indiretas ("**That's an interesting idea**" pode significar "não gostei"). Brasileiros costumam suavizar críticas e valorizar a relação. Em equipes internacionais, **read between the lines** — e, se não tiver certeza, pergunte.

summary_pt: Passivo: being told / to be taken.

remember/forget + -ing (passado) x + to (fazer).
stop/try/regret mudam de sentido com -ing ou to.

grammar.title: Collocations and idioms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Collocations com verbos "leves"**
- **make** (criar, produzir, resultado): make a mistake, a decision, a plan, a complaint, an effort, progress, money, friends, a difference, an excuse, a phone call
- **do** (tarefas, trabalho, atividades): do homework, the housework, research, business, a course, your best, a favour, damage, exercise
- **take** (ações, oportunidades): take a break, a risk, a photo, an exam, part in, place, advantage of, responsibility for, care of
- **have** (experiências, refeições): have a look, a chat, a good time, an argument, a shower, lunch, a go
- **pay** (dar algo): pay attention, a visit, a compliment, the price

**2. Adjetivo + substantivo** ("forte" muda em inglês!):
- **heavy** rain / traffic / smoker · **strong** coffee / wind / accent · **high** temperature / price / risk · **deep** sleep / concern · **bitter** disappointment · **close** friend · **broad** smile

**3. Advérbio + adjetivo** (intensificadores naturais):
- **highly** recommended / unlikely / successful · **deeply** grateful / concerned · **bitterly** disappointed / cold · **fully** aware · **completely** different · **perfectly** normal

**4. Idioms (expressões idiomáticas)**
- Use com moderação — idioms demais soam forçados.
- Muitos são **parecidos** com o português (break the ice = quebrar o gelo), mas outros **não**: "it's raining cats and dogs" ≈ "está chovendo canivetes"; "cost an arm and a leg" ≈ "custar os olhos da cara".
- Idioms são **fixos**: não troque palavras (❌ "a piece of pie").

**Estratégia:** ao aprender uma palavra nova, anote **com o que ela combina**, não só a tradução.

homework, research, your best, a favour, business, exercise
a break, a risk, part in, place, advantage of, care of

grammar.tip_pt: Os erros de collocation mais comuns de brasileiros: ❌ "do a mistake" (✅ make), ❌ "make a question" (✅ **ask** a question), ❌ "take a decision" (✅ **make** — embora "take" seja aceito no inglês britânico), ❌ "strong rain" (✅ heavy rain), ❌ "lose the bus" (✅ **miss** the bus).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Collocations e idioms são pronunciados como **um bloco só**, com as palavras ligadas: "make a mistake" = "mêikamistêik", "take a break" = "têikabrêik", "a piece of cake" = "apísovkêik". Aprender em blocos melhora a **fluência** e a **velocidade**.

listening.title: Idioms around the world
listening.context_pt: Um podcast compara expressões idiomáticas em diferentes línguas.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Today we're comparing idioms from different languages. Let's start with rain. In English, when it's raining heavily, people sometimes say "it's raining cats and dogs" — though, honestly, most people just say "it's pouring". In Brazilian Portuguese, it's "raining pocket knives".

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.en: I love that one! And when something is very expensive, English speakers say it "costs an arm and a leg", whereas Brazilians say it "costs the eyes of the face". Same idea — very valuable parts of the body!

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Exactly. And some idioms are almost identical. "Break the ice" exists in English, Portuguese and many other languages.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.en: My advice to learners: don't try to use too many idioms. Collocations are more important. If you say "make a decision" and "heavy traffic" correctly, you'll sound more natural than if you use five idioms in one sentence!

questions.answer: "Custar os olhos da cara" (cost the eyes of the face).

questions.q: What is the guest's advice to learners?
questions.answer: Don't use too many idioms; collocations are more important.

reading.title: Chunks, not words
reading.text: For most of the twentieth century, language teaching focused on two things: grammar rules and individual words. But in the 1990s, the linguist Michael Lewis proposed what he called the "Lexical Approach". His central idea was simple but powerful: language is not made of grammar and words, but largely of "chunks" — groups of words that native speakers store and use as single units. Phrases like "by the way", "I'm not sure", "make a decision" or "as far as I know" are not built word by word each time we speak; they come ready-made. Corpus research — the study of very large collections of real texts — supports this view, showing that a large part of everyday language consists of recurring combinations. This helps explain why learners can know thousands of words and still sound unnatural: they combine words in ways that are grammatically correct but that native speakers simply don't use, like "do a decision" or "strong rain". It also explains why fluent speakers can talk so quickly: they don't need to build every sentence from scratch. For learners, the practical lesson is clear. When you meet a new word, don't just learn its translation. Notice the words around it, write down the whole chunk, and practise it until it comes out automatically.

questions.q: What did Michael Lewis propose?
questions.answer: The Lexical Approach: language is largely made of chunks.

questions.q: What does corpus research show?
questions.answer: A large part of everyday language consists of recurring combinations.

questions.q: Why can learners know many words and still sound unnatural?
questions.answer: They combine words in ways native speakers don't use.

questions.q: What is the practical lesson for learners?
questions.answer: Learn whole chunks, not just translations, and practise them.

writing.model:
Review: A weekend at Pousada Mar Azul, Ilhabela

I'd been working long hours for months, so I decided to take a break and spend a weekend on Ilhabela. A friend had highly recommended Pousada Mar Azul, and I'm deeply grateful she did.

The staff made a real effort to make us feel welcome. The owner, Dona Célia, paid us a visit on the first evening, broke the ice with some funny stories about the island and gave us excellent advice about where to go.

The rooms are simple but spotlessly clean, with a breathtaking view of the sea. On the second day there was heavy rain, but it turned out to be a blessing in disguise: we had a long chat with other guests in the lounge and made friends with a lovely couple from Chile.

Breakfast deserves a special mention. The coffee was strong, the fruit was fresh and the homemade cakes were absolutely delicious.

The only downside? Getting there. The ferry queue on a Friday afternoon can be extremely long, so pay attention to the timetable and arrive early.

It isn't cheap, but it certainly doesn't cost an arm and a leg either, especially compared with other places on the island. All in all, it's a perfect place to relax, and I'd have no hesitation in recommending it. Five stars.

culture_note.title: Idioms que confundem
culture_note.text_pt: Cuidado com idioms que **parecem** traduções mas não são: **"to pull someone's leg"** = zoar alguém (não "puxar o pé"); **"break a leg!"** = boa sorte (no teatro); **"it's not my cup of tea"** = não é a minha praia; **"once in a blue moon"** = muito raramente. E o português **"pagar mico"** seria **"to make a fool of yourself"**.

grammar.title: B2 review and exam strategies
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Revisão das grandes estruturas do B2:**
- **Narrativa:** past perfect continuous, would / used to, inversão ("Never have I...")
- **Futuro:** future continuous / perfect ("By 2030, I'll have finished...")
- **Passiva e reporting:** "It is believed that...", "He is said to be..."
- **Condicionais:** third, mixed, wish / if only, alternativas ao if
- **Orações:** relative clauses avançadas, participle clauses
- **Coesão:** although / despite / whereas / however, linkers formais
- **Modais no passado:** needn't have, should have, could have, might have
- **Gerúndio / infinitivo:** being told, having done, to have done
- **Léxico:** collocations e idioms

**Formato das provas:**

**Cambridge B2 First** — 4 partes:
- **Reading & Use of English** (1h15): gramática, vocabulário e leitura
- **Writing** (1h20): essay obrigatório + uma tarefa à escolha (artigo, e-mail/carta, relatório ou resenha)
- **Listening** (cerca de 40 min)
- **Speaking** (cerca de 14 min, **em dupla**): entrevista, comparação de fotos, tarefa colaborativa e discussão

**IELTS Speaking** (11–14 min, individual):
- **Part 1**: perguntas sobre você (casa, trabalho, hobbies)
- **Part 2**: fale **1–2 minutos** sobre um tema de um cartão (1 min para preparar)
- **Part 3**: discussão mais abstrata sobre o tema da Part 2
- Critérios: fluência e coerência, vocabulário, gramática e pronúncia. No IELTS, B2 corresponde aproximadamente às bandas 5.5–6.5.

**Estratégias para o speaking:**
1. **Ganhe tempo** com naturalidade: "That's an interesting question...", "Let me think..."
2. **Desenvolva** (elaborate): responda + motivo + exemplo. Nunca só "yes" ou "no".
3. **Parafraseie** quando faltar uma palavra: "It's a kind of... / It's something you use to..."
4. **Autocorrija-se** rapidamente: "I goed — sorry, I went..."  — isso mostra controle.
5. Na prova em dupla, **interaja**: "What do you think?", "I see your point, but..."
6. **Mostre variedade**: use estruturas do B2 de propósito (conditionals, passivas, relative clauses).

rows: That's a good question. / Let me think about that for a second.
I can't remember the word, but it's a kind of... / It's what you use to...
The main reason is... For example, ... That's why...
What do you think? / Would you agree? / I see your point, but...
Sorry, could you repeat the question? / Do you mean...?
So, all in all, I'd say... / To sum up, ...

examples.en: That's an interesting question. I've never really thought about it, but I'd say that technology has made us more connected and, at the same time, lonelier.
examples.pt: Que pergunta interessante. Nunca pensei muito nisso, mas eu diria que a tecnologia nos tornou mais conectados e, ao mesmo tempo, mais solitários.

examples.en: I can't remember the exact word, but it's a kind of tool you use to measure temperature.
examples.pt: Não lembro a palavra exata, mas é um tipo de ferramenta que você usa para medir temperatura.

examples.en: If I had known how useful English would be, I would have started studying much earlier.
examples.pt: Se eu soubesse o quanto o inglês seria útil, teria começado a estudar bem mais cedo.

grammar.tip_pt: Na prova oral, **o examinador avalia o seu inglês, não as suas ideias**. Você não precisa dizer algo brilhante — precisa dizer algo **claro, desenvolvido e com variedade**. Se não tiver opinião, invente uma!

common_mistakes.wrong: Examiner: Do you like reading? — Student: Yes.
common_mistakes.right: Yes, I do, especially novels. I usually read before bed, because it helps me relax.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Sempre desenvolva: resposta + motivo + exemplo.

common_mistakes.wrong: I don't know how to say this in English, so... (silêncio)
common_mistakes.right: I can't think of the word, but it's a kind of...
common_mistakes.why_pt: Parafraseie em vez de parar.

common_mistakes.wrong: Usar só estruturas simples para não errar.
common_mistakes.right: Arriscar estruturas do B2 (If I had..., It is said that..., Having...)
common_mistakes.why_pt: A variedade conta pontos — pequenos erros com estruturas complexas são aceitáveis.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Fluência não é falar rápido — é falar **sem pausas longas no lugar errado**. Faça pausas **entre** blocos de sentido (não no meio de um chunk), use **fillers** naturais (well, actually, I mean, you know) com moderação e ligue as palavras dentro de cada bloco.

lines.en: Shall we start with exercise? I think it's one of the most effective options. It is often said that even a short walk can improve your mood. What do you think?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: I agree, although not everyone has time to go to the gym. Having said that, you don't need a gym — you could just walk to work.
lines.pt: Concordo, embora nem todo mundo tenha tempo de ir à academia. Dito isso, você não precisa de academia — poderia simplesmente ir a pé para o trabalho.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: That's a good point. What about social media? If I had spent less time on my phone last year, I think I would have been much less anxious.
lines.pt: Bom argumento. E as redes sociais? Se eu tivesse passado menos tempo no celular no ano passado, acho que teria ficado bem menos ansiosa.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Me too. But I wouldn't say it's all negative. It can also help you stay in touch with friends who live far away, which links to the next idea.
lines.pt: Eu também. Mas eu não diria que é tudo negativo. Também pode ajudar a manter contato com amigos que moram longe, o que se liga à próxima ideia.

lines.speaker: Ana

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.en: OK, so I'd like to talk about a skill that has been incredibly useful to me, which is speaking English. I started learning it at school, but to be honest, I didn't take it very seriously back then. It wasn't until I was about twenty-five, having just been offered a job in an international company, that I realized how much I needed it. So I signed up for an evening course. At first, it was really challenging — I remember being terrified of speaking in class. But my teacher encouraged us to make mistakes, which made a huge difference. The skill has been useful in so many ways. At work, I now lead meetings with colleagues in four countries. I've also travelled a lot more, and I've made friends from all over the world. If I hadn't learned English, I wouldn't have the job I have today. Looking back, I wish I'd started taking it seriously much earlier — I needn't have waited until I was twenty-five!

reading.title: What does B2 really mean?
reading.text: According to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), a B2 user is an "independent user" who can understand the main ideas of complex texts, interact with native speakers with a degree of fluency and spontaneity, and produce clear, detailed texts on a wide range of subjects. In practical terms, this is a significant milestone. Many universities around the world accept B2 as a minimum level of English for some courses, and many international employers consider it the point at which someone can work effectively in English. However, reaching B2 does not mean that you will understand everything. You may still struggle with fast speech, strong regional accents, jokes and cultural references. You will continue to make mistakes — but, crucially, they will rarely prevent communication, and you will often be able to notice and correct them yourself. Perhaps the most important change is psychological. At B2, English stops being only a subject that you study and becomes a tool that you use: to read the news, watch series without subtitles, follow a TED talk or argue your point in a meeting. From here, progress depends less on courses and more on exposure. The more you read, listen and speak, the closer you will get to C1 — and, more importantly, the richer your life in English will become.

questions.q: How does the CEFR describe a B2 user?
questions.answer: An independent user who understands complex texts, interacts with fluency and produces clear, detailed texts.

questions.q: Why is B2 a significant milestone?
questions.answer: Many universities and employers accept it as a minimum level.

questions.q: What might you still struggle with at B2?
questions.answer: Fast speech, strong accents, jokes and cultural references.

questions.q: What does progress depend on after B2?
questions.answer: More on exposure (reading, listening, speaking) than on courses.

writing.model:
Is learning languages still necessary?

Translation apps have improved enormously in recent years. As a result, it could be argued that learning a foreign language is no longer worth the effort. However, I believe this view is mistaken.

Firstly, language is not only about exchanging information but also about building relationships. Although an app can translate words, it cannot easily capture humour, emotion or cultural references. Having made friends abroad, I know that real connection happens when you speak someone's language.

Secondly, in the job market, speaking English is still seen as an essential skill. Employers want people who can lead meetings and negotiate, which is extremely difficult to do through an app.

Finally, learning a language changes the way we think. It is widely believed that bilingual people are more flexible and open to other cultures.

In conclusion, while translation technology is a useful tool, it is not a substitute for learning. If I had relied on apps, I would never have had the experiences that English has given me.

grammar.title: Verb forms: nuance and attitude
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Stative verbs no continuous** — verbos de estado (be, think, have, see, feel, love...) normalmente não vão para o continuous. Quando vão, o **sentido muda**:
- **be** → comportamento temporário: "He **is** rude." (é grosso) x "He**'s being** rude." (está sendo grosso agora)
- **think** → opinião x processo: "I **think** it's a good idea." x "I**'m thinking** about moving abroad." (considerando)
- **see** → ver x encontrar/namorar: "I **see** what you mean." x "I**'m seeing** the doctor at 3." / "She**'s seeing** someone."
- **have** → posse x atividade: "I **have** two sisters." x "We**'re having** dinner."
- **love / like** no continuous → entusiasmo informal com algo atual: "I**'m loving** this new job!"

**2. Passado e continuous para distanciamento ("tentative")** — tornam pedidos e opiniões mais suaves e educados:
- "I **was wondering** if you could..." (mais educado que "I wonder")
- "I **was hoping** we could talk." / "We **were thinking** of leaving early."
- "**Did** you **want** a coffee?" (oferta educada, sobre o presente)
- "I **thought** you might like this."

**3. Always / constantly / forever + continuous** → hábito irritante ou marcante:
- "He's **always interrupting** me!" / "She was **forever** losing her keys."
- Também pode ser positivo: "She's **always doing** nice things for people."

**4. Present perfect para novidades** (notícias, anúncios), seguido do past simple para os detalhes:
- "Scientists **have discovered** a new species. It **was found** in the Amazon last month."

grammar.tip_pt: Em português, usamos o **futuro do pretérito** para suavizar ("Eu **gostaria** de saber..."). Em inglês, o mesmo efeito vem do **passado continuous**: "I **was wondering**..." — é uma das marcas mais claras de um falante C1.

listening.title: The stories we tell about ourselves
listening.context_pt: Trecho de um podcast de psicologia sobre identidade narrativa.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Psychologists who study what they call "narrative identity" argue that we don't just have experiences — we turn them into stories, and those stories become who we are. The researcher Dan McAdams has spent decades studying these life stories. One pattern that comes up again and again is what he calls a "redemption sequence": a story in which something bad turns into something good. "I lost my job, but it led me to find my real calling." Research in this area suggests that people who tell their lives this way tend to report higher well-being. Now, I'm not saying we should invent happy endings. But it's worth asking: what story are you telling about yourself? And is it the only possible version? Because, as it turns out, we have more freedom to rewrite it than we usually think.

reading.title: The myth of the fixed self
reading.text: Ask people whether their personality will change much over the next ten years and most will say no. Ask them how much it has changed over the past ten years, however, and they will readily admit that it has changed considerably. Psychologists Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson called this the "end of history illusion": at every age, we seem to believe that the person we are today is, more or less, the finished product. Their study, published in Science in 2013, surveyed thousands of adults and found that people consistently underestimated how much their values, preferences and personalities would change in the future. The illusion has practical consequences. Because we assume our current tastes will last, we may pay too much today for things our future selves won't value — a tattoo, say, or a ticket to see a favourite band a decade from now. Longitudinal research on personality offers a more nuanced picture still. Traits such as conscientiousness and emotional stability tend to increase gradually throughout adulthood, a pattern sometimes described as "maturation". None of this means that we are endlessly changeable; there is real continuity in who we are. But it does suggest that the question "Who am I?" is better answered in pencil than in ink. The self, it seems, is less a statue than a river.

writing.model:
The person I used to think I was

For most of my twenties, I was convinced I was an introvert. I was always making excuses to leave parties early, and I genuinely believed that I simply wasn't "a people person". It was a label I had picked up at school, where a teacher once described me as "quiet but reliable", and I wore it for years without questioning it.

Things started to shift when I moved to Recife for work. I didn't know anyone, so I had no choice but to start conversations — with neighbours, with colleagues, with the man who sold coconut water on the corner. To my surprise, I was enjoying it. I remember calling my sister after a few months and saying, "I think I'm being someone else here." She laughed and replied that perhaps I was finally being myself.

Looking back, I suspect I wasn't really an introvert at all. I was anxious, which is a very different thing. Being quiet had felt safer than risking rejection, and the label gave me a convenient explanation.

None of this means I've become the life and soul of the party. I still need time alone to recharge, and there are evenings when I'd much rather read than go out. But I've stopped thinking of myself as a fixed type. These days, if someone asks me whether I'm an introvert or an extrovert, I usually answer, "It depends on the day."

If I could talk to my younger self, I think I'd simply say: "I was wondering whether you'd ever considered that the story you tell about yourself might be wrong." Labels can be useful, but they are descriptions, not destinies.

grammar.title: Ellipsis and substitution
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Substituição** = trocar uma parte da frase por uma palavra curta. **Elipse** = simplesmente omitir o que já está claro.

**1. so / not** substituem uma oração inteira depois de think, hope, expect, suppose, believe, guess, be afraid, appear, seem:
- "Is she coming?" — "I **think so**." / "I **hope not**." / "I'm **afraid not**."
- Negativa com think/believe/expect: **I don't think so** (mais natural que "I think not", que soa formal).
- **If so / If not**: "Are you free on Friday? **If so**, let's meet."
- Formal: **do so** substitui verbo + complemento: "Applicants must register online. Those who fail to **do so** will be excluded."

**2. one / ones** substituem substantivos contáveis:
- "I don't like this shirt. Can I see the red **one**?" / "These shoes are nicer than the old **ones**."
- ⚠️ Não use one com incontáveis: ❌ "I prefer the French one wine" → "I prefer French wine."

**3. Infinitivo reduzido (to)** — repete-se só o **to**:
- "Do you want to come?" — "I'd **love to**." / "I don't **want to**." / "I **meant to**, but I forgot."

**4. Auxiliares (elipse do verbo principal):**
- "I can't speak Japanese, but my sister **can**."
- "She said she'd call, and she **did**."
- "I haven't finished yet, but I **will have** by Friday."

**5. Elipse em orações coordenadas** (muito comum na escrita):
- "Some of the participants spoke English, others (spoke) Spanish."
- "I'd like to help, but (I) can't."

listening.title: Does language shape thought?
listening.context_pt: Uma linguista explica, numa aula aberta, pesquisas sobre língua e pensamento.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Does the language you speak change the way you think? For much of the twentieth century, the strong version of this idea — that language determines thought — was largely rejected. But a weaker version has gained support. The cognitive scientist Lera Boroditsky and others have studied, for instance, an Aboriginal community in Australia, the Kuuk Thaayorre, whose language uses cardinal directions — north, south, east, west — instead of "left" and "right". Speakers have been reported to stay remarkably well oriented, even indoors. Other studies have looked at colour: Russian has separate basic words for light blue and dark blue, and some experiments found that Russian speakers were slightly faster at distinguishing those shades. Does this mean we're prisoners of our language? Most researchers would say not. But it does suggest that each language trains our attention in particular ways — and that learning another one can show us the world from a slightly different angle.

questions.q: Which version of the idea was largely rejected?
questions.answer: The strong version: that language determines thought.

questions.q: What is special about Kuuk Thaayorre?
questions.answer: It uses cardinal directions instead of left and right.

questions.q: What did some experiments find about Russian speakers?
questions.answer: They were slightly faster at distinguishing light and dark blue.

questions.q: What is the speaker's conclusion?
questions.answer: Languages train our attention in particular ways; learning one shows a new angle.

reading.title: The translator's dilemma
reading.text: Every translator faces the same impossible choice: be faithful to the words or to the meaning. Translate too literally, and the result may be accurate but lifeless; translate too freely, and you risk replacing the author's voice with your own. Nowhere is this clearer than with humour, poetry and culturally loaded words. Take the Portuguese "jeitinho". A dictionary might offer "knack" or "way around something", but neither conveys the mixture of creativity, flexibility and occasional rule-bending the word suggests to Brazilians. A translator can choose to keep the original word and explain it, to find an approximate equivalent, or to rewrite the sentence entirely. Each option gains something and loses something. Machine translation has transformed the field in recent years. For everyday texts — instructions, emails, the gist of a news article — modern tools are remarkably good, and many professional translators now use them as a first draft. Literary translation, however, remains a stubbornly human craft. A novel's rhythm, ambiguity and wordplay depend on choices that require an understanding not only of two languages but of two cultures. Perhaps the best definition of a good translation is one that makes the reader forget it is one. If so, the translator's greatest achievement is to become invisible — which may explain why so few readers can name the translators of their favourite books.

questions.q: What is the translator's "impossible choice"?
questions.answer: To be faithful to the words or to the meaning.

questions.q: Why is "jeitinho" hard to translate?
questions.answer: No English word conveys its mix of creativity, flexibility and rule-bending.

questions.q: How do many professionals use machine translation?
questions.answer: As a first draft.

questions.q: Why does literary translation remain human?
questions.answer: Rhythm, ambiguity and wordplay require understanding two languages and two cultures.

writing.model:
Five Brazilian words the world needs

Every language has words that others envy. English speakers have borrowed "schadenfreude" from German and "hygge" from Danish; perhaps it's time they borrowed a few from Brazilian Portuguese too.

1. Saudade. Often described as untranslatable, saudade is a bittersweet longing for someone or something absent. Is it the same as nostalgia? Not quite. You can feel it for a person who is alive and well, or even for a future that hasn't happened yet.

2. Cafuné. The act of gently running your fingers through someone's hair. Many languages have no single word for it; Portuguese does, which may say something about how much Brazilians value physical affection.

3. Gambiarra. An improvised, often ingenious fix — holding a broken door shut with a chair, say. Engineers might frown at it; most Brazilians, if they're honest, admire it.

4. Jeitinho. Closely related to gambiarra but applied to rules rather than objects, jeitinho means finding a creative way around an obstacle. Is it always positive? I don't think so. It can describe both admirable flexibility and questionable shortcuts.

5. Xodó. Someone's xodó is their favourite person or thing — the one they spoil and adore. A grandmother might call her youngest grandchild her xodó; a teenager might use the word for a new phone.

What do these words reveal? Perhaps a culture that values warmth, improvisation and emotional honesty. Of course, no list can capture a whole country, and this one doesn't try to. But if English speakers ever need a word for the feeling of missing a place they've never been to, they'll know where to find one.

grammar.title: Emphatic structures
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. do / does / did enfático** (em frases afirmativas) — reforça, contrasta ou corrige:
- "I **do** like your new haircut!" (gosto mesmo)
- "You never listen to me!" — "I **do** listen!" (contradizer)
- "She **did** warn us, to be fair." (admitir)
- No imperativo, soa insistente e caloroso: "**Do** come in!" / "**Do** sit down."
- Na fala, o **do** é sempre **acentuado**.

**2. Fronting** — mover um elemento para o início para dar destaque:
- **Adjetivo/advérbio + as + sujeito + verbo** (concessão = "por mais... que"):
  "**Strange as it may seem**, ..." / "**Tired as she was**, she kept going." / "**Hard as I tried**, I couldn't settle in."
- **Much as** + oração (= although, "por mais que"): "**Much as I love** my hometown, I couldn't live there again."
- Objeto no início (estilo literário/falado): "**That** I don't understand." / "**Some things** you never forget."

**3. so / such... that**
- **so + adjetivo/advérbio + that**: "The city was **so** noisy **that** I couldn't sleep."
- **such + (a/an) + adjetivo + substantivo + that**: "It was **such a** warm welcome **that** I cried."
- **so much / many / little / few + substantivo**: "There were **so many** people **that**..."

**4. Inversão com so / such** (formal/literário):
- "**So** strong **was** the feeling **that** I cried."
- "**Such was** her homesickness **that** she flew back after a month."

listening.title: Third culture kids
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre crianças que crescem entre culturas.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: The term "third culture kids" was coined in the 1950s by the American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem, who studied children of families living abroad. The idea is that these children grow up between their parents' culture and the culture of the country where they live, and end up creating a third culture of their own. Ask one of them "Where are you from?" and you may get a long pause. Many describe a feeling of belonging everywhere and nowhere. Strange as it may seem, they often feel most at home with other third culture kids, regardless of nationality. There are clear advantages: adaptability, language skills, an ability to see situations from several perspectives. But there are challenges too. Repeated goodbyes can make some people reluctant to form deep attachments. So common is this experience that many international schools now run programmes to help students deal with transitions.

questions.q: Who coined the term, and when?
questions.answer: Ruth Hill Useem, an American sociologist, in the 1950s.

questions.q: What is the "third culture"?
questions.answer: A culture of their own, created between their parents' culture and the host culture.

questions.q: Who do they often feel most at home with?
questions.answer: Other third culture kids.

questions.q: What challenge is mentioned?
questions.answer: Repeated goodbyes can make them reluctant to form deep attachments.

reading.title: What makes a place home?
reading.text: Much as we talk about home as a place, researchers who study belonging suggest it is better understood as a set of relationships. In one influential framework, environmental psychologists describe "place attachment" as developing through three overlapping dimensions: the people we share a place with, the meaningful experiences we have there, and the physical features we come to know intimately — the smell of a particular bakery, the sound of the street at dawn. This helps explain a phenomenon that puzzles many migrants. Returning to their hometown after years away, they find the streets unchanged but the feeling gone. Their friends have moved on, the rhythms of daily life have changed, and they themselves are no longer the same people. Home, it turns out, does not stay where we left it. Brazil offers a vivid illustration. Over the twentieth century, millions of people moved from the countryside and the Northeast to cities in the Southeast. Many of them recreated home in their new neighbourhoods through food, music and festivals: the forró halls and Northeastern fairs of São Paulo are a direct result of this. Such was the scale of the movement that it transformed the culture of the cities that received it. Perhaps the lesson is that belonging is not something we find but something we build. Small as they are, the daily rituals of a place — a greeting from a neighbour, a familiar route to work — slowly turn a city into home.

questions.q: How do researchers suggest home is better understood?
questions.answer: As a set of relationships rather than just a place.

writing.model:
The place I call home

When people ask me where I'm from, I usually say Campina Grande, because that's where I was born. But if they asked where home is, I'd have to think much harder.

I left Paraíba at eighteen to study in Porto Alegre, more than three thousand kilometres away. The first winter was so cold that I slept in two jumpers and a hat. Such was the shock — the climate, the accent, the reserved way people greeted each other — that I seriously considered going back after the first semester.

I didn't, of course. Slowly, the city began to change, or perhaps I did. I found a bakery where the owner remembered my order. I joined a football team made up almost entirely of other "outsiders" from different states. I learned to drink chimarrão, and, strange as it may seem, I came to love it.

That was fifteen years ago. Today, I have a flat, a partner, a dog and a job I enjoy. I've put down roots. And yet, every June, I do feel a pull towards the Northeast. Much as I love Porto Alegre, nothing compares to the festa junina in Campina Grande: the forró, the bonfires, the smell of canjica and pamonha.

So where is home? I've come to believe that it isn't a single place. Home is wherever my people are, and wherever I feel I can be fully myself. Some days that's a street in the South; other days, it's a memory of the Northeast.

I do sometimes envy people who have never left the place where they were born. But I wouldn't change my two homes for anything.

grammar.title: Spoken discourse markers and vague language
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Discourse markers da fala** — organizam a conversa e mostram sua atitude:
- **Mudar / voltar ao assunto:** anyway, by the way, incidentally, speaking of which, as I was saying
- **Acrescentar uma ressalva:** **mind you** ("se bem que"), **that said / having said that**, then again
- **Coincidência / informação relevante:** **as it happens**, actually, funnily enough
- **Reconsiderar:** **come to think of it**, now that I think about it, on second thoughts
- **Resumir / concluir:** so, basically, at the end of the day, all in all
- **Ganhar tempo / suavizar:** well, I mean, you know, let me see

"The hotel was a bit far from the centre. **Mind you**, the view was incredible."
"Are you going to the conference? — **As it happens**, I'm giving a talk there."

**2. Vague language** — imprecisão **intencional**, típica da fala natural (não é erro!):
- **Aproximar números/horários:** about, around, roughly, **or so**, **-ish** (sevenish, fortyish), give or take
- **Categorias:** **and stuff (like that)**, **and things**, **or something (like that)**, **and so on**
- **Suavizar:** **sort of / kind of**, a bit, slightly, quite
- **Palavras "coringa":** thing, stuff, whatsit, thingy (muito informal)

"I've been there twenty times **or so**." / "She's **sort of** shy at first." / "We talked about work **and stuff**."

⚠️ **Registro:** vague language é para a **fala informal**. Em redações e e-mails formais, seja preciso.

rows: mind you, that said, then again
come to think of it, on second thoughts
or so, -ish, roughly, give or take
and stuff, or something, and things like that
sort of, kind of, a bit

listening.title: In defence of small talk
listening.context_pt: Um comentarista de rádio defende a importância do small talk.

lines.speaker: Commentator
lines.en: Small talk has a pretty bad reputation. People call it shallow, fake, a waste of time. But, as it happens, research suggests otherwise. In one well-known study, the psychologists Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn asked people to have a brief, friendly exchange with a barista instead of just ordering and leaving. Those who chatted reported a better mood and a greater sense of belonging. Sandstrom has also found that our interactions with so-called "weak ties" — the neighbour, the bus driver, the person at the gym — contribute to our happiness more than we tend to assume. Mind you, I'm not saying you should corner strangers and talk about the weather for half an hour. But a two-minute chat is sort of like social glue. It's how relationships start. Come to think of it, most of my close friends began as people I made small talk with.

questions.answer: Shallow, fake, a waste of time.

questions.q: What metaphor does the speaker use for small talk?

reading.title: The strength of weak ties
reading.text: In 1973, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a deliberately paradoxical title: "The Strength of Weak Ties". Studying how people in a Boston suburb had found their jobs, he noticed something surprising. Many had heard about the opportunity not from close friends but from acquaintances — people they saw only occasionally. His explanation was elegant. Our close friends tend to move in the same circles we do, so they mostly know what we already know. Acquaintances, by contrast, connect us to different networks and therefore to new information. The idea has since become one of the most cited in the social sciences, and recent research has largely supported it. A large study of LinkedIn users, published in Science in 2022, found that moderately weak ties were the most useful for job mobility. That said, weak ties do more than help us find work. They also seem to matter for our well-being. A quick chat with a neighbour or a familiar face at the market can make a city feel friendlier and less anonymous. Perhaps this is why so many people felt strangely lonely during the pandemic lockdowns, even when they kept in touch with close friends online: what had disappeared were the small, casual encounters that once filled their days. Small talk, it seems, is not so small after all.

questions.q: What did Granovetter notice about how people found jobs?
questions.answer: Many heard about opportunities from acquaintances, not close friends.

questions.q: Why are weak ties useful, according to his explanation?
questions.answer: They connect us to different networks and new information.

questions.q: What did the 2022 LinkedIn study find?
questions.answer: Moderately weak ties were the most useful for job mobility.

questions.q: Why might people have felt lonely during lockdowns?
questions.answer: The small, casual encounters with weak ties had disappeared.

writing.model:
How I learned to love small talk

I'll be honest: for most of my life, I hated small talk. Chatting about the weather, the traffic, the weekend — it all seemed sort of pointless. If I wanted to talk to someone, I wanted to talk about something real.

That changed about three years ago, when I started working from home. At first, I loved it. No commute, no office politics, no awkward conversations by the coffee machine. Then, after six months or so, I noticed something strange. I felt lonely — and not because I missed my close friends. I spoke to them all the time. What I missed were the tiny, meaningless chats: the security guard asking about my weekend, the colleague who always complained about the air conditioning, that kind of thing.

As it happens, I'd just read an article about "weak ties" — the acquaintances who make up a big part of our social world. Apparently, brief exchanges with them can genuinely improve our mood. So I tried an experiment. For a month, I made a point of chatting to at least one stranger a day: the woman at the bakery, the guy who walks the same dog route as me, people at the gym and so on.

The results? Well, I didn't make any best friends. Mind you, I did start looking forward to my morning bread run. Come to think of it, I also ended up joining a running group thanks to the dog guy.

Anyway, the point is this: small talk isn't really about the weather. It's about saying, "I see you, and I'm friendly." That said, I still draw the line at talking about the traffic for more than two minutes!

culture_note.title: Small talk pelo mundo
culture_note.text_pt: Nos EUA, small talk com desconhecidos (no elevador, na fila) é comum e esperado. No Reino Unido, o **tempo** é o tema clássico — e reclamar dele é quase um ritual. Na Finlândia, ao contrário, o silêncio entre desconhecidos é confortável e normal. Brasileiros costumam ser calorosos e pessoais rapidamente — às vezes **pessoais demais** para padrões anglo-saxões (idade, salário, religião e vida amorosa são temas a evitar no início).

grammar.title: Inversion after negative and limiting adverbials
grammar.explanation_pt:
Quando uma expressão **negativa ou restritiva** abre a frase, invertemos sujeito e auxiliar, **como numa pergunta**. O efeito é **formal e enfático**.

**Estrutura:** expressão + **auxiliar + sujeito** + verbo
(se não houver auxiliar, use **do / does / did**)

**1. Never / Rarely / Seldom / Hardly ever**
- "**Never before had** a product sold so fast."
- "**Rarely do** start-ups survive their first five years."

**2. Not only... but (also)**
- "**Not only did** they lose money, **but** they **also** lost their reputation."

**3. Little** (= não fazer ideia)
- "**Little did** they **know** that a small start-up would replace them."

**4. Sequências rápidas: No sooner... than / Hardly... when / Scarcely... when** (geralmente com past perfect)
- "**No sooner had** they launched the app **than** it crashed."
- "**Hardly had** the CEO resigned **when** the share price rose."

**5. Only + expressão de tempo/condição** → a inversão vem na **oração principal**:
- "**Only when** sales collapsed **did they realize** the problem."
- "**Only after** the merger **was** the extent of the debt revealed."
- "**Not until** 2010 **did** the company **launch** its first app."
- "**Only by** listening to customers **can** you succeed."

**6. Expressões com "no"**
- "**Under no circumstances should** you share your password."
- "**On no account must** this information leave the room."
- "**At no time did** the board **consider** selling."
- "**In no way is** this a criticism."

⚠️ **Não inverta** se a expressão não for negativa/restritiva ou não estiver no início: "They **had never** seen..." (sem inversão).
⚠️ **Not only** no meio da frase não inverte: "They **not only** lost money **but also**..."

listening.title: The innovator's dilemma
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de administração explica a teoria da inovação disruptiva.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: In 1997, the Harvard professor Clayton Christensen published The Innovator's Dilemma, a book that changed how business leaders think about innovation. His central question was a puzzling one: why do successful, well-managed companies fail? His answer was that they often fail precisely because they do the right things — they listen to their best customers and focus on improving their most profitable products. Meanwhile, a new technology appears at the bottom of the market. At first, it's cheaper, simpler and, frankly, worse. Established firms ignore it, because their best customers don't want it. But the new technology improves, and by the time it's good enough for mainstream customers, it's too late. Not only have the newcomers taken the low end of the market; they've learned how to move up. Kodak is often cited as an example: one of its own engineers built an early digital camera in 1975, yet the company struggled to embrace the technology that eventually helped to bring it down.

questions.answer: Why do successful, well-managed companies fail?

questions.q: Why do established companies ignore the new technology?
questions.answer: Because their best customers don't want it at first.

questions.q: What is the new technology like at first?
questions.answer: Cheaper, simpler and worse.

questions.q: Why is Kodak cited as an example?
questions.answer: Its engineer built an early digital camera in 1975, but it struggled to embrace digital technology.

reading.title: Brazil's banking revolution
reading.text: For decades, opening a bank account in Brazil was, for many people, a frustrating experience. Fees were high, branches were crowded and the paperwork seemed endless. Large numbers of adults, particularly among lower-income groups, had no account at all. Then, in the 2010s, a wave of digital banks began to change the picture. Offering free accounts and credit cards that could be managed entirely through an app, companies such as Nubank attracted millions of customers who had long been ignored or poorly served by traditional institutions. Never before had so many Brazilians been able to open an account in a matter of minutes, from their phones. The traditional banks, at first, appeared unconcerned. Only when the new players had gathered tens of millions of customers did several of them respond seriously, launching their own digital brands and cutting fees. The changes did not stop there. In 2020, the Central Bank launched Pix, an instant payment system that is free for individuals. Not only did Pix make transfers immediate, but it also allowed small businesses and informal workers to accept payments without expensive card machines. Its adoption was remarkably fast: within a few years it had become one of the most widely used payment methods in the country. Seldom has a public innovation been embraced so quickly. Experts still debate the risks, from fraud to rising household debt. Yet few would deny that, in little more than a decade, the relationship between Brazilians and their money has been transformed.

questions.q: What problems did many Brazilians face with traditional banks?
questions.answer: High fees, crowded branches and endless paperwork; many had no account.

questions.q: What did digital banks offer?
questions.answer: Free accounts and credit cards managed entirely through an app.

questions.q: When did traditional banks respond seriously?
questions.answer: Only when the new players had gathered tens of millions of customers.

questions.q: What two benefits of Pix are mentioned?
questions.answer: Immediate transfers and allowing small businesses to accept payments without card machines.

writing.model:
The phone that swallowed the world

When Apple unveiled the first iPhone in January 2007, many industry experts were unimpressed. It had no physical keyboard, it was expensive, and at launch it couldn't run apps made by other companies. Little did they know that they were looking at the device that would transform not only the phone industry but almost every industry it touched.

At the time, the market leaders were Nokia and BlackBerry. Seldom had any company dominated a sector as completely as Nokia did in the mid-2000s, and BlackBerry was the undisputed favourite of business users. Both believed that their strengths — reliable hardware and physical keyboards — would protect them. Only when their customers began switching in large numbers did they accept that the rules of the game had changed.

What made the smartphone so disruptive? Not only did it combine a phone, a music player and an internet browser in one device, but, with the launch of the App Store in 2008, it became a platform on which other businesses could be built. No sooner had the store opened than developers began creating products that nobody had imagined: ride-hailing, mobile banking, food delivery, dating apps.

The consequences went far beyond technology. Cameras, maps, alarm clocks and even torches were absorbed into a single device. Rarely has a product rendered so many others obsolete so quickly.

There is, of course, a darker side. Not until years later did researchers and parents begin to seriously question the effects of constant connectivity on attention and mental health, a debate that continues today.

The lesson for business leaders is clear. Under no circumstances should a company assume that today's market leadership guarantees tomorrow's survival. In technology, as Nokia discovered, the fall can be as fast as the rise.

grammar.title: Nominalisation and formal register
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Nominalização** = transformar **verbos** ou **adjetivos** em **substantivos**. O resultado é um texto mais **denso, impessoal e objetivo** — o estilo de relatórios, artigos e textos acadêmicos.

**Comparação:**
- Fala: "Prices **went up** sharply, so people **bought** less."
- Formal: "The sharp **rise** in prices led to a **fall** in consumption."

**Sufixos comuns:**
- **-tion / -sion:** introduce → introduction, decide → decision, expand → expansion
- **-ment:** develop → development, improve → improvement
- **-ance / -ence:** perform → performance, depend → dependence
- **-ity:** flexible → flexibility, secure → security
- **-ness:** aware → awareness, effective → effectiveness
- **-al:** arrive → arrival, refuse → refusal
- Mesma forma: increase, decline, rise, fall, change, cut, demand

**Como nominalizar:**
1. Transforme o verbo principal em substantivo.
2. O sujeito vira **possessivo** ou **of**: "The government **regulated** apps" → "The government's **regulation** of apps" / "**the regulation of** apps **by** the government".
3. Advérbio vira **adjetivo**: "increased **sharply**" → "a **sharp** increase".
4. Conectores viram **verbos/preposições de causa**: because/so → **led to, resulted in, caused, due to, as a result of**.

**Collocations formais com substantivos:**
carry out (research / an investigation / a survey) · make (an improvement / a recommendation / a contribution) · have (an impact / an effect on) · take (measures / steps / action) · reach (a conclusion / an agreement) · pose (a threat / a risk)

⚠️ **Cuidado com o exagero:** nominalização demais deixa o texto pesado e difícil. Equilibre com verbos fortes.

listening.title: The four-day week
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista apresenta resultados de testes da semana de quatro dias.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: One of the most talked-about experiments in the world of work in recent years has been the four-day week. In 2022, a large pilot programme in the UK involved around sixty companies, whose employees moved to a four-day week with no loss of pay, on the condition that productivity was maintained. The results, published in 2023, attracted international attention. Most of the participating companies said they would continue with the new schedule. Researchers reported reductions in stress and burnout among employees, as well as improvements in sleep and work-life balance. Similar trials have since been carried out in other countries, including Brazil. Critics point out, however, that the companies involved chose to take part, which may have influenced the results, and that the model is far harder to implement in sectors such as healthcare or retail. The debate, in other words, is far from over.

questions.answer: No loss of pay, as long as productivity was maintained.

questions.answer: To continue with the four-day week.

questions.q: What improvements did researchers report?

reading.title: Working for the algorithm
reading.text: The expansion of app-based work has been one of the most significant changes in the labour market of the past decade. In Brazil, as in many other countries, the growth of ride-hailing and food delivery platforms has created opportunities for hundreds of thousands of people, particularly during periods of high unemployment. For many workers, the attraction lies in the flexibility these platforms offer: the ability to choose when and how long to work, and the absence of a boss in the traditional sense. However, this flexibility comes at a price. Unlike conventional employees, most platform workers do not have access to paid holidays, sick pay or guaranteed minimum earnings. Their income depends on fluctuations in demand and on decisions made by algorithms over which they have little control or understanding. The suspension of an account, for example, can mean the immediate loss of a worker's livelihood, often without a clear explanation. These concerns have led to growing pressure for regulation. Governments in several countries, including Brazil, have attempted to introduce rules guaranteeing minimum standards of pay and social protection, though such proposals have frequently met with resistance from both companies and some workers, who fear the loss of flexibility. The challenge for policymakers, therefore, lies in the development of a model that combines the advantages of flexibility with an adequate level of security. The outcome of this debate will have a profound impact not only on platform workers, but on the future of work as a whole.

questions.q: What attracts many workers to platforms?
questions.answer: Flexibility: choosing when and how long to work, and no traditional boss.

questions.q: What do most platform workers lack?
questions.answer: Paid holidays, sick pay and guaranteed minimum earnings.

questions.q: Why can an account suspension be serious?
questions.answer: It can mean the immediate loss of a livelihood, often without explanation.

questions.q: Why have some workers resisted regulation?
questions.answer: They fear losing flexibility.

writing.model:
Report on the hybrid working trial

Introduction
The aim of this report is to evaluate the results of the six-month hybrid working trial carried out in the marketing and finance departments between January and June, and to make recommendations regarding its continuation. The findings are based on an online survey of 85 employees, interviews with team leaders and an analysis of performance data.

Findings
Overall, the introduction of hybrid working was well received. Approximately 80% of respondents reported an improvement in their work-life balance, largely as a result of the reduction in commuting time. Performance data showed no decline in productivity; in fact, the finance department recorded a slight increase in the number of tasks completed on time.

However, the trial also revealed some concerns. Several employees mentioned a lack of contact with colleagues and a sense of isolation, particularly among new staff. Team leaders also highlighted difficulties in the coordination of projects when team members were rarely in the office on the same days. In addition, the absence of clear guidelines led to some confusion regarding availability and response times.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, the following measures are recommended:
• the continuation of the hybrid model, with a minimum of two office days per week;
• the introduction of fixed "team days" to facilitate collaboration;
• the creation of a mentoring programme for new employees;
• the publication of clear guidelines on working hours and communication.

Conclusion
The trial has demonstrated that hybrid working can lead to greater employee satisfaction without any loss of productivity. Provided that the issues of isolation and coordination are addressed, the adoption of the model on a permanent basis would be of considerable benefit to the company.

grammar.title: Advanced modals: probability and attitude
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Graduando a probabilidade (do mais certo ao menos certo):**
- **will / be bound to / be sure to / be certain to** → certeza: "There**'s bound to** be resistance." (com certeza)
- **should / ought to** → expectativa lógica: "The report **should be** ready by Friday." (é o esperado)
- **may well / might well / could well** → **bem provável** (o "well" aumenta a chance): "She **might well** get the job."
- **may / might / could** → possível
- **might just / could just** → pequena chance (às vezes com esperança): "It **might just** work!"
- **be unlikely to / I doubt** → improvável

**2. May / might as well** → "é melhor / tanto faz, então..." (sugestão sem entusiasmo, porque não há opção melhor):
- "The meeting is cancelled. We **may as well** go home."
- "Nobody's listening. I **might as well** be talking to a wall." (= é como se...)

**3. Could hardly / can't possibly** → quase impossível:
- "I **could hardly** say no to my boss." / "We **can't possibly** finish by Monday."

**4. Would para expectativa e crítica:**
- "You**'d think** a manager **would** know that." (seria de esperar)
- "She **would** say that, wouldn't she?" (típico dela)
- "I**'d have thought** so." (eu acharia que sim)

**5. No passado:** might well have, is bound to have, should have (expectativa: "They **should have arrived** by now.")

rows: be bound to / be sure to

examples.en: If you micromanage talented people, they may well start looking for another job.

grammar.tip_pt: Atenção: **should** de probabilidade ("It **should** be easy" = deve ser fácil) é diferente de **should** de conselho. O contexto decide. E **may well** NÃO significa "pode bem" no sentido de "tem permissão" — significa **"é bem provável"**.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em **may well / might well / could well**, o **well** é acentuado: "She might **WELL** get the job." Em **may as well**, o acento recai no verbo principal: "We may as well **GO**." E **bound to** = "báundtu".

listening.title: What makes a team work?
listening.context_pt: Um consultor fala sobre pesquisas sobre equipes eficazes.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: A few years ago, Google ran an internal research project, known as Project Aristotle, to find out why some of its teams performed better than others. You'd think the answer would be about talent — put the smartest people together and you're bound to succeed. But that's not what they found. According to the company's own summary, the most important factor was psychological safety: whether team members feel safe to take risks, ask questions and admit mistakes without being embarrassed or punished. The concept was developed by Amy Edmondson, a professor at Harvard Business School. Her early research in hospitals produced a surprising result: the better teams appeared to report more errors — not because they made more, she concluded, but because people felt safe enough to talk about them. So, if you're a leader, the message is clear. Your team may well be hiding problems from you. And if they are, you might as well be flying blind.

reading.title: The humble leader
reading.text: For much of the twentieth century, the ideal leader was imagined as a confident, decisive figure who had all the answers. That image may well be changing. A growing body of research suggests that some of the most effective leaders combine ambition with a quality that is rarely associated with power: humility. In his influential study of companies that had made the leap from good to great performance, the management writer Jim Collins described what he called "Level 5 leaders" — executives who blended intense professional will with personal modesty. They were quick to give credit to others for success and to take responsibility for failure. Later studies have pointed in a similar direction, linking humble leadership with greater team engagement and learning. Why should humility matter so much? One explanation is that no leader, however talented, can possibly know everything in a complex organization. Leaders who admit what they don't know are more likely to ask for input, and their teams are more likely to offer it. Arrogant leaders, by contrast, are bound to hear only what they want to hear. None of this means that leaders should be passive or indecisive. Teams still need direction, and there will be moments when someone simply has to decide. But the old idea that admitting a mistake is a sign of weakness looks increasingly outdated. You'd think, after decades of evidence, that this lesson would be widely accepted. In many workplaces, however, it is still waiting to be learned.

questions.answer: A confident, decisive figure who had all the answers.

questions.q: Why does humility matter, according to the text?
questions.answer: No leader can know everything; humble leaders ask for input and get it.

questions.q: Does the text say leaders should be passive?
questions.answer: No — teams still need direction and decisions.

Subject: Hello from your new team leader

Dear all,

As most of you will know by now, I'm joining the customer experience team as your new leader from Monday. I wanted to take this opportunity to introduce myself and share a few thoughts about how I like to work.

I've spent the last eight years in customer service, first as an agent and later as a supervisor, so I have a pretty good idea of what your days look like — the good, the bad and the frustrating. That said, every team is different, and I'm bound to have a lot to learn about how things work here. Over the next few weeks, I'd like to meet each of you individually. The meetings should take about thirty minutes, and Ana will send out a schedule shortly.

In terms of style, I try to be hands-on without micromanaging. I'll set clear goals, but I trust you to decide how to reach them. I'd much rather you came to me with a problem early than tried to hide it — mistakes are inevitable, and you'll find I'm the first to own mine.

You may well have heard that the company is planning to introduce a new support platform later this year. I know changes like this can cause anxiety, and there may well be some difficult moments during the transition. However, I can promise that you'll be involved in the process from the start. After all, you know our customers better than anyone, so it would hardly make sense to plan this without you.

Finally, my door — or my Teams chat — is always open. If you have questions, ideas or concerns, you might as well send them now rather than wait for our meeting!

Looking forward to working with you all.

Best wishes,
Gabriela

grammar.title: Rhetorical devices and cleft sentences
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Regra de três (tricolon)** — três elementos paralelos soam completos e memoráveis:
- "Our app is **faster, cheaper and safer**."
- "**We listened, we learned, and we built** something better."

**2. Perguntas retóricas** — envolvem o público (você responde logo em seguida):
- "**How many of you** have waited an hour for a doctor's appointment? **Exactly.**"
- "**So, why does this matter?** Because..."

**3. Contraste e antítese:**
- "It's **not about** working harder; **it's about** working smarter."
- "**Yesterday**, it took three days. **Today**, it takes three minutes."

**4. Repetição (anáfora)** — repetir o início das frases:
- "**Every day**, families lose time. **Every day**, businesses lose money. **Every day**, we wait."

**5. Cleft sentences para foco** (revisão e expansão do B2):
- **What** + oração + **is/was**: "**What we need is** a simpler solution." / "**What surprised us was** the demand."
- **All** + oração (= a única coisa): "**All you need is** a phone."
- **The reason (why)... is that**: "**The reason why** we're different **is that** we listen."
- **The thing / The problem / The truth is (that)**: "**The problem is that** nobody trusts the current system."
- **It is/was... that/who**: "**It was** our customers **who** gave us this idea."

**6. Signposting** — sinaliza a estrutura:
- Começo: "I'd like to start by... / Let me begin with a question."
- Transição: "Let's move on to... / This brings me to... / Turning now to..."
- Ênfase: "I'd like to stress that... / The key point here is..."
- Fim: "To wrap up... / Let me leave you with one thought..."

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na **regra de três**, a entonação sobe nos dois primeiros itens e **cai** no último: "faster ↗, cheaper ↗ and safer ↘". Depois de uma **pergunta retórica**, faça uma **pausa de 1–2 segundos** — o silêncio cria impacto. Em **cleft sentences**, enfatize o elemento focado.

listening.title: Three tricks from the ancient world
listening.context_pt: Um professor de oratória explica recursos retóricos clássicos.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: More than two thousand years ago, Aristotle argued that persuasion rests on three pillars: ethos, your credibility; pathos, the emotions you create; and logos, your logic and evidence. Notice, by the way, that even his theory comes in three parts. The rule of three is everywhere in rhetoric. Julius Caesar's famous message, often quoted as "veni, vidi, vici" — "I came, I saw, I conquered" — is perhaps the most famous example. Why does it work? Psychologists suggest that three is the smallest number that creates a pattern. Two items feel like a comparison; four start to feel like a list. Three feels complete. The second trick is antithesis — putting opposites side by side. Think of Neil Armstrong's line about "one small step for man" and "one giant leap for mankind". And the third is the rhetorical question, which turns a lecture into a conversation. So, what do these techniques have in common? They make your message easier to remember. And in a pitch, what matters most is what people remember after you've left the room.

questions.q: What are Aristotle's three pillars of persuasion?
questions.answer: Ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion) and logos (logic and evidence).

questions.q: Why does the rule of three work?
questions.answer: Three is the smallest number that creates a pattern; it feels complete.

questions.q: What is antithesis?
questions.answer: Putting opposites side by side.

questions.q: What do the three techniques have in common?
questions.answer: They make the message easier to remember.

reading.title: Why most pitches fail
reading.text: Every year, thousands of founders stand in front of investors hoping to secure funding. Most of them fail — and, according to experienced investors, the reason is rarely the idea itself. What sinks most pitches is the way the idea is communicated. The first mistake is starting in the wrong place. Many founders open with their company history or a detailed description of their technology. Investors, however, want to understand the problem before they care about the solution. A strong pitch begins with a pain point the audience can feel — ideally one that is large, urgent and growing. The second mistake is trying to say too much. Faced with a short time slot, nervous presenters often try to cram every feature onto their slides. The result is confusion. What investors remember is a single clear message: who the product is for, what it does, and why it is better than the alternatives. The third mistake is neglecting evidence. Enthusiasm is necessary, but it is not sufficient. Investors want to see traction — paying customers, growth rates, partnerships — that proves the idea works outside the founder's imagination. Finally, many pitches simply end. The speaker reaches the last slide, says "thank you" and waits for questions. A compelling pitch, by contrast, finishes with a clear call to action: what the founder is asking for and what the investor will gain. The best founders understand that a pitch is not a lecture. It is the beginning of a relationship. And, as with any relationship, first impressions matter enormously.

writing.model:
Pitch script: AulaViva

How many of you had a teacher who changed your life? (Pause.) Now imagine if that teacher, after retiring, could keep changing lives — from home, a few hours a week.

That's the idea behind AulaViva.

Let me start with the problem. Across Brazil, many students who struggle at school have no access to extra help. Private tutoring is expensive, and public schools are often overloaded. At the same time, thousands of experienced teachers retire every year. They have the knowledge, the patience and, very often, the desire to keep teaching. What's missing is a bridge between these two groups.

AulaViva is that bridge. We're an online platform that connects retired teachers with students who need support. Sessions are affordable for families, flexible for teachers and free for students from low-income households, thanks to sponsorship from local businesses.

This brings me to our results. We launched a pilot in two cities last year. In six months, 120 retired teachers joined the platform and delivered more than 3,000 hours of tutoring. Participating schools reported that most students improved their maths grades. But it was the teachers who surprised us most: many told us they felt useful and connected again.

So, what makes us different? It's not just a tutoring app; it's a community. The reason why our teachers stay is that they feel valued, not just paid.

Now, let's look at the opportunity. Brazil has millions of students who could benefit, and the number of retired teachers is growing every year. We're ready to expand to ten more cities.

To wrap up, we're looking for an investment of two million reais to fund this expansion and develop our mobile app. In return, we're offering a 15% stake in a company with proven impact, a scalable model and a mission that matters.

What we're asking for today isn't charity. It's a partnership. Thank you.

grammar.title: Advanced passive forms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Modal + passive**
- Presente/futuro: **modal + be + particípio**: "The results **must be checked**." / "This **could be done** faster."
- Passado: **modal + have been + particípio**: "The sample **must have been contaminated**." / "The disease **could have been prevented**."
- Contínuo (raro): "The data **might be being analysed** right now."

**2. Get passive** (informal) → eventos **inesperados, acidentais** ou **negativos**; também mudança de estado:
- "He **got bitten** by a snake." / "Our flight **got cancelled**." / "She **got promoted**."
- Mais comum na fala; evite em textos acadêmicos.

**3. Have / get something done** (causativo)
- **Serviço** feito por outra pessoa: "I **had** my car **repaired**." / "We need to **get** the samples **analysed**."
- **Experiência negativa** (alguém fez algo com você): "She **had** her bag **stolen**." / "He **had** his application **rejected** three times."

**4. Verbos com dois objetos** (give, send, offer, award, show, lend, tell, promise):
- "They **gave** the scientists a prize." →
  • "The scientists **were given** a prize." (mais comum: pessoa como sujeito)
  • "A prize **was given to** the scientists."

**5. Passiva com preposição no final:**
- "The problem **was dealt with** quickly." / "This theory **has been argued about** for years."

**6. Passiva com verbos de percepção + infinitivo com to:**
- Ativa: "They **saw** him **leave**." → Passiva: "He **was seen to leave**."
- "She **was made to** repeat the experiment." (ativa: They made her repeat...)

listening.title: Science in Brazil

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: When people think of great scientific discoveries, Brazil isn't always the first country that comes to mind. Yet Brazilian scientists have made important contributions. In 1909, the physician Carlos Chagas described a new disease — now known as Chagas disease — identifying the parasite that causes it, the insect that transmits it and its clinical symptoms, an achievement that is often described as unique in the history of medicine. The country has also been praised for its agricultural research: Embrapa, the public agricultural research company founded in the 1970s, is widely credited with helping to transform the tropical savannah of the Cerrado into productive farmland — though the environmental costs of that transformation are still debated. And during the Zika outbreak of 2015 and 2016, Brazilian researchers were among the first to establish the link between the virus and microcephaly in newborns. These achievements could not have been made without public funding, which is why cuts to research budgets are a constant concern for the scientific community.
