reading.title: The scientist nobody believed
reading.text: For decades, the Hungarian-born biochemist Katalin Karikó was considered, by many of her colleagues, to be chasing an impossible dream. Her idea was to use messenger RNA — the molecule that carries genetic instructions inside cells — to make the body produce its own proteins, which could then be used to treat or prevent disease. The problem was that synthetic mRNA, when injected into animals, triggered a strong inflammatory reaction. Grant applications were rejected repeatedly, and in the 1990s she was demoted at the University of Pennsylvania. Most researchers would have given up. Karikó did not. In the early 2000s, working with the immunologist Drew Weissman, she discovered that the inflammatory reaction could be largely avoided if one of the building blocks of the mRNA was slightly modified. Their paper, published in 2005, attracted little attention at the time. Fifteen years later, it was fundamental to one of the fastest medical responses in history. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck, vaccines based on modified mRNA were developed, tested and approved in less than a year — a process that had traditionally taken a decade or more. Hundreds of millions of doses were administered worldwide. In 2023, Karikó and Weissman were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her story is often told as a lesson in persistence. But it also raises uncomfortable questions about the way science is funded. How many other good ideas have been abandoned because they could not be explained in a short grant proposal, or did not produce quick results?

questions.answer: To use mRNA to make the body produce its own proteins to treat or prevent disease.

questions.q: What was the main problem with synthetic mRNA?
questions.answer: It triggered a strong inflammatory reaction.

questions.q: What did Karikó and Weissman discover?
questions.answer: The reaction could be avoided by slightly modifying one of the mRNA's building blocks.

questions.q: What uncomfortable question does the story raise?
questions.answer: How many good ideas have been abandoned because of the way science is funded?

writing.model:
Ignaz Semmelweis: the doctor who asked for clean hands

In the 1840s, the maternity wards of Vienna General Hospital were divided into two clinics. In the first, women were attended by doctors and medical students; in the second, by midwives. Strangely, the death rate from a condition called childbed fever was far higher in the first clinic. Many mothers begged to be admitted to the second.

The young Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis was determined to find out why. A breakthrough was made in 1847, when a colleague died after being cut accidentally during an autopsy. His symptoms were remarkably similar to those of the dying mothers. Semmelweis concluded that the disease must have been carried by doctors who went straight from dissecting bodies to examining patients.

His solution was simple: all staff were required to have their hands washed in a chlorine solution before touching patients. The results were dramatic. Within months, the death rate in the first clinic had fallen sharply.

Yet his ideas were not welcomed. Many senior doctors were offended by the suggestion that they themselves could be responsible for their patients' deaths. Germ theory had not yet been developed, so his findings could not be fully explained. Semmelweis was not given a permanent position, and he eventually left Vienna.

His later years were tragic. His behaviour became increasingly erratic, and in 1865 he was committed to an asylum, where he died shortly afterwards, apparently after being beaten by guards.

Only years later, after the work of Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister, was Semmelweis recognized as a pioneer of antiseptic practice. Today he is often called "the saviour of mothers". His story is a painful reminder that good evidence can be ignored when it challenges powerful people — and that many lives might have been saved if he had been listened to.

grammar.title: The subjunctive and formal structures
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Subjuntivo presente** = **verbo base** para **todas as pessoas** (sem -s, sem do, sem tempo passado).
Aparece depois de verbos e adjetivos de **exigência, recomendação ou importância**:
- Verbos: **recommend, suggest, insist, demand, propose, request, require, ask, urge** + **that**
- Adjetivos: **it is essential / vital / crucial / important / necessary / imperative that**

"The doctor **recommended that** she **take** a break." (não "takes")
"They **insisted that** the trial **be** stopped." (não "is" / "was")
"It is **vital that** he **not** be informed yet." (negativa: **not** + base)

⚠️ O tempo do verbo principal **não muda** o subjuntivo: "They **demanded** that he **resign**."

**Alternativa britânica (menos formal):** **should** + verbo: "They recommended that the study **should be** suspended." Ambas são corretas.

**2. Should no lugar de if (inversão)** — hipóteses educadas e formais:
- "**Should you need** any further information, do not hesitate to contact us." (= If you need...)

**3. Were it not for / Had it not been for** (= se não fosse por):
- "**Were it not for** vaccines, millions more would die every year."
- "**Had it not been for** the transplant, he would have died."

**4. Expressões fixas com subjuntivo** (muito comuns!):
- **Be that as it may** (seja como for)
- **Come what may** (aconteça o que acontecer)
- **God save the King / Long live...**
- **Suffice it to say** (basta dizer)
- **If need be** (se for necessário)
- **So be it** (que assim seja)
- **..., be it X or Y** (seja X ou Y): "All life, **be it** human or animal, deserves respect."

dialogue.title: The ethics committee
dialogue.context_pt: Uma reunião de comitê de ética avalia uma proposta de pesquisa genética (situação fictícia).

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: Let's move on to the gene therapy proposal. Dr. Lima, could you summarize your concerns?
lines.pt: Vamos para a proposta de terapia gênica. Dr. Lima, poderia resumir suas preocupações?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lima
lines.en: Certainly. The science is promising, but I would recommend that the trial be limited to adult patients at first.
lines.pt: Claro. A ciência é promissora, mas eu recomendaria que o ensaio fosse limitado a pacientes adultos inicialmente.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: And informed consent?
lines.pt: E o consentimento informado?

lines.speaker: Dr. Lima
lines.en: That's my main point. It is essential that every participant fully understand the risks. Some of these patients are desperate, and desperation can affect judgement.
lines.pt: Esse é meu ponto principal. É essencial que cada participante entenda plenamente os riscos. Alguns desses pacientes estão desesperados, e o desespero pode afetar o julgamento.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: With respect, were it not for trials like this, these patients would have no hope at all. Delaying it also has a cost.
lines.pt: Com todo o respeito, não fossem ensaios como este, esses pacientes não teriam esperança nenhuma. Adiar também tem um custo.

lines.speaker: Dr. Lima
lines.en: Be that as it may, we have a duty to protect them. I'd also insist that an independent team monitor the results.
lines.pt: Seja como for, temos o dever de protegê-los. Eu também insistiria que uma equipe independente monitorasse os resultados.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: That's reasonable. Should any serious side effects appear, the trial could be stopped immediately.
lines.pt: Isso é razoável. Caso surjam efeitos colaterais graves, o ensaio poderia ser interrompido imediatamente.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.en: So, I propose that we approve the trial, subject to those two conditions. All in favour?
lines.pt: Então, proponho que aprovemos o ensaio, sujeito a essas duas condições. Todos a favor?

listening.title: The CRISPR babies
listening.context_pt: Uma jornalista científica relata o caso dos bebês editados geneticamente na China.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: In November 2018, the Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced that he had used the gene-editing tool CRISPR to alter the DNA of human embryos, resulting in the birth of twin girls. His stated aim was to make them resistant to HIV. The reaction from the scientific community was almost universally negative. Critics argued that the procedure was medically unnecessary, that its long-term effects were unknown, and that the changes could be passed on to future generations. Many questioned whether the parents had given truly informed consent. He was later sentenced to prison in China. The case led to calls from leading scientists that a global moratorium be placed on heritable genome editing until its safety and ethics could be properly assessed. It's worth noting that gene editing in non-reproductive cells — which only affects the patient — is a different matter, and therapies of this kind have already been approved in some countries. The line, most experts agree, is crossed when changes are made that will be inherited.

questions.q: What did He Jiankui announce in 2018?
questions.answer: He had edited the DNA of human embryos, resulting in the birth of twin girls.

questions.q: Name two criticisms of the procedure.
questions.answer: It was medically unnecessary / long-term effects unknown / changes could be inherited / doubts about consent.

questions.q: What did leading scientists call for?
questions.answer: A global moratorium on heritable genome editing.

questions.q: Where is the line crossed, according to most experts?
questions.answer: When changes are made that will be inherited.

reading.title: Who decides?
reading.text: Few technologies have raised hopes and fears as dramatically as gene editing. Tools such as CRISPR, whose developers Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020, allow scientists to modify DNA with a precision that would have been unimaginable a generation ago. The potential benefits are enormous. Inherited diseases that have caused suffering for centuries could, in theory, be corrected. In 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved the first therapy based on CRISPR, designed to treat sickle cell disease. Yet the same technology raises profound ethical questions. If it becomes possible to eliminate a disease, should it also be possible to select for height, intelligence or appearance? Critics warn of a slippery slope towards "designer babies" and a world in which genetic advantages are available only to the wealthy. Disability rights advocates have also asked who gets to decide which human traits count as "defects". Most scientific bodies currently insist that a clear distinction be maintained between somatic editing, which affects only the individual patient, and germline editing, whose changes would be inherited by future generations. The first is increasingly accepted; the second remains, in most countries, prohibited. But laws vary from one country to another, and technology tends to move faster than regulation. Were it not for international cooperation, the rules could easily be bypassed by researchers moving to countries with weaker oversight. Perhaps the most important question is not what science can do, but who should decide what it ought to do — scientists, governments, patients or society as a whole. Be that as it may, it seems essential that these decisions not be left to a few laboratories alone.

questions.q: Who developed CRISPR and what were they awarded?
questions.answer: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier; the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

questions.q: What was approved in 2023?
questions.answer: The first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle cell disease (UK and US).

questions.q: What is the difference between somatic and germline editing?
questions.answer: Somatic affects only the patient; germline changes are inherited.

questions.q: Why is international cooperation important?
questions.answer: Otherwise researchers could move to countries with weaker oversight.

writing.task: Write a formal essay (280–320 words): "Gene editing should be used only to treat disease, never to enhance human abilities." Discuss both sides and give your opinion. Use at least four subjunctive forms and two other formal structures from this lesson.

writing.model:
Treatment or enhancement? The limits of gene editing

Advances in gene-editing technology have made it possible, for the first time in history, to alter human DNA with remarkable precision. While few would object to its use in curing devastating diseases, many experts insist that a firm line be drawn between treatment and enhancement. This essay will examine whether such a line is both desirable and realistic.

The case for restricting gene editing to medical treatment is a strong one. Were it not for clear limits, the technology could easily be used to create genetic advantages for those who could afford them, deepening existing inequalities. Moreover, our understanding of the human genome remains incomplete. A change intended to improve one characteristic might have unforeseen consequences elsewhere, and if made in embryos, those consequences would be inherited by future generations. It is therefore vital that any intervention be justified by a serious medical need.

On the other hand, critics argue that the distinction between treatment and enhancement is far from clear. Is strengthening the immune system a treatment or an enhancement? What about reducing the risk of a condition that may never develop? Some have also pointed out that we already accept many forms of enhancement, from vaccines to education, and that refusing genetic improvements on principle may be inconsistent.

Be that as it may, I believe the risks of allowing enhancement currently outweigh the potential benefits. The technology is too new, its long-term effects too uncertain and its social consequences too unpredictable. I would therefore recommend that its use be limited to the treatment of serious diseases, and that any change to that policy be decided through public debate rather than by scientists or companies alone. Should our knowledge improve significantly in the future, the question could be reconsidered. Until then, caution seems the wisest course.

grammar.title: Describing data and academic hedging
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Descrevendo tendências** — duas estruturas equivalentes:
- **Verbo + advérbio:** "Sales **rose sharply**." / "Prices **fell slightly**."
- **Adjetivo + substantivo:** "There was **a sharp rise** in sales." / "**a slight fall** in prices."

**Verbos:** rise, increase, grow, climb, **soar**, **rocket** ↗ · fall, decrease, drop, decline, **plummet**, **plunge** ↘ · **fluctuate** ↕ · **level off**, **stabilize**, remain steady → · **peak**, reach a high/low
**Advérbios/adjetivos de intensidade:** dramatically, sharply, significantly, considerably, steadily, gradually, slightly, marginally

**Preposições** (erro comum!):
- rose **from** 10% **to** 25% · rose **by** 15 percentage points · **a** rise **in** prices · **a** rise **of** 15% · peaked **at** 30%

**Multiplicadores:** doubled / tripled / a **threefold** increase / **twice as many as** / **three times as high as**

**2. Aproximações:**
- **just over / just under / roughly / approximately / around / nearly / almost**
- **the vast majority / a significant minority / a small proportion / one in five / a quarter**

**3. Hedging acadêmico** (suavizar quando a evidência é limitada):
- Verbos: **appear to, seem to, tend to, suggest, indicate**
- Modais: **may, might, could**
- Expressões: **it would appear that / there is evidence to suggest that / to some extent / in some cases / it is likely that**
- Advérbios: **possibly, probably, arguably, apparently**

Compare:
- Forte demais: "Social media **causes** depression."
- Acadêmico: "There **is some evidence to suggest** that heavy social media use **may be associated with** higher rates of depression."

**Boosters** (quando a evidência é forte): clearly, undoubtedly, it is evident that, the data **demonstrate**.

examples.en: The number of internet users in Brazil rose steadily throughout the 2010s, reaching the vast majority of the population by the end of the decade.

examples.en: Just under a third of respondents said they had never used a public library.
examples.pt: Pouco menos de um terço dos entrevistados disse nunca ter usado uma biblioteca pública.

listening.title: Describing a graph

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Let's look at this example. The line graph shows the number of daily bicycle trips in a fictional city between 2010 and 2025. Overall, cycling increased dramatically over the period, although there were some fluctuations. In 2010, there were roughly 20,000 daily trips. This figure remained fairly stable until 2014, when the city opened its first network of cycle lanes. Over the following four years, the number of trips more than doubled, reaching just over 45,000 in 2018. There was a sharp fall in 2020, when trips plummeted to around 25,000, which would appear to be linked to lockdown restrictions. However, the figure recovered rapidly, peaking at approximately 60,000 in 2023 — a threefold increase compared with 2010 — before levelling off. Notice what I did there: an overview first, then the key figures, and a careful "would appear to be linked" — because the graph alone can't prove the cause.

reading.title: How to lie with statistics
reading.text: In 1954, the American writer Darrell Huff published a small book with a provocative title: How to Lie with Statistics. Despite its age, many of its warnings remain remarkably relevant. Perhaps the most common trap is confusing correlation with causation. Countries that consume more chocolate per person, for example, tend to have won more Nobel Prizes per capita — a correlation highlighted, half-jokingly, in a 2012 article in a medical journal. Few would seriously conclude that chocolate makes people smarter. A far more likely explanation is that both are associated with a third factor: national wealth. Yet similar reasoning appears regularly in headlines about diet, technology and health. A second trap involves relative and absolute risk. A headline announcing that a medicine "doubles the risk" of a side effect sounds alarming. But if the risk rises from one in 10,000 to two in 10,000, the absolute increase is tiny. Both statements are technically true; only one gives the reader a fair picture. Third, there is the problem of the sample. A survey of 200 enthusiastic app users cannot tell us much about the population as a whole, however impressive its results may appear. Finally, graphs themselves can mislead. By starting the vertical axis at a number other than zero, a designer can make a marginal change look dramatic. None of this means that statistics are useless — quite the opposite. Used carefully, they are among the most powerful tools we have for understanding the world. The point is that numbers, like words, need to be read critically. As a rule of thumb, it would seem wise to ask three questions of any statistic: compared to what, measured how, and according to whom?

questions.q: What is the chocolate example meant to show?
questions.answer: That correlation doesn't imply causation (both linked to national wealth).

questions.q: What is the difference between relative and absolute risk in the example?
questions.answer: "Doubles" sounds big, but the absolute rise is only from 1 to 2 in 10,000.

questions.q: How can graphs mislead?
questions.answer: By starting the vertical axis at a number other than zero.

questions.q: What three questions does the writer suggest asking?
questions.answer: Compared to what, measured how, and according to whom?

grammar.title: Advanced concession
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. However / Whatever / Whoever / Wherever / Whenever + oração** (= não importa como/o que/quem...)
- **However + adjetivo/advérbio + S + V**: "**However hard** I try, I can't understand it." / "**However much** it costs, we'll pay."
- "**Whatever** you decide, I'll support you." / "**Whoever** wins, the country will be divided."
- Com **may** (mais formal): "**However** difficult it **may** be, ..."

**2. No matter + what / how / who / where / when**
- "**No matter how** many times I explain, he doesn't listen." (≈ However many times...)
- "**No matter what** happens, stay calm."

**3. Adjetivo / advérbio + though / as + S + V** (formal, enfático):
- "**Difficult though** it is, we must decide." / "**Tempting as** it may be, we should not lie."

**4. Concessão com advérbios e expressões** (reconhecer → contrapor):
- **Admittedly**, ... / **Granted**, ... / **It is true that** ..., **but** ...
- **While it is true that** ..., ... / **Although it may be argued that** ..., ...
- **Be that as it may**, ... / **Even so**, ... / **All the same**, ... / **That said**, ...
- "**Admittedly**, lying can sometimes protect people. **Even so**, I believe honesty is the better policy in the long run."

**5. Much as / However much** (revisão da M1-L3): "**Much as** I admire her, I can't agree."

**Estrutura de argumento concessivo:**
**reconhecer** (Admittedly / Granted / While it is true that...) → **contrapor** (However / Even so / Be that as it may) → **reforçar a sua posição**.

dialogue.context_pt: Dois engenheiros discutem como programar um carro autônomo para situações de acidente inevitável.

lines.speaker: Rodrigo
lines.en: Here's the scenario we have to program for: the brakes fail, and the car must either hit a group of pedestrians or swerve into a wall, possibly killing the passenger.

listening.title: The Moral Machine
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora apresenta os resultados de um grande experimento online sobre dilemas morais.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: In 2016, researchers at MIT launched an online experiment called the Moral Machine. It presented visitors with variations of the famous trolley problem, adapted for self-driving cars: should the car save its passengers or the pedestrians? The young or the elderly? More lives or fewer? Millions of people from over two hundred countries and territories took part, and the results were published in Nature in 2018. Some preferences were broadly shared: in general, people chose to spare more lives rather than fewer, humans rather than animals, and the young rather than the old. But there were also notable cultural differences. Participants from some regions, for example, showed a weaker preference for sparing younger people. Whatever you think of the method — and it has been criticized for oversimplifying real situations — the study raises a difficult question. However universal our moral instincts may seem, they may not be the same everywhere. So whose values should a machine follow?

reading.title: Is it ever right to lie?
reading.text: Few moral questions are as old, or as practical, as this one. The eighteenth-century philosopher Immanuel Kant took an uncompromising position. Lying, he argued, is always wrong, whatever the consequences — even, in a much-debated example, when a murderer comes to your door asking where your friend is hiding. However extreme this may sound, Kant's reasoning was that a lie treats other people as mere instruments and undermines the trust on which all communication depends. Most people find this conclusion hard to accept. Admittedly, honesty is a value almost every culture shares. Even so, few of us believe we should tell a friend that their wedding speech was boring, or tell a terrified patient every grim statistic at once. Consequentialist philosophers, following thinkers such as John Stuart Mill, argue that the morality of an action depends on its outcomes. If a lie prevents serious harm, it may be not only permissible but right. Yet this view has its own difficulties. Who decides which consequences matter, and how far ahead must we look? A "white lie" that spares someone's feelings today may damage their trust tomorrow. Psychologists add an interesting twist. Research suggests that most of us lie more often than we think, and that we tend to judge our own lies far more generously than those of others. Much as we may admire honesty in principle, our everyday behaviour is more complicated. Perhaps the most realistic answer is that honesty is a strong default, not an absolute rule. Granted, that leaves us with grey areas. But moral life, whatever philosophers may wish, has always been full of them.

questions.q: What was Kant's position on lying?
questions.answer: Lying is always wrong, whatever the consequences.

questions.q: Why did Kant believe this?
questions.answer: A lie treats people as instruments and undermines trust.

questions.q: What do consequentialists argue?
questions.answer: The morality of an action depends on its outcomes.

questions.q: What does research suggest about how we judge lies?
questions.answer: We judge our own lies more generously than others'.

writing.model:
Is it ever right to break the law?

In a democratic society, laws are meant to reflect shared values and protect citizens. It might therefore seem obvious that they should always be obeyed. However, history offers numerous examples of people who broke the law and are now remembered as heroes. This essay will consider whether breaking the law can ever be justified.

There are strong arguments for obeying the law in all circumstances. If individuals could ignore any law they disagreed with, the result would be chaos. Whatever our personal views, the rule of law protects the weak from the strong and allows disagreements to be resolved peacefully. Admittedly, laws are sometimes unjust. Even so, democratic societies offer legal ways of changing them, such as elections, protests and the courts.

On the other hand, it is difficult to argue that every law deserves obedience. Rosa Parks broke the law when she refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, yet few people today would say she was wrong. However legitimate a government may appear, its laws can still be deeply immoral, and legal routes to change can be slow or blocked entirely. In such cases, peaceful civil disobedience may be the only way to draw attention to injustice.

Granted, the line between principled disobedience and simple law-breaking is not always clear. Much as we may admire activists, we should be wary of anyone who claims the right to decide which laws apply to them.

In conclusion, I believe that breaking the law can be justified, but only in exceptional circumstances: when the law is clearly unjust, when legal options have been exhausted, and when the act is peaceful and open, with the person willing to accept the consequences. Difficult though it may be to define these limits precisely, they distinguish conscience from mere convenience.

grammar.title: Descriptive language
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Adjetivos compostos** (duas palavras + hífen, antes do substantivo):
- **adjetivo/advérbio + particípio:** well-known, long-awaited, badly-paid, newly-built, highly-respected
- **substantivo + particípio:** sun-drenched, rain-soaked, home-made, hand-written, tear-stained
- **adjetivo + substantivo-ed:** blue-eyed, broken-hearted, open-minded, short-tempered, bad-tempered
- **substantivo/adjetivo + -ing:** heart-warming, record-breaking, mouth-watering, good-looking, never-ending
- **número + substantivo (singular!):** a **ten-minute** walk, a **five-star** hotel, a **two-hour** film

**2. Verbos expressivos** (mostram **como**):
- **walk:** stroll (sem pressa), stride (confiante), stagger (cambaleando), tiptoe (na ponta dos pés), wander (sem rumo), limp (mancando)
- **say:** whisper, mutter, mumble, yell, snap (irritado), sigh, stammer
- **look:** glance, stare, gaze (com admiração), peer (com dificuldade), glimpse
- **laugh:** giggle, chuckle, burst out laughing · **cry:** sob, weep

**3. Ordem dos adjetivos** (nativos seguem intuitivamente):
**opinião → tamanho → idade → forma → cor → origem → material → propósito + substantivo**
"a **lovely little old** **white** **Portuguese** **stone** cottage"
Na prática, use no máximo 2–3 adjetivos seguidos.

**4. "Show, don't tell"** — em vez de **dizer** a emoção, **mostre** com ações e detalhes:
- Tell: "She was nervous."
- Show: "She **glanced** at the clock for the third time, **twisting** her ring around her finger."

lines.en: "The man walked into the bar. He was sad because his wife had left him."

lines.en: OK. The information's there, but it's telling, not showing. How did he walk in?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: So find a verb that does that work. Did he stagger? Trudge? Drag himself?

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Much better! Now, instead of saying he's sad, show me a detail.
lines.pt: Muito melhor! Agora, em vez de dizer que ele está triste, me mostre um detalhe.

lines.speaker: Caio
lines.en: "He turned his wedding ring round and round, staring at the empty seat beside him."
lines.pt: "Ele girava a aliança sem parar, olhando fixamente para o lugar vazio ao lado."

lines.speaker: Teacher
lines.en: Now that's a story I want to keep reading. You don't need to tell me his wife left — I can feel it.
lines.pt: Agora sim, essa é uma história que eu quero continuar lendo. Você não precisa me dizer que a esposa foi embora — eu sinto.

listening.title: Why our brains love stories
listening.context_pt: Um neurocientista explica, num podcast, como o cérebro reage a histórias.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Why do stories grip us so powerfully? Part of the answer may lie in the brain. When we read a list of facts, the areas involved in processing language become active. But a number of studies have suggested that vivid descriptions can engage other areas too. In one experiment, words with strong smell associations, like "coffee" or "perfume", appeared to activate regions linked to the sense of smell. Metaphors involving texture — "a rough day", "a velvety voice" — seemed to engage areas related to touch. Researchers are cautious about these findings, and brain-imaging studies are notoriously difficult to interpret. But they're consistent with something writers have always known: a well-told story isn't just understood, it's experienced. That's also why stories are remembered so much better than statistics. Tell people that thousands of children are hungry, and they nod. Tell them about one child — her name, her face, what she had for breakfast — and they act.

questions.q: What happens in the brain when we read a list of facts?
questions.answer: The language-processing areas become active.

questions.q: What did words like "coffee" appear to activate?
questions.answer: Regions linked to the sense of smell.

questions.q: Why are researchers cautious?
questions.answer: Brain-imaging studies are notoriously difficult to interpret.

questions.q: Why are stories more effective than statistics?
questions.answer: People connect with an individual story and act; statistics just make them nod.

reading.title: Six words
reading.text: "For sale: baby shoes, never worn." These six words are often described as the shortest story ever written, and they are frequently attributed to Ernest Hemingway, who is said to have written them to win a bet. There is, however, no reliable evidence that he did; similar newspaper adverts had appeared years before. Whoever wrote it, the story is a perfect illustration of a principle at the heart of good writing: what is left out can be as powerful as what is put in. The reader is never told what happened. There is no description of grief, no explanation, no ending. And yet most readers feel a sudden, heart-breaking weight. The story works precisely because the reader's imagination does the work. Hemingway himself described a similar idea, sometimes called the "iceberg theory": a writer who knows his subject well can omit much of it, and the reader will still sense what lies beneath the surface. Many writing teachers express the same idea with the phrase "show, don't tell". Rather than stating that a character is lonely, a writer might describe him setting the table for two out of habit, then slowly putting one plate away. Rather than declaring that a city is poor, she might describe children playing football with a ball made of plastic bags. Of course, the rule can be overused. Sometimes the clearest, most efficient choice is simply to tell. But the six-word story reminds us of something worth remembering in any kind of writing, from novels to emails: readers are not passive recipients of information. Given the right details, they will build the world themselves.

questions.q: Is there evidence that Hemingway wrote the six-word story?
questions.answer: No reliable evidence; similar adverts had appeared before.

questions.q: Why does the story work?
questions.answer: The reader's imagination does the work; what is left out is powerful.

questions.q: What is the "iceberg theory"?
questions.answer: A writer can omit much of what they know, and the reader will sense what lies beneath.

questions.q: Give one example of "showing" from the text.
questions.answer: A man setting the table for two, then putting one plate away / children playing with a ball of plastic bags.

writing.model:
The letter

Nobody noticed the letter for three days.

It lay face down on the dusty hall table, half-hidden beneath a pile of pizza menus and electricity bills. The Oliveiras were a busy, fast-moving family: Paulo strode out of the house at six every morning, his phone already pressed to his ear; Cláudia rushed the twins to school, a half-eaten piece of toast in one hand; and sixteen-year-old Bia drifted in and out like a ghost, earphones permanently in place.

It was Dona Lurdes, the grandmother, who finally found it. She had shuffled into the hall on Thursday evening, searching for her reading glasses, when she glimpsed the familiar handwriting on the envelope. Her hands began to tremble.

She lowered herself slowly onto the stairs and peered at the faded stamp. Portugal. The postmark was three weeks old.

For a long time she simply sat there, turning the envelope over and over, as if it might disappear. Upstairs, a door slammed. Somewhere, a television roared with recorded laughter.

When Cláudia came looking for her, she found her mother-in-law still sitting on the bottom step, the letter open on her lap, tear-stained but smiling.

"Dona Lurdes? What's wrong?"

The old woman didn't answer at first. She smoothed out the thin, hand-written pages and pointed to the signature at the bottom.

"Fernando," she whispered. "My brother. I haven't heard his voice in fifty-two years."

Cláudia sat down beside her. Neither of them spoke. In the kitchen, the dinner was burning, and for once, nobody cared.

Later that night, the whole family gathered around the dining table — even Bia, who had taken her earphones out — while Dona Lurdes read the letter aloud. It was a long, rambling, heart-warming account of a life lived on the other side of the ocean: a fishing boat, a wife, four children, eleven grandchildren.

At the end, there was a phone number.

grammar.title: Word formation
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Prefixos negativos** (o contrário):
- **un-**: unpredictable, unconvincing, unforgettable, unrealistic
- **in-**: inaccurate, incomplete, insensitive
- **im-** (antes de m, p, b): impossible, impatient, immature
- **ir-** (antes de r): irrelevant, irresistible, irresponsible
- **il-** (antes de l): illogical, illegal, illiterate
- **dis-**: dishonest, dislike, disappointing, disagree
- **non-**: non-fiction, non-existent

**2. Prefixos de sentido:**
- **mis-** (errado): misunderstand, misinterpret, miscast, mislead
- **over- / under-** (demais / de menos): overrated / underrated, overpriced, underestimate
- **re-** (de novo): remake, reread, reinvent
- **out-** (superar): outperform, outsell, outlive
- **counter-** (contra): counterproductive, counterpart
- **co-**: co-star, co-writer

**3. Sufixos que formam substantivos:**
- **-ness**: darkness, awareness, effectiveness
- **-ity**: originality, creativity, popularity, authenticity
- **-ment**: disappointment, achievement, entertainment
- **-tion/-sion**: production, adaptation, tension
- **-ance/-ence**: performance, relevance, existence
- **-ship / -hood**: relationship, childhood

**4. Sufixos que formam adjetivos:**
- **-able/-ible**: predictable, forgettable, believable, incredible
- **-ive**: impressive, creative, repetitive
- **-ful / -less**: powerful, pointless, meaningless
- **-ous**: ambitious, humorous, glamorous
- **-al / -ic**: emotional, dramatic, iconic

**5. Sufixos que formam verbos e advérbios:**
- **-ize/-ise**: dramatize, criticize, romanticize · **-en**: strengthen, shorten · **-ify**: intensify, simplify
- **-ly**: surprisingly, unexpectedly, convincingly

**Dica de prova:** leia a frase toda e pergunte: preciso de **substantivo, adjetivo, verbo ou advérbio**? **Positivo ou negativo**? **Singular ou plural**?

examples.pt: Apesar da enorme popularidade, a série foi criticada pelos diálogos irrealistas.

examples.en: The remake is surprisingly faithful to the original, but it lacks originality.
examples.pt: O remake é surpreendentemente fiel ao original, mas falta originalidade.

grammar.tip_pt: Cuidado com os prefixos negativos que **não** seguem o português: **in**ac**cur**ate (impreciso), **un**able (incapaz), **dis**honest (desonesto), **un**comfortable (desconfortável), **ir**responsible. Na dúvida, consulte o dicionário — e anote a família inteira.

common_mistakes.why_pt: predict + -able → predictable.

common_mistakes.wrong: The ending was a big deception.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Decepção = disappointment; deception = enganação.

common_mistakes.wrong: It's an inbelievable story.

common_mistakes.why_pt: believable → unbelievable (un-, não in-).

pronunciation.tip_pt: O acento se move com os sufixos: **CRI**tic → **CRI**ticize → criti**CIS**m? Não! **CRI**ticism. Mas: o**RI**ginal → origi**NA**lity; **PHO**tograph → pho**TO**graphy → photo**GRA**phic; pre**DICT** → pre**DIC**table. Sufixos como **-ity, -ic, -ion** puxam o acento para a sílaba anterior.

listening.title: Can we trust online ratings?
listening.context_pt: Um especialista em mídia fala sobre avaliações online de filmes e séries.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Before watching a film, millions of people check a score — the percentage of positive reviews on an aggregator site, or the star rating on a streaming platform. These numbers are useful, but they can be misleading. First, a high percentage doesn't necessarily mean a film is outstanding; it means most critics found it at least acceptable. A film that nobody loves but nobody hates can score higher than a bold, divisive masterpiece. Second, audience ratings can be manipulated. There have been well-documented cases of "review bombing", in which groups of users deliberately flood a film with negative ratings, sometimes before it has even been released. And third, critics and audiences often disagree. Some films are critically acclaimed but commercially unsuccessful; others are box-office hits that critics dismiss. My advice? Don't rely on a single number. Read two or three reviews from critics whose taste you know — and remember that disagreement is part of the pleasure of art.

questions.q: What does a high percentage on an aggregator site mean?
questions.answer: Most critics found the film at least acceptable — not necessarily outstanding.

questions.q: Why can a divisive masterpiece score lower?
questions.answer: A film nobody loves or hates can get more positive reviews overall.

questions.q: What is "review bombing"?
questions.answer: Groups deliberately flooding a film with negative ratings.

questions.q: What is the speaker's advice?
questions.answer: Don't rely on a single number; read reviews from critics whose taste you know.

reading.title: In defence of the bad review
reading.text: In an age of star ratings and thumbs-up icons, the traditional film critic can seem like an endangered species. Many newspapers have reduced their arts coverage, and audiences increasingly rely on algorithms and influencers to decide what to watch. Some argue that critics have become irrelevant — or worse, that they are snobbish gatekeepers out of touch with what ordinary people enjoy. It is worth defending them, however, and especially their least popular product: the negative review. A thoughtful bad review is not simply an expression of dislike. At its best, it is an explanation — of why a story feels unconvincing, why a performance seems mechanical, why a film that cost hundreds of millions to make leaves no lasting impression. In explaining their disappointment, critics help readers understand what makes art work, and sharpen their own judgement in the process. Negative reviews also perform a useful function in an industry dominated by marketing. Studios spend enormous sums persuading audiences that every release is unmissable. Independent criticism offers a counterweight to that pressure, reminding us that our time and money are limited. Of course, criticism can be unfair, careless or simply cruel. A review that ridicules without explaining contributes little. And critics are not infallible: history is full of works that were dismissed on release and later recognized as masterpieces. But the solution to bad criticism is better criticism, not none at all. In the end, a culture in which everything is "amazing" is a culture in which nothing is. The willingness to say "this doesn't work, and here's why" may be one of the most valuable things a critic can offer.

questions.q: Why can critics seem like an endangered species?
questions.answer: Newspapers have reduced arts coverage, and audiences rely on algorithms and influencers.

questions.q: What is a thoughtful bad review, at its best?
questions.answer: An explanation of why something doesn't work.

questions.q: What function do negative reviews perform against marketing?
questions.answer: They offer a counterweight to studios' pressure that every release is unmissable.

questions.q: What does the final sentence mean: "a culture in which everything is amazing is a culture in which nothing is"?
questions.answer: If everything is praised, praise loses its meaning.

writing.model:
Review: City of the Tides (series, season 1)

There has been no shortage of hype around City of the Tides, the new eight-episode Brazilian thriller set in a fictional fishing town on the coast of Bahia. Expectations were high, and for the most part, the series lives up to them.

The story follows Inês, a marine biologist who returns to her childhood home after twenty years to investigate the mysterious disappearance of a research boat. What begins as a straightforward mystery gradually develops into a thought-provoking drama about memory, family loyalty and the environmental destruction of the coast.

The series' greatest strength is its atmosphere. The photography is breathtaking: sun-drenched beaches and storm-darkened skies create a sense of beauty that is constantly threatened. The lead actress gives a remarkably powerful performance, conveying her character's guilt and determination with impressive subtlety. The supporting cast is equally convincing, particularly the actor playing her estranged father.

Unfortunately, the series is not without its weaknesses. The middle episodes are overlong and somewhat repetitive, and a subplot involving a corrupt politician feels underdeveloped and, at times, frankly unbelievable. Some viewers may also find the final twist a little predictable — although, to be fair, it is handled with considerable emotional intensity.

Despite these flaws, City of the Tides is an ambitious and genuinely original piece of television. It avoids the temptation to oversimplify its themes, and it trusts its audience to draw their own conclusions. The cliffhanger at the end of the final episode makes a second season almost irresistible.

Verdict: not quite the masterpiece some critics have claimed, but a gripping, beautifully made series that deserves a wide international audience. Definitely worth a binge-watch.

Rating: ★★★★☆

warmup.text_pt: Um britânico diz que um filme horrível foi "**not bad**" ou que uma tempestade é "**a bit of rain**". Isso é **understatement** — e entender isso é essencial no C1! Hoje você vai aprender a mostrar **atitude** com advérbios como "**frankly**", "**arguably**", "**ironically**" e a entender o humor em inglês.
questions: What makes you laugh? Is your sense of humour typically Brazilian?
Have you ever told a joke in English that nobody understood?

grammar.title: Comment adverbs and attitude
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Comment adverbs** (ou **sentence adverbs**) comentam a **frase inteira**, mostrando sua atitude. Geralmente vêm **no início**, seguidos de vírgula.

**1. Honestidade / franqueza:** frankly, honestly, to be honest, candidly, quite frankly
"**Frankly**, the show was a waste of money."

**2. Concessão:** admittedly, granted, of course, to be fair
"**Admittedly**, the jokes were a bit old. **To be fair**, the audience loved them."

**3. Opinião / grau de certeza:** arguably (possivelmente — defensável), apparently, presumably, supposedly (supostamente — com dúvida), undoubtedly, evidently, clearly
"It is **arguably** the funniest series of the decade."

**4. Reação emocional:** surprisingly, unsurprisingly, ironically, fortunately, sadly, luckily, oddly / strangely enough, predictably, understandably
"**Ironically**, the comedian who mocked technology became famous on TikTok."

**5. Óbvio:** needless to say, obviously, naturally, of course
"**Needless to say**, I never told that joke again."

**Understatement** (dizer menos do que se quer dizer) — típico do humor britânico:
- "It was **a bit** chilly." (= estava congelando)
- "He's **not the most** patient person." (= ele é muito impaciente)
- "That **could have gone better**." (= foi um desastre)
- "**Not bad**" pode significar "muito bom" — o tom decide.

**Ironia verbal** = dizer o contrário do que se pensa, geralmente com tom marcado:
- (Durante uma tempestade) "**Lovely** weather for a picnic!"
- **Sarcasmo** = ironia com intenção de criticar ou ferir: "Oh, **great** job, really."

⚠️ Ironia e sarcasmo **não funcionam bem por escrito** sem contexto — em e-mails profissionais, evite!

rows: Frankly, I didn't get the joke.
To be fair, it was his first show.
Ironically, the expert got it wrong.
Needless to say, I was late.

examples.en: Admittedly, some of the jokes haven't aged well. Even so, it's arguably one of the most influential sitcoms ever made.
examples.pt: É verdade que algumas piadas envelheceram mal. Mesmo assim, é possivelmente uma das sitcoms mais influentes já feitas.

examples.en: The film is supposedly a comedy, but, quite frankly, I didn't laugh once.
examples.pt: O filme supostamente é uma comédia, mas, francamente, eu não ri uma vez.

examples.en: Ironically, the meeting about improving communication was cancelled because nobody received the invitation.
examples.pt: Ironicamente, a reunião sobre melhorar a comunicação foi cancelada porque ninguém recebeu o convite.

grammar.tip_pt: **Arguably** NÃO é "discutivelmente" no sentido negativo! Significa "**pode-se argumentar que / possivelmente**": "It's **arguably** the best film" = muitos diriam que é o melhor. E **eventually** ≠ eventualmente (= finalmente).

common_mistakes.wrong: Arguably, the film is terrible. (= é discutível)
common_mistakes.right: The film is arguably the best of the year. (= pode-se dizer que é)
common_mistakes.why_pt: Arguably reforça uma opinião defensável, não a põe em dúvida.

common_mistakes.wrong: Needless to say, but I was late.
common_mistakes.right: Needless to say, I was late.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Needless to say + frase direta, sem but.

common_mistakes.wrong: Ironically, it rained on my birthday. (simples azar)
common_mistakes.right: Ironically, the weather forecaster got caught in the storm.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Ironically = uma contradição inesperada, não só falta de sorte.

pronunciation.tip_pt: A ironia em inglês costuma vir com entonação **exagerada** ou **completamente plana** (deadpan): "Oh, **lovely** weather." (tom plano) / "**Great**. Just **great**." Understatement britânico é dito de forma **calma e neutra** — e é isso que o torna engraçado.
practice: (deadpan) Oh, lovely weather for a picnic.
(calm) Well, that could have gone better.

listening.title: Is humour universal?
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre humor em diferentes culturas.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: Laughter itself appears to be universal. Babies laugh long before they can speak, and researchers have observed play vocalizations resembling laughter in apes and other animals. But what people find funny varies enormously. British humour, for instance, is famous for understatement and irony. Saying "It's a bit damp" during a flood is, for many Britons, both funny and polite. Many Americans, by contrast, are often described as preferring a more direct, energetic style. In Brazil, humour is frequently warm and teasing, and it's often used to cope with difficult situations — there's a long tradition of making jokes about politics, inflation and everyday frustrations. Interestingly, what travels best across cultures tends to be physical comedy. Charlie Chaplin and Mr. Bean are loved almost everywhere, partly because they don't depend on words. Puns and wordplay, on the other hand, are notoriously difficult to translate. So, if you want to be funny in another language, my advice is: start with self-deprecation and situations people recognize, and save the puns for later.

questions.q: What evidence suggests laughter is universal?
questions.answer: Babies laugh before they speak, and animals like apes make laughter-like sounds.

questions.q: What is British humour famous for?
questions.answer: Understatement and irony.

questions.q: How is Brazilian humour described?
questions.answer: Warm, teasing and often used to cope with difficult situations.

questions.q: What type of comedy travels best, and why?
questions.answer: Physical comedy, because it doesn't depend on words.

reading.title: The serious science of humour
reading.text: Why do we laugh? For a phenomenon so familiar, humour has proved surprisingly difficult to explain. Philosophers have offered several theories over the centuries. The oldest, associated with Plato and Thomas Hobbes, is the "superiority theory": we laugh at the misfortunes or foolishness of others because it makes us feel superior. This arguably explains slapstick and some teasing, but it hardly accounts for a clever pun. A second explanation, the "relief theory", linked to Sigmund Freud among others, suggests that laughter releases nervous energy or suppressed feelings — which may explain why people sometimes laugh at funerals or after a frightening experience. The most widely discussed today, however, is the "incongruity theory": we laugh when something violates our expectations in a way that makes sense on second thought. A punchline works because it forces us to reinterpret what came before. More recently, the researchers Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren proposed what they call the "benign violation theory". According to this idea, something is funny when it is simultaneously wrong in some way — a violation of how things should be — and yet harmless, or benign. Tickling is a good illustration: a mild physical "attack" that is clearly not dangerous. The theory also helps explain why a joke can fail in two opposite ways. If it is too safe, it is boring; if the violation feels too real or too painful, it is offensive. Needless to say, no theory captures everything. Humour depends heavily on context, culture and timing, and attempts to analyse a joke tend, ironically, to kill it. As the American writer E. B. White reportedly put it, analysing humour is like dissecting a frog: few people are interested, and the frog dies.

questions.q: What does the superiority theory claim?
questions.answer: We laugh at others' misfortunes because it makes us feel superior.

questions.q: What does the incongruity theory claim?
questions.answer: We laugh when expectations are violated in a way that makes sense on second thought.

questions.q: What is the benign violation theory?
questions.answer: Something is funny when it is wrong in some way but harmless.

questions.q: In what two ways can a joke fail, according to this theory?
questions.answer: It can be too safe (boring) or too painful (offensive).

writing.task: Write an opinion column (280–320 words) titled "Is anything off-limits in comedy?". Use at least six different comment adverbs and one example of irony or understatement.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma coluna de opinião (280–320 palavras) intitulada "Existe algum limite no humor?". Use pelo menos seis comment adverbs diferentes e um exemplo de ironia ou understatement.
writing.model:
Is anything off-limits in comedy?

Few debates generate as much heat, and, ironically, as little laughter, as the question of what comedians should be allowed to joke about. Every few months, a comedian somewhere is accused of crossing a line, and the same arguments are repeated: either we are "too sensitive" or comedians are "punching down".

Admittedly, comedy has always depended on taking risks. Many of the most celebrated comedians in history became famous precisely because they said things others didn't dare to. Satire, in particular, has long been one of the few weapons ordinary people have against the powerful. Unsurprisingly, authoritarian governments tend to have very little tolerance for jokes about themselves.

To be fair, however, freedom to joke is not the same as freedom from criticism. If a comedian makes a joke that audiences find cruel, they are entitled to say so — and to stop buying tickets. That is not censorship; it is feedback. Frankly, the comedians who complain loudest about "cancel culture" often seem to have more media attention than ever.

What matters, arguably, is not the topic itself but the target. Joking about a tragedy is not necessarily wrong; joking at the expense of its victims usually is. Some of the funniest comedy I've seen dealt with illness, grief and racism — but the people being laughed at were the powerful, the absurd or the comedian themselves, not those already suffering.

Needless to say, there will never be a rulebook that everyone agrees on. Humour depends on context, timing and trust between performer and audience. A joke that works in a small comedy club may fall flat on social media, where context disappears.

So, is anything off-limits? Perhaps not in principle. But a comedian who ignores the difference between laughing with people and laughing at them is, to put it mildly, not doing their job very well.

culture_note.title: Humor britânico x brasileiro
culture_note.text_pt: O humor britânico é famoso por **ironia, understatement e autodepreciação** (pense em *Monty Python* ou *The Office* britânico). O brasileiro tende a ser mais **caloroso, exagerado e provocador**, com forte tradição de sátira política (de Chico Anysio a grupos de humor da internet). Uma dica: quando um britânico diz **"That's very brave"** sobre sua ideia, pode ser que ele ache a ideia péssima!

summary_pt: Franqueza: frankly, honestly · Concessão: admittedly, to be fair.

grammar.title: Advanced cleft sentences
grammar.explanation_pt:
Cleft sentences dividem uma frase em duas partes para **destacar** uma informação. Revisão: "**What** I need **is** a break." / "**It was** Ana **who** called."

**1. What-cleft com ações (do / happen):**
- "**What she did was** (to) leave the room." (destaca a ação)
- "**What happened was (that)** the alarm went off."
- "**What I'd do is** call the gallery directly."

**2. All-cleft** (= a única coisa, só):
- "**All I want is** an honest opinion." / "**All he did was** sign his name."
- "**All** you need to do **is** ask."

**3. Substantivos gerais + cleft:**
- **The thing (that)... is**: "**The thing that** annoys me **is** the price."
- **The reason (why)... is that**: "**The reason** it's famous **is that** it was stolen."
- **The person who / The place where / The day when / The way**: "**The place where** you really see her talent **is** in her drawings."
- **Where / When / Why / How** sem antecedente: "**Where** the film works **is** in its silences." / "**How** he did it **is** a mystery."

**4. It's not that... it's (just) that...** (corrigir um mal-entendido):
- "**It's not that** I hate modern art; **it's just that** some of it feels empty."
- "**It isn't** the price **that** bothers me; **it's** the attitude."

**5. Cleft reverso** (a informação destacada vem primeiro):
- "A good night's sleep **is what** I need." / "That**'s why** I left." / "That**'s where** we disagree."

**Fala informal:** "**The thing is**, ..." / "**What happened was**, ..." são muito comuns como **marcadores de discurso**.

listening.title: The painting that shredded itself
listening.context_pt: Uma repórter relata um dos episódios mais famosos do mercado de arte recente.

lines.speaker: Reporter
lines.en: In October 2018, at an auction at Sotheby's in London, a framed copy of Banksy's Girl with Balloon was sold for just over one million pounds. What happened next stunned the room. Moments after the hammer came down, an alarm sounded and the canvas began to slide through a shredder hidden inside the frame. Halfway through, the shredder stopped. Banksy later posted a video suggesting that he had built the device years earlier, in case the work was ever put up for auction. Many people assumed the stunt would destroy the painting's value. What it actually did was the opposite. The half-shredded work was renamed Love is in the Bin, and in 2021 it was sold again — this time for more than eighteen million pounds. The reason it became so valuable is that the shredding itself became part of the artwork, and, arguably, part of art history. It's not that the art market missed the joke; it's that the market turned the joke into a product.

questions.q: What happened just after the painting was sold in 2018?
questions.answer: A hidden shredder in the frame began to shred the canvas.

questions.q: Why had Banksy built the device, according to his video?

reading.title: What is art worth?
reading.text: In 2019, at the Art Basel fair in Miami, the Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan exhibited a work called Comedian: a real banana, attached to a wall with grey duct tape. Editions of the work were reportedly sold for around 120,000 dollars each. Then, to the delight of photographers, a performance artist peeled the banana off the wall and ate it. The gallery was unconcerned. What the buyers had purchased, it explained, was not the fruit itself but a certificate of authenticity and instructions for replacing it. The episode provoked a familiar mixture of laughter and outrage. For many people, it confirmed their suspicion that contemporary art is a joke played on the rich. Yet the story raises a serious question: where does the value of art actually lie? It is not that the materials of most great art are especially precious; paint, canvas and stone are relatively cheap. What we pay for, arguably, is something less tangible: an idea, a reputation, a story, a moment in history. Vincent van Gogh is often said to have sold only one painting in his lifetime — an oversimplification, but one that captures how little his work was valued while he lived. Today, his paintings rank among the most expensive ever sold. Nothing about the canvases changed. What changed was how people saw them. None of this means that every expensive work is a masterpiece, or that every unknown artist is a misunderstood genius. Markets can be driven by fashion, speculation and the desire for status. But perhaps the banana on the wall was doing exactly what art has always done: making us look again at something ordinary and ask what it means. The thing is, whether that is worth 120,000 dollars is a question no theory can answer for us.

questions.q: What might the banana have been doing, according to the writer?

writing.model:
Why I changed my mind about contemporary art

For years, my opinion of contemporary art could be summed up in one sentence: "My nephew could have done that." It's not that I disliked art in general — I loved Renaissance paintings and the bright, bold canvases of Tarsila do Amaral. It's just that I couldn't see the point of empty rooms, piles of bricks or a single line on a white wall.

What changed my mind was a weekend at Inhotim, the enormous art park in Minas Gerais, a few years ago. I went reluctantly, mainly because a friend had already bought the tickets.

The first surprise was the setting. Instead of white walls and silent guards, what I found were tropical gardens, lakes and pavilions hidden among the trees. The thing that struck me most, though, was how differently I felt when I wasn't being told what to think.

One installation in particular stayed with me. All it consisted of was a dark room and a sound recording of the earth itself. I had no idea what I was supposed to understand. What I actually did was sit there for twenty minutes, completely absorbed, feeling something I couldn't name.

That's when I realized what I'd been getting wrong. I'd been treating contemporary art like a puzzle with a correct answer, and getting annoyed when I couldn't solve it. Where it really works, I think, is in creating an experience rather than delivering a message.

I still don't like everything, of course. Some works seem to me pretentious, and the prices at international auctions are, frankly, absurd. But the reason I keep going back to galleries now is that I've stopped asking "What does it mean?" and started asking "What does it do to me?"

My nephew, incidentally, is now studying fine art. Perhaps he could have done it after all.

grammar.title: Formal future forms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Previsões (jornalismo, relatórios):**
- **be set to** + verbo: muito provável, já encaminhado — "Renewables **are set to** overtake coal."
- **be expected / likely / predicted to**: "Temperatures **are expected to** rise by..."
- **be poised to**: pronto para agir, prestes a — "The country **is poised to** become a leader in green hydrogen."
- **be bound to**: certeza (revisão C1-M2)

**2. Iminência:**
- **be about to** + verbo: prestes a (muito em breve) — "The meeting **is about to** start."
- **be on the verge / point / brink of** + substantivo ou -ing: à beira de
  "on the **verge of** a breakthrough" / "on the **point of** leaving" / "on the **brink of** extinction" (brink = algo negativo, catastrófico)

**3. Horários e cronogramas:**
- **be due to** + verbo / **be due** + tempo: previsto para — "The report **is due to** be published in May." / "The train **is due** at 5."

**4. be to + verbo** (formal): planos oficiais, ordens, instruções, destino
- Plano oficial: "The summit **is to be held** in Belém." / "The president **is to visit** the Amazon."
- Ordem/instrução: "You **are to report** to the director immediately." / "All staff **are not to** leave the building."
- Em condicionais: "If we **are to** meet our targets, we must act now." (= se quisermos)
- Passado (destino): "He **was** never **to** see his homeland again." (nunca mais veria)

**5. Futuro no passado** (revisão): was going to / was about to / was to have + pp (plano frustrado: "The bridge **was to have opened** in 2020.")

**Manchetes:** omitem o **be**: "Emissions **set to** fall" / "PM **to** resign" / "Species **on brink of** extinction".

reading.title: The Amazon at a tipping point?
reading.text: For decades, scientists have warned that the Amazon rainforest may be approaching a critical threshold. The concept is relatively simple. The forest generates a large share of its own rainfall: trees release moisture into the air, which forms clouds that carry rain further inland. As deforestation and climate change reduce the number of trees and increase temperatures, this cycle weakens. Beyond a certain point — a "tipping point" — parts of the forest could be unable to sustain themselves and might gradually turn into a drier, savannah-like ecosystem. Estimates of where exactly that point lies vary. In widely cited work, the Brazilian climate scientist Carlos Nobre and the American biologist Thomas Lovejoy suggested that it might be reached if deforestation exceeded around 20 to 25 percent of the original forest. Some studies indicate that parts of the eastern Amazon are already showing signs of stress, with longer dry seasons and, in certain areas, the forest releasing more carbon than it absorbs. Not all researchers agree on how close the tipping point is, and the forest is likely to respond differently from region to region. What is broadly accepted, however, is that the consequences of large-scale dieback would extend far beyond the Amazon itself. Rainfall in other parts of South America, including Brazil's agricultural heartland, depends partly on moisture from the forest. There are reasons for cautious hope. Deforestation rates have fallen significantly in some recent years, demonstrating that policy and enforcement can make a difference. Restoration projects are also under way. But if the Amazon is to remain a rainforest, many scientists argue, the next two decades are likely to be decisive.

questions.q: How does the Amazon generate its own rainfall?
questions.answer: Trees release moisture that forms clouds carrying rain further inland.

questions.q: What might happen beyond the tipping point?
questions.answer: Parts of the forest could turn into a drier, savannah-like ecosystem.

questions.q: What threshold did Nobre and Lovejoy suggest?
questions.answer: Around 20–25% deforestation of the original forest.

questions.q: Why would the consequences extend beyond the Amazon?
questions.answer: Rainfall elsewhere in South America, including farming regions, depends partly on the forest's moisture.

Coastal city set to build "sponge parks" to fight flooding

A coastal city in southern Brazil is set to become one of the first in the country to adopt "sponge city" techniques on a large scale, as it struggles to cope with increasingly frequent floods. (Fictional story created for this lesson.)

The city council is due to vote next Tuesday on a plan to transform six urban areas into parks designed to absorb rainwater, along with permeable pavements and rain gardens in several neighbourhoods. If approved, work is to begin in March, with the first park expected to open within eighteen months.

The plan comes after a series of floods last year left thousands of residents temporarily homeless. "We were on the verge of losing an entire neighbourhood," said the mayor at a press conference on Monday. "If we are to protect our citizens, we cannot simply build higher walls. We need to work with nature, not against it."

The concept of the "sponge city" was popularized in China, where cities have used green spaces, wetlands and permeable surfaces to reduce flooding. Experts say similar approaches are poised to spread across Latin America as extreme rainfall becomes more common.

Not everyone is convinced. Some business owners have warned that construction work is bound to disrupt trade in the city centre, while opposition councillors have questioned the project's estimated cost of 180 million reais.

Environmental scientist Dr. Helena Prado, who advised the council, said the investment would pay for itself. "Every flood costs the city millions in repairs and lost income," she explained. "The real question is not whether we can afford to do this, but whether we can afford not to."

The council's decision is expected to be announced on Tuesday evening.

grammar.title: Multi-word verbs with abstract meanings
grammar.explanation_pt:
Muitos phrasal verbs têm um **sentido literal** (B1/B2) e um **sentido abstrato** (C1), que aparece em textos formais.

**1. Causa e origem:**
- **bring about** = causar, provocar (mudança): "The war **brought about** mass migration."
- **stem from** = originar-se de: "Many problems **stem from** a lack of documents."
- **give rise to** = dar origem a: "Climate change **gives rise to** new forms of displacement."
- **lead to / result in** (revisão)

**2. Explicar e quantificar:**
- **account for** = representar (proporção) / explicar: "Women **account for** half of all migrants." / "How do you **account for** the increase?"
- **bear out** = confirmar: "The data **bear out** this theory."
- **point to** = indicar: "Studies **point to** economic factors."

**3. Enfrentar e lidar:**
- **come up against** = deparar-se com (obstáculo)
- **face up to** = encarar (realidade difícil)
- **grapple / contend with** = lutar com, lidar com
- **cope with / deal with** (revisão)

**4. Começar, propor-se, eliminar:**
- **set out to** = propor-se a / **set up** = criar, estabelecer
- **embark on** = embarcar em, começar (projeto, jornada)
- **do away with** = abolir / **phase out** = eliminar gradualmente
- **draw up** = elaborar (plano, documento) / **carry out** = realizar

**5. Outros úteis:**
- **fall through** = fracassar (plano) · **put forward** = propor (ideia) · **rule out** = descartar · **look into** = investigar · **bring up** = mencionar · **step up** = intensificar

**Registro:** muitos phrasal verbs têm equivalentes latinos mais formais:
bring about = **cause** · set up = **establish** · look into = **investigate** · do away with = **abolish** · put forward = **propose** · rule out = **exclude**
Em redações C1, uma **mistura** dos dois soa natural; só latinos soa pesado.

**Gramática:** verbos de três partes são **inseparáveis**: "face up **to** it" (não "face it up to").

rows: We must face up to the facts.
They did away with the visa.

examples.en: Much of the hostility towards migrants stems from misinformation about their impact on jobs and public services.
examples.pt: Grande parte da hostilidade contra migrantes vem da desinformação sobre seu impacto nos empregos e serviços públicos.

examples.en: Many newly arrived refugees come up against language barriers, bureaucracy and, at times, open prejudice.
examples.pt: Muitos refugiados recém-chegados esbarram em barreiras linguísticas, burocracia e, às vezes, preconceito aberto.

examples.en: Remittances account for a significant share of the economy in several Latin American countries.
examples.pt: As remessas representam uma parcela significativa da economia em vários países latino-americanos.

grammar.tip_pt: **Account for** é muito útil e muito confundido: "Migrants **account for** 10% of the population" (= representam) / "This **accounts for** the rise" (= explica). Não confunda com "count" ou "represent for".

pronunciation.tip_pt: Em phrasal verbs, o acento costuma cair na **partícula**: bring a**BOUT**, set **UP**, rule **OUT**. Em verbos de três partes, acento na **segunda** palavra: come up a**GAINST**? Não — come **UP** against, face **UP** to, do a**WAY** with.

They did aWAY with the rule.

dialogue.title: Starting again
dialogue.context_pt: Uma jornalista entrevista um homem venezuelano que reconstruiu a vida em Roraima e depois em Curitiba.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Thank you for talking to us, Diego. What brought about your decision to leave Venezuela?
lines.pt: Obrigada por conversar conosco, Diego. O que provocou sua decisão de sair da Venezuela?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.en: It stemmed from many things — shortages, no medicine for my mother, no future for my children. In the end, we simply couldn't cope with it any more.
lines.pt: Veio de muitas coisas — escassez, falta de remédio para minha mãe, nenhum futuro para meus filhos. No fim, simplesmente não conseguíamos mais lidar com aquilo.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: What were the first months in Brazil like?
lines.pt: Como foram os primeiros meses no Brasil?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.en: Hard. We came up against so many obstacles — the language, documents, finding work. I'm an engineer, but at first I worked in a supermarket.
lines.pt: Difíceis. Esbarramos em muitos obstáculos — a língua, documentos, achar trabalho. Sou engenheiro, mas no começo trabalhei num supermercado.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: And how did you end up in Curitiba?
lines.pt: E como você acabou em Curitiba?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.en: Through a relocation programme that helps people move from the border to other cities with more jobs. A local NGO helped us set up our life here.
lines.pt: Por meio de um programa de interiorização que ajuda pessoas a se mudarem da fronteira para outras cidades com mais empregos. Uma ONG local nos ajudou a montar nossa vida aqui.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: And now?
lines.pt: E agora?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.en: I had my qualifications recognized last year, and I'm working as an engineer again. And I've set out to help other newcomers — I give free Portuguese classes on Saturdays.
lines.pt: Tive meu diploma reconhecido ano passado e estou trabalhando como engenheiro de novo. E me propus a ajudar outros recém-chegados — dou aulas gratuitas de português aos sábados.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: What would you say to Brazilians who are suspicious of migrants?
lines.pt: O que você diria aos brasileiros que desconfiam dos migrantes?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.en: That most of that fear stems from not knowing us. Come and have a coffee with us. Most of us just want to work and give something back.
lines.pt: Que a maior parte desse medo vem de não nos conhecer. Venham tomar um café com a gente. A maioria de nós só quer trabalhar e retribuir.

listening.title: A nation of migrants
listening.context_pt: Um historiador fala sobre a história da migração no Brasil.

lines.speaker: Historian
lines.en: Brazil has been shaped by migration — much of it forced. Over three centuries, an estimated four to five million enslaved Africans were brought to Brazil, more than to any other country in the Americas. Their descendants account for a large part of today's population, and African influences run through Brazilian culture, from music and religion to food and language. From the late nineteenth century, a new wave of immigration began, much of it brought about by government policies to attract European labour after the abolition of slavery in 1888. Italians, Portuguese, Spaniards and Germans arrived in large numbers, followed by Japanese immigrants from 1908 — today, Brazil is home to the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan. Lebanese and Syrian communities also set down deep roots. In recent decades, the picture has changed again: Brazil has received people from Haiti, Venezuela, Bolivia and African countries, while hundreds of thousands of Brazilians have themselves emigrated, to places such as the United States, Portugal and Japan.

questions.q: How many enslaved Africans were brought to Brazil, according to estimates?
questions.answer: Four to five million.

questions.q: What brought about the wave of European immigration?
questions.answer: Government policies to attract European labour after the abolition of slavery in 1888.

questions.q: What is notable about the Japanese community in Brazil?
questions.answer: It's the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan.

questions.q: Where have many Brazilians emigrated to?
questions.answer: The United States, Portugal and Japan.

reading.title: The economics of migration
reading.text: Few issues provoke as much political debate as migration, and few are as widely misunderstood. Public opinion surveys in many countries suggest that people tend to overestimate the number of immigrants living among them, sometimes considerably. Much of the anxiety surrounding migration stems from economic fears: that newcomers will take jobs, push down wages or place an unbearable burden on public services. What does the evidence say? On the question of jobs, most economic research has failed to bear out the most pessimistic predictions. Migrants often take up work that local workers are unwilling or unavailable to do, or set up businesses that create new employment. Their effect on average wages is generally found to be small, although some studies point to modest negative effects for specific groups of low-skilled workers, particularly in the short term. Migrants also tend to be of working age, which means that, in ageing societies, they can help to pay for pensions and healthcare. At the same time, it would be naive to rule out real challenges. Rapid arrivals can put pressure on housing, schools and health services in particular areas, especially when governments fail to plan or invest accordingly. Integration does not happen automatically: newcomers frequently come up against language barriers, unrecognized qualifications and discrimination, all of which can prevent them from contributing fully. Emigration, meanwhile, has its own consequences for countries of origin. The "brain drain" of doctors, engineers and other professionals can weaken health and education systems, although remittances sent home by migrants account for a substantial share of income in many developing economies. Ultimately, the evidence suggests that migration is neither the catastrophe some fear nor the simple solution others claim. Its effects depend largely on how societies choose to face up to it.

questions.q: What do people tend to overestimate?
questions.answer: The number of immigrants living among them.

questions.q: What does most research say about migrants and jobs?
questions.answer: It has failed to bear out pessimistic predictions; effects on wages are generally small.

questions.q: What real challenges does the text mention?
questions.answer: Pressure on housing, schools and health services; integration barriers.

questions.q: What are the consequences for countries of origin?
questions.answer: Brain drain, but also significant income from remittances.
