writing.task: Write a formal proposal (280–320 words) to your city council suggesting a programme to help migrants and refugees integrate. Describe the problems they face, your proposal and its expected benefits. Use at least eight multi-word verbs.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma proposta formal (280–320 palavras) para a câmara municipal sugerindo um programa para ajudar migrantes e refugiados a se integrarem. Descreva os problemas, a proposta e os benefícios esperados. Use pelo menos oito multi-word verbs.
writing.model:
Proposal: The "Welcome Neighbour" integration programme

Introduction
The aim of this proposal is to put forward a programme to help the growing number of migrants and refugees in our city to integrate more quickly and fully into local life. Over the past five years, newcomers from Venezuela, Haiti and several African countries have come to account for a visible share of our population, yet support services remain limited.

Current situation
Interviews carried out by our association with more than sixty migrant families suggest that most of their difficulties stem from three sources: language barriers, the slow recognition of professional qualifications and a lack of information about public services. Many highly qualified people, including nurses and engineers, come up against so much bureaucracy that they end up in low-paid, informal work. This represents a waste of talent that the city cannot afford.

Proposal
We propose that the council set up a "Welcome Neighbour" centre, run in partnership with local NGOs and universities. The centre would:
• offer free Portuguese classes at different levels, including evening and weekend options;
• help newcomers draw up the documents needed to have their qualifications recognized;
• pair each family with a local volunteer "neighbour" for their first six months;
• organize regular cultural events to bring migrant and local communities together.

Expected benefits
The programme is likely to bring about faster integration into the job market, which would in turn increase tax revenue and reduce dependence on social support. Perhaps more importantly, it would help to do away with the misunderstandings and prejudice that often arise when communities live side by side without meeting.

Conclusion
We are aware that the council is facing budget constraints. However, the costs of the programme would be modest, and we believe the city cannot afford to ignore the issue. We would welcome the opportunity to present the proposal in more detail.

lessons.title: Truth and trust
lessons.subtitle_pt: Distanciamento: allegedly, reportedly, is alleged to have, reporting verbs com nuance
source_refs: CEFR / EAQUALS Core Inventory – C1 (distancing, reporting verbs)
Cambridge C1 Advanced – Reading and Use of English Part 7
objectives: Usar advérbios de distanciamento (allegedly, reportedly, supposedly, purportedly)
Usar passivas de relato em todos os tempos (is alleged to have been...)
Escolher reporting verbs que mostram atitude (claim, admit, deny, insist, concede)
Analisar desinformação e checar fatos

warmup.text_pt: Um jornal sério nunca diz "O político roubou dinheiro" antes de uma condenação. Diz: "The politician **allegedly** stole..." ou "He **is alleged to have** stolen...". Essa linguagem de **distanciamento** protege o autor e mostra ao leitor o **grau de certeza**. Tema: **desinformação e confiança**.

grammar.title: Distancing language
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Advérbios de distanciamento** — mostram que a informação **não foi confirmada** pelo autor:
- **allegedly** (acusação ainda não provada): "The mayor **allegedly** used public funds."
- **reportedly** (segundo relatos/a imprensa): "The singer is **reportedly** planning a tour."
- **supposedly** (supostamente — com dúvida/ironia): "The diet **supposedly** cures everything."
- **apparently** (ao que parece), **purportedly** (formal, = supostamente), **ostensibly** (aparentemente, mas na verdade não)

**2. Passivas de relato** (revisão B2 + todos os tempos):
- **It is + particípio + that**: "**It is alleged that** he lied." / "**It has been reported that**..."
- **Sujeito + be + particípio + infinitivo**:
  • presente: "He **is said to be** in Portugal."
  • contínuo: "He **is thought to be hiding** abroad."
  • passado: "He **is alleged to have lied**."
  • passado passivo: "The data **are believed to have been manipulated**."
  • passado do relato: "She **was reported to have left** the country."
- **There is said / thought to be**: "**There are thought to be** thousands of fake accounts."

**3. Reporting verbs que mostram atitude:**
- **Neutro:** say, state, report, explain
- **Dúvida do autor:** **claim** (afirmar, sem prova), **allege**, **purport**
- **Admitir:** **admit**, **concede** (admitir a contragosto), **acknowledge**
- **Negar:** **deny** (+ -ing / that), **reject**, **dismiss** (descartar como sem importância)
- **Insistir:** **insist**, **maintain** (sustentar), **assert**
- **Prometer/ameaçar:** pledge, vow, threaten

Compare: "The CEO **said** profits were stable" (neutro) x "The CEO **claimed** profits were stable" (o jornalista duvida) x "The CEO **conceded** profits had fallen" (admitiu a contragosto).

rows: It is claimed that the photo is fake.
She is said to be very ill.
S + is + pp + to have + pp
He is believed to have fled.
The votes are alleged to have been altered.
There are thought to be 200 victims.
He denied having seen the email.

examples.en: The video, which is reported to have been viewed millions of times, was later shown to be a deepfake.

examples.en: There are thought to be thousands of automated accounts spreading political content.

grammar.tip_pt: **Claim** em inglês carrega **dúvida**: "He **claims** to be a doctor" sugere que talvez não seja. Para relatar de forma neutra, use **say** ou **state**. Escolher o verbo certo é escolher sua **atitude** em relação à informação.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **Allegedly** = "a-LÉ-djid-li" (4 sílabas, o -ed é pronunciado "id"!). **Reportedly** = "ri-PÓR-tid-li". **Supposedly** = "sa-PÔU-zid-li" (não "supposably"!).

dialogue.title: Is this true?
dialogue.context_pt: Uma checadora de fatos ajuda o pai a verificar uma mensagem que ele recebeu no grupo da família.

lines.speaker: Dad
lines.en: Look at this message from the family group. It says a famous doctor has discovered that lemon water cures diabetes!
lines.pt: Olha essa mensagem do grupo da família. Diz que um médico famoso descobriu que água com limão cura diabetes!

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.en: Hmm. Who's the doctor? Is there a link to a study?
lines.pt: Hmm. Quem é o médico? Tem link para algum estudo?

lines.speaker: Dad
lines.en: It just says he's "a renowned specialist". And it's supposedly been shared a million times.
lines.pt: Só diz que é "um especialista renomado". E supostamente foi compartilhado um milhão de vezes.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.en: That's a classic sign. Let me search... OK, here. Fact-checkers debunked this months ago. The "doctor" is alleged to be a fake profile, and the photo is reported to have been taken from a stock image site.
lines.pt: Esse é um sinal clássico. Deixa eu pesquisar... OK, aqui. Checadores desmentiram isso meses atrás. Alega-se que o "médico" é um perfil falso, e a foto teria sido tirada de um banco de imagens.

lines.speaker: Dad
lines.en: But your aunt insisted it was true!
lines.pt: Mas sua tia insistiu que era verdade!

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.en: I'm sure she meant well. But the people behind it are thought to be selling a "miracle" supplement. That's what the link at the bottom is for.
lines.pt: Tenho certeza de que ela teve boa intenção. Mas acredita-se que quem está por trás disso vende um suplemento "milagroso". É para isso que serve o link no final.

lines.speaker: Dad
lines.en: Oh. I almost bought it. OK, I concede — I should have checked.
lines.pt: Ah. Quase comprei. OK, admito — eu deveria ter checado.

lines.speaker: Fernanda
lines.en: Don't worry. Just remember: if a message makes you feel shocked or excited and asks you to share urgently, stop and check first.
lines.pt: Não se preocupe. Só lembra: se uma mensagem te deixa chocado ou empolgado e pede para compartilhar com urgência, pare e verifique antes.

listening.title: Why lies spread faster
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre um estudo famoso sobre notícias falsas no Twitter.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: In 2018, a team of researchers at MIT published a study in the journal Science that analysed around 126,000 stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017. Each story had been checked by independent fact-checking organizations. The findings were striking. False stories were found to spread significantly further, faster and more widely than true ones. According to the study, false news was about 70 percent more likely to be retweeted than the truth. Why? The researchers suggested that false stories tend to be more novel and surprising, and that they provoke stronger emotional reactions, such as disgust and fear. Interestingly, the study concluded that it was humans, not automated bots, who were primarily responsible for the difference. Bots were found to spread true and false stories at similar rates. The implication is uncomfortable. If we want to fight misinformation, it is not enough to blame algorithms or foreign agents. We also have to look at our own behaviour — and pause before we click "share".

questions.q: What did the MIT study analyse?
questions.answer: Around 126,000 stories shared on Twitter between 2006 and 2017.

questions.q: How much more likely was false news to be retweeted?
questions.answer: About 70 percent more likely.

questions.q: Why do false stories spread faster, according to the researchers?
questions.answer: They are more novel and provoke stronger emotions.

questions.q: Who was primarily responsible for spreading false news?
questions.answer: Humans, not bots.

reading.title: The age of deepfakes
reading.text: In 2018, a video appeared online in which former US president Barack Obama seemed to insult his successor. The video was not real. It had been created by the media company BuzzFeed, in collaboration with the filmmaker Jordan Peele, who voiced the words, to warn the public about a new kind of technology: deepfakes. Since then, the tools needed to produce convincing fake video and audio have become dramatically cheaper and easier to use. What once required a professional studio can now reportedly be done in minutes with a laptop or even a phone. The consequences are already visible. Fake audio recordings of politicians have allegedly been circulated shortly before elections in several countries, when there is little time to debunk them. Criminals are reported to have used cloned voices of company executives to persuade employees to transfer money. Ordinary people, too, have been targeted with fabricated images. Perhaps the most worrying effect, however, is not that people will believe fake content but that they will stop believing real content. Researchers have called this the "liar's dividend": when anything could be fake, those caught on camera doing something wrong can simply claim that the evidence has been fabricated. Truth itself becomes a matter of opinion. There are responses. Technology companies are said to be developing tools to detect manipulated media and to label AI-generated content, and several governments have introduced or proposed regulations. Journalists and fact-checkers are increasingly trained in verification techniques. But most experts concede that technology alone cannot solve the problem. In the end, the best defence may be an old-fashioned one: a healthy scepticism, combined with trust in reliable, accountable sources.

Health app accused of selling users' data

A popular fitness app with more than five million Brazilian users is alleged to have sold sensitive health information to advertisers without users' consent, according to an investigation published yesterday. (Fictional story created for this lesson.)

The company, VidaFit, reportedly shared data including users' weight, sleep patterns and menstrual cycles with at least three marketing firms between 2022 and 2024. Internal emails seen by journalists are said to show that senior managers were aware of the practice.

In a statement released on Monday evening, VidaFit's CEO, Marcos Teixeira, denied that the company had "ever sold personal data". He insisted that all information shared with partners had been "fully anonymized" and claimed that users had agreed to the practice when accepting the app's terms and conditions.

Privacy experts, however, dismissed this explanation. "Health data is extremely difficult to anonymize," said Dr. Larissa Moura, a specialist in digital rights. "And it is hard to argue that consent buried on page forty of the terms is genuine consent."

The national data protection authority is understood to have opened a preliminary investigation. If the allegations are confirmed, the company could face fines of up to 2% of its revenue in Brazil, as provided for under the General Data Protection Law (LGPD).

By Tuesday afternoon, the company appeared to be changing its position. A spokesperson conceded that "communication with users could have been clearer" and announced that the data-sharing programme had been suspended "as a precaution".

The case has prompted calls for stricter rules on health apps. Thousands of users are thought to have deleted their accounts since the story broke, and a consumer group has threatened to take legal action.

grammar.title: Cohesion in writing
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Coesão** = os mecanismos que **ligam** frases e parágrafos. Um texto C1 usa vários, **sem exagerar nos conectores**.

**1. Referência (para trás):**
- **this / that / these / those** + substantivo: "Many cities have introduced bike lanes. **This policy** has..."
- **such** + substantivo (= desse tipo): "**Such measures** are expensive." / "**Such a policy**..."
- **the former / the latter** (o primeiro / o último de **dois**): "Investing in schools or hospitals? **The former** has long-term benefits; **the latter** saves lives now."
- **it / they / which** (pronomes — cuidado com ambiguidade!)

**2. "Umbrella nouns"** — substantivos gerais que resumem uma ideia anterior:
**this issue / problem / trend / approach / development / situation / view / claim / argument / measure / phenomenon**
"Young people are increasingly leaving rural areas. **This trend** has serious consequences..."

**3. Sinônimos e variação lexical** — evite repetir a mesma palavra:
public transport → the transport network → buses and trains → the system

**4. Substituição e elipse** (revisão C1-M1-L2): do so, one(s), so/not.

**5. Transições entre parágrafos** (ligam ideia anterior + nova):
- "**Turning now to** healthcare, ..."
- "**Another area which deserves attention is**..."
- "**While** improving transport would clearly benefit commuters, **investing in** education might have more far-reaching effects."
- "**Having considered** X, **it is worth examining** Y."

**6. Estrutura do essay C1 Advanced (avaliar 2 de 3 opções):**
1. **Introdução:** apresente o tema e diga quais duas opções vai discutir.
2. **Parágrafo 1:** opção A — vantagens, exemplos, possíveis limitações.
3. **Parágrafo 2:** opção B — idem.
4. **Conclusão:** diga **qual é mais importante/eficaz** e **por quê** (obrigatório!).

⚠️ **Dica:** um conector por frase é muito. Use **referência e vocabulário** para criar coesão — isso é o que distingue C1.

lines.speaker: Teacher

listening.title: What examiners look for
listening.context_pt: Uma examinadora explica os critérios de correção do essay C1.

lines.speaker: Examiner
lines.en: At C1 level, the difference between a good essay and an excellent one is often not the ideas but the organization. We assess writing in four areas: content, communicative achievement, organization and language. Under organization, we're looking for a text that is well structured and cohesive, using a variety of devices — not just linking words. Many candidates think that the more "furthermore" and "moreover" they use, the higher their score will be. In fact, overusing linking words can make a text feel mechanical. What really impresses examiners is when ideas flow naturally: when a sentence refers back to the previous one using "this problem" or "such an approach", and when paragraphs are connected by a clear line of argument. The other common mistake is forgetting part of the task. In the essay, you must clearly state which option you consider more important, and give reasons. If you don't, your content score will suffer, however good your English is.

questions.q: What is often the difference between good and excellent essays at C1?
questions.answer: The organization, not the ideas.

questions.q: What mistake do many candidates make with linking words?
questions.answer: They overuse them, making the text feel mechanical.

questions.q: What really impresses examiners?
questions.answer: Ideas flowing naturally, with reference (this problem, such an approach) and a clear line of argument.

questions.q: What part of the task do candidates often forget?
questions.answer: Stating which option is more important and giving reasons.

reading.title: Model essay: Improving life in cities
reading.text:
Over half of the world's population now lives in cities, and this proportion is expected to keep rising. As a result, the question of how to make urban life healthier and more sustainable has become increasingly urgent. Of the various measures available to governments, investment in public transport and the provision of affordable housing are two of the most frequently discussed.

An efficient public transport system can transform daily life. When buses and trains are frequent, safe and affordable, fewer people depend on cars, which in turn reduces congestion, air pollution and carbon emissions. Such a network also widens access to jobs and education, particularly for those living on the outskirts. However, this kind of infrastructure is costly and can take years to build, and its benefits depend heavily on good planning and maintenance.

Affordable housing, by contrast, addresses a more fundamental need. In many cities, soaring rents have pushed low-income families into informal settlements or distant suburbs, where they face long commutes and limited services. Providing decent homes closer to city centres would not only improve living conditions but also reduce the very travel demands that transport investment seeks to meet. Admittedly, such programmes can be poorly managed and may concentrate poverty if they are badly designed.

On balance, although both measures are valuable, I believe the latter should be the priority. Without a secure, affordable place to live, people cannot fully benefit from any other improvement a city has to offer. Moreover, well-located housing reduces the need for long journeys in the first place, making it, in the long term, the more far-reaching solution.

questions.q: Which two measures does the essay discuss?
questions.answer: Investment in public transport and affordable housing.

questions.q: What benefits of public transport are mentioned?
questions.answer: Less congestion, pollution and emissions; wider access to jobs and education.

questions.answer: Such a network / this kind of infrastructure / which in turn / However.

questions.q: Which option does the writer prioritize, and why?
questions.answer: Affordable housing (the latter): it's a fundamental need and reduces the need for long journeys.

writing.model:
Reducing inequality: where should governments begin?

Inequality remains one of the most persistent challenges facing countries such as Brazil. Of the many policies proposed to address this issue, a guaranteed minimum income and investment in early childhood education are among the most widely debated.

A guaranteed minimum income offers immediate relief. By ensuring that every household has enough to cover its basic needs, such a scheme can reduce extreme poverty almost overnight. Cash transfer programmes have been credited with lowering poverty rates in several countries, including Brazil, and they allow families to decide for themselves how best to spend the money. Nevertheless, this approach is expensive and, on its own, does little to change the conditions that cause poverty in the first place.

Early childhood education, by contrast, targets those underlying conditions. Research suggests that the first years of life are crucial for cognitive and social development, and that children from poorer families who attend high-quality nurseries and pre-schools are more likely to succeed later on. The benefits of this investment, however, take many years to appear, which makes it politically less attractive.

On balance, although both measures have clear merits, I believe the latter is ultimately more effective. While a minimum income alleviates the symptoms of inequality, early education addresses one of its root causes, giving children a fairer start regardless of their background. Ideally, the two policies would work together; if only one can be prioritized, however, investing in the youngest citizens is likely to have the most far-reaching impact.

grammar.title: Diplomatic language and softening
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Qualificadores e advérbios suavizadores:**
- **not entirely / not quite / not really / not particularly**: "I'm **not entirely** happy with this." (= não estou feliz)
- **slightly / a bit / somewhat / rather**: "The price is **slightly** higher than we expected."
- **a little / a few**: "There are **a few** issues we need to discuss."

**2. Modais e condicionais** (tornam afirmações hipotéticas e menos impositivas):
- "That **would** be difficult." (= é difícil/impossível)
- "We **might** need to rethink this." / "It **could** be a problem."
- "**It might be worth** + -ing": "It might be worth checking the figures again."

**3. Passado e contínuo de distanciamento** (revisão C1-M1-L1):
- "I **was wondering** if..." / "We **were hoping** for a lower price." / "I **was thinking** we could..."

**4. Perguntas negativas** (sugerir sem impor):
- "**Wouldn't it be** better to wait?" / "**Shouldn't we** check with the client first?" / "**Isn't** there a risk that...?"

**5. Understatement e negação do oposto:**
- "That's **not ideal**." (= é ruim) / "It's **not the best** solution." / "I'm **not a huge fan of**..."
- Negue o positivo em vez de afirmar o negativo: "It's **not very** clear" (em vez de "It's confusing").

**6. Passiva e impessoalidade** (tirar o foco da pessoa):
- "**You made** a mistake" → "**A mistake seems to have been made**" / "**There seems to be** an error in..."

**7. Frases de transição e preparação:**
- "**I see your point, but**..." / "**With respect**, ..." / "**I take your point. However**, ..." / "**To be honest**, ..." / "**I'm afraid** that..."

⚠️ **Não exagere:** diplomacia demais pode soar falsa ou confusa. Em culturas diretas (Holanda, Alemanha, Israel), seja mais claro.

listening.title: Getting to yes
listening.context_pt: Um especialista em negociação fala sobre o método de Harvard.

lines.speaker: Expert
lines.en: In 1981, Roger Fisher and William Ury of the Harvard Negotiation Project published Getting to Yes, a book that became one of the most influential guides to negotiation ever written. Their central idea was to move away from what they called "positional bargaining", where each side digs in and defends a fixed position, towards "principled negotiation". This rests on a few key principles. First, separate the people from the problem: you can be tough on the issue while remaining respectful to the person. Second, focus on interests, not positions. Two people might both demand the same orange — but if one wants the juice and the other wants the peel for a cake, there's a solution that satisfies both. Third, invent options for mutual gain before deciding. And fourth, insist on objective criteria, such as market prices or expert opinion, rather than a contest of wills. Diplomatic language is essential here. It allows you to challenge ideas without attacking people — which is often what makes agreement possible.

questions.q: What does the orange example illustrate?

reading.title: Lost in diplomacy
reading.text: Every culture has its own rules about how directly people should express disagreement, and misunderstandings between cultures can be costly. In her influential book The Culture Map, Erin Meyer, a professor at the business school INSEAD, describes a scale ranging from cultures where negative feedback is delivered directly to those where it is delivered indirectly. In the Netherlands, Israel and Germany, she argues, people tend to give criticism frankly, often using "upgraders" such as "absolutely" or "totally": "This is totally inappropriate." In the United Kingdom, Japan and much of Southeast Asia, by contrast, criticism is typically softened with "downgraders": "This might be slightly inappropriate." The problem arises when the two styles meet. A Dutch manager who tells a British colleague that his presentation was "a bit weak" may think she is being helpful; the British colleague may hear something far more devastating, because in his culture "a bit weak" is how one might describe a disaster. Conversely, a British manager who describes a project as "not quite what we were hoping for" may be shocked to discover that a Dutch employee interpreted this as minor feedback. Brazil occupies an interesting position. Brazilians are often described as expressive and warm, and comfortable showing emotion. Yet when it comes to negative feedback, especially towards superiors or in public, many Brazilians tend to soften their message considerably — sometimes so much that the criticism is missed entirely. The lesson is not that one style is superior. It is that effective communicators learn to recognize the code being used and, when necessary, check their understanding. A simple question — "Just to make sure I understand, are you saying that we need to redo this?" — can prevent a great deal of confusion.

questions.q: What scale does Erin Meyer describe?
questions.answer: From cultures where negative feedback is direct to those where it is indirect.

questions.q: What are "upgraders" and "downgraders"?
questions.answer: Words that intensify (absolutely, totally) or soften (slightly, might) criticism.

questions.q: Why might a British colleague be devastated by "a bit weak"?
questions.answer: In his culture, "a bit weak" can describe a disaster.

questions.q: What simple strategy does the text recommend?
questions.answer: Check your understanding with a clarifying question.

Subject: Your proposal for the São Paulo event

Dear Ms. Walker,

Thank you very much for sending us your proposal for the launch event in São Paulo, and for the time your team has clearly put into it. We were particularly impressed by the creative concept and the attention to detail in the programme.

Having discussed the proposal internally, however, there are a few points we would like to raise before moving forward.

Firstly, I'm afraid the overall budget is somewhat higher than we had anticipated. We were hoping to keep the total closer to 250,000 reais, and we wondered whether there might be some flexibility, perhaps in the catering or decoration costs.

Secondly, while we can see the appeal of holding the event at a hotel, we are not entirely convinced that this would be the best choice for our audience. Many of our guests are from the creative industries, and a more informal space — such as a converted warehouse — might create a more suitable atmosphere. Would it be possible to suggest one or two alternative venues?

Finally, there seems to be a slight discrepancy in the dates. The proposal refers to 14 March, whereas we had discussed the following week. It might be worth confirming this as soon as possible, as several of our speakers have limited availability.

None of these points should detract from the overall quality of your work, and we remain very keen to work with you. Perhaps we could arrange a short video call early next week to discuss possible adjustments?

Thank you once again, and I look forward to hearing from you.

Kind regards,

Camila Rocha
Marketing Director

grammar.title: Advanced conditionals
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Condicionais invertidos** (formais, sem if):
- **Should + S + verbo** (= if... should / if, possibilidade remota — 1º condicional): "**Should** the flight **be** delayed, we will inform you."
- **Were + S + to + verbo** (= if... were to — 2º condicional, hipótese): "**Were** the company **to** close, 500 people would lose their jobs."
- **Were + S + noun/adj** (com be): "**Were** I in your position, I'd accept."
- **Had + S + particípio** (3º condicional): "**Had** we **known**, we would have acted."
- **Negativas:** "**Should** you **not** wish to continue..." / "**Had** it **not been** for..." (nunca "Hadn't it...")

**2. If + will / would** (exceções!):
- **Pedidos educados:** "**If you'll** follow me, I'll show you to your seat." / "**If you would** sign here, please."
- **Resultado na oração do if:** "I'll give you £10 **if it'll** help." (= se isso for ajudar)
- **Insistência/teimosia:** "**If you will** eat so much sugar, of course you'll feel ill!" (will acentuado)

**3. If + should / happen to** (possibilidade remota):
- "**If** you **should** see Ana, tell her to call me." / "**If** you **happen to** pass the bakery..."

**4. Alternativas formais ao if:**
- **Assuming (that) / Supposing (that)**: "**Assuming** the weather is good, we'll go."
- **Given that** (= considerando que): "**Given that** costs are rising, we must act."
- **In the event of** + substantivo / **in the event that**: "**In the event of** fire, use the stairs."
- **On condition that / Provided (that) / As long as** (revisão)
- **But for** + substantivo (= se não fosse por): "**But for** her help, I'd have failed."
- **Otherwise / Or else** (revisão B2)
- **If so / If not** (revisão C1-M1)

**5. Mixed e implícitos:**
- "I'd have called you, **but** I lost my phone." (condição implícita)
- "**Without** your support, this **wouldn't have been** possible."

listening.title: Pre-mortem: imagine it failed
listening.context_pt: Uma consultora explica uma técnica para avaliar riscos antes de tomar decisões.

lines.speaker: Consultant
lines.en: Most teams evaluate risks by asking, "What could go wrong?" The problem is that, once a team is excited about a project, few people want to be seen as negative. The psychologist Gary Klein proposed a clever alternative called the "pre-mortem". Before making a final decision, the team imagines that it's a year later and the project has failed completely. Then each person writes down, independently, the reasons why it failed. Research on what's called "prospective hindsight" suggests that imagining that an event has already happened can make it easier to identify its causes. So instead of "Were we to fail, what might the reasons be?", you say, "We failed. Why?" People suddenly feel free to mention concerns they'd otherwise keep to themselves. Had more organizations used this technique, many expensive disasters might have been avoided. And it costs nothing but an hour of honest conversation.

questions.answer: Once excited, few people want to seem negative.

questions.q: What is "prospective hindsight"?

questions.q: What does the technique cost?

reading.title: Thinking in bets
reading.text: In her book Thinking in Bets, the former professional poker player Annie Duke argues that most of us make a fundamental mistake when judging our decisions: we evaluate them by their outcomes. Poker players call this "resulting". If a decision turns out well, we assume it was a good one; if it turns out badly, we conclude it was a mistake. But, as Duke points out, the quality of a decision and the quality of its outcome are not the same thing. Imagine you drive home after drinking too much and arrive safely. Was it a good decision? Clearly not. Had you crashed, nobody would have questioned that conclusion; the fact that you were lucky does not change it. Conversely, a well-reasoned business decision might fail for reasons nobody could have foreseen. Were we to judge every choice purely by what happened afterwards, we would learn the wrong lessons from both. The alternative, Duke suggests, is to think of decisions as bets on an uncertain future. Before deciding, ask: what are the possible outcomes, how likely is each, and what would each cost or gain me? Assuming you have made a reasonable estimate with the information available, you have made a good decision — whatever happens next. This way of thinking has practical benefits. It encourages people to seek out information that might prove them wrong, to admit uncertainty ("I'm about 70 percent sure") and to review their decisions more honestly. Should a plan fail, the question becomes not "Who is to blame?" but "Was this bad luck, bad information or bad judgement?" Given that almost every important decision in life involves uncertainty, that may be one of the most useful questions we can learn to ask.

questions.q: What is "resulting"?
questions.answer: Judging a decision by its outcome.

questions.q: What does the drink-driving example show?
questions.answer: A good outcome doesn't make a bad decision good.

questions.q: What questions should you ask before deciding, according to Duke?
questions.answer: What are the possible outcomes, how likely is each, and what would each cost or gain?

writing.model:
Risk assessment: Open-air music festival, Parque das Águas

Introduction
The purpose of this report is to identify the main risks associated with the proposed one-day music festival in Parque das Águas in October, and to recommend measures to reduce them. Assuming the council approves the plan, the event is expected to attract around 8,000 visitors.

Weather
Given that October is the beginning of the rainy season, heavy rain is a significant risk. Were a storm to occur during the event, the main stage and electrical equipment could be damaged and visitors put at risk. It is therefore recommended that a covered stage be hired and that the weather forecast be reviewed daily in the week before the festival. In the event of severe weather warnings, the event should be postponed to the reserve date in November.

Crowd safety
The park has only two main entrances. Should a large number of visitors arrive at the same time, there is a serious risk of overcrowding. We recommend opening a third, temporary entrance and introducing staggered entry times for ticket holders.

Financial risk
The budget depends heavily on ticket sales. Were sales to fall below 5,000, the organizers would make a loss. To reduce this risk, we suggest securing at least two local sponsors before tickets go on sale. Had a similar measure been taken last year, the previous festival would not have ended with a deficit.

Conclusion
Provided that the measures outlined above are implemented, the risks associated with the festival can be kept at an acceptable level. Should the council require any further information, the organizing committee would be happy to provide it.

grammar.title: Register: formal, neutral and informal
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Marcas de registro formal:**
- Vocabulário de origem **latina**: obtain, require, commence, assist, inform, purchase, sufficient, regarding
- **Passiva** e **impessoalidade**: "It has been decided that..." / "Payment is required..."
- **Nominalização**: "the cancellation of the event" (em vez de "we cancelled the event")
- **Sem contrações**: I am, we will, do not
- **Condicionais invertidos e subjuntivo**: Should you require..., It is essential that he be...
- Frases mais **longas e complexas**

**Marcas de registro informal:**
- **Phrasal verbs** e vocabulário anglo-saxão: get, start, help, find out, put off, sort out
- **Contrações**: I'm, we'll, don't
- **Elipse**: "(Are you) Coming tonight?" / "(I) Hope you're well."
- **Discourse markers e vague language**: anyway, by the way, and stuff, -ish
- **Perguntas diretas e exclamações**: "Guess what!" / "How cool is that?"
- Palavras como **guys, stuff, loads of, a bit, pretty (= bastante)**

**Pares formal ↔ informal:**
- request ↔ ask for · receive ↔ get · inform ↔ tell · investigate ↔ look into · tolerate ↔ put up with · postpone ↔ put off · discover ↔ find out · establish ↔ set up · reduce ↔ cut down on · contact ↔ get in touch with · however ↔ but · therefore ↔ so · in addition ↔ also / plus

**Abertura e fechamento de e-mails:**
- **Formal:** Dear Mr./Ms. Smith / Dear Sir or Madam → Yours sincerely (nome conhecido) / Yours faithfully (nome desconhecido, britânico) / Kind regards
- **Neutro:** Dear Ana / Hello Ana → Best regards / Best wishes
- **Informal:** Hi Ana / Hey! → Cheers / Take care / Love / See you soon

⚠️ **Formal demais também é erro:** num e-mail para um colega próximo, "I am writing to enquire whether you would be available for lunch" soa estranho ou irônico!

common_mistakes.why_pt: No britânico: nome desconhecido → Yours faithfully.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Mensagem informal não combina com linguagem formal.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na fala, o registro muda o **ritmo e as reduções**: no informal, "going to" vira "**gonna**", "want to" → "**wanna**", "got to" → "**gotta**", "don't know" → "**dunno**". No formal, pronuncie as palavras completas e com mais clareza. Nunca escreva gonna/wanna em textos formais!

reading.title: Why register matters
reading.text: Linguists use the term "register" to describe the way language varies according to its context: who is speaking to whom, about what, and through which medium. We all switch registers constantly, usually without thinking. The same person might say "Could you possibly pass the salt?" at a formal dinner, "Pass the salt, please" at home and simply "Salt?" to a close friend. For language learners, however, register can be a hidden trap. Textbooks often teach a fairly neutral style, while films and social media expose learners to very informal speech. The result can be an awkward mixture: an email to a university professor that begins "Hey!" or a casual chat sprinkled with expressions like "furthermore" and "I hereby". Neither is grammatically wrong, but both send an unintended social message. English has a particular feature that makes register especially noticeable: its double vocabulary. After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French became the language of the ruling class in England for centuries, while English continued to be spoken by ordinary people. As a result, English today often has two words for the same idea — a shorter, everyday word of Germanic origin and a longer, more formal one from French or Latin: help and assist, buy and purchase, ask and enquire, begin and commence. A famous illustration involves animals and food. The farm animals kept by English-speaking peasants have Germanic names — cow, pig, sheep — while the meat served at aristocratic tables took French-derived names: beef, pork, mutton. Mastering register, then, is not about learning to be formal. It is about choosing the right words for the right situation. A C1 speaker is not someone who always sounds sophisticated, but someone who knows when not to.

questions.q: What is register, according to linguists?
questions.answer: The way language varies according to context: who, to whom, about what and through which medium.

Subject: Leadership training course, 12–13 May

Dear Ms. Harris,

I am writing on behalf of the twelve employees of Grupo Nova who attended your leadership training course on 12 and 13 May, in order to bring several issues to your attention.

Firstly, the course commenced almost an hour late on the first day, owing to technical problems with the projector. As a result, two of the planned sessions were shortened considerably. Secondly, the course materials, which we were assured would be provided in advance, were not received until the second morning. Finally, the trainer appeared to be unaware that our group consisted of experienced managers, and much of the content was, in our view, more suitable for new supervisors.

While we appreciated the trainer's enthusiasm, we feel that the course did not meet the standards described in your proposal. We would therefore be grateful if you could consider offering a partial refund or an additional half-day session free of charge.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Rafaela Costa
HR Coordinator

Hi Tiago,

culture_note.title: Sincerely ou faithfully?

Hoje, em e-mails profissionais, **Kind regards** e **Best regards** são aceitos quase universalmente — e são uma escolha segura.

grammar.title: C1 review and exam strategies
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Revisão das estruturas do C1:**
- **Nuance verbal:** stative no continuous, I was wondering, always + continuous
- **Coesão:** elipse e substituição (so, not, do so, one), referência (this issue, such, the former/latter)
- **Ênfase:** do/did, fronting (Strange as it may seem), so/such + inversão, cleft sentences (What..., All..., It's not that...)
- **Inversão:** Not only..., Little did..., No sooner..., Only when..., Should/Were/Had
- **Registro formal:** nominalização, subjuntivo, passivas avançadas, distanciamento (is alleged to have)
- **Modais e futuro:** might well, be bound to, may as well, be set to, be on the verge of, be to
- **Léxico:** formação de palavras, multi-word verbs abstratos, collocations, comment adverbs, vague language, discourse markers
- **Pragmática:** linguagem diplomática, hedging, understatement, troca de registro

**Cambridge C1 Advanced** (4 partes):
- **Reading and Use of English** (1h30, 8 partes): múltipla escolha de vocabulário, lacunas, **formação de palavras**, **key word transformations**, textos longos
- **Writing** (1h30): **essay** obrigatório (220–260 palavras) + uma tarefa à escolha (carta/e-mail, proposta, relatório ou resenha)
- **Listening** (cerca de 40 min, 4 partes)
- **Speaking** (cerca de 15 min, **em dupla**): entrevista, comparação de fotos, tarefa colaborativa, discussão

**IELTS:** C1 corresponde aproximadamente às bandas **7.0–8.0**. Speaking com 3 partes (11–14 min), Writing com 2 tarefas (a Task 2 com no mínimo 250 palavras).

**Estratégias C1:**
1. **Reading:** leia **perguntas antes do texto**; cuidado com **distractors** (palavras do texto usadas com outro sentido); procure **paráfrases**, não palavras idênticas.
2. **Use of English:** em key word transformations, procure a **estrutura testada** (inversão, passiva, phrasal verb, expressão fixa); a palavra dada **não pode mudar**; conte as palavras (3–6, contrações contam como duas).
3. **Writing:** **planeje 5–10 minutos**; responda **todos os pontos**; ajuste o **registro** ao leitor; mostre **variedade** sem forçar; revise erros "bobos" (artigos, preposições, -s).
4. **Listening:** antecipe o conteúdo pelas perguntas; atenção a **atitudes e opiniões** (Part 3/4), não só fatos.
5. **Speaking:** **desenvolva** (resposta + razão + exemplo + contraste); **interaja** com o parceiro ("I'd like to pick up on what you said..."); **parafraseie** em vez de parar; mostre **variedade** naturalmente.

rows: Leia as perguntas primeiro; procure paráfrases; cuidado com distractors.
Identifique a estrutura testada; não mude a palavra dada; 3–6 palavras.
Planeje; responda tudo; registro certo; revise.
Antecipe; foque em atitudes e opiniões.

grammar.tip_pt: No C1, **pequenos erros são aceitáveis** — o que conta é a **flexibilidade, a precisão e a variedade**. Um examinador prefere ver você **arriscar** uma inversão com um pequeno deslize do que repetir estruturas B1 perfeitas.

common_mistakes.wrong: Key word transformation: changing the given word (ALTHOUGH → although's).
common_mistakes.right: Use the given word exactly as it is.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A palavra dada não pode ser alterada.

common_mistakes.wrong: Essay: discussing all three options and not choosing one.
common_mistakes.right: Discuss two options and clearly state which is more important.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Não responder parte da tarefa reduz a nota de conteúdo.

common_mistakes.wrong: Speaking: giving one-sentence answers to avoid mistakes.
common_mistakes.right: Develop: answer + reason + example + contrast.
common_mistakes.why_pt: No C1, a extensão e variedade das respostas são avaliadas.

pronunciation.tip_pt: No C1, o objetivo não é perder o sotaque, mas ter **prosódia clara**: acento correto nas palavras, ênfase nas informações importantes, pausas nos lugares certos e entonação que mostra atitude. Grave-se e compare com falantes nativos — foque em **ritmo** mais do que em sons isolados.

dialogue.title: Mock C1 speaking test – Part 4
dialogue.context_pt: Simulação da Parte 4 da prova oral C1 Advanced: o examinador faz perguntas de discussão a dois candidatos.

lines.speaker: Examiner
lines.en: Some people say that in the age of AI translation, learning foreign languages is becoming less important. What do you think?
lines.pt: Algumas pessoas dizem que, na era da tradução por IA, aprender línguas estrangeiras está se tornando menos importante. O que vocês acham?

lines.speaker: Luiza
lines.en: That's a fascinating question. I can see why people might think so — the tools have become remarkably accurate. That said, I'd argue that a language isn't just a code to be translated. What you lose with an app is the nuance: humour, irony, the things people leave unsaid.
lines.pt: Que pergunta fascinante. Entendo por que as pessoas pensam assim — as ferramentas ficaram muito precisas. Dito isso, eu diria que uma língua não é só um código a ser traduzido. O que se perde com um app é a nuance: o humor, a ironia, o que as pessoas não dizem.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: I'd like to pick up on that. I agree about nuance, but I also think we shouldn't underestimate how much these tools help people who would otherwise have no access at all — tourists, migrants, small businesses.
lines.pt: Gostaria de retomar isso. Concordo sobre a nuance, mas também acho que não devemos subestimar o quanto essas ferramentas ajudam pessoas que, de outra forma, não teriam acesso nenhum — turistas, migrantes, pequenas empresas.

lines.speaker: Luiza
lines.en: That's a fair point. So perhaps it's not that languages are becoming less important; it's that the reasons for learning them are changing.
lines.pt: Bom argumento. Então talvez não seja que as línguas estejam ficando menos importantes; é que os motivos para aprendê-las estão mudando.

lines.speaker: Examiner
lines.en: In what way?
lines.pt: De que forma?

lines.speaker: Luiza
lines.en: Well, in the past, many people learned English mainly for practical reasons — to get a job, for instance. Were those reasons to disappear, what would remain is the human side: building relationships, understanding other cultures from the inside.
lines.pt: Bom, no passado, muita gente aprendia inglês principalmente por motivos práticos — para conseguir um emprego, por exemplo. Se esses motivos desaparecessem, o que restaria seria o lado humano: construir relações, entender outras culturas por dentro.

lines.speaker: Rafael
lines.en: Absolutely. And, if I'm honest, I can't imagine having the friendships I have now through an app. Some things simply can't be outsourced.
lines.pt: Com certeza. E, sinceramente, não consigo imaginar ter as amizades que tenho hoje por meio de um app. Algumas coisas simplesmente não podem ser terceirizadas.

lines.speaker: Examiner
lines.en: Thank you. That is the end of the test.
lines.pt: Obrigado. Este é o fim da prova.

listening.title: Beyond C1
listening.context_pt: Uma linguista fala sobre como continuar progredindo depois do C1.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Reaching C1 is a remarkable achievement. According to the CEFR, a C1 user can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, recognize implicit meaning, express themselves fluently and spontaneously, and use language flexibly for social, academic and professional purposes. But what comes next? Progress beyond this level tends to be slower and less visible, which can be frustrating. You no longer learn new grammar every week; instead, you refine. My advice is threefold. First, read widely — novels, long-form journalism, academic articles — because this is where your vocabulary will grow most. Second, specialize: develop the English of your profession or passion in depth. And third, use English to create, not just to consume: write, present, debate, teach. Interestingly, many highly proficient speakers say the moment they felt truly fluent wasn't when they passed an exam. It was when they laughed at a joke without having to think — or when they realized they'd been dreaming in English.

questions.q: What can a C1 user do, according to the CEFR?
questions.answer: Understand demanding texts, recognize implicit meaning, express themselves fluently and use language flexibly.

questions.q: Why can progress beyond C1 be frustrating?
questions.answer: It tends to be slower and less visible.

questions.q: What are the speaker's three pieces of advice?
questions.answer: Read widely, specialize, and use English to create, not just consume.

questions.q: When do many speakers say they felt truly fluent?
questions.answer: When they laughed at a joke without thinking, or dreamt in English.

reading.title: The plateau and how to break it
reading.text: Almost every advanced learner eventually encounters what teachers call the "intermediate plateau" — and its more subtle cousin, the advanced plateau. In the early stages of learning a language, progress is fast and obvious: every week brings new words, new structures and new abilities. At higher levels, however, the gains become smaller and harder to notice. Learners who could once measure their improvement in leaps now find it difficult to see any improvement at all. Part of the explanation is that the remaining gaps are less visible. A B1 learner knows when she does not understand a sentence. A C1 learner usually understands, but may not notice that a native speaker would have chosen a different collocation, a more precise verb or a subtler level of politeness. Such gaps rarely cause communication to break down, which means there is little pressure to fix them. Research on expertise offers some useful insights. The psychologist Anders Ericsson, whose work on expert performance became widely known, argued that improvement at advanced levels depends less on the amount of practice than on its quality. What he called "deliberate practice" involves working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of one's ability, with immediate feedback. For language learners, this might mean recording yourself and comparing your speech with a model, rewriting a paragraph three times in different registers, or noting down every unfamiliar collocation you meet in a week. Equally important is motivation. At C1, the external rewards — passing an exam, getting a job — have often already been achieved. Learners who continue to improve tend to be those who have found intrinsic reasons: a love of literature, an international friendship, a professional passion. In the end, the plateau is not a wall but a change of terrain. The climb continues; it simply requires a different kind of walking.

questions.q: Why does progress seem slower at advanced levels?
questions.answer: The remaining gaps are less visible and rarely cause communication to break down.

questions.q: What is "deliberate practice"?
questions.answer: Working on specific weaknesses, at the edge of your ability, with immediate feedback.

questions.q: Give two examples of deliberate practice for language learners.
questions.answer: Recording yourself and comparing with a model / rewriting in different registers / noting collocations.

questions.q: What kind of motivation helps learners continue improving?
questions.answer: Intrinsic reasons, such as a love of literature, friendships or professional passion.

exercises.title: Speaking Part 4: develop your answer
exercises.instruction: Answer each discussion question in 4–5 sentences, including a reason, an example, a contrasting view and a conclusion.
exercises.instruction_pt: Responda cada pergunta em 4–5 frases, com motivo, exemplo, visão contrária e conclusão.

items.prompt: Is it better to be an expert in one field or to have broad general knowledge?
items.answer: Model: I'd argue that, in today's world, a combination is ideal. Deep expertise makes you valuable — a surgeon, for instance, needs years of specialized training. That said, people with broad knowledge are often better at connecting ideas across fields, which is where innovation tends to happen. So, all things considered, I'd say the best approach is to be deep in one area and curious about many others.

items.prompt: Should people be required to learn a second language at school?
items.answer: Model: On the whole, I think so. Not only does it open professional doors, but it also helps students understand other cultures. Admittedly, schools already have crowded timetables, and some students struggle with core subjects. Even so, I believe the long-term benefits outweigh the costs, provided that languages are taught in a practical, communicative way.

speaking.instruction: "Final talk": give a 6–8 minute presentation titled "What English has given me" (or a topic of your choice). Include a hook, a personal story (narrative + emphasis), an argument with concession, data or evidence (hedging), and a memorable conclusion (rhetorical devices). Then answer three questions from the class.
speaking.instruction_pt: "Palestra final": faça uma apresentação de 6–8 minutos intitulada "O que o inglês me deu" (ou um tema à sua escolha). Inclua um gancho, uma história pessoal (narrativa + ênfase), um argumento com concessão, dados ou evidências (hedging) e uma conclusão memorável (recursos retóricos). Depois responda três perguntas da turma.

Will AI make learning languages unnecessary?

What advice would you give to someone starting English from zero?
How will you keep improving after C1?

writing.task: C1 Advanced essay (220–260 words): "Your class has discussed three factors that help people learn a language successfully: formal instruction, living in a country where the language is spoken, and personal motivation. Write an essay discussing two of these, explaining which is more important and why." Show a wide range of C1 structures.
writing.task_pt: Essay C1 Advanced (220–260 palavras): "Sua turma discutiu três fatores que ajudam as pessoas a aprender uma língua com sucesso: instrução formal, morar num país onde a língua é falada e motivação pessoal. Discuta dois deles, explicando qual é mais importante e por quê." Mostre ampla variedade de estruturas C1.
writing.model:
What really makes a successful language learner?

Why do some people master a foreign language while others, despite years of study, never progress beyond the basics? Of the many factors involved, formal instruction and personal motivation are arguably two of the most influential.

Formal instruction provides structure. A good teacher can explain grammar systematically, correct persistent errors and expose learners to language they might never encounter on their own. Without such guidance, many learners develop a fluent but inaccurate style which becomes increasingly difficult to correct. That said, instruction alone rarely produces proficiency. Countless students have spent years in classrooms and yet remain unable to hold a conversation.

Personal motivation, by contrast, determines what happens outside the classroom. Learners who genuinely want to read a novel, make a friend or build a career in another language tend to seek out opportunities to practise, and to persist when progress slows. Admittedly, motivation can fade, and enthusiasm is no substitute for knowledge. Nevertheless, it is motivation that turns a few hours of lessons a week into a daily habit of listening, reading and speaking.

On balance, although both factors are valuable, I believe the latter is ultimately more important. Not only does motivation lead learners to find their own resources, but it also sustains them through the inevitable plateaus. Instruction can show the way; only motivation ensures that the learner keeps walking.

culture_note.title: Depois do C1
culture_note.text_pt: O próximo nível é o **C2 (Mastery / Proficiency)**, certificado por provas como o **Cambridge C2 Proficiency** e por bandas 8.5–9 no IELTS. Mas, para muitos, o C1 já é o ponto em que o inglês deixa de ser **matéria** e vira **ferramenta de vida**. A partir daqui: leia literatura, ouça podcasts especializados, escreva, apresente e ensine. **Congratulations — and never stop learning!**

grammar.title: Near-synonyms: connotation, collocation and register
grammar.explanation_pt:
No C2, quase-sinônimos raramente são intercambiáveis. Eles se diferenciam em **quatro dimensões**:

**1. Conotação (juízo de valor)**
- positivo → neutro → negativo: **slender** → **thin** → **skinny** → **scrawny**
- **determined** (+) / **persistent** (=) / **stubborn** (−) / **obstinate** (− formal)
- **frugal / thrifty** (+) / **careful with money** (=) / **mean / stingy / tight-fisted** (−)
- **confident** (+) / **self-assured** (=) / **arrogant / cocky** (−)

**2. Collocation (com o que a palavra combina)**
- **commit** a crime / an error ✔ · **make** a mistake ✔ · ❌ commit a mistake
- **heavy** rain / **strong** wind / **high** temperature
- **utterly** combina com palavras negativas ou extremas: utterly **ridiculous / exhausted** (raro: utterly delighted)
- **broad** daylight, **bitterly** cold, **acutely** aware, **painfully** shy, **blissfully** unaware

**3. Registro**
- **commence** (formal) / **start** (neutro) / **kick off** (informal)
- **deceased** (formal/jurídico) / **dead** (neutro) / **passed away** (eufemismo)
- **inebriated** (formal/humorístico) / **drunk** (neutro) / **hammered** (gíria)

**4. Intensidade**
- **like** < **be fond of** < **adore** < **worship**
- **annoyed** < **irritated** < **angry** < **furious** < **livid**
- **interesting** < **fascinating** < **riveting**

**Uso estratégico:** a escolha de palavras revela **posição**. Jornalistas, políticos e advogados escolhem com cuidado: "**reform**" (+) x "**cuts**" (−); "**protesters**" x "**rioters**"; "**estate tax**" x "**death tax**".

examples.en: What her supporters call principled, her critics call obstinate.
examples.pt: O que seus apoiadores chamam de íntegro, seus críticos chamam de obstinado.

examples.en: He was blissfully unaware that the whole office had been talking about him.
examples.pt: Ele estava felizmente alheio ao fato de que o escritório inteiro andava falando dele.

examples.en: The government described the measures as "reforms"; the unions called them "cuts".
examples.pt: O governo descreveu as medidas como "reformas"; os sindicatos as chamaram de "cortes".

grammar.tip_pt: Use um **dicionário de collocations** (como o *Oxford Collocations Dictionary*) e um **corpus** (buscadores de frases reais) para checar combinações. No C2, a pergunta não é "essa palavra existe?", mas "**um nativo diria assim?**"

common_mistakes.wrong: She's very skinny and elegant.
common_mistakes.right: She's very slender and elegant.
common_mistakes.why_pt: skinny tem conotação negativa; slender combina com elegância.

common_mistakes.wrong: He committed a mistake.
common_mistakes.right: He made a mistake. / He committed an error (formal).
common_mistakes.why_pt: commit combina com crime, error, offence — não com mistake.

common_mistakes.wrong: I was utterly pleased with the result.
common_mistakes.right: I was thoroughly / immensely pleased with the result.
common_mistakes.why_pt: utterly costuma combinar com palavras negativas ou absolutas.

pronunciation.tip_pt: A conotação também está no **tom**. A mesma palavra neutra pode ficar negativa com ênfase e entonação: "He's very... *confident*" (com pausa e tom descendente = arrogante). No C2, perceba e use essa camada.

dialogue.title: Writing the reference letter
dialogue.context_pt: Dois gerentes discutem como redigir uma carta de recomendação para uma ex-funcionária difícil.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: So, how do we describe Patrícia in this reference? Honestly, she was a nightmare in meetings.
lines.pt: Então, como descrevemos a Patrícia nesta carta de referência? Sinceramente, ela era um pesadelo nas reuniões.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: We can't say that. But we can't lie either. What about "assertive"?
lines.pt: Não podemos dizer isso. Mas também não podemos mentir. Que tal "assertiva"?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: "Assertive" is generous. "Pushy" would be nearer the mark.
lines.pt: "Assertiva" é generoso. "Insistente demais" seria mais preciso.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: True, but she got results. She never gave up on a client. I'd call that determined rather than stubborn.
lines.pt: Verdade, mas ela trazia resultados. Nunca desistia de um cliente. Eu chamaria isso de determinação, não de teimosia.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: Fair enough. And she was very... direct with junior staff.
lines.pt: Justo. E ela era muito... direta com os funcionários juniores.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: "Direct" is fine — it's neutral. Any reader with experience will read between the lines anyway.
lines.pt: "Direta" está bom — é neutro. Qualquer leitor experiente vai ler nas entrelinhas de qualquer jeito.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: So: "a determined and results-driven professional with a direct communication style".
lines.pt: Então: "uma profissional determinada e orientada a resultados, com estilo de comunicação direto".

listening.title: Same facts, different words
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de linguística mostra como a escolha de palavras muda a percepção de um mesmo fato.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: In a classic experiment published in 1974, the psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed participants films of car accidents and then asked them how fast the cars were going. The only difference between the groups was a single verb. Some were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" each other; others heard "collided", "bumped", "hit" or "contacted". Those who heard "smashed" gave the highest speed estimates. A week later, they were also more likely to report having seen broken glass — even though there was none in the film. One word changed not just how people judged the event, but what they remembered. Journalists, lawyers and politicians understand this intuitively. Is a sudden rise in prices a "spike" or a "correction"? Are people who cross a border "migrants", "refugees" or "illegals"? Each choice is a small argument in disguise. And at the highest level of language, noticing those choices — and making them consciously — is perhaps the most important skill of all.

questions.q: What did participants in the 1974 experiment watch?
questions.answer: Films of car accidents.

questions.q: What was the only difference between the groups?
questions.answer: The verb used in the question (smashed, collided, bumped, hit, contacted).

questions.q: What happened a week later?
questions.answer: The "smashed" group were more likely to report seeing broken glass, though there was none.

questions.q: What does the speaker mean by "a small argument in disguise"?

reading.title: The tyranny of the thesaurus
reading.text: Every writing teacher has encountered it: the essay in which every second word appears to have been lifted from a thesaurus. "The protagonist perambulated pensively through the verdant arboretum", writes the student, when what he means is that the main character walked through the park, thinking. The impulse is understandable. Learners — and, for that matter, many native speakers — are often taught that variety is a virtue and that repetition is a sin. A thesaurus seems to offer an endless supply of alternatives. The difficulty is that a thesaurus lists words that are similar, not words that are interchangeable. "Slender", "skinny", "gaunt" and "emaciated" all denote thinness, but they evoke four very different people. "Notorious" and "famous" both describe someone widely known, yet only one would be welcome on a reference letter. Even apparently neutral synonyms differ in collocation and register: one "commences" a legal procedure but rarely "commences" a holiday. Linguists sometimes claim that there are no true synonyms in any language — that if two words were genuinely identical in every context, one of them would eventually fall out of use or acquire a distinct meaning. Whether or not this is strictly true, it captures something important. Words carry histories, associations and social signals that no list can fully record. The solution is not to abandon the thesaurus but to treat it as a starting point rather than an answer. Before adopting an unfamiliar word, a careful writer checks how it is actually used: in which contexts, with which neighbours, in what tone. Precision, not variety, is the hallmark of good writing — and, at the highest levels of proficiency, of good speaking too. As the novelist Elmore Leonard memorably advised: if it sounds like writing, rewrite it.

questions.q: What is the problem with the student's sentence?
questions.answer: It uses unnecessarily elaborate thesaurus words instead of simple, natural ones.

questions.q: What does a thesaurus list, according to the text?
questions.answer: Words that are similar, not interchangeable.

questions.q: What do some linguists claim about synonyms?
questions.answer: That there are no true synonyms; identical words would fall out of use or change meaning.

questions.q: What is the hallmark of good writing, according to the writer?
questions.answer: Precision, not variety.

writing.model:
Reference for Mr. André Santos

To whom it may concern,

I am pleased to provide a reference for André Santos, who worked as a Senior Analyst in my team at Horizonte Consultoria from March 2021 to June 2025.

André is a highly capable analyst with an exceptional eye for detail. His reports were consistently thorough and meticulously researched, and on several occasions he identified errors in financial models that others had overlooked. Clients frequently commented on the clarity of his written work.

He is also a determined professional. When a project encountered difficulties, he was invariably the last person to give up, and he often worked well beyond what was expected of him to meet a deadline. This persistence was particularly valuable during a complex restructuring project in 2023, which he helped to bring to a successful conclusion.

André holds strong views on how work should be done and expresses them directly. While this occasionally led to lively discussions within the team, his contributions were always motivated by a genuine commitment to quality. He would, I believe, thrive in a role that allows him a degree of independence and values precision above speed.

I have no hesitation in recommending him for a position that requires analytical rigour and dedication. Should you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me.

Yours faithfully,

Mariana Duarte
Head of Analysis, Horizonte Consultoria

—
Word choices: "determined" rather than "stubborn" emphasizes the positive side of his persistence; "expresses them directly" is a neutral way of acknowledging that he could be blunt; "lively discussions" signals conflict without exaggerating it.

O que **não** se diz também comunica!

lessons.title: Between the lines
lessons.subtitle_pt: Negação enfática e litotes: by no means, far from, none too, not unlike
source_refs: CEFR – C2 descriptors (implicit meaning, fine shades of meaning)
Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading and Use of English Part 4
objectives: Usar negação enfática (by no means, not in the least, far from, anything but)
Usar litotes — afirmar negando o contrário (not bad, not unlike, no small feat)
Usar none too / none the + comparativo / not so much... as
Interpretar implicaturas e o que fica subentendido

warmup.text_pt: "Ela **não é nada boba**" significa que ela é esperta. "**Não foi pouca coisa**" significa que foi uma grande conquista. Essa figura — afirmar algo **negando o contrário** — se chama **litotes**, e o inglês adora: "**not bad**", "**no small achievement**", "**not unlike**". No C2, você também precisa dominar as **negações enfáticas**: "by no means", "far from", "anything but".

grammar.title: Emphatic negation and litotes
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Negação enfática** — reforça o "não":
- **by no means / not by any means** (de modo algum): "The result is **by no means** certain."
- **not in the least / not in the slightest / not at all**: "I'm **not in the least** worried."
- **far from** + adjetivo/-ing/substantivo (longe de): "The plan is **far from** perfect." / "**Far from** helping, he made things worse."
- **anything but** (tudo menos): "The meeting was **anything but** productive."
- **nowhere near** (nem perto de): "We're **nowhere near** ready."
- **not remotely / not the least bit**: "It's **not remotely** funny."
- No início da frase → **inversão**: "**By no means** is this the end." / "**In no way** am I criticizing you."

**2. None too / none the + comparativo**
- **none too** + adjetivo (= not very, irônico): "He was **none too** happy about it."
- **none the** + comparativo (= not at all + comparativo): "I read the instructions twice and was **none the wiser**." (não entendi nada mais) / "He fell but was **none the worse for** it." (não sofreu nada)

**3. Litotes** — afirmar algo negando o oposto (understatement elegante):
- **not bad** (= bom) · **not uncommon** (= bastante comum) · **not unlike** (= parecido com) · **not without** (= com algum) · **no small** / **no mean** (= grande)
- "It was **no mean feat**." / "The idea is **not without** its problems." / "His style is **not unlike** Hemingway's."
- Efeito: soa **cauteloso, irônico ou modesto**.

**4. Not so much X as Y** (não tanto X, mas sim Y):
- "It's **not so much** a problem **as** an opportunity."

**5. Implicatura** — o que se comunica sem dizer:
- "Some of the students passed." → implica que **nem todos** passaram.
- "Can you pass the salt?" → não é uma pergunta sobre habilidade.
- "He's a good typist." (numa carta de referência para professor universitário) → implica que **não há nada mais** a elogiar.

Not so much a job as a calling.

grammar.tip_pt: Português também tem litotes: "**não é nada mau**", "**não é de se jogar fora**", "**não foi pouca coisa**". O equivalente mais natural em inglês geralmente é **not bad at all**, **not to be sniffed at** (informal) ou **no mean feat**.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Litotes dependem do tom. "**Not BAD**" com entonação ascendente-descendente e sorriso = bom de verdade. Com tom plano = só razoável. Em **anything but**, o acento vai em **ANYthing**: "It was **ANY**thing but relaxing."

listening.title: What we mean when we don't say it
listening.context_pt: Um filósofo da linguagem explica as máximas de Grice num podcast.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: In the 1960s and 1970s, the British philosopher Paul Grice proposed that conversation is guided by what he called the Cooperative Principle. We assume that the people we talk to are trying to communicate efficiently, and he described several "maxims" they generally follow: say as much as is needed but no more; say what you believe to be true; be relevant; and be clear. The fascinating part is what happens when someone appears to break a maxim. Suppose I ask a friend, "How was the restaurant?" and she replies, "Well, the parking was easy." She's apparently being irrelevant. But because I assume she's cooperating, I infer something she hasn't said: the food was by no means good. Grice called this kind of meaning an "implicature". It's how irony works, how politeness works, and how a great deal of everyday communication works. And it's often where advanced learners struggle — not with the words, but with what lies between them.

questions.q: What is the Cooperative Principle?
questions.answer: The assumption that people in conversation are trying to communicate efficiently.

questions.q: Name two of Grice's maxims.
questions.answer: Say as much as needed; say what you believe true; be relevant; be clear.

questions.q: What does the friend imply by "the parking was easy"?
questions.answer: That the food was not good.

questions.q: Where do advanced learners often struggle, according to the speaker?
questions.answer: With what lies between the words — implied meaning.

reading.title: The art of saying less
reading.text: English, and British English in particular, has a reputation for understatement, and few devices capture this more neatly than litotes: the practice of asserting something by denying its opposite. To describe a brilliant performance as "not bad", a catastrophic error as "not ideal" or a significant achievement as "no mean feat" is to communicate, paradoxically, by appearing to say less than one means. The device is far from new. It appears in Old English poetry, where a hero might be said to be "not unfamiliar" with battle, and it was a favourite of classical rhetoricians, who valued it as a way of sounding modest while making a strong point. Why should speakers choose such an indirect route? Part of the answer lies in social risk. Unrestrained praise can sound insincere; unrestrained criticism can sound aggressive. Litotes offers a way of expressing judgement while leaving room for retreat. A manager who calls a report "not without its problems" can, if challenged, insist that she meant only minor issues — even if both parties know she meant something rather more serious. There is also an aesthetic dimension. Understatement invites the listener to participate, to reconstruct the full meaning from the restrained version. When it works, it creates a sense of shared understanding, almost of complicity. Yet the same quality makes litotes treacherous for anyone unfamiliar with the code. A visitor who takes "not bad" at face value may underestimate genuine enthusiasm, while one who takes "it's not the worst idea I've heard" as encouragement may be in for a disappointment. At the highest levels of proficiency, then, understanding English is by no means simply a matter of knowing words. It is a matter of knowing how much — and how little — they are being asked to carry.

questions.q: What is litotes?
questions.answer: Asserting something by denying its opposite.

questions.q: Is the device new? Give evidence.
questions.answer: No — it appears in Old English poetry and classical rhetoric.

questions.q: Why might speakers choose litotes, according to the text?
questions.answer: To reduce social risk: to express judgement while leaving room for retreat.

questions.q: Why can litotes be treacherous for outsiders?
questions.answer: They may take it at face value and misjudge enthusiasm or criticism.

writing.model:
Review: The Golden Fork, Vila Madalena

The Golden Fork has been open for six months and has already acquired a reputation, though not, perhaps, the one its owners were hoping for. I visited on a Friday evening, which, given that the restaurant was anything but crowded, was no mean feat of timing.

The décor is not unlike that of an airport lounge in the late 1990s: a great deal of chrome, a certain amount of beige and lighting that can only be described as candid. The music, I was assured, was jazz. I am none the wiser as to which jazz.

The menu is ambitious. It is by no means short, running to some forty dishes across seven cuisines, a range that would challenge a far larger kitchen. I ordered the "signature" seafood risotto. It arrived promptly, which I have learned to regard as not entirely a good sign. The rice was far from undercooked; indeed, it had clearly been cooked for some time, possibly that morning. The prawns, to their credit, were present.

Service was attentive, in the sense that our waiter returned to the table on eleven occasions to ask whether everything was all right. I was not in the least tempted to tell him.

Dessert was the high point of the evening. The chocolate mousse was not bad at all — light, rich and genuinely delicious — and it would not be unfair to say that I would return for it alone. Whether I would wish to pass through the rest of the menu to reach it is another question.

At around 200 reais per person without wine, The Golden Fork is none too cheap. It is, however, unforgettable. I shall leave readers to decide which of those qualities matters more.

Rating: ★★☆☆☆ (one of them is for the mousse)

culture_note.title: "Quite good" é bom?

É exagerada e humorística — mas revela algo real sobre a cultura da **understatement**.

summary_pt: Negação enfática: by no means, not in the least, far from, anything but, nowhere near.
none too + adj; none the wiser / none the worse.

lessons.title: Part and parcel
lessons.subtitle_pt: Binômios, provérbios e expressões fixas — e sua manipulação criativa
source_refs: CEFR – C2 descriptors (idiomatic expressions and colloquialisms)
Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading and Use of English Part 2
objectives: Usar binômios e trinômios fixos (by and large, part and parcel, sooner or later)
Usar provérbios de forma natural (muitas vezes só a primeira metade)
Reconhecer a manipulação criativa de expressões fixas em manchetes e publicidade

Em inglês, eles são chamados de **binomials**, e a ordem é **fixa**: "salt and pepper", nunca "pepper and salt". grammar.title: Binomials, proverbs and creative manipulation
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Binômios (binomials)** — pares de palavras ligados por **and / or / but**, com **ordem fixa**:
- **Sinônimos/reforço:** safe and sound, peace and quiet, pick and choose, first and foremost
- **Opostos:** pros and cons, ups and downs, give and take, sooner or later, black and white, back and forth
- **Repetição/rima:** neck and neck (empatados), touch and go, wear and tear, high and dry, rough and ready
- **Preposições:** by and large, on and off, over and above, out and about
⚠️ A ordem **não muda**: ❌ "sound and safe", ❌ "cons and pros".

**Trinômios:** lock, stock and barrel (tudo); hook, line and sinker (completamente); tall, dark and handsome.

**2. Provérbios** — nativos frequentemente dizem **só a primeira metade**:
- "When in Rome..." (do as the Romans do)
- "Speak of the devil..." (and he shall appear) — quando alguém de quem se falava aparece
- "Too many cooks..." (spoil the broth)
- "The early bird..." (catches the worm)
- "Every cloud..." (has a silver lining)
- "Don't count your chickens..." (before they hatch)

**3. Manipulação criativa** — manchetes, publicidade e humor alteram expressões fixas, e o leitor C2 precisa reconhecer o original:
- "**Every cloud has a silver lining**" → manchete sobre computação em nuvem: "**Every cloud has a cyber lining**"
- "**Better late than never**" → "**Better late than pregnant**" (humor)
- "**All's well that ends well**" → "All's well that **sends** well" (anúncio de correio)

**4. Uso adequado** — idioms em excesso soam **artificiais** ("It's raining cats and dogs, so let's kill two birds with one stone..."). Use-os **com moderação** e no **registro certo**: "by and large" e "first and foremost" funcionam até em textos formais; "lock, stock and barrel" é mais informal/jornalístico.
