listening.title: Why can't we say "pepper and salt"?
listening.context_pt: Uma linguista explica por que binômios têm ordem fixa.

lines.speaker: Linguist
lines.en: Why do English speakers say "salt and pepper" but never "pepper and salt"? Or "rock and roll", "black and white", "ladies and gentlemen"? Linguists have identified several tendencies — not strict rules, but strong patterns. First, the shorter word tends to come first: "salt and pepper", "bread and butter". Second, when vowels differ, words with higher, front vowels — like the "i" in "zig" — tend to precede lower, back vowels, like the "a" in "zag". That's why it's "zig-zag", "tick-tock", "flip-flop" and never the other way round. Third, cultural or logical priority often matters: "cause and effect", "before and after", "husband and wife" — though the last example also shows how these orders can reflect social hierarchies of the past. Interestingly, Portuguese often shows similar patterns. But when the orders differ between languages, learners tend to transfer their own — which is why, at C2, these small, fixed pairs are worth learning as single units.

questions.q: Which word tends to come first in a binomial?
questions.answer: The shorter word.

questions.q: What vowel pattern explains "zig-zag" and "tick-tock"?
questions.answer: Higher, front vowels tend to come before lower, back vowels.

questions.q: What does "husband and wife" show?
questions.answer: Orders can reflect social hierarchies of the past.

questions.q: Why should learners learn binomials as units?
questions.answer: Because when orders differ between languages, learners transfer their own.

reading.title: The headline writer's toolkit
reading.text: Few writers handle fixed expressions with as much mischief as the authors of newspaper headlines. Limited to a handful of words and competing for the reader's attention, headline writers — sub-editors, in British newsrooms — have long relied on a simple trick: take a familiar phrase and twist it. A story about a theft from a cheese factory becomes "Grate Expectations"; an article on the decline of hand-written letters is headed "Signed, Sealed, Deleted"; a report on rising house prices in a seaside town appears as "Home and Dry? Not Any More". The technique depends entirely on recognition. The reader must instantly recall the original — Dickens's Great Expectations, the song "Signed, Sealed, Delivered", the idiom "home and dry" — and register the change. The pleasure lies in the gap between the expected and the actual, and in the small flash of understanding that bridges it. Advertising uses the same mechanism, as do comedians, politicians and, increasingly, social media users. For language learners, this presents a particular challenge. It is perfectly possible to understand every word of a headline and still miss its point entirely. A learner unfamiliar with "Every cloud has a silver lining" will find nothing remarkable in a technology column titled "Every Cloud Has a Cyber Lining"; the native reader, by contrast, sees a joke, an argument and a cultural reference compressed into six words. This is why fixed expressions matter far more at the highest levels than their apparent triviality might suggest. They are part and parcel of a shared cultural memory — the background against which a great deal of creative language is written. To read like an insider, one must first know what the insiders know by heart. Only then can one appreciate, and eventually produce, the twist.

questions.q: What trick do headline writers use?
questions.answer: They take a familiar phrase and twist it.

questions.q: What does the technique depend on?
questions.answer: Recognition of the original expression.

questions.q: Why can learners miss the point of a headline?
questions.answer: They may understand every word but not recognize the original expression.

questions.q: Why are fixed expressions important at the highest levels?
questions.answer: They're part of a shared cultural memory against which creative language is written.

writing.model:
Home Sweet Office

When my company announced that we would be working from home "for the foreseeable future", I was, first and foremost, delighted. No more traffic, no more crowded lifts, no more colleagues reheating fish in the office microwave. Peace and quiet at last.

That was three years ago. By and large, I don't regret it. But I have learned that working from home has its ups and downs, and that some of them are not entirely obvious at first.

Take the kitchen table. In theory, it's a temporary workspace. In practice, it has become my office lock, stock and barrel: laptop, second screen, a mountain of papers and an assortment of odds and ends that I'm afraid to throw away. My family now eats dinner on the sofa.

Then there are the interruptions. Unexpected deliveries, the neighbour's renovations and a cat who believes my keyboard is a heated bed are, it seems, part and parcel of the arrangement. Last month, during an important video call with a client, it was touch and go whether I would finish my presentation before the drilling next door began. (It began.)

The biggest surprise, however, has been loneliness. Real conversations with colleagues are now few and far between. I never imagined I would miss Paulo from accounts and his endless stories about his weekend fishing trips. But I do.

So, after weighing up the pros and cons, I've reached a compromise. Twice a week, I go to a co-working space. It's rough and ready — the coffee is terrible — but there are people, and conversation, and nobody is drilling.

Is working from home the be-all and end-all? Not quite. But sooner or later, I suspect, most of us will find our own balance. Meanwhile, the cat has the keyboard.

grammar.title: Absolute constructions
grammar.explanation_pt:
Uma **oração absoluta** tem **sujeito próprio** (diferente do da oração principal) e um particípio, adjetivo, advérbio ou locução — **sem verbo conjugado**. Ela acrescenta circunstância (tempo, causa, condição, descrição).

**1. Substantivo + particípio (-ing / -ed)**
- "**The work done**, we went home." (= When the work was done...)
- "**The sun having set**, the temperature dropped."
- "**Weather permitting**, the ceremony will be held outdoors."
- "**Other things being equal**, the cheaper option is better."

**2. Substantivo + adjetivo / advérbio / locução** (muito comum em descrições literárias):
- "**The meeting over**, they left."
- "She stood at the window, **her face pale**."
- "He walked in, **hands in his pockets**."
- "The children ran out, **their schoolbags forgotten**."

**3. With / Without + objeto + particípio/adjetivo/locução** (mais natural na fala):
- "**With prices rising**, families are cutting back."
- "**With the deadline approaching**, nobody slept."
- "She fell asleep **with the light on**."
- "**Without anyone noticing**, he slipped out."

**4. Expressões absolutas fixas** (sem sujeito explícito, aceitas como "comentário"):
- **generally / strictly / broadly / frankly speaking** · **all things considered** · **considering** + noun · **given** + noun · **judging by / from** · **assuming** · **that said / that being said** · **talking of** · **taking everything into account**

**5. Cuidado com o dangling participle** (erro de sujeito):
- ❌ "**Walking** to the station, **the rain** started." (a chuva estava andando?)
- ✅ "**Walking** to the station, **I** got caught in the rain." (mesmo sujeito)
- ✅ "**I was walking** to the station **when** the rain started."
- As **expressões fixas** do item 4 são exceções aceitas.

listening.title: Travel writing at its best
listening.context_pt: Um editor de literatura de viagem fala sobre o que torna um relato memorável.

lines.speaker: Editor
lines.en: What separates great travel writing from a guidebook? Generally speaking, it's the shift from information to experience. A guidebook tells you the museum opens at nine. A travel writer puts you on the steps outside at ten to nine, the street still wet from the night's rain, a stray dog asleep in a patch of sunlight. Notice the grammar there — those little phrases with their own subjects, "the street still wet", "a dog asleep". They let a writer add layers of detail without stopping the flow of the sentence. Writers like Jan Morris, Bruce Chatwin and Paul Theroux used them constantly. The other ingredient is honesty. The best travel writers aren't afraid to describe disappointment, boredom or their own prejudices — and, all things considered, that's what makes us trust them when they describe wonder.

questions.q: What separates travel writing from a guidebook?
questions.answer: The shift from information to experience.

questions.q: What grammatical feature does the editor point out?
questions.answer: Absolute phrases with their own subjects ("the street still wet").

questions.q: What do these phrases allow writers to do?
questions.answer: Add layers of detail without stopping the flow of the sentence.

questions.q: Why do we trust travel writers who describe disappointment?
questions.answer: Their honesty makes us believe them when they describe wonder.

reading.title: Dawn in Ouro Preto
reading.text: I arrived in Ouro Preto after midnight, the bus from Belo Horizonte having been delayed by fog on the mountain road, and I remember almost nothing of that first night except the cold and the sound of rain on a tiled roof. It was the morning that stayed with me. I woke before six, the room still dark, and, unable to sleep, went out to walk. The town, built on hills so steep that some streets seem to defy gravity, was entirely silent. Mist lay in the valleys between the churches, their towers rising out of it like the masts of ships at anchor. The cobblestones, polished by three centuries of feet and that night's rain, shone under the last of the streetlamps. Somewhere below, a dog barked once, then thought better of it. I climbed towards the Church of São Francisco de Assis, my breath visible in the air, my legs protesting at every step. With the light growing stronger, details began to emerge: the soapstone carvings above the doorway, the blue and white of colonial façades, a woman in a doorway sweeping her front step, her radio murmuring a morning programme. She nodded to me without a word, as if strangers at dawn were part and parcel of her day. History in Ouro Preto is not a subject but an atmosphere. Gold made the town rich in the eighteenth century, its wealth flowing to Lisbon and beyond, and the beauty that remains was built, in large part, by enslaved labour — a fact no honest visitor should forget. Yet that morning, the streets empty and the mist slowly lifting, it felt less like a museum than a place still dreaming. By eight, the first tour buses had arrived. The spell broken, I went in search of coffee. All things considered, I have rarely spent two hours better.

writing.model:
Saturday at the Ver-o-Peso

I arrived at the Ver-o-Peso market in Belém just after five, the sky over the Guajará Bay still the colour of slate. The boats had come in during the night, their decks piled high with baskets of açaí, and men were already carrying them ashore, the purple fruit glistening in the half-light.

The noise came first. Vendors shouted prices to one another across the stalls, a radio somewhere played brega at full volume, and the vultures — there are always vultures at the Ver-o-Peso — circled above the fish market with an air of patient expectation. Then came the smells: river mud, diesel, coriander, the sharp, sweet scent of cupuaçu.

I wandered through the herb section, where women sat behind tables crowded with bottles and roots, each labelled with promises. One mixture, I was told, would bring luck in love; another, prosperity in business; a third, a combination of both. The seller, a woman in her seventies, her hair tied back in a bright scarf, explained each one with the seriousness of a pharmacist. When I asked whether they really worked, she smiled and said nothing, which seemed the most honest answer possible.

By seven, the heat had arrived. With the sun climbing higher and the crowds growing thicker, I retreated to a stall by the water for breakfast: fried fish, farinha and a bowl of açaí so thick that the spoon stood upright in it. Around me, porters sat in silence, their work done for the morning, staring out at the river.

The market will doubtless change. There are always plans to modernize, to clean up, to make it more "tourist-friendly". Some of those changes may be welcome. But that morning, the river shining and the vultures still circling, it felt like the beating heart of the city — chaotic, generous and entirely alive.

All things considered, I can think of few better places to understand the Amazon without leaving the city.

grammar.title: Literary inversion and fronting
grammar.explanation_pt:
Além da inversão após expressões negativas (C1), o inglês formal e literário usa outros tipos de **fronting** (deslocar um elemento para o início) com **inversão do sujeito e do verbo**:

**1. Expressões de lugar / movimento + verbo + sujeito** (verbos intransitivos como come, go, stand, lie, sit, walk):
- "**Here comes** the bus." / "**There goes** my chance."
- "**Into the room walked** the president." / "**On the hill stood** an old church."
- "**Beneath the city lie** the remains of a Roman fort."
⚠️ Com pronome, **não** inverta: "Here **it comes**" (não "Here comes it").

**2. Particípio / adjetivo no início + be + sujeito:**
- "**Gone are the days** when..." (Os dias em que... já se foram)
- "**Equally important is** the question of..." / "**Of particular concern is**..."
- "**Attached is** a copy of the contract." / "**Enclosed are**..."
- "**Far more serious was** the damage to his reputation."

**3. Such / So + inversão** (resultado intenso):
- "**Such is** the power of television **that** elections are often won on screen."
- "**So great was** the demand **that** tickets sold out in minutes."
- "**Such was** his influence **that** no one dared to contradict him."

**4. Nowhere / Seldom / Rarely + comparativo:**
- "**Nowhere is** the divide **more** visible **than** in our cities."
- "**Rarely has** a speech had **such** an impact."

**5. So / Neither / Nor + auxiliar + sujeito** (concordância):
- "The president supported the law, **as did** most of the parliament." (as + auxiliar + sujeito — formal)
- "He didn't apologize, **nor did** he resign."

**6. So it was that...** (narrativo, solene): "**So it was that** a small protest became a national movement."

**Efeito:** dramaticidade, ênfase e ritmo. **Use com moderação**: uma ou duas por parágrafo são impactantes; mais que isso soa teatral.

listening.title: Ethos, pathos, logos — and kairos
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de retórica fala sobre os elementos da persuasão.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: You may have heard of Aristotle's three modes of persuasion: ethos, the character and credibility of the speaker; pathos, the emotions of the audience; and logos, the logic of the argument. Less well known, but no less important, is a fourth concept the Greeks discussed: kairos, the opportune moment. Such is the importance of timing that the same words can inspire a nation on one day and fall completely flat on another. Think of a leader addressing the country after a disaster. Rarely is an audience more ready to listen, and rarely does a speaker have more power — or more responsibility. Gone, of course, are the days when a speech reached people only once, in a hall or on the radio. Today, every phrase can be clipped, replayed and reinterpreted in a different context, months or years later. Kairos has become far more complicated. A sentence that was perfectly judged at the time may sound tone-deaf when it resurfaces. Nowhere is this more evident than on social media.

questions.answer: Credibility of the speaker, emotions of the audience, logic of the argument.

questions.q: What is kairos?
questions.answer: The opportune moment — timing.

questions.q: Why has kairos become more complicated?
questions.answer: Phrases can be clipped and replayed in different contexts later.

reading.title: The age of the soundbite
reading.text: Gone are the days when political arguments unfolded over hours. In nineteenth-century America, the famous debates between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas could last three hours, with each candidate speaking for an hour or more while crowds stood and listened. Such was the appetite for political oratory that newspapers printed the speeches in full, and readers studied them line by line. The contrast with today could hardly be sharper. Studies of American television news have documented a dramatic shrinking of the "soundbite" — the length of time a candidate is shown speaking without interruption. According to research frequently cited by media scholars, the average soundbite on the evening news fell from more than forty seconds in the late 1960s to under ten seconds by the end of the 1980s. Social media has accelerated the trend still further. Today, a political career can be made or broken by a phrase short enough to fit on a placard. What has been lost? Critics argue that complexity is the first casualty. Few serious problems — climate change, healthcare, inequality — can be explained in a single sentence, and politicians who attempt to do so are forced to oversimplify. Equally worrying is the effect on public trust. When every statement is designed to be clipped and shared, politicians speak less to persuade than to avoid giving their opponents ammunition. Yet it would be wrong to romanticize the past. Long speeches were by no means guaranteed to be wise, and many nineteenth-century orators were skilled demagogues. Nor is brevity always a vice: some of the most powerful phrases in political history are also among the shortest. Perhaps the real question is not how long political speech should be, but whether audiences still have the patience — and the platforms — to hear arguments that cannot be reduced to a slogan.

questions.q: How did the average TV soundbite change, according to research?
questions.answer: From over forty seconds in the late 1960s to under ten seconds by the late 1980s.

questions.q: What two negative effects are mentioned?
questions.answer: Loss of complexity and loss of public trust.

writing.model:
The disappearing public square

Gone are the days when a town's most important conversations took place in its square. For centuries, the praça was where Brazilians met, argued, celebrated and protested. Today, those conversations have largely moved online — and our democracy is the poorer for it.

Such is the convenience of social media that it has become, for millions of people, the main source of political information. It is easy to see why. Platforms are free, immediate and available at any hour. Yet they were not designed to foster debate. They were designed to capture attention, and nothing captures attention quite like outrage.

Nowhere is the consequence more visible than in the tone of our political life. Opponents are no longer people with different views but enemies to be defeated. Nuance is punished; certainty is rewarded. A politician who admits doubt is mocked, while one who shouts is shared.

Equally troubling is the fragmentation of reality itself. In the old square, people heard the same speeches, read the same newspapers and, even when they disagreed, argued about the same facts. Online, each of us inhabits a separate world, shaped by algorithms we do not understand. So complete has this separation become that neighbours may now hold entirely different beliefs about events that happened in their own street.

None of this means we should abandon technology, nor should we romanticize a past that excluded many voices. But it does mean we must deliberately rebuild spaces — physical and digital — where citizens can encounter one another as people rather than profiles: public libraries, community meetings, local newspapers, platforms designed for discussion rather than division.

On the walls of many old town halls hangs an image of citizens gathered in a square, listening to one another. It is worth asking whether our grandchildren will understand what it means. Democracy, after all, is not only a system of voting. It is a habit of talking — and habits, once lost, are hard to recover.

grammar.title: The language of spin
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Eufemismos** — palavras suaves para realidades duras:
- **Trabalho:** downsizing, rightsizing, restructuring, letting people go, workforce adjustment, "exploring other opportunities" (= demitido)
- **Economia:** negative growth (= recessão), revenue enhancement (= aumento de impostos), price adjustment (= aumento de preço), correction (= queda)
- **Guerra:** collateral damage, neutralize, friendly fire, enhanced interrogation
- **Vida pessoal:** passed away, between jobs, economically disadvantaged
⚠️ Nem todo eufemismo é manipulação: "passed away" é **delicadeza**; "collateral damage" pode **desumanizar**.

**2. Weasel words** — criam a **impressão** de uma afirmação sem afirmar nada verificável:
- **Fontes vagas:** "Some experts say...", "Studies show...", "It is widely believed...", "Many people are saying..."
- **Qualificadores:** "**up to** 70% off" (pode ser 5%), "**helps** reduce" (não diz quanto), "**virtually** invisible", "**can** improve", "**as much as**"
- **Comparações incompletas:** "**40% more** effective" (do que o quê?)

**3. Gramática para ocultar o agente:**
- **Passiva sem agente:** "Mistakes **were made**." / "The data **was lost**." / "Shots **were fired**."
- **Nominalização:** "There has been **a reduction in staff**" (em vez de "We fired 300 people")
- **Verbos ergativos** (sem agente): "The project **failed**." / "Prices **rose**." / "The ship **sank**."
- **Sujeitos abstratos:** "**The situation** has led to job losses."

**4. O falso pedido de desculpas (non-apology):**
- "I'm sorry **if** anyone was offended." (coloca a culpa em quem se ofendeu)
- "I regret that **you feel** that way."
- "Mistakes were made, **but** ..."
- Um pedido real: "**I** was wrong. **I** apologize for **what I said**. **It** won't happen again."

**Antídoto C2:** pergunte sempre **quem fez o quê, a quem, quanto e segundo quem?**

rows: I'm sorry if you were offended.
I'm sorry for what I said.

examples.en: The company announced a "strategic workforce realignment", which, stripped of the jargon, meant that 400 people would lose their jobs.
examples.pt: A empresa anunciou um "realinhamento estratégico da força de trabalho", o que, sem o jargão, significava que 400 pessoas perderiam o emprego.

examples.en: "Mistakes were made" is a classic example of the passive voice being used to avoid responsibility.
examples.pt: "Erros foram cometidos" é um exemplo clássico da voz passiva sendo usada para evitar responsabilidade.

examples.en: The advert claims the cream "helps reduce the appearance of wrinkles" — a sentence carefully designed to promise almost nothing.
examples.pt: O anúncio afirma que o creme "ajuda a reduzir a aparência de rugas" — uma frase cuidadosamente construída para prometer quase nada.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português também temos: "**colaboradores desligados**" (demitidos), "**ajuste tarifário**" (aumento), "**comunidade**" (às vezes para evitar "favela"). Perceber o eufemismo nas duas línguas é sinal de leitura crítica madura.

common_mistakes.wrong: Treating "Studies show..." as a reliable source.
common_mistakes.right: Ask: which studies, by whom, published where?
common_mistakes.why_pt: Weasel words imitam autoridade sem fornecer evidência.

common_mistakes.wrong: I'm sorry if you were upset by my comment. (as a real apology)
common_mistakes.right: I'm sorry for my comment. It was wrong.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Um pedido real assume responsabilidade, sem "if".

common_mistakes.wrong: Using "collateral damage" in a neutral news report about civilian deaths.
common_mistakes.right: Use clear language: "civilians were killed".
common_mistakes.why_pt: Eufemismos de guerra podem desumanizar vítimas.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Ao citar um eufemismo de forma crítica, falantes nativos usam um tom **ligeiramente irônico**, muitas vezes com **air quotes** (aspas no ar) ou expressões como "so-called": "They're not firing people, they're... *rightsizing*." / "the **so-called** 'price adjustment'".

dialogue.title: The press release
dialogue.context_pt: Uma jornalista e um assessor de imprensa discutem um comunicado de uma empresa.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Your press release says the company is "optimizing its operational footprint". What does that actually mean?
lines.pt: Seu comunicado diz que a empresa está "otimizando sua presença operacional". O que isso significa de fato?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: It means we're making the business more efficient for the long term.
lines.pt: Significa que estamos tornando o negócio mais eficiente no longo prazo.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Are you closing the factory in Joinville?
lines.pt: Vocês vão fechar a fábrica de Joinville?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: The Joinville facility will be transitioning to a new model.
lines.pt: A unidade de Joinville passará por uma transição para um novo modelo.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: Will the 600 workers there lose their jobs?
lines.pt: Os 600 trabalhadores de lá vão perder o emprego?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: Some roles will be affected, yes. We'll be supporting colleagues as they explore new opportunities.
lines.pt: Algumas funções serão afetadas, sim. Vamos apoiar os colaboradores enquanto exploram novas oportunidades.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: So, in plain English: the factory is closing and around 600 people will be made redundant.
lines.pt: Então, em português claro: a fábrica vai fechar e cerca de 600 pessoas serão demitidas.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: I wouldn't put it quite like that.
lines.pt: Eu não colocaria exatamente assim.

lines.speaker: Journalist
lines.en: No — but I will. My readers deserve to know what's happening, not what it's being called.
lines.pt: Não — mas eu vou colocar. Meus leitores merecem saber o que está acontecendo, não como isso está sendo chamado.

listening.title: Politics and the English language
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de literatura fala sobre o ensaio de George Orwell sobre linguagem política.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: In 1946, George Orwell published an essay called "Politics and the English Language". His argument was that political language is often designed to make the indefensible sound reasonable. He gave examples from his own time: villages bombed and inhabitants driven out were described as "pacification". Rather than describe brutal events directly, officials reached for abstract, Latinate words that created a kind of fog. Orwell also attacked lazy writing more generally — dying metaphors, pretentious vocabulary, unnecessary passives — because he believed that sloppy language makes sloppy thinking easier. He ended with six rules, the most famous of which is probably: "Never use a long word where a short one will do." He was also honest enough to add a final rule allowing writers to break any of the others rather than say anything outright barbarous. Almost eighty years later, the essay is still widely read, and its central warning still applies. When language stops describing reality and starts concealing it, democracy has a problem.

questions.q: What was Orwell's main argument?
questions.answer: Political language is often designed to make the indefensible sound reasonable.

questions.q: What euphemism did he give as an example?
questions.answer: "Pacification" for bombing villages and driving out inhabitants.

questions.q: Why did he criticize lazy writing in general?
questions.answer: Sloppy language makes sloppy thinking easier.

questions.q: What is his most famous rule?
questions.answer: Never use a long word where a short one will do.

reading.title: The anatomy of a non-apology
reading.text: Few genres of public communication have been studied as closely, or mocked as mercilessly, as the corporate apology. When a company is caught polluting a river, mistreating customers or leaking personal data, its statement tends to follow a predictable pattern — one that linguists and public relations experts have learned to dissect. It typically begins with an expression of regret, rather than an apology: "We regret any inconvenience this may have caused." The verb "regret" is significant. One can regret a storm; regret does not imply responsibility. The phrase "any inconvenience" minimizes the harm, while "may have caused" leaves open the possibility that nothing was caused at all. Next comes the passive voice. "Mistakes were made" and "data was accessed" describe events without naming anyone who performed them. The agent — the company, its executives, a specific decision — quietly vanishes from the sentence. Then there is the conditional apology: "We apologize to anyone who was affected" or "We're sorry if customers felt let down." By placing the problem in the reactions of others, the statement implies that the fault lies, at least partly, in their sensitivity. Finally, the statement moves swiftly to the future: "We are committed to the highest standards and are reviewing our processes." The past, with all its awkward details, is left behind. Research on apologies suggests that the most effective ones do almost exactly the opposite. They acknowledge responsibility clearly, name the specific harm, express genuine remorse, explain what went wrong and offer concrete repair. They are short, specific and active. "We broke your trust. Here is what we did, here is why it happened, and here is what we will do to put it right." Such apologies are rare, not because they are hard to write, but because they are hard to say. They require something the language of spin is designed to avoid: accepting the blame.

questions.q: Why is "regret" different from "apologize"?
questions.answer: Regret doesn't imply responsibility.

questions.q: How does the passive voice help companies?
questions.answer: It describes events without naming who caused them.

questions.q: What does a conditional apology imply?
questions.answer: That the fault lies partly in others' sensitivity.

questions.q: What do effective apologies do?
questions.answer: Acknowledge responsibility, name the harm, show remorse, explain, and offer repair.

writing.model:
Version 1 — Spin

Statement from RotaFácil

At RotaFácil, the safety and satisfaction of our valued customers have always been our highest priorities. We are aware of recent reports concerning a technical incident affecting a limited number of journeys on our platform. Some passengers may have experienced unexpected route variations and adjusted fare calculations. We sincerely regret any inconvenience this may have caused. Mistakes were made in the implementation of a system update, and the matter is being reviewed. We are committed to continuous improvement and to delivering the seamless experience our customers expect. Going forward, enhanced monitoring processes will be put in place. We thank our community for its patience and understanding.

Version 2 — Honest

An apology from RotaFácil

On 3 and 4 June, a software update we released contained an error. As a result, our app charged around 12,000 customers more than it should have — in some cases, twice the correct fare — and sent some drivers on unnecessarily long routes.

This was our fault. We did not test the update properly before releasing it, and when customers first complained, we were too slow to respond.

We are sorry. Every customer who was overcharged will receive a full refund, plus a credit of R$20, by 15 June. You don't need to do anything: the money will be returned automatically. Drivers who lost earnings will also be compensated.

We have changed how we test updates so that this cannot happen again, and we will publish a report on what went wrong next month.

If you have any questions, our team is available on 0800-555-0199.

Marina Lopes
CEO, RotaFácil

culture_note.title: "Economical with the truth"
culture_note.text_pt: A expressão **"economical with the truth"** ficou famosa em 1986, quando o alto funcionário britânico **Sir Robert Armstrong** a usou num tribunal australiano para descrever uma carta enganosa. Hoje é um eufemismo irônico para "mentir por omissão". Outras expressões semelhantes: **"terminological inexactitude"** (Churchill, 1906) e **"alternative facts"** (2017).

summary_pt: Eufemismos: rightsizing, letting go, negative growth, collateral damage.
Weasel words: some experts say, up to, helps, virtually, X% more (than what?).
Ocultar o agente: passiva sem agente, nominalização, verbos ergativos.
Pedido real: I + responsabilidade + dano específico + reparação; sem "if".

lessons.title: The fine print
lessons.subtitle_pt: Conectores formais: whereby, notwithstanding, insofar as, lest, albeit, hence, thereby
source_refs: CEFR – C2 descriptors (formal and legal register)
Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading and Use of English Part 2
objectives: Usar conectores formais raros (notwithstanding, albeit, insofar as, inasmuch as)
Usar whereby, thereby, hence, thus, whereupon

warmup.text_pt: Já leu os **termos de uso** de um app até o fim? Provavelmente não — e não foi por falta de inglês. Contratos e regulamentos usam um vocabulário próprio: "**Notwithstanding** the above...", "...**whereby** the user agrees...", "**albeit** with limitations". No C2, você precisa entender — e usar com precisão — esses conectores, que também aparecem em textos acadêmicos e na prova C2 Proficiency.

grammar.title: Formal connectives
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Concessão formal:**
- **notwithstanding** (= despite / however) — antes ou depois do substantivo: "**Notwithstanding** the delay, the project was completed." / "The delay **notwithstanding**, ..."; também advérbio: "It was expensive; it was, **notwithstanding**, a success."
- **albeit** (= although) + adjetivo/advérbio/frase sem verbo: "a significant, **albeit** temporary, improvement" / "He agreed, **albeit** reluctantly."
- **be that as it may** (C1) / **that said** / **nonetheless**

**2. Extensão / grau:**
- **insofar as / in so far as** (= to the extent that): "The plan is fair **insofar as** everyone pays the same."
- **inasmuch as** (= since / to the extent that, formal): "He is responsible **inasmuch as** he signed the document."

**3. Meio / relação:**
- **whereby** (= by which, através do qual): "a system **whereby** employees can buy shares"
- **wherein / whereupon**: "the document **wherein** the terms are stated" / "He signed, **whereupon** the meeting ended." (= depois do que)

**4. Resultado / consequência:**
- **hence** (= portanto / daí) — muitas vezes sem verbo: "The data were incomplete, **hence** the delay."
- **thus** (= assim, portanto): "Costs fell; **thus**, prices could be reduced."
- **thereby** + -ing (= com isso, desse modo): "The bank raised rates, **thereby** reducing inflation."

**5. Finalidade negativa:**
- **lest** + (should) + verbo base (= para que não, formal/literário): "Keep a copy **lest** the original **be** lost."
- **for fear that / for fear of** + -ing: "He kept quiet **for fear of** losing his job."

**6. Linguagem jurídica (here- / there-):**
- **hereby** (por meio deste), **herein** (neste documento), **hereinafter** (doravante denominado), **thereof** (dele/disso), **therein** (nele)
- "The Company (**hereinafter** "the Provider") **hereby** agrees..."

⚠️ **Use com critério:** em e-mails comuns, "hereby" e "lest" soam arcaicos. São adequados em **textos jurídicos, acadêmicos e muito formais**.

examples.en: Notwithstanding any other provision of this agreement, the user remains responsible for the security of their password.

examples.en: The government introduced a scheme whereby low-income families receive a monthly payment, thereby reducing extreme poverty.

grammar.tip_pt: Muitos desses conectores têm equivalente direto no português jurídico: **notwithstanding** = não obstante; **hereby** = por meio deste / pelo presente; **whereby** = pelo qual; **hence** = daí; **albeit** = ainda que. Saber isso ajuda muito na tradução de contratos.

common_mistakes.wrong: Albeit it was expensive, it was worth it.
common_mistakes.right: Although it was expensive, it was worth it. / It was expensive, albeit worth it.
common_mistakes.why_pt: albeit normalmente não introduz uma oração completa com sujeito e verbo.

common_mistakes.wrong: The data was incomplete, hence we delayed the report.
common_mistakes.right: The data was incomplete; hence the delay. / ..., and hence we delayed the report.
common_mistakes.why_pt: hence costuma vir com substantivo ou depois de ponto e vírgula/and.

common_mistakes.wrong: Write it down lest you will forget.
common_mistakes.right: Write it down lest you forget / lest you should forget.
common_mistakes.why_pt: lest + verbo base (ou should).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Atenção à pronúncia: **notwithstanding** = "not-uiθ-STÉN-din"; **albeit** = "ól-BÍ-it" (3 sílabas!); **insofar** = "in-sou-FÁR"; **whereby** = "uér-BÁI"; **hereinafter** = "hír-in-ÉF-ter"; **lest** = "lést".

dialogue.title: Before you sign
dialogue.context_pt: Uma advogada explica um contrato de aluguel comercial a um cliente.

lines.speaker: Lawyer
lines.en: Before you sign, let's look at clause 12. It says: "Notwithstanding clause 4, the landlord may increase the rent annually in accordance with inflation."
lines.pt: Antes de assinar, vamos olhar a cláusula 12. Diz: "Não obstante a cláusula 4, o locador poderá reajustar o aluguel anualmente de acordo com a inflação."

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: But clause 4 says the rent is fixed for three years!
lines.pt: Mas a cláusula 4 diz que o aluguel é fixo por três anos!

lines.speaker: Lawyer
lines.en: Exactly. "Notwithstanding" means clause 12 overrides it. Hence my concern.
lines.pt: Exatamente. "Não obstante" significa que a cláusula 12 prevalece. Daí minha preocupação.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: So the rent isn't really fixed at all.
lines.pt: Então o aluguel não é fixo de verdade.

lines.speaker: Lawyer
lines.en: Only insofar as it can't rise above inflation. And here, clause 15 sets up an arrangement whereby you're liable for all structural repairs.
lines.pt: Só na medida em que não pode subir acima da inflação. E aqui, a cláusula 15 estabelece um arranjo pelo qual você é responsável por todos os reparos estruturais.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Structural? Even the roof?
lines.pt: Estruturais? Até o telhado?

lines.speaker: Lawyer
lines.en: Even the roof. It's unusual, albeit not illegal. I'd recommend negotiating it out, thereby protecting yourself from a very large bill.
lines.pt: Até o telhado. É incomum, embora não ilegal. Eu recomendaria negociar a retirada, protegendo-se assim de uma conta muito alta.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Thank you. I'm glad I didn't just sign it, lest I regret it for the next three years.
lines.pt: Obrigado. Ainda bem que não assinei direto, para não me arrepender nos próximos três anos.

listening.title: Nobody reads the terms
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora de direito digital fala sobre termos de uso.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: Almost everyone clicks "I agree" without reading. In one well-known experiment, published in 2016, researchers Jonathan Obar and Anne Oeldorf-Hirsch created a fictitious social network and asked students to sign up. Buried in the terms of service was a clause whereby users agreed to give up their first-born child as payment. The overwhelming majority of participants agreed — most of them, apparently, without noticing. The study was, admittedly, an exaggeration, albeit a revealing one. Real terms of service rarely demand children, but they frequently contain provisions whereby users waive important rights: allowing companies to share data with third parties, to change the terms at any time, or to resolve disputes through private arbitration rather than in court. Several jurisdictions, including the European Union, have introduced rules requiring that key information be presented clearly, thereby giving consumers a better chance of understanding what they're signing. Notwithstanding these efforts, the basic problem remains: terms are long, readers are busy, and the default is to trust.

questions.q: What did the fictitious social network's terms include?
questions.answer: A clause where users agreed to give up their first-born child.

questions.q: How did most participants react?
questions.answer: They agreed, mostly without noticing.

questions.q: What real provisions do terms of service often contain?
questions.answer: Data sharing, changing terms at any time, private arbitration instead of court.

questions.q: What has the EU done?
questions.answer: Introduced rules requiring key information to be presented clearly.

reading.title: In defence of legalese?
reading.text: Few styles of writing are as widely disliked as "legalese": the dense, archaic and seemingly impenetrable language of contracts, statutes and terms of service. Critics have long argued that it serves mainly to exclude ordinary readers, thereby protecting the interests of lawyers and the powerful. Movements for "plain language" in law have won significant victories, and in many countries, government documents and consumer contracts must now be written in a way that the average reader can understand. Yet legal language is not merely the product of tradition or self-interest. Many of its peculiarities exist for a reason. Words such as "notwithstanding", "hereinafter" and "whereby" allow drafters to establish precise relationships between different parts of a document — which clause overrides which, how a term is defined, by what mechanism an obligation arises. Ordinary words, by contrast, tend to be vague, and vagueness in a contract can lead to years of costly litigation. Repetition, too, has a purpose: a lawyer who writes "the Buyer" fifty times rather than switching to "they" or "the customer" ensures that no court can later argue that the parties meant different people. Some features, admittedly, are harder to defend. Doublets and triplets such as "null and void", "cease and desist" and "give, devise and bequeath" are largely historical relics, dating from a time when English law drew on English, French and Latin and drafters used all three to be safe. Long sentences with multiple embedded clauses serve the convenience of the writer far more than the comprehension of the reader. The challenge, then, is not to abolish legal language but to distinguish precision from obscurity. A good contract should be as exact as necessary — albeit no more complicated than it needs to be. Insofar as plain language can achieve that, it is not the enemy of the law but its ally.

Terms and Conditions — Horta Viva Community Garden

1. Definitions
In these Terms, "the Association" refers to the Horta Viva Residents' Association, and "the Member" refers to any person allocated a plot (hereinafter "the Plot").

2. Allocation
Plots are allocated in accordance with a waiting list whereby priority is given to residents of the neighbourhood. The Association hereby reserves the right to refuse an application where the applicant has previously breached these Terms.

3. Use of the Plot
The Member shall cultivate the Plot regularly, albeit with reasonable flexibility during periods of illness or travel. A Plot left uncultivated for more than three consecutive months may be reallocated, notwithstanding any fees previously paid.

4. Water and resources
Water is shared and limited; hence, hoses may only be used before 9 a.m. or after 5 p.m. Members are encouraged to use rainwater collection systems, thereby reducing costs for the whole community.

5. Liability
Insofar as the law permits, the Association shall not be liable for loss of or damage to tools, plants or personal property. Members are therefore advised to store valuables at home lest they be lost or stolen.

6. Termination
Either party may terminate the agreement with thirty days' written notice, whereupon the Member shall return the Plot in a clean and usable condition.

7. Changes
The Association may amend these Terms, provided that Members are notified at least two weeks in advance.

— Plain English summary —
You get a plot because you live nearby. Look after it — if you leave it for three months, we may give it to someone else. Only water early or late in the day. We're not responsible if your tools are stolen, so don't leave valuables here. You can leave with 30 days' notice. We'll tell you two weeks before we change any rules.

grammar.title: Rhetorical figures
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Paralelismo** — estruturas gramaticais **iguais** em sequência (a base de quase todas as figuras):
- ❌ "She likes swimming, to run and cycles." ✅ "She likes **swimming, running and cycling**."
- "We will **build** schools, **train** teachers and **support** families."

**2. Tricolon** (C1, revisão): três elementos paralelos, geralmente com o último mais longo ou forte.
- "government **of** the people, **by** the people, **for** the people" (Lincoln, 1863)

**3. Anáfora** — repetição no **início** de frases/orações:
- "**We shall fight** on the beaches, **we shall fight** on the landing grounds, **we shall fight** in the fields..." (Churchill, 1940)

**4. Epístrofe** — repetição no **final**:
- "...government of the people, by the **people**, for the **people**."
- "When I was a child, I spoke as a **child**, I understood as a **child**, I thought as a **child**." (Bíblia, King James)

**5. Antítese** — ideias opostas em estrutura paralela:
- "...**not because** they are **easy**, **but because** they are **hard**." (Kennedy, 1962)
- "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind." (Armstrong, 1969)

**6. Quiasmo** — repetição **invertida** (A-B / B-A):
- "Ask not what **your country** can do for **you** — ask what **you** can do for **your country**." (Kennedy, 1961)
- "**Eat** to **live**, not **live** to **eat**."
- "It's not the **years** in your **life**, it's the **life** in your **years**."

**7. Aliteração e assonância** — repetição de sons: "**b**igger, **b**etter, **b**older"; "**p**eace, **p**rosperity and **p**rogress"

**8. Perguntas retóricas e pausas** (C1, revisão).

**Gramática do paralelismo:** ao listar ações, mantenha a **mesma forma** (todos verbos base, todos -ing, todos substantivos); ao contrastar, use **estruturas idênticas**: "not X but Y", "less X, more Y", "the more X, the more Y".

Ao escrever em inglês, comece pelo **paralelismo**: ele torna frases mais claras **e** mais memoráveis. listening.title: Anatomy of a famous speech
listening.context_pt: Um historiador analisa o Discurso de Gettysburg, de Abraham Lincoln (1863).

lines.speaker: Historian
lines.en: On 19 November 1863, at the dedication of a military cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, Abraham Lincoln spoke for around two minutes. The main speaker that day, the celebrated orator Edward Everett, had spoken for about two hours. It is Lincoln's speech that is remembered. Why? Partly because of its brevity — fewer than three hundred words — and partly because of its extraordinary craftsmanship. Lincoln uses antithesis repeatedly: the world "will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here." He uses a tricolon of verbs: "we can not dedicate — we can not consecrate — we can not hallow — this ground." And he ends with perhaps the most famous example of epistrophe in American history, describing a government "of the people, by the people, for the people". Notice, too, the irony of that first antithesis: Lincoln claimed the world would not remember his words. Rarely has a prediction been so completely wrong.

questions.q: How long did Lincoln speak, compared with Edward Everett?
questions.answer: About two minutes, compared with about two hours.

questions.q: Give an example of antithesis from the speech.
questions.answer: "The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here."

questions.q: What tricolon of verbs does Lincoln use?
questions.answer: Dedicate, consecrate, hallow.

questions.q: What is ironic about the first antithesis?
questions.answer: Lincoln said the world wouldn't remember his words, but it did.

reading.title: Why rhetoric still matters
reading.text: For much of Western history, rhetoric — the art of persuasive speech — stood at the centre of education. Roman schoolboys practised declamation; medieval universities taught it as one of the three foundational arts, alongside grammar and logic; and well into the nineteenth century, educated people were expected to recognize, and to use, figures such as anaphora and chiasmus. In the twentieth century, however, rhetoric acquired a bad name. After decades of wartime propaganda and, later, the polished manipulations of advertising, the word came to suggest empty or deceptive speech: "mere rhetoric". Many schools quietly dropped it from the curriculum. This is unfortunate, for two reasons. First, the techniques of rhetoric have not disappeared; they have simply become less visible. Every political speech, advertising campaign and viral post draws on the same toolkit that Cicero and Quintilian described two thousand years ago. Citizens who cannot recognize these techniques are, in a sense, defenceless against them. To identify a false antithesis — "either you are with us or you are against us" — is already to begin to resist it. Second, rhetoric is not only a weapon of the powerful. It has also been the instrument of those seeking to challenge power. Abolitionists, suffragists and civil rights leaders were, almost without exception, masters of persuasive language; their speeches combined moral clarity with carefully crafted rhythm, repetition and contrast. To dismiss rhetoric as manipulation is, in effect, to give up one of the most effective tools of democratic change. Perhaps the solution is to return rhetoric to its original place: not as a set of tricks but as a discipline of both speaking and listening. A society that teaches its citizens to recognize persuasion, to analyse it and to use it responsibly is far better equipped to govern itself than one that merely hopes its leaders will speak honestly.

questions.q: What were the three foundational arts in medieval universities?
questions.answer: Grammar, logic and rhetoric.

questions.q: Why did rhetoric acquire a bad name in the twentieth century?
questions.answer: Because of wartime propaganda and advertising manipulation.

questions.q: What is the first reason it's unfortunate to drop rhetoric from education?
questions.answer: The techniques are still used; citizens who can't recognize them are defenceless.

questions.q: What is the second reason?
questions.answer: Rhetoric has also been a tool for challenging power and democratic change.

writing.model:
Opening of the Vila Esperança Community Library

Friends, neighbours, children of Vila Esperança,

Three years ago, on this very spot, there was nothing but a broken wall and a pile of rubbish. Today, there are four thousand books.

They told us it was impossible. They told us there was no money. They told us that nobody here would read. Look around you. Every shelf in this room is an answer to them.

This library was not built by the government, nor by a company, nor by a single generous donor. It was built by you: by the bricklayer who gave his weekends, by the grandmother who organized the book drive, by the teenagers who painted these walls. It was built not with money, but with time; not with promises, but with hands.

Some people say that books belong to the past — that our children need screens, not stories. I say they need both. But a screen can show you the world; a book can show you yourself.

Here, a child who has never left this neighbourhood can travel to the Amazon, to Lisbon, to the moon. Here, an adult who never finished school can finally finish a book. Here, every one of us can find a quiet place in a noisy world.

We did not build this library because it was easy. We built it because it was necessary.

So, to the children of Vila Esperança, I have just one request. Don't just read the books in this room — one day, write the books that will fill it. Because a community that reads can change its story; a community that writes its story can change the world.

Welcome to your library.

— Figures used: anaphora ("They told us...", "Here..."), tricolon (bricklayer, grandmother, teenagers), antithesis (not with money, but with time), chiasmus ("a community that reads can change its story; a community that writes its story..."), parallel antithesis ("not because it was easy... because it was necessary").

grammar.title: Fine-grained epistemic modality
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Escala de certeza com expressões nominais e adverbiais** (do mais certo ao menos):
- **certo:** it's a foregone conclusion · undoubtedly · without a doubt · there's no question that
- **quase certo:** in all likelihood · in all probability · there's every chance / reason to believe · the odds are (that)
- **provável:** it's (highly) likely that · S is likely to · chances are (that)
- **possível:** conceivably · it's not inconceivable that (litotes!) · there's a (slim / outside) chance that
- **improvável:** it's doubtful whether · S is unlikely to · it's a long shot
- **impossível:** it's inconceivable / unthinkable that · there's no way that (informal)

**2. Modais + advérbios** (graduação fina):
- **may / might / could well** (bem provável) x **may / might just** (pequena chance)
- **can't possibly / couldn't possibly** (impossível) — "She **can't possibly have** known."
- **needn't necessarily** (não implica obrigatoriamente) — "A fall in sales **needn't necessarily** mean a crisis."
- **must surely / must have surely** (dedução forte, com ênfase)
- **would probably / would almost certainly**

**3. It + adjetivo + that / whether:**
- "**It is doubtful whether** the plan will work."
- "**It is highly improbable that**..." / "**It is by no means certain that**..."
- "**It is not inconceivable that**..." (= é possível — mais cauteloso)

**4. Atenção ao "no passado":**
- **must have / can't have / might have + particípio** (dedução)
- "**In all likelihood**, the letter **was** lost in the post."
- "There**'s every chance** he **has** already **left**."

**5. Comunicar incerteza:** separe **o que se sabe**, **o que é provável** e **o que é desconhecido**. Evite falsa precisão ("exactly 73.4%") e falsa certeza ("science proves").

rows: in all likelihood, there's every chance, the odds are
conceivably, it's not inconceivable, may well
it's doubtful whether, a long shot, might just

examples.en: In all likelihood, the virus was circulating for several weeks before the first case was identified.
examples.pt: Muito provavelmente, o vírus estava circulando por várias semanas antes de o primeiro caso ser identificado.

examples.en: A single cold winter needn't necessarily contradict the evidence for global warming.
examples.pt: Um único inverno frio não contradiz necessariamente as evidências do aquecimento global.

examples.en: It is doubtful whether the new treatment will be available before the end of the decade.
examples.pt: É duvidoso que o novo tratamento esteja disponível antes do fim da década.

grammar.tip_pt: "**Needn't necessarily**" é muito útil para **evitar conclusões precipitadas**: "Correlation needn't necessarily imply causation." E "**It's not inconceivable**" (litotes) soa mais cauteloso que "it's possible".

common_mistakes.why_pt: Expressão fixa no singular.

common_mistakes.why_pt: doubtful + whether ou that, sem if duplo.

common_mistakes.wrong: She can't possibly knew.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Modal + have + particípio para o passado.

pronunciation.tip_pt: O grau de certeza também está na voz. Em **can't POSSibly** e **needn't NEcessarily**, o advérbio é **muito acentuado**. Em expressões de incerteza, a entonação tende a ser **mais lenta e suspensa**: "It's... conceivable ↗, I suppose."

listening.title: What does "likely" mean?
listening.context_pt: Um especialista em comunicação de riscos fala sobre como as pessoas interpretam palavras de probabilidade.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: In the 1960s, an analyst at the CIA, Sherman Kent, noticed a worrying problem. Intelligence reports used words like "probable", "likely" and "a serious possibility", but when he asked colleagues what probability these words represented, their answers varied enormously. For some, "a serious possibility" meant a 20 percent chance; for others, 80. Later surveys of the general public have found the same pattern. The word "likely" might mean 60 percent to one person and 90 to another. This matters. A doctor who says a treatment will "probably" work, or a climate report that describes an outcome as "very likely", may be understood very differently by different people. That's why some organizations — the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, for instance — attach specific numerical ranges to their words: "very likely", in their reports, means 90 to 100 percent. The lesson for all of us? When it really matters, it's worth adding a number.

questions.q: What problem did Sherman Kent notice?
questions.answer: Probability words in reports were interpreted very differently by different people.

questions.q: How differently was "a serious possibility" interpreted?
questions.answer: From about 20 percent to 80 percent.

questions.q: What does "very likely" mean in IPCC reports?
questions.answer: 90 to 100 percent.

questions.q: What is the speaker's advice?
questions.answer: When it matters, add a number.

reading.title: The science of saying "we don't know"
reading.text: In the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, scientists faced a communication challenge of unprecedented scale. They were being asked, daily and in front of enormous audiences, to answer questions that could not yet be answered with confidence. How easily does the virus spread? How deadly is it? Do masks help? The honest answer to many of these questions was, at first, "We don't know — but here is what we think is likely." That answer proved remarkably difficult to communicate. Audiences, understandably, wanted certainty. Politicians often preferred clear messages. And when advice changed as evidence accumulated — as it inevitably did — many people concluded that the experts had been wrong, or worse, dishonest. Yet changing one's mind in response to new evidence is not a failure of science; it is the very essence of it. Researchers who study risk communication have drawn several lessons from the experience. First, uncertainty should be acknowledged openly and early. Studies suggest that admitting uncertainty does not necessarily damage trust; in some cases, audiences find it more credible than false confidence. Second, it helps to distinguish clearly between what is known, what is probable and what is still unknown. Third, communicators should explain in advance that advice may change, and why. If people expect revisions, they are less likely to interpret them as contradictions. None of this is easy. A message hedged with qualifications is, in all likelihood, less memorable than a confident slogan. But there is every reason to believe that, over time, honesty about uncertainty builds a deeper and more durable kind of trust — one that can survive the inevitable moments when the evidence shifts.

questions.q: What was the honest answer to many early pandemic questions?
questions.answer: "We don't know — but here is what we think is likely."

questions.q: Why did changing advice cause problems?
questions.answer: Many people concluded the experts had been wrong or dishonest.

questions.q: Does admitting uncertainty damage trust, according to studies?
questions.answer: Not necessarily; sometimes it's seen as more credible.

questions.q: Name two lessons from risk communication research.
questions.answer: Acknowledge uncertainty early; distinguish known/probable/unknown; explain in advance that advice may change.

writing.model:
Will we ever talk to animals?

In recent years, a number of research projects have begun using artificial intelligence to analyse the sounds of animals — from sperm whales to bats to crows — in the hope of decoding their communication. Headlines have promised that we may soon be able to "talk to" other species. How realistic is that?

What we know is this: many animals use complex vocal systems. Some species of birds and whales produce sequences of sounds that follow regular patterns, and researchers have shown that certain calls are associated with particular situations, such as warnings of specific predators. It is beyond doubt that animals communicate, and in some cases in surprisingly sophisticated ways.

What is likely is that AI will help scientists detect patterns that humans would never notice. Machine learning is remarkably good at finding structure in large amounts of data, and there is every reason to believe that it will reveal more about how and when animals use particular sounds. In all likelihood, we will soon have much more detailed "dictionaries" of animal calls.

What remains unknown — and is, frankly, doubtful — is whether any animal communication system is a language in the human sense, with grammar and the ability to express new ideas. Finding patterns needn't necessarily mean finding meaning. A model might predict which sound a whale will make next without understanding what, if anything, the sound refers to.

As for a two-way conversation, that remains a long shot. Even if we could produce the right sounds, it is by no means certain that animals would interpret them as we intend. It is not inconceivable that we will one day exchange simple signals with another species. But the odds are that the first breakthroughs will be smaller, stranger and more interesting than the headlines suggest.

grammar.title: Complex noun phrases and reporting verbs
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Sintagma nominal complexo** = núcleo + **pré-modificadores** + **pós-modificadores**:

[the] [**recent**] [**large-scale**] [**rural-to-urban**] **migration** [**of young people**] [**in north-eastern Brazil**] [**over the past two decades**]

- **Pré-modificação:** adjetivos, substantivos como adjetivos (*labour market*, *health policy*), adjetivos compostos (*low-income*, *evidence-based*), particípios (*the growing demand*)
- **Pós-modificação:** preposições (*of, in, for, on*), orações relativas reduzidas (*the data collected in 2020*, *students attending public schools*), infinitivos (*the decision to expand*), orações relativas (*a policy which...*)

**Dica:** substantivos como adjetivos ficam no **singular**: *a three-year study*, *a labour market policy* (não "labours market").

**2. Verbos de citação (reporting verbs) — posição do autor original:**
- **Neutros:** state, note, report, describe, observe, suggest, propose
- **Argumentativos (o autor defende):** argue, contend, maintain, claim, assert, posit, insist
- **Concessão:** acknowledge, concede, admit, recognize
- **Discordância:** dispute, challenge, question, reject, refute (= provar que é falso!), dismiss
- **Evidência:** demonstrate, show, find, establish, confirm

**3. Sua posição (stance) em relação à fonte:**
- **Aceitando:** "As Silva **rightly** points out..." / "Silva **convincingly** demonstrates..."
- **Distanciando:** "Silva **claims** that..." (dúvida) / "**According to** Silva..."
- **Rejeitando:** "Silva's argument **fails to account for**..." / "This view **overlooks**..."

**4. Tempo verbal nas citações:**
- **Presente** para ideias/argumentos ainda relevantes: "Smith (2020) **argues** that..."
- **Passado** para estudos específicos e resultados: "Smith (2020) **found** that 40% of..."
- **Present perfect** para panorama: "Several studies **have shown**..."

listening.title: Why is academic English so dense?
listening.context_pt: Um linguista explica a densidade da escrita acadêmica.

lines.speaker: Linguist
lines.en: If you've ever struggled with an academic article, you're not alone. Corpus research led by linguists such as Douglas Biber has shown that academic writing differs from conversation in a striking way. Conversation is dominated by verbs and clauses: "We went out, and then it started raining, so we came back." Academic prose, by contrast, is dominated by nouns and noun phrases: "The sudden onset of heavy rainfall necessitated an early return." Information is packed into long, complex noun phrases, which allows writers to express a great deal very concisely — but also places heavy demands on the reader. This density isn't simply pretentiousness. It allows academics to treat processes as objects that can be discussed, compared and measured. Once "people moved to the cities" becomes "urbanization", you can ask about the rate of urbanization, the causes of urbanization, the effects of urbanization. That said, many style guides now encourage academics to balance density with clarity — and to remember that a paper nobody can read is a paper nobody will cite.

reading.title: The replication crisis
reading.text: Over the past fifteen years, a growing body of research has raised uncomfortable questions about the reliability of published scientific findings. The concern, often referred to as the "replication crisis", emerged most visibly in psychology. In a large-scale collaborative project published in Science in 2015, the Open Science Collaboration attempted to reproduce one hundred studies previously published in leading psychology journals. While nearly all the original studies had reported statistically significant results, only around a third to a half of the replications, depending on the criteria used, produced comparable findings. The causes of this problem are widely debated. A number of researchers contend that the incentive structures of academic publishing bear a considerable share of the responsibility. Journals have traditionally favoured novel, positive results over replications or null findings, thereby encouraging what critics describe as "questionable research practices": analysing data in multiple ways until a significant result emerges, or reporting only the outcomes that support the original hypothesis. Others emphasize methodological factors, including small sample sizes and insufficient statistical power. Not all scholars accept the more pessimistic interpretations, however. Some have argued that the replication studies themselves suffered from methodological limitations, and that differences between original and replication findings may reflect variations in populations or procedures rather than flawed original research. These objections notwithstanding, the episode has prompted significant reforms. Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans, the sharing of data and materials, and the publication of registered reports — in which journals commit to publishing a study before its results are known — have become increasingly common. Whether these measures will substantially improve the reliability of the scientific record remains, at present, an open empirical question.

questions.answer: Reproduce one hundred previously published psychology studies.

questions.q: What incentive problem do some researchers identify?

writing.model:
Remote learning and educational inequality: a brief review

(Note: the sources cited below are fictional and created for this exercise.)

The sudden shift to remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic has generated a substantial body of research on its consequences for educational inequality. Much of this literature points in a similar direction, although important disagreements remain regarding both the scale and the duration of the effects.

Drawing on national assessment data from over 3,000 public schools, Almeida and Rocha (2022) contend that the prolonged closure of schools in low-income urban areas resulted in significant learning losses, particularly in mathematics. Crucially, they demonstrate that these losses were considerably smaller in schools with pre-existing digital infrastructure, suggesting that access to technology acted as a key mediating factor.

This interpretation is broadly supported by Nunes (2023), whose qualitative study of teachers in rural Pernambuco highlights the practical barriers faced by families without reliable internet connections. Nunes acknowledges, however, that the small size of her sample limits the generalizability of her findings.

Not all researchers share this emphasis on technology. Barros (2023) challenges what he describes as a "technological determinism" in the literature, arguing that the quality of teacher–student relationships and the availability of parental support were more decisive than devices or connectivity. While Barros rightly draws attention to these often-overlooked social factors, his argument arguably underestimates the extent to which digital exclusion itself constrained such relationships during the pandemic.

Taken together, these studies suggest that the effects of remote learning cannot be attributed to any single cause. Further longitudinal research is needed to establish whether the observed learning losses have been recovered, and which interventions have proved most effective in narrowing the resulting gaps.

grammar.title: Complex hypothetical forms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. As if / as though + formas irreais** (comparações hipotéticas):
- **Presente irreal** → past simple / were: "He talks **as if** he **owned** the place." (mas não é dono) / "She looks **as though** she **were** about to cry."
- **Passado irreal** → past perfect: "She acted **as though** nothing **had happened**."
- **Comparação real/provável** → tempo normal: "It looks **as if** it**'s going to** rain." (provavelmente vai)
- **It's as if / It's not as if** (= não é como se): "Why are you worried? **It's not as if** you **failed** the exam."

**2. Desejos literários e enfáticos:**
- **Would that** + past / past perfect (literário, arcaico): "**Would that** I **had** more time!" / "**Would that** we **had known**."
- **If only** (B2) + past / past perfect / would
- **Oh, to be / Oh, for** (exclamação poética): "**Oh, to be** young again!" / "**Oh, for** a cup of tea!"

**3. Suppose / Supposing / Say / Imagine** com diferentes tempos:
- Possibilidade real: "**Suppose** the bus **is** late — what then?"
- Hipótese presente: "**Supposing** you **won** the lottery..."
- Contrafactual passado: "**Suppose** the Portuguese **had never reached** Brazil..."
- "**Say** you **had** a million reais — what would you do?"

**4. Subjuntivo fixo em contrafactuais e argumentos:**
- **if need be** (se for preciso) · **be it X or Y** (seja X ou Y) · **come what may** · **so be it** · **far be it from me to** (longe de mim...) · **as it were** (por assim dizer)
- "**Far be it from me to** criticize, but..." (ironia: vou criticar)

**5. Contrafactuais mistos e cadeias (revisão B2 + extensão):**
- "Had the Portuguese crown **not** moved to Rio in 1808, Brazil **might well have** split into several countries — and we **would** perhaps **be speaking** of 'the Brazils' today."

listening.title: The uses of counterfactual history
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de história fala sobre o valor e os riscos da história contrafactual.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: For a long time, many professional historians dismissed counterfactual history as a parlour game. The British historian E. H. Carr famously mocked it, and plenty of scholars still regard it with suspicion. Yet, in a sense, all historical explanation is counterfactual. To say that an event caused another is to imply that, had the first not happened, the second would not have happened either. Suppose a historian claims that a drought caused a revolution. That claim only makes sense if we can imagine the same society without the drought — and ask whether the revolution would still have occurred. Used carefully, counterfactuals help us test explanations and resist the illusion that the past was inevitable. Used carelessly, however, they become fantasy, with each imaginary step piled on another as though we could know the consequences decades later. The trick, most historians who use them would say, is to stay close to the moment: change one thing, ask what was realistically possible, and stop before you start writing a novel.

questions.q: How did many historians view counterfactual history?
questions.answer: As a parlour game; some, like E. H. Carr, mocked it.

questions.q: Why is all historical explanation counterfactual in a sense?
questions.answer: Saying A caused B implies that without A, B wouldn't have happened.

questions.q: What is the "trick" to using them well?

reading.title: The illusion of inevitability
reading.text: Looking back, it is tempting to see history as a path leading inexorably towards the present. Empires rise and fall as though following a script; revolutions break out because they "had to"; technologies appear exactly when the world is ready for them. Psychologists have a name for part of this tendency: hindsight bias, the inclination, once we know an outcome, to believe that it was predictable all along. In a series of classic experiments in the 1970s, the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff found that people who were told the outcome of a historical event rated that outcome as considerably more likely than people who were not told — and frequently believed they would have predicted it themselves. Counterfactual thinking is one of the most effective antidotes to this illusion. By asking "what if?", we are forced to reconstruct the uncertainty that people at the time actually faced. Suppose an assassination attempt had failed, a ship had sailed a day earlier, or a vote had gone the other way by a handful of ballots. Would the world look the same? Very often, the honest answer is that we cannot be sure — and that uncertainty is itself a valuable insight. It reminds us that the people of the past were not characters walking towards a known ending, but individuals making difficult choices with incomplete information, much as we do. There is a moral dimension to this, too. If the past was inevitable, then nobody was truly responsible for it: things simply happened as they had to. If, on the other hand, outcomes hinged on decisions that could have been different, then those decisions — and the people who made them — can be judged. Far from being idle speculation, then, the question "what if?" may be one of the most serious questions historians, and citizens, can ask. Would that it were asked more often.

questions.q: What is hindsight bias?
questions.answer: Believing, once we know an outcome, that it was predictable all along.

questions.q: What did Fischhoff's experiments find?
questions.answer: People told the outcome rated it as more likely and believed they'd have predicted it.

questions.q: How does counterfactual thinking help?
questions.answer: It forces us to reconstruct the uncertainty people faced at the time.

questions.q: What is the moral dimension of the argument?
questions.answer: If outcomes weren't inevitable, decisions and decision-makers can be judged.

writing.model:
What if Brasília had never been built?

In 1956, Juscelino Kubitschek became president of Brazil with an extraordinary promise: to build a new capital in the empty centre of the country within a single term. Brasília was inaugurated in 1960. Today, it is so familiar that we speak of it as though it had always been inevitable. It was not.

Suppose Kubitschek had abandoned the project, as many of his critics demanded. The capital would, in all likelihood, have remained in Rio de Janeiro. Rio would have kept not only its political power but also the jobs, investment and prestige that came with it — and the city's later decline, which many historians partly attribute to the loss of its capital status, might well have been less severe.

The effects on the interior would arguably have been even greater. Brasília was intended, as it were, as a heart that would pump life into the centre of the country. Had it never been built, the roads connecting the Centre-West to the rest of Brazil might have taken decades longer to appear, and the development of the Cerrado — for better and for worse — could have followed a very different path.

Of course, it is not as if the interior would have remained empty forever. Agricultural expansion was already under way, and some form of integration would doubtless have happened sooner or later. Nor would Brazil necessarily have been better off. Brasília was enormously expensive, and many economists link its cost to the inflation that troubled the country in the following years.

Far be it from me to claim certainty about any of this. Counterfactuals cannot be tested; they can only be argued. Yet the exercise is valuable precisely because it reminds us that the Brazil we know hinged on a series of human decisions — bold, controversial and, at the time, deeply uncertain. Would that we remembered this when we assume that today's choices do not matter.

grammar.title: Sophisticated comparisons
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. all the + comparativo (+ because / for)** — intensificação por causa de algo:
- "The victory was **all the sweeter** because nobody expected it."
- "Her criticism made me **all the more** determined."

**2. none the + comparativo** — sem mudança (ver C2-M1-L2):
- "I listened to the explanation but was **none the wiser**." / "He was **none the worse for** the accident."

**3. the + comparativo..., the + comparativo** (com estruturas complexas):
- "**The more** evidence we collect, **the less** certain the answer becomes."
- "**The sooner** we act, **the better**." (sem verbo)

**4. Correção e reformulação:**
- **not so much X as Y** (não tanto X, mas Y): "It's **not so much** a problem **as** a challenge."
- **more (of) a X than a Y**: "He's **more of** a teacher **than** a manager."
- **less X than Y**: "The decision was **less** rational **than** emotional."
- **rather than**: "We need to think **rather than** react."

**5. Ênfase com quantidade:**
- **no less than / no fewer than** (ênfase no número grande): "**No fewer than** 40 studies have confirmed it."
- **no more than** (ênfase no número pequeno): "It took **no more than** five minutes."
- **nothing short of** (nada menos que): "The result was **nothing short of** miraculous."

**6. Igualdade e proporção:**
- **every bit as + adj + as** (tão... quanto, enfático): "She's **every bit as** capable **as** he is."
- **nowhere near / nothing like as + adj + as** (nem de longe tão...): "It's **nowhere near as** easy **as** it looks."
- **twice / three times as likely to**: "People are **twice as likely to** remember a story **as** a statistic."
- **by far / far and away** + superlativo: "**by far the most** common bias"
