listening.title: Two systems of thinking
listening.context_pt: Uma psicóloga explica a ideia dos "dois sistemas" de Daniel Kahneman.

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: In his best-selling book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002, popularized a useful way of describing the mind. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, reads a simple sentence, or tells you instantly that two plus two is four. System 2 is slow, effortful and deliberate: it's what you use to calculate 17 times 24 or fill in a tax form. Most of the time, System 1 serves us well. The problem is that it's not so much accurate as confident. It jumps to conclusions, relies on rules of thumb and is easily influenced by irrelevant information — a number you saw a minute ago, for example, can affect your estimate of something completely unrelated. That's called anchoring. System 2 can correct these errors, but it's lazy; it takes effort, and we're often happy to accept the first answer that comes to mind. The lesson isn't that intuition is useless. It's that, the higher the stakes, the more it pays to slow down.

questions.q: How is System 1 described?
questions.answer: Fast, automatic and intuitive.

questions.q: How is System 2 described?
questions.answer: Slow, effortful and deliberate.

questions.q: What is anchoring?
questions.answer: Being influenced by an irrelevant number when making an estimate.

questions.q: What is the speaker's lesson?
questions.answer: The higher the stakes, the more it pays to slow down.

reading.title: The expert's blind spot
reading.text: It is natural to assume that expertise protects us from error. The more we know about a subject, surely, the better our judgements become. In many domains, this is true: an experienced radiologist is far more likely to spot a tumour than a beginner, and a chess grandmaster sees patterns invisible to a novice. Yet research on expert judgement offers a more complicated picture. In a famous long-term study, the political scientist Philip Tetlock collected thousands of predictions from experts in politics and economics over many years. When he compared their forecasts with what actually happened, the results were sobering. Many experts performed only slightly better than chance, and in some cases no better than simple statistical rules. Strikingly, the most famous experts — those most often quoted in the media — were often among the least accurate. Tetlock drew on an image from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin to explain the difference. "Hedgehogs" know one big thing: they view the world through a single theory and make bold, confident predictions. "Foxes" know many small things: they draw on multiple perspectives, are comfortable with uncertainty and readily change their minds. On average, foxes made more accurate forecasts. Hedgehogs, however, were all the more appealing to audiences precisely because of their confidence. The lesson is not so much that experts are useless as that confidence and accuracy are by no means the same thing. Indeed, the Dunning–Kruger effect — the finding that people with limited knowledge in a field tend to overestimate their competence — suggests that confidence can sometimes be a sign of ignorance rather than mastery. The best thinkers, it seems, are every bit as knowledgeable as the boldest ones, but nowhere near as certain. For those of us who listen to experts, the implication is clear: be wary of anyone who is never in doubt.

questions.q: What did Tetlock's study involve?
questions.answer: Collecting thousands of expert predictions over many years and comparing them with what happened.

questions.q: What was surprising about the most famous experts?
questions.answer: They were often among the least accurate.

questions.q: What is the difference between "hedgehogs" and "foxes"?
questions.answer: Hedgehogs know one big thing and are confident; foxes know many things, accept uncertainty and change their minds.

questions.q: What is the main lesson of the text?
questions.answer: Confidence and accuracy are not the same; be wary of people who are never in doubt.

writing.model:
Should we trust experts?

In recent years, "trust the experts" has become both a rallying cry and an object of ridicule. For some, experts are our best defence against misinformation; for others, they are an arrogant elite whose predictions are frequently wrong. The truth, I would argue, is not so much somewhere in the middle as more interesting than either position allows.

Let us begin with what experts do well. In fields with clear rules and rapid feedback — medicine, engineering, chess — expertise is nothing short of essential. A trained surgeon is not merely somewhat better than an amateur; she is incomparably better. To dismiss such knowledge would be every bit as foolish as refusing to use a map because maps occasionally contain errors.

The picture becomes far murkier, however, when experts attempt to predict complex systems such as economies or elections. Here, research suggests, expert forecasts are often nowhere near as accurate as their confident tone implies. Ironically, the more famous the expert, the more likely he or she is to make bold predictions — and bold predictions are, by definition, the ones most likely to fail.

Part of the problem lies in the biases that affect us all. Experts are no less vulnerable to confirmation bias than anyone else; indeed, their reputations may make them all the more reluctant to admit mistakes. Overconfidence, too, is less a sign of deep knowledge than of a failure to appreciate uncertainty.

So should we trust experts? Yes — but selectively and intelligently. We should trust them far more in areas where their knowledge can be tested than in areas of pure speculation. We should value those who acknowledge uncertainty over those who never express doubt. And we should judge them by their track record rather than their fame.

Ultimately, trusting experts is less a matter of faith than of judgement. The question is not whether to listen to them, but how.

grammar.title: Free indirect speech and the historic present
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Os três modos de representar pensamento:**
- **Discurso direto:** She thought, "**Why does** he always **do** this? **I'm** tired of it."
- **Discurso indireto:** She wondered **why he always did** that. She **was** tired of it.
- **Discurso indireto livre:** She looked at the clock. **Late again. Why did he always do this? Well, she was tired of it.**

**Características do discurso indireto livre:**
- **Terceira pessoa e passado** (como no indireto): "she was", "did he"
- **Sem verbo introdutório** ("she thought", "she wondered") — a mente da personagem entra direto na narração
- **Marcas da fala/pensamento da personagem:** perguntas, exclamações, interjeições, gírias, frases incompletas, dêiticos como **now, here, today, tomorrow** (em vez de then, there, the next day)
  - "Tomorrow she **would** tell him. **Yes**, tomorrow. **Enough** was enough!"
- **Efeito:** intimidade com a personagem **e** distância irônica ao mesmo tempo — o leitor nunca sabe se o julgamento é do narrador ou da personagem.

**2. O presente histórico** — narrar o passado no presente para criar **imediatismo**:
- Na fala informal: "So **I'm** at the bus stop, and this guy **comes** up to me and **says**..."
- Na ficção: "It **is** 1964. A woman **stands** at the window, waiting."
- Em manchetes e resumos de enredo: "In chapter 3, Capitu **meets** Bentinho..." (convenção para resumir obras!)

**3. Distância narrativa:**
- **Onisciente:** o narrador sabe tudo, entra em várias mentes.
- **Limitado:** segue uma personagem.
- **Não confiável:** o narrador distorce ou ignora a verdade (ex.: Bento Santiago em *Dom Casmurro*).

**4. Tempo verbal ao escrever sobre literatura:** use o **presente** ("literary present"): "Austen **uses** irony to..." / "The narrator **reveals**..."

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: Free indirect speech is so common in modern fiction that we hardly notice it. But it wasn't always there. Scholars often point to Jane Austen, writing in the early nineteenth century, as one of the first novelists in English to use it with real sophistication. In her novels, the narrator's voice slides almost imperceptibly into a character's thoughts — and back out again — so that we see the world through a character's eyes while also sensing the narrator's ironic distance. A century later, modernist writers like Virginia Woolf and James Joyce pushed the technique further, towards what's called stream of consciousness: the attempt to represent the flow of thought itself, with all its jumps, associations and fragments. In Brazilian literature, writers like Graciliano Ramos and Clarice Lispector explored similar territory. What all these writers share is a fascination with the gap between what people say and what they think — and the conviction that fiction is uniquely able to show us both.

questions.q: What is stream of consciousness?
questions.answer: An attempt to represent the flow of thought itself, with jumps, associations and fragments.

reading.title: Whose voice is it?
reading.text: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." Few opening lines in English literature are as famous as the first sentence of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, published in 1813. Read quickly, it sounds like a solemn general statement. Read carefully, it is something far more slippery. Is it really a universal truth? Of course not. The sentence is ironic: what it describes is not a law of nature but the belief — or rather the hope — of the families with unmarried daughters who populate the novel. The next sentence confirms the joke: the "truth", we learn, is fixed in the minds of the neighbours, who regard any wealthy newcomer as "the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters". The real subject of the opening, then, is not rich men but the society that schemes to marry them. This ability to say one thing while meaning another — to adopt the voice of a character or a community while quietly mocking it — is at the heart of Austen's art, and it depends heavily on free indirect speech. Throughout the novel, the narrator moves in and out of characters' minds, especially that of the heroine, Elizabeth Bennet. We share her quick judgements and sharp observations, and we only gradually realize, as she does, how mistaken some of them are. The reader experiences prejudice from the inside before recognizing it from the outside. Two centuries later, the technique remains one of the most powerful tools available to novelists. It allows fiction to do something that no other art form can do so easily: to place us simultaneously inside and outside another person's mind. To read like a writer is, in large part, to learn to hear those two voices at once — and to ask, at every turn, whose voice we are really hearing.

questions.q: Why is the opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice ironic?
questions.answer: It presents a social belief/hope as a universal truth.

questions.q: What is the real subject of the opening, according to the text?

questions.q: How does free indirect speech affect our experience of Elizabeth Bennet?

questions.q: What can fiction do, according to the last paragraph?

writing.model:
The promotion

Renata arrived at the office forty minutes early, as she had every day for the past six years. The cleaning staff were still mopping the floors. Good. She liked the building like this: silent, orderly, waiting.

Today was the day. The director had called her in for a meeting at nine — "just a quick chat", he had said, which was exactly what people said when they didn't want to spoil a surprise. Who else could it be? Marcos was talented, of course, but he arrived at ten and left at six, and everyone knew he spent half the afternoon on his phone. No, it had to be her. Six years of early mornings. Six years of weekends answering emails. People noticed these things. They had to.

She made herself a coffee and sat down to review the quarterly figures one last time. Not that she needed to; she knew them by heart. But it never hurt to be prepared. Her mother had always said that luck was simply what happened when preparation met opportunity, and her mother had been right about most things, except perhaps about Renata's ex-husband.

At eight-thirty, Marcos walked in. Early, for once. He was wearing a new jacket — rather a nice one, actually — and he looked unusually pleased with himself.

"Morning, Renata! Big day today," he said, with a wink.

Big day? What did he mean by that? Surely he couldn't know about her meeting. Unless — no. The director would never discuss something like that with Marcos.

She smiled politely and returned to her spreadsheet. The numbers swam a little in front of her eyes. Well, it was early. She had slept badly. That was all.

At nine o'clock exactly, the director put his head round the door.

"Ah, both of you are here," he said. "Perfect. Marcos, would you come in first?"

grammar.title: Sound devices and rhythm
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Repetição de sons:**
- **Aliteração** — consoantes iniciais: "**P**eter **P**iper **p**icked...", "**b**ig **b**old **b**rands", "**c**ool, **c**alm and **c**ollected"
- **Assonância** — vogais: "the r**ai**n in Sp**ai**n st**ay**s m**ai**nly...", "h**ea**r the m**e**llow w**e**dding b**e**lls"
- **Consonância** — consoantes no meio/fim: "pi**tt**er-pa**tt**er", "bla**nk** and thi**nk**"
- **Rima** (final ou **interna**): "Once upon a midnight dr**eary**, while I pondered, weak and w**eary**" (Poe, 1845)

**2. Onomatopeia** — palavras que imitam sons: buzz, hiss, whisper, crash, murmur, sizzle, splash, thud, rustle, crackle, tick-tock
- Note que muitas são **verbos** em inglês: "The fire **crackled**." / "Leaves **rustled**."

**3. Ritmo acentual (stress-timed rhythm)**
- O inglês alterna sílabas **fortes** e **fracas**; as fortes caem em intervalos mais ou menos regulares e as fracas são **reduzidas** (schwa /ə/).
- "I **WANT** to **GO** to the **SHOPS**." (3 batidas) — "to the" quase some.
- Isso é muito diferente do português (mais "silábico"), e é uma das razões do sotaque estrangeiro.

**4. Métrica:**
- **Iambo** = fraca + **forte** (da-**DUM**): "be**LIEVE**", "to**DAY**"
- **Pentâmetro iâmbico** = 5 iambos por verso (10 sílabas) — o metro de Shakespeare:
  "Shall **I** com**PARE** thee **TO** a **SUM**mer's **DAY**?"
- **Troqueu** = **forte** + fraca (**DUM**-da): "**DOUB**le, **DOUB**le, **TOIL** and **TROU**ble" (*Macbeth*)

**5. Uso prático:** slogans ("**B**uy **b**etter, **b**uild **b**etter"), títulos ("*Pride and Prejudice*", "*Sense and Sensibility*"), marcas (Coca-Cola, Kit Kat), discursos e escrita criativa.

listening.title: Why we remember rhymes
listening.context_pt: Um psicólogo fala sobre o efeito da rima na memória e na credibilidade.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Why do children learn nursery rhymes so easily? Why do advertising jingles get stuck in our heads? Sound patterns like rhyme, rhythm and alliteration make language easier to process and to remember — which is why oral traditions all over the world, from ancient epic poetry to Brazilian cordel, relied on them long before writing was common. But there's a more surprising effect. In a study published in 2000, psychologists Matthew McGlone and Jessica Tofighbakhsh presented people with sayings in two versions: one that rhymed, like "Woes unite foes", and one that meant the same thing but didn't rhyme, like "Woes unite enemies". Participants judged the rhyming versions to be more accurate. Researchers sometimes call this the "rhyme-as-reason" effect. The sound of a statement, it seems, can influence whether we believe it. Which is a useful thing to know — both if you're writing a slogan, and if you're trying not to be fooled by one.

questions.q: Why did oral traditions rely on sound patterns?
questions.answer: They make language easier to process and remember.

questions.q: What is the "rhyme-as-reason" effect?

reading.title: Poetry for the ear
reading.text: For most of human history, poetry was something heard rather than read. Long before printed books, communities preserved their histories, laws and stories in verse, recited from memory by bards, griots and storytellers. Rhythm, rhyme and repetition were not decorations but tools: they made long texts easier to memorize and more pleasurable to hear. The Old English epic Beowulf, for instance, relies on heavy alliteration, each line typically linking two or three stressed words that begin with the same sound. Printing gradually changed the relationship between poetry and sound. As poems came to be read silently on the page, poets began to experiment with visual effects — line breaks, spacing, even the shape of the text. By the twentieth century, many poets had abandoned regular metre and rhyme altogether in favour of free verse, which follows the rhythms of natural speech rather than a fixed pattern. Some critics complained that poetry had lost its music, and with it much of its audience. In recent decades, however, the ear has made a remarkable comeback. Spoken word and slam poetry, performed live and shared online, have attracted a new generation of poets and listeners, many of whom would never have opened a poetry anthology. Hip-hop, with its intricate internal rhymes and rhythmic complexity, has been described by many critics as one of the most significant poetic forms of our time. In Brazil, repentistas improvising in verse, cordel writers and slam competitions in city squares have kept the oral tradition vividly alive. Perhaps the lesson is that poetry has never really stopped being music. Even the quietest poem on a page asks to be heard, if only in the reader's head. To read poetry well — in any language — is to listen as much as to look.

questions.q: Why were rhythm and rhyme important in oral cultures?
questions.answer: They made long texts easier to memorize and more pleasurable to hear.

questions.q: What sound feature characterizes Beowulf?
questions.answer: Heavy alliteration.

questions.q: How did printing change poetry?
questions.answer: Poems were read silently; poets experimented with visual effects and free verse.

questions.q: What forms have brought "the ear" back to poetry?
questions.answer: Spoken word, slam poetry, hip-hop, and in Brazil repentistas, cordel and slams.

writing.model:
Rain in Belém, three o'clock

It begins, as it always begins, with a whisper.

A few fat drops tap on the tin roof of the market: tap, tap, tap, like a polite visitor. The vendors glance up, then down again. They know what's coming.

Then the sky splits. The rain rushes in, roaring on the roofs, drumming on the awnings, hammering the river until the whole city seems to hum. Gutters gurgle and overflow. Car tyres hiss through the flooded streets. A bus splashes past, and a woman shrieks, then laughs, her shopping bags soaked.

Under the mango trees, the world shrinks to a single sound — a steady, silver static, so loud it swallows every voice. Somewhere a radio crackles, fighting to be heard. A dog whimpers in a doorway. A child stamps in a puddle, delighted, defiant.

And then, as suddenly as it started, it stops.

Drip. Drip. Drip.

The leaves let go of the last of the water. The sun slides out from behind the clouds, and the steam rises softly from the warm, wet stones. The vendors shake their tarpaulins and shout their prices again. Birds begin, cautiously, to sing.

In Belém, they say you can set your watch by the rain. Three o'clock, every afternoon: the city's own symphony, played loud and short and true.

— Choices: onomatopoeia (tap, roaring, gurgle, hiss, splashes, shrieks, crackles, whimpers, drip) recreates the soundscape; alliteration (steady, silver static; delighted, defiant) and short sentences mimic the rhythm of the storm.

Ambos mostram que a poesia oral, baseada em ritmo e rima, continua viva.

grammar.title: Punctuation for meaning and style
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Ponto e vírgula (;)** — liga **duas orações completas** relacionadas, sem conjunção:
- "It was late; everyone had gone home."
- Antes de advérbios conectivos: "The plan was risky; **however**, it worked."
- Em listas complexas com vírgulas internas: "We visited Recife, Pernambuco; Salvador, Bahia; and Natal, Rio Grande do Norte."

**2. Dois-pontos (:)** — **anuncia** o que vem: explicação, lista, citação, conclusão.
- "She had one goal: to win." / "The reason was simple: money."
- ⚠️ O que vem **antes** dos dois-pontos deve ser uma oração completa: ❌ "The ingredients are: eggs, flour..." ✅ "You need three ingredients: eggs, flour and milk."

**3. Travessão (—)** — interrupção, ênfase, reviravolta, aposto dramático:
- "He said yes — eventually."
- "Three people — my mother, my sister and a stranger — saw it happen."
- Mais informal e enfático que parênteses; em textos acadêmicos, use com moderação.

**4. Erros clássicos:**
- **Comma splice** (duas orações completas só com vírgula): ❌ "It was late, everyone had gone home." → use ponto, ponto e vírgula ou conjunção.
- ❌ "The plan was risky, however it worked." → "The plan was risky; however, it worked."
- **Run-on sentence:** duas orações sem nenhuma pontuação.

**5. Vírgula de Oxford** (antes do *and* final de uma lista) — opcional, mas evita ambiguidades:
- "I'd like to thank my parents, Ana**,** and God." (três grupos, não "meus pais, que são Ana e Deus")

**6. Variedade de frases (estilo):**
- **Frase cumulativa** — ideia principal no início, detalhes acumulados depois: "She walked into the sea, the water cold against her legs, the sun low over the horizon, the gulls crying above."
- **Frase periódica** — suspense, ideia principal **no fim**: "After years of struggle, countless rejections and one long, sleepless night, she finally said yes."
- **Fragmento intencional** — impacto: "He never came back. Never."
- **Regra de ouro:** alterne frases longas e curtas. Uma frase curta depois de várias longas **chama atenção**.

rows: It was hard; however, we finished.

grammar.tip_pt: O **comma splice** é o erro de pontuação mais comum de brasileiros escrevendo em inglês, porque em português é mais tolerado. Revise seus textos procurando vírgulas que separam duas orações completas — e troque por **ponto, ponto e vírgula ou conjunção**.

Leia um parágrafo respeitando essas pausas.

lines.en: Your story is moving, Igor. But the punctuation is getting in the way. Look at this sentence: "I arrived in London, it was raining, I didn't know anyone."

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.en: In English, it's a comma splice — three complete clauses joined only by commas. You could use full stops: "I arrived in London. It was raining. I didn't know anyone."
lines.pt: Em inglês, é um comma splice — três orações completas ligadas só por vírgulas. Você poderia usar pontos: "I arrived in London. It was raining. I didn't know anyone."

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.en: That sounds very dramatic. Very lonely.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.en: Which is exactly what you were feeling, isn't it? Short sentences create that effect. Or, if you want it smoother: "I arrived in London on a rainy Tuesday; I didn't know a single person."
lines.pt: Que é exatamente o que você estava sentindo, não? Frases curtas criam esse efeito. Ou, se quiser mais fluido: "Cheguei a Londres numa terça chuvosa; não conhecia uma única pessoa."

lines.speaker: Igor

lines.pt: Prefiro a versão curta. E aqui — usei muitos parênteses.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.en: Try a dash instead when you want emphasis: "My first job was washing dishes — for twelve hours a day." The dash makes the reader feel the weight of it.
lines.pt: Tente um travessão quando quiser ênfase: "Meu primeiro emprego foi lavar pratos — doze horas por dia." O travessão faz o leitor sentir o peso disso.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.en: I see. Punctuation isn't just grammar; it's rhythm.
lines.pt: Entendo. Pontuação não é só gramática; é ritmo.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.en: Exactly — and you've just used a semicolon perfectly.
lines.pt: Exatamente — e você acabou de usar um ponto e vírgula perfeitamente.

listening.title: The semicolon wars
listening.context_pt: Um colunista fala, com humor, sobre o debate em torno do ponto e vírgula.

lines.speaker: Columnist
lines.en: Few punctuation marks inspire as much passion as the semicolon. Kurt Vonnegut famously advised writers not to use them at all, mocking them as pretentious — before, with typical irony, using one himself a few pages later. Other writers adore them. To their fans, the semicolon is the most elegant mark in the language: stronger than a comma, gentler than a full stop, it joins two ideas that belong together without forcing them into a single sentence. The truth, as usual, lies somewhere in between. Overused, semicolons can make writing feel heavy and academic. Used well, they create subtle connections that no other mark can manage. My advice? Before you use one, ask yourself a simple question: could each side stand alone as a sentence? If not, it's the wrong mark. And if yes — ask whether the two ideas are close enough to share a breath. If they are, go ahead. If not, a full stop will do the job; it usually does.

questions.q: What did Kurt Vonnegut say about semicolons?
questions.answer: Not to use them; he mocked them as pretentious (but used one himself later).

questions.q: How do fans of the semicolon describe it?
questions.answer: Stronger than a comma, gentler than a full stop; it joins ideas that belong together.

questions.q: What question should you ask before using a semicolon?
questions.answer: Could each side stand alone as a sentence?

questions.q: Find the semicolon in the speaker's last sentence. Is it used correctly?
questions.answer: "...will do the job; it usually does." Yes — two complete, closely related clauses.

reading.title: The rhythm of prose
reading.text: Writers have long understood that prose, like music, has rhythm, and that rhythm depends not only on words but on the shape of sentences. In a much-quoted passage from his book The Way We Write, the American writing teacher Gary Provost demonstrated this with a simple experiment. He wrote a paragraph composed entirely of five-word sentences. It was grammatically perfect. It was also, as he pointed out, monotonous. Then he varied the length: a short sentence, a medium one, and then a long, rolling sentence that built and built until it reached its climax. The second version, he argued, did not merely inform; it sang. The lesson is easily overlooked by learners, who often focus on accuracy at the expense of rhythm. A text made entirely of short sentences can sound childish or breathless. A text made entirely of long, complex sentences can exhaust the reader, however impressive each individual sentence may be. The most effective writers alternate. They use long, cumulative sentences to describe and accumulate detail, allowing the reader to settle into a scene; they use periodic sentences, which delay the main point until the end, to build suspense; and they use short sentences — sometimes no more than a word or two — for emphasis, surprise or finality. Punctuation is the instrument that makes this possible. The comma lets a sentence breathe. The semicolon holds two ideas in balance. The colon creates expectation: something important is coming. The dash interrupts, adds, surprises. And the full stop, the most underestimated of all, gives the reader a moment of silence in which a sentence can resonate. None of this can be learned from rules alone. It must be heard. Reading good prose aloud, slowly, remains one of the best ways to develop an ear for rhythm. So does reading your own writing aloud. If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long. If it sounds like a list, it probably needs a variation. Try it.

questions.q: What did Gary Provost's experiment show?
questions.answer: Sentences of the same length are monotonous; varying length creates rhythm.

questions.q: What are cumulative sentences good for?
questions.answer: Describing and accumulating detail.

questions.q: What are periodic sentences good for?
questions.answer: Building suspense by delaying the main point.

questions.q: What practical advice does the text give?
questions.answer: Read good prose and your own writing aloud to develop an ear for rhythm.

writing.model:
The phone call

I was nineteen when the phone rang at three in the morning. Nobody calls at three in the morning with good news; I knew that even before I picked it up.

It was my uncle. His voice was strange — flat, careful, as if each word had been chosen in advance. My father had been taken to hospital. A heart attack. They didn't know yet.

I remember very little of the drive. I remember the empty avenues, the traffic lights changing for nobody, the orange glow of the streetlamps sliding across the windscreen, my mother's hand gripping the door handle so tightly that her knuckles were white. I remember thinking one thing over and over: not yet.

The hospital was too bright. Everything in it was too bright: the floors, the walls, the forced smiles of the nurses who told us to wait. So we waited. We waited for four hours; it felt like four days.

And then, after a night of silence, after the coffee from the machine and the prayers I didn't know I remembered, after watching every door open and close and open again, a young doctor walked towards us and smiled.

He was going to be fine.

My father lived for another twenty-two years. He became, if anything, more stubborn after that night — he refused to give up salt, coffee or football — but he also became softer in ways I hadn't expected. He started telling us he loved us. Often. Sometimes too often, my sister used to joke.

I still think about that drive whenever my phone rings at night. Fear, I learned, is not the opposite of love; it is one of its shapes. And gratitude, when it finally comes, arrives quietly: a doctor's smile, a corridor, a door that opens the right way.

grammar.title: Evaluative language and review structure
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Vocabulário avaliativo preciso** — substitua "good / bad / interesting":
- **Positivo:** accomplished, assured, compelling, luminous, nuanced, haunting, exhilarating, beautifully observed, a tour de force
- **Negativo:** derivative, formulaic, self-indulgent, overwrought, heavy-handed, laboured, uneven, patchy, forgettable
- **Neutro/descritivo:** understated, ambitious, sprawling, experimental, slow-paced, unconventional

**2. Avaliação com nuance** — o crítico C2 raramente é totalmente positivo ou negativo:
- **if / albeit** concessivo: "an **accomplished, if uneven**, debut" / "a **powerful, albeit flawed**, film"
- **never quite / not entirely / falls short of**: "The ending **never quite** convinces." / "It **falls short of** its ambitions."
- **what it lacks in X, it makes up for in Y**: "**What it lacks in** originality, **it makes up for in** charm."
- **for all its flaws / for all its brilliance** (apesar de): "**For all its flaws**, it's a remarkable achievement."
- **the film / book is at its best when...**: "The novel **is at its best when** it focuses on the family."

**3. Estrutura de uma review C2 (280–320 palavras):**
1. **Abertura com gancho + contexto** (autor/diretor, gênero, expectativa)
2. **Resumo breve** (sem spoilers!), no **presente**
3. **Análise** de 2–3 aspectos (atuação, roteiro, estilo, temas) com exemplos
4. **Pontos fracos** com nuance
5. **Avaliação final + recomendação** (para quem?)

**4. Registro:** semiformal, com personalidade; pode usar humor e opinião pessoal, mas sempre **justificada**.

rows: The plot never quite comes together.
It falls short of the original.
What it lacks in depth, it makes up for in style.
For all its length, it never drags.

grammar.tip_pt: Na prova C2, o examinador procura **vocabulário avaliativo variado** e **opinião justificada**. Evite "very good" e "very interesting". Uma boa técnica: para cada adjetivo avaliativo, dê **um exemplo concreto** da obra que o justifique.

listening.title: What makes a good critic?
listening.context_pt: Uma editora de cultura de um jornal fala sobre o papel da crítica.

lines.speaker: Editor
lines.en: People sometimes assume that a critic's job is simply to tell you whether something is good or bad. That's the least interesting part of it. A good critic does three things. First, they describe the work vividly enough that you can imagine it, without giving away what shouldn't be given away. Second, they analyse — they explain how the work achieves its effects, or why it fails to. And third, they place it in context: what is this artist trying to do, how does it relate to their earlier work, or to the tradition it belongs to? The verdict comes last, and it should feel earned. The worst reviews, in my experience, are the ones that are either entirely gushing or entirely dismissive. Real works of art are rarely perfect or worthless. Even a masterpiece has weaknesses; even a failure may contain moments of genuine brilliance. A critic's real value lies in noticing both — and in helping readers see what they might otherwise have missed.

questions.q: What is the least interesting part of a critic's job, according to the editor?
questions.answer: Simply saying whether something is good or bad.

questions.q: What are the three things a good critic does?
questions.answer: Describe vividly, analyse how the work achieves its effects, and place it in context.

questions.q: What kinds of reviews does she consider the worst?
questions.answer: Entirely gushing or entirely dismissive ones.

questions.q: Where does a critic's real value lie?
questions.answer: In noticing both strengths and weaknesses and helping readers see what they might miss.

reading.title: Review: The House of the Two Rivers
reading.text:
(The novel reviewed below is fictional and was created for this lesson.)

Few debut novels arrive with as much expectation as The House of the Two Rivers, the first book by the Manaus-born writer Helena Barros. Shortlisted for a major prize before its publication in English, it has been described by its publishers as "the great Amazonian family saga". It is not quite that — but it is something more interesting.

The novel follows three generations of the Andrade family, rubber merchants whose fortunes rise and fall with the boom and collapse of the trade in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. At its centre is the family's crumbling mansion, built where two rivers meet, and Dona Clara, the formidable matriarch who refuses to leave it even as the city around her decays.

Barros is at her best when she slows down. Her descriptions of the river at dawn, of the humid stillness of the house in the afternoon, of the small rituals of a family pretending nothing has changed, are luminous. Her prose is understated yet precise, and her use of free indirect speech allows us to inhabit Clara's mind while quietly exposing her illusions. The scenes between Clara and her granddaughter, in particular, are a masterclass in what goes unsaid.

The novel is less assured when it tries to cover too much ground. A subplot involving a foreign engineer feels heavy-handed, and the final section, which jumps abruptly to the 1970s, reads more like an epilogue than a conclusion. At over five hundred pages, the book occasionally sags, and a firmer editorial hand might have produced a tighter, more powerful novel.

For all its flaws, however, this is an accomplished and haunting debut. What it lacks in structural discipline, it more than makes up for in atmosphere, emotional intelligence and sheer beauty of language. Readers who enjoy slow, immersive fiction will find much to admire. Barros is a writer to watch; her second novel may well be a masterpiece.

questions.q: How does the reviewer respond to the publisher's description?
questions.answer: It's not quite "the great Amazonian family saga" — but something more interesting.

questions.q: When is the writer "at her best"?
questions.answer: When she slows down — in descriptions and quiet family scenes.

questions.q: What weaknesses does the reviewer identify?
questions.answer: A heavy-handed subplot, an abrupt final section, and occasional sagging due to length.

questions.q: Who does the reviewer recommend the novel to?
questions.answer: Readers who enjoy slow, immersive fiction.

writing.model:
Vidas Secas (Barren Lives), by Graciliano Ramos

Few novels manage to say so much in so few pages. First published in 1938 and available in English as Barren Lives, Graciliano Ramos's portrait of a family of migrants fleeing drought in the Brazilian sertão is barely 150 pages long, yet it remains one of the most powerful works of Brazilian literature.

The novel follows Fabiano, his wife Sinha Vitória, their two sons and their dog, Baleia, as they wander across the parched landscape of the Northeast in search of work and water. Very little happens, in the conventional sense. The family finds shelter on an abandoned farm, endures the cruelty of a landowner and a soldier, and is eventually forced to move on again.

What makes the book extraordinary is its form. Each chapter focuses on a different character, and Ramos uses free indirect speech to enter minds that have almost no words of their own. Fabiano struggles to express his anger; the children ask questions nobody can answer; and in the most famous chapter, the narrative enters the consciousness of the dying dog with a tenderness that is almost unbearable. Ramos's prose is spare, precise and utterly unsentimental — as dry, one might say, as the landscape it describes.

The novel is not without its challenges for international readers. Its episodic structure can feel fragmentary, and some cultural and historical references may be unfamiliar without a good introduction. Its bleakness, too, will not be to everyone's taste.

For all that, it is a masterpiece that has stood the test of time remarkably well. In an age of climate migration and growing inequality, its portrait of people driven from their land by forces beyond their control feels anything but dated. Readers who admire the restraint of writers such as Steinbeck or Coetzee will find in Ramos a kindred spirit — and a voice the world should hear far more often.

Rating: ★★★★★

grammar.title: How new words are made
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Blends (palavras-valise)** — partes de duas palavras:
- brunch (breakfast + lunch), smog (smoke + fog), motel (motor + hotel), podcast (iPod + broadcast), staycation (stay + vacation), Brexit (Britain + exit), infodemic (information + epidemic)

**2. Conversão** — a palavra muda de **classe** sem mudar de forma:
- substantivo → verbo: **to google**, **to text**, **to email**, **to friend**, **to adult** (informal), **to gift**
- verbo → substantivo: **an ask** ("a big ask"), **a read** ("a good read"), **a must-have**, **a fail**
- adjetivo → verbo: **to green** (a cidade), **to empty**

**3. Afixos produtivos:**
- **-ify / -ize**: gamify, monetize, weaponize, Uberize
- **-esque / -ian**: Kafkaesque, Orwellian, Dickensian (como na obra de...)
- **-ism / -ist**: ageism, lookism, ableism
- **-ish**: sevenish, greenish, "Are you happy?" "**Ish.**" (informal)
- **-ee / -er**: trainee, influencer
- **hyper- / mega- / post- / micro- / e- / cyber-**: hyperlocal, mega-rich, post-truth, microplastics, e-learning, cybercrime
- **un-** criativo: unfriend, unfollow, unsend

**4. Compostos:** deepfake, doomscrolling, screen time, side hustle, cancel culture

**5. Siglas:**
- **Acronym** (lido como palavra): NASA, laser (light amplification by...), FOMO, YOLO
- **Initialism** (soletrada): FAQ, DIY, BBC

**6. Back-formation** — criar uma palavra "mais simples" a partir de uma mais longa: **edit** (de editor), **babysit** (de babysitter), **donate** (de donation), **burgle** (de burglar)

**7. Empréstimos:** emoji (japonês), tsunami, schadenfreude (alemão), hygge (dinamarquês) — e do português: **samba, caipirinha, favela, capoeira, piranha**.

**Registro:** neologismos informais (ghosting, adulting) funcionam na fala e em textos leves; em textos formais, prefira termos estabelecidos ou explique o neologismo ("so-called 'doomscrolling'").

listening.title: How a word gets into the dictionary
listening.context_pt: Uma lexicógrafa explica como os dicionários decidem incluir palavras novas.

lines.speaker: Lexicographer
lines.en: People often ask me who decides whether a word is "real". The honest answer is: nobody — and everybody. Dictionaries of English don't create words, and they don't approve them. They observe them. Lexicographers track huge collections of real language — books, newspapers, websites, transcripts — looking for words that are being used widely, by many different people, over a sustained period. A word that appears once in a viral post and then disappears won't make it. But if a word keeps appearing in different contexts, across different types of writing, for several years, it's likely to be added. That's how words like "selfie", "emoji" and "podcast" found their way into major dictionaries. This is quite different from languages that have official academies — Portuguese and French, for example, have institutions that publish official vocabularies or spelling rules. English has never had an equivalent. Its dictionaries are descriptive: they tell you how people actually use the language, not how they ought to.

questions.q: Who decides whether an English word is "real"?
questions.answer: Nobody and everybody — dictionaries observe usage.

questions.q: What do lexicographers look for?
questions.answer: Words used widely, by many people, in different contexts, over a sustained period.

questions.q: Why won't a word from one viral post be included?
questions.answer: It isn't used widely over time.

questions.q: How is English different from Portuguese and French in this respect?
questions.answer: English has no official academy; its dictionaries are descriptive.

reading.title: Is English being ruined?
reading.text: Complaints about the decline of the English language are almost as old as the language itself. In the eighteenth century, Jonathan Swift lamented the "corruptions" introduced by fashionable young writers and proposed an academy to fix the language once and for all. Two centuries later, critics worried about the influence of American films; more recently, the targets have been text messages, social media and teenagers. Each generation, it seems, is convinced that it is witnessing the end of proper English. Linguists tend to be considerably more relaxed. From their perspective, change is not a sign of decay but a condition of life. Every living language constantly gains new words and loses old ones, shifts its pronunciation and adjusts its grammar. Many words now considered perfectly respectable began as slang or as "errors". "Mob", for example, was once a disreputable abbreviation of the Latin mobile vulgus; "nice" originally meant "foolish"; and the verb "to contact", now indispensable in any office, was widely condemned as vulgar American usage in the early twentieth century. The digital age has undoubtedly accelerated the process. New words can now spread across the globe in days rather than decades, and the boundaries between speech and writing have blurred. Yet research on young people's writing has generally found little evidence that texting damages literacy; some studies even suggest that playful abbreviation requires a sophisticated awareness of how language works. None of this means that every innovation deserves to survive, or that standards no longer matter. Clear, precise language remains essential in law, science and public life, and most speakers are perfectly capable of switching between registers. The real skill, perhaps, is not resisting change but navigating it: knowing when "ghosting" is the perfect word, and when it would be entirely out of place.

questions.q: What did Jonathan Swift propose?
questions.answer: An academy to fix the English language once and for all.

questions.q: How do linguists view language change?
questions.answer: Not as decay but as a normal condition of a living language.

questions.q: Give one example of a word that changed status or meaning.
questions.answer: "Mob" (once disreputable), "nice" (once meant foolish), "to contact" (once considered vulgar).

questions.q: What has research found about texting and literacy?
questions.answer: Little evidence that it damages literacy; it may even show linguistic awareness.

writing.model:
Language change: decline or evolution?

Every few years, a new wave of anxiety sweeps through the media: young people are destroying the language. Their texts are full of abbreviations, their speech full of slang, and words like "ghosting", "adulting" and "doomscrolling" are invading the dictionary. Is this evidence of decline, or simply evolution in action?

There is no doubt that English is changing rapidly. Digital technology has accelerated the creation and spread of new words, many of them formed through familiar processes. Blends such as "staycation" and "infodemic" combine existing words; conversion has turned nouns like "google" and "text" into verbs; and productive suffixes allow speakers to coin terms such as "gamify" or "Uberization" almost effortlessly. Far from being chaotic, these innovations follow patterns that have shaped English for centuries.

Indeed, history suggests that today's "corruption" is often tomorrow's standard. Words such as "mob" and "bus" were once condemned as vulgar abbreviations, and the use of "contact" as a verb provoked indignation in the early twentieth century. Few people would now consider them anything but ordinary English. The same process is visible in Portuguese, which has absorbed words like "deletar" and "printar", to the dismay of some purists.

That said, it would be naive to claim that all change is neutral. Rapidly multiplying jargon can exclude older people or non-specialists, and the informality of online communication can make it harder for some young people to master formal registers when they need them — in job applications, legal documents or academic writing.

The solution, however, is not to resist change but to teach flexibility. A speaker who can use "ghosted" with friends and "failed to respond" in a formal complaint is not a victim of linguistic decline but a skilled user of the language.

In conclusion, language change is neither a catastrophe nor a cause for unqualified celebration. It is, quite simply, what living languages do. Our task is not to stop it, but to understand it — and to use every register well.

grammar.title: Varieties of English
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Britânico x americano** (as diferenças mais comuns):
- **Vocabulário:** flat/apartment, lift/elevator, queue/line, holiday/vacation, pavement/sidewalk, autumn/fall, mobile/cell phone, rubbish/trash, chemist/pharmacy, motorway/highway
- **Ortografia:** colour/color, centre/center, organise/organize (ambos aceitos no UK), travelled/traveled, programme/program, defence/defense
- **Gramática:**
  - **have got** (UK) / **have** (US): "Have you got...?" / "Do you have...?"
  - **Present perfect** mais usado no UK: "I've just eaten" (UK) x "I just ate" (US, comum)
  - **Substantivos coletivos:** "The team **are** playing well" (UK, possível) x "The team **is**..." (US)
  - **Preposições:** at the weekend (UK) / on the weekend (US); different from/to (UK) / different from/than (US)
  - **gotten** (US) / got (UK)
- **Pronúncia:** o "r" final (rhotic no US, non-rhotic em RP: car = "kaa"); o "t" entre vogais (US: water ≈ "wárer"); vogais (bath, can't, tomato)

**2. World Englishes** — variedades legítimas com normas próprias:
- **Inglês indiano:** "do the needful", "prepone" (antecipar, oposto de postpone), "revert" (= responder), "cousin-brother"; uso frequente do contínuo ("I am knowing him")
- **Inglês nigeriano:** "to off the light" (desligar), "to on the TV", "well done" como saudação a quem trabalha
- **Singlish (Singapura):** partículas como **lah**, **lor**, **meh**; "Can or not?", "Got or not?"
- **Inglês sul-africano:** "now-now" (já, já), "just now" (daqui a pouco, às vezes!), "robot" (semáforo)
- **Inglês australiano:** arvo (afternoon), brekkie (breakfast), "no worries"
- **Inglês caribenho/crioulos:** sistemas gramaticais próprios (ex.: Jamaican Patois)

**3. Inglês como língua franca (ELF):** em comunicação internacional, **inteligibilidade** importa mais que sotaque "nativo". Pesquisadores como **Jennifer Jenkins** identificaram um "núcleo" de características de pronúncia que mais afetam a compreensão (certas consoantes, vogais longas x curtas, acento nas palavras importantes) — o resto, como o "th", pode variar sem prejudicar a comunicação.

**4. Atitude C2:** reconheça e **respeite** a variação. Escolha uma variedade-base para escrever (UK ou US) e seja **consistente** na ortografia.

examples.en: In Indian English, "Please revert at the earliest" simply means "Please reply as soon as possible".
examples.pt: No inglês indiano, "Please revert at the earliest" significa simplesmente "Por favor, responda o quanto antes".

grammar.tip_pt: Para melhorar a compreensão de sotaques, **varie suas fontes**: ouça podcasts e entrevistas com falantes da Índia, Nigéria, Escócia, Austrália, Irlanda, África do Sul. Na prova C2 Proficiency, o Listening inclui uma variedade de sotaques.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Consistência ortográfica é esperada em textos formais.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Algumas pistas rápidas: **r final** pronunciado (US, Escócia, Irlanda, Índia) ou não (RP, Austrália, África do Sul); **t entre vogais** como "r" rápido (US, Austrália); **bath / can't** com /ɑː/ longo (sul da Inglaterra) ou /æ/ (US, norte da Inglaterra). Ouça "water", "car" e "bath" em vários sotaques.

listening.title: Whose English is it?
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre a expansão global do inglês.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: The linguist Braj Kachru, who was born in Kashmir and worked in the United States, proposed an influential model of English around the world, often pictured as three concentric circles. The inner circle includes countries where English is the main first language: the UK, the US, Australia and so on. The outer circle includes countries where English has an official or institutional role as a second language, often as a result of colonial history: India, Nigeria, Singapore, the Philippines. And the expanding circle includes countries where English is learned as a foreign language for international communication — Brazil, China, Japan, Germany, and most of the world. The model has been criticized and revised, but its central insight remains powerful: English no longer belongs only to its native speakers. In fact, most interactions in English today probably take place between people for whom it isn't a first language at all. Which raises a fascinating question: who, now, sets the standard?

questions.q: Who proposed the three-circle model?
questions.answer: Braj Kachru.

questions.q: What is the inner circle?
questions.answer: Countries where English is the main first language (UK, US, Australia...).

questions.q: Which circle does Brazil belong to?
questions.answer: The expanding circle.

questions.q: What is the central insight of the model?
questions.answer: English no longer belongs only to its native speakers.

reading.title: The myth of the perfect accent
reading.text: For decades, many language learners have pursued a single, elusive goal: to sound like a native speaker. Textbooks offered recordings in "standard" British or American accents; learners practised minimal pairs late into the night; and those who failed to eliminate every trace of their first language often felt that they had, in some sense, failed. In recent years, this ideal has come under sustained criticism. The first problem is practical. There is no single native accent to imitate. A speaker from Glasgow sounds very different from one from London, Dublin, Texas or Sydney, and none of these accents is inherently more correct than the others. Even the "standard" British accent traditionally taught to learners, Received Pronunciation, is spoken natively by only a small minority of people in the United Kingdom. The second problem concerns purpose. For the vast majority of learners, English is a means of communicating with people from many different countries, most of whom are not native speakers themselves. In these situations, what matters is not whether one sounds British or American but whether one is understood. Research on English as a lingua franca has suggested that certain features — word stress, the distinction between some long and short vowels, and a number of consonant sounds — are far more important for intelligibility than others. A Brazilian speaker who pronounces "think" as "fink" will almost always be understood; one who misplaces the stress in "comfortable" or "development" may cause genuine confusion. None of this means that pronunciation does not matter. Clear pronunciation is a courtesy to one's listeners, and many learners find great satisfaction in mastering the sounds of a new language. But the goal has shifted from imitation to intelligibility, and from shame to confidence. An accent, after all, is not a defect. It is a sign that someone has learned to live in more than one language — which is, by any measure, an achievement.

questions.q: What goal have many learners pursued?
questions.answer: To sound like a native speaker.

questions.q: Why is there no single native accent to imitate?
questions.answer: Native accents vary enormously; none is inherently more correct.

questions.q: What matters most in lingua franca communication?
questions.answer: Being understood (intelligibility), not sounding British or American.

questions.q: Which features does research suggest are most important for intelligibility?
questions.answer: Word stress, long/short vowel distinctions and some consonant sounds.

writing.model:
Whose English is it anyway?

When I started learning English as a child in Brazil, I believed there was one "correct" version of the language, spoken by people in London or New York, and that my job was to imitate it as closely as possible. Every trace of my Portuguese accent felt like a mistake. It took me many years — and many conversations with people from very different places — to realize how wrong that idea was.

English today is spoken by an estimated one and a half billion people, but only a minority of them learned it as their first language. It is the official or institutional language of countries as diverse as India, Nigeria, Singapore and the Philippines, each of which has developed its own vocabulary, rhythms and expressions. An Indian colleague might ask me to "revert" on an email; a Nigerian friend might ask me to "off the light"; a Singaporean classmate might end a sentence with "lah". These are not errors. They are features of established varieties of English, as legitimate as the British "queue" or the American "sidewalk".

For learners, this has liberating implications. First, there is no single accent we are obliged to imitate. What matters in international communication is intelligibility: speaking clearly, stressing the right syllables and adapting to our listeners. Second, we are not merely visitors in someone else's language. As members of the global community of English users, we have a stake in it — and perhaps even a right to shape it.

That does not mean anything goes. In formal writing, consistency and accuracy still matter, and learners benefit from understanding the major standard varieties. But the old hierarchy, in which native speakers were the only judges of what was correct, is giving way to something more democratic.

So whose English is it? The honest answer is: everyone's who uses it. And that, I believe, is the best reason of all to keep learning it — accent and all.

grammar.title: Modals and expressions of obligation in legal texts
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Shall** — em leis e contratos, expressa **obrigação** ou **determinação legal** (não futuro):
- "The tenant **shall** pay the rent on the first day of each month." (= deve pagar)
- "Everyone **shall** have the right to..." (= terá/tem garantido)
- **Shall not** = proibição: "No one **shall** be held in slavery."
- ⚠️ Muitos especialistas em *plain English* recomendam substituir **shall** por **must** (obrigação) ou pelo presente ("Everyone **has** the right..."), pois "shall" pode ser ambíguo.

**2. Must / must not** — obrigação / proibição clara.

**3. May / may not** — em textos legais:
- **may** = **permissão** ou **possibilidade**: "The landlord **may** inspect the property with 24 hours' notice."
- **may not** = **proibição** (= is not allowed to): "Tenants **may not** sublet the property."

**4. Expressões com be + adjetivo/particípio:**
- **be entitled to** + substantivo/verbo (ter direito a): "Workers **are entitled to** thirty days' leave." / "...entitled to receive..."
- **be liable for** (ser responsável por) / **be liable to** (estar sujeito a — pena, multa): "Offenders **are liable to** a fine of up to..."
- **be obliged / required to** (ser obrigado a)
- **be prohibited / barred / forbidden from** + -ing: "Members **are prohibited from** sharing..."
- **be subject to** (estar sujeito a): "**Subject to** approval" / "Prices **are subject to** change."
- **be eligible for / to** (ser elegível)
- **be exempt from** (ser isento de)

**5. Passiva e linguagem impessoal** — típicas de leis: "It **is hereby** enacted...", "Any person who... **shall be guilty of** an offence."

**6. Explicando em linguagem simples:** "The tenant shall not keep pets" → "You're not allowed to have pets."

examples.en: Under the law, consumers are entitled to cancel online purchases within seven days.
examples.pt: Segundo a lei, os consumidores têm direito a cancelar compras online em até sete dias.

grammar.tip_pt: Atenção: **shall** em contratos **não** é futuro! E **may not** em regulamentos é **proibição**, não "talvez não". Ao ler um contrato em inglês, pergunte sempre: isto é um **direito** (entitled, may), um **dever** (shall, must, required) ou uma **proibição** (shall not, may not, prohibited)?

listening.title: The Universal Declaration
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de direito internacional fala sobre a Declaração Universal dos Direitos Humanos.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: On 10 December 1948, the General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Drafted in the aftermath of the Second World War, it set out, for the first time, a list of rights that all human beings are entitled to, regardless of nationality, race, sex, religion or any other status. The committee that drafted it was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, and it included representatives from many countries and traditions. Its thirty articles cover civil and political rights — such as the right to life, liberty and a fair trial — as well as economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to education and to work. Notice the language: "No one shall be held in slavery"; "Everyone has the right to education". Technically, the Declaration itself is not a binding treaty. But it has inspired many later legally binding agreements and national constitutions, including Brazil's 1988 Constitution. It has also been translated into more languages than almost any other document in the world.

questions.q: When was the Universal Declaration adopted?
questions.answer: On 10 December 1948.

questions.q: Who chaired the drafting committee?
questions.answer: Eleanor Roosevelt.

questions.q: What two broad types of rights does it cover?
questions.answer: Civil and political rights, and economic, social and cultural rights.

questions.q: Is the Declaration legally binding?
questions.answer: Not itself, but it inspired binding treaties and constitutions.

reading.title: Rights in the digital age
reading.text: When the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was drafted in 1948, its authors could not have imagined smartphones, social media or artificial intelligence. Yet many of the most urgent debates about rights today concern precisely these technologies. Article 12 of the Declaration states that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy. What does that mean in a world where vast amounts of personal data are collected, analysed and sold, often without users fully understanding what they have agreed to? In response, a growing number of jurisdictions have adopted data protection laws. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which came into force in 2018, has been particularly influential; Brazil's own General Data Protection Law (LGPD) followed shortly afterwards. Under such laws, individuals are typically entitled to know what data is held about them, to request its correction and, in certain circumstances, to have it deleted. Organizations that process data are obliged to have a legal basis for doing so and may be liable to substantial fines if they fail to protect it. New questions continue to emerge. Should people have a right to an explanation when an algorithm denies them a loan or a job? Is internet access itself becoming a basic right, given that so many essential services now depend on it? To what extent should platforms be held liable for harmful content posted by their users? These debates are far from settled. What is clear is that rights are not fixed for all time. They are interpreted, extended and sometimes contested as societies change. The language of the law may sound timeless — "shall", "entitled", "liable" — but the questions it must answer are constantly new.

questions.q: What does Article 12 of the Declaration protect?
questions.answer: Privacy, against arbitrary interference.

questions.q: What rights do individuals typically have under data protection laws?
questions.answer: To know what data is held, request correction and, in some cases, deletion.

questions.q: What may happen to organizations that fail to protect data?
questions.answer: They may be liable to substantial fines.

questions.q: Name one new question about rights in the digital age.
questions.answer: Right to an explanation from algorithms / internet access as a right / platform liability for content.

writing.model:
Charter of Rights and Responsibilities — Riverside Online Learning Community

Preamble
This Charter sets out the rights and responsibilities of all members of the Riverside Online Learning Community ("the Community"). By joining the Community, members agree to abide by its provisions.

Article 1 — Respect
Every member shall have the right to participate in discussions without being subjected to harassment, discrimination or personal attacks. Members shall treat one another with courtesy, regardless of nationality, age, gender, religion or level of English.

Article 2 — Freedom of expression
Members are entitled to express their opinions freely, subject to the limits set out in Article 1. Disagreement is welcome; abuse is not.

Article 3 — Privacy
Members may not share other members' personal information, including photographs, messages or contact details, without their explicit consent. The Community shall not sell or disclose members' data to third parties.

Article 4 — Academic integrity
Members shall submit only their own work. Members found to have plagiarised may be liable to suspension from the Community.

Article 5 — Moderation
Moderators may remove content that breaches this Charter. Any member whose content has been removed shall be entitled to request an explanation and to appeal the decision within fourteen days.

Article 6 — Amendments
This Charter may be amended by a majority vote of members, provided that all members are notified at least one month in advance.

— Plain English summary —
Be respectful: no harassment or discrimination. You can say what you think, but don't attack people. Don't share other people's personal information; we won't sell yours. Only submit your own work — if you copy, you may be suspended. Moderators can delete posts that break the rules, but you can ask why and appeal. Rules can change only if most members vote for it, with a month's notice.

grammar.title: Paraphrasing and synthesizing
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Técnicas de paráfrase** (combine várias!):
- **Sinônimos:** "children" → "young people"; "harmful" → "detrimental"
- **Mudar a classe da palavra:** "Technology **has transformed** education" → "Education **has undergone a transformation** because of technology"
- **Mudar a estrutura (ativa/passiva, ordem):** "Schools should ban phones" → "Phones ought to be prohibited in schools"
- **Generalizar / abstrair:** "teachers, parents and pupils" → "the whole school community"
- **Usar um verbo de citação que mostra a posição do autor:** "The writer **contends / warns / dismisses the idea that**..."
⚠️ **Não copie** sequências de 3+ palavras do texto original (exceto termos técnicos).

**2. Resumir:** identifique **a tese** e **2–3 argumentos de cada texto**; ignore exemplos e detalhes.

**3. Sintetizar (comparar os textos):**
- **Concordância:** "Both writers **agree / concur** that..." / "The second text **echoes** this view..."
- **Divergência:** "**Whereas** the first writer..., the second..." / "The second writer **takes issue with**..." / "**Where they diverge** is..."
- **Complemento:** "The second text **adds** a further dimension..." / "...**goes further**, arguing that..."

**4. Avaliar (sua opinião):**
- "I find the first argument **more convincing** because..."
- "**While** the second writer **rightly points out**..., she **overlooks**..."
- "**In my view**, the most persuasive point is..."

**5. Estrutura do essay C2 Part 1 (240–280 palavras):**
1. **Introdução:** tema geral + o que os dois textos discutem
2. **Texto 1:** ideias principais (parafraseadas) + sua avaliação
3. **Texto 2:** ideias principais + relação com o texto 1 + sua avaliação
4. **Conclusão:** sua posição geral
(Alternativa: organizar por **temas**, comparando os dois textos em cada parágrafo.)

rows: Social media is harmful to teenagers.
Young people's well-being may be damaged by online platforms.
Mobile devices ought to be prohibited in classrooms.
Education has undergone a profound transformation as a result of technology.
This view is far from universally accepted.
It costs a lot of money.

grammar.tip_pt: Na prova, **planeje 10 minutos**: sublinhe a tese e os argumentos de cada texto, anote **sinônimos** antes de escrever e decida sua opinião. O erro mais comum é **copiar frases inteiras** do texto — isso é penalizado. O segundo mais comum é **esquecer a avaliação**.

listening.title: Two views on homework
listening.context_pt: Dois especialistas apresentam visões diferentes sobre lição de casa num programa de rádio.

lines.speaker: Voice 1
lines.en: Homework, in my view, remains an essential part of learning. It reinforces what students have studied in class, develops independent study habits and gives parents a window into their children's education. Without it, many pupils would simply forget what they had learned. The problem is not homework itself but bad homework: repetitive tasks that take hours and teach nothing new.

lines.speaker: Voice 2
lines.en: I'd go further. The research on homework, particularly for younger children, is mixed at best. Some studies suggest a modest benefit for older students, but for primary school pupils, the evidence is weak. Meanwhile, homework can increase stress and inequality: children with educated parents and quiet places to study benefit, while others fall further behind. I'd abolish it for under-twelves and drastically reduce it for everyone else.

questions.q: What does the first speaker think homework is good for?
questions.answer: Reinforcing learning, developing study habits and involving parents.

questions.q: What does the first speaker see as the real problem?
questions.answer: Bad homework — repetitive, time-consuming and not useful.

questions.q: What does the second speaker say about the research?
questions.answer: It's mixed; weak evidence for young children, some benefit for older students.

questions.q: Where do the speakers agree and diverge? (synthesis)
questions.answer: Both criticize bad/excessive homework; they diverge on whether homework is essential (1) or should be abolished for young children (2).

reading.title: C2 Part 1 practice: two texts on tourism
reading.text:
Text 1 — The case for tourism
For many regions, tourism is not merely an industry but a lifeline. It brings income to places where few other opportunities exist, creates jobs for young people who might otherwise be forced to migrate, and provides funding for the preservation of historic buildings and natural landscapes. Moreover, travel broadens the mind: visitors who encounter other cultures at first hand often return home more tolerant and curious. To condemn tourism wholesale, as some critics now do, is to ignore the livelihoods of millions and the very real benefits of human contact across borders.

Text 2 — The cost of popularity
Across the world, a growing number of cities and natural sites are struggling under the weight of their own popularity. In some historic centres, short-term rentals have driven up housing costs so steeply that local residents can no longer afford to live there; neighbourhoods once full of life now resemble theme parks. Fragile ecosystems are damaged by crowds, and much of the money generated by tourism flows to international companies rather than local communities. This is not an argument against travel itself, but against an unregulated model that treats places as products. Without limits, tourism risks destroying the very things that make destinations worth visiting.

Model essay
Both texts address the impact of tourism on the places that receive it, but they reach rather different conclusions.

The first writer presents tourism as vital for many communities, arguing that it generates income and employment in areas with few alternatives and helps finance the conservation of heritage and nature. The text also emphasizes the cultural value of travel, suggesting that contact with other ways of life fosters open-mindedness. While these points are undoubtedly valid, the writer arguably overstates the case by dismissing critics so readily.

The second text, by contrast, focuses on the consequences of excessive tourism. Its author contends that soaring demand for holiday accommodation has priced residents out of their own neighbourhoods, that natural environments are suffering, and that the economic benefits often bypass local people. Crucially, however, the writer does not reject travel as such, but rather a model that lacks regulation.

In my view, the second text offers the more nuanced analysis. It acknowledges, at least implicitly, the advantages highlighted in the first text, while identifying real problems that a purely positive account ignores. The challenge, as I see it, is not to choose between tourism and its critics, but to strike a balance: to welcome visitors while ensuring that communities retain control over their homes, their environment and their economy.

questions.q: What are the main arguments of Text 1?
questions.answer: Tourism provides income and jobs, funds preservation and broadens the mind.

questions.q: What are the main arguments of Text 2?
questions.answer: Overtourism raises housing costs, damages ecosystems and benefits international companies more than locals; it needs regulation.

questions.q: Find two paraphrases in the model essay.
questions.answer: Examples: "priced residents out" (local residents can no longer afford...); "bypass local people" (flows to international companies); "fosters open-mindedness" (broadens the mind).

questions.q: What is the writer's own evaluation?
questions.answer: Text 2 is more nuanced; the solution is to strike a balance through regulation.

writing.model:
Homework: essential or outdated?

The value of homework has long divided educators and parents, and the two contributions considered here illustrate the debate well.

The first speaker defends homework as a fundamental component of education. In her view, tasks completed at home consolidate classroom learning, encourage pupils to work independently and allow families to follow their children's progress. Importantly, she acknowledges that much homework is poorly designed, attributing the problem not to the practice itself but to repetitive, time-consuming assignments that add little to students' understanding. This distinction seems to me a sensible one, although she offers little evidence to support her confidence in homework's benefits.

The second speaker takes a considerably more sceptical position. Drawing on research, he argues that the advantages of homework are, at best, uncertain, particularly in primary education. Furthermore, he raises the important issue of fairness: pupils from more privileged homes, he contends, are far better placed to benefit from work set outside school, so homework may actually widen educational gaps. His proposal — to eliminate homework for younger children and greatly reduce it for older ones — follows logically from this analysis.

On balance, I find the second argument more persuasive, largely because it addresses the question of equity, which the first speaker overlooks. That said, both contributions converge on one crucial point: the quantity and quality of homework matter far more than whether it exists at all. A reasonable compromise, I would suggest, might be to limit homework to short, purposeful tasks — such as reading — for younger pupils, while ensuring that schools provide quiet study spaces for those who lack them at home.

grammar.title: The language of mediation
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Reformular e simplificar:**
- "**In other words**, ..." / "**To put it simply / To put it another way**, ..."
- "**What this means (in practice) is that**..." (cleft — útil para destacar a consequência)
- "**Basically / Essentially**, ..." (na fala)
- "**The key point / The bottom line is**..."

**2. Analogias e comparações:**
- "**Think of it as / It's a bit like**..." / "**Imagine**..."
- "**It works in much the same way as**..."
- "**If X is a..., then Y is a...**" (analogia estruturada)

**3. Decompor (signposting):**
- "**Let me break that down.** **First**, ... **Then**, ... **Finally**, ..."
- "**There are three things you need to know.**"

**4. Verificar compreensão e convidar perguntas:**
- "**Does that make sense (so far)?**" / "**Is that clear?**" / "**Shall I go over that again?**"
- Evite "Do you understand?" (pode soar condescendente) — prefira "**Have I explained that clearly?**" (assume a responsabilidade)

**5. Mediar entre pessoas (relaying and clarifying):**
- "**What I think she's saying is**..." / "**If I understand you correctly, you mean**..."
- "**Both of you seem to agree that**...; **the difference is**..."
- "**Could you say a bit more about**...?"

**6. Princípios:**
- **Começar pelo que o público já sabe.**
- **Um conceito de cada vez.**
- **Exemplos concretos** antes de definições abstratas.
- Evitar a **"curse of knowledge"** (esquecer como é não saber).
- **Simplificar sem distorcer** (não "dumb down").

lines.pt: Desculpe — sou filha dele, e meu português não é muito bom. Poderia explicar em inglês também?

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: Of course. Think of the heart as having its own electrical system, a bit like the wiring in a house. Normally, it sends regular signals, so the heart beats in a steady rhythm.
lines.pt: Claro. Pense no coração como tendo seu próprio sistema elétrico, parecido com a fiação de uma casa. Normalmente ele envia sinais regulares, então o coração bate num ritmo estável.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: And in his case, the wiring is faulty?
lines.pt: E no caso dele, a fiação está com defeito?

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: In a sense. The upper chambers are receiving chaotic signals, so the rhythm becomes irregular. What that means in practice is that he may feel tired or short of breath, and there's a higher risk of blood clots.
lines.pt: De certa forma. As câmaras superiores estão recebendo sinais caóticos, então o ritmo fica irregular. O que isso significa na prática é que ele pode se sentir cansado ou sem fôlego, e há um risco maior de coágulos.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: Is it dangerous?
lines.pt: É perigoso?

lines.speaker: Dr. Silva
lines.en: It can be if it's not treated. But it's common and very manageable. To put it simply: medication to control the rhythm, and another to thin the blood. Does that make sense so far?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: Yes, completely. Thank you — that's the first time anyone has explained it so clearly.
lines.pt: Sim, totalmente. Obrigada — é a primeira vez que alguém explica com tanta clareza.

listening.title: The curse of knowledge
listening.context_pt: Uma psicóloga explica por que especialistas têm dificuldade em explicar o que sabem.

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: In 1990, a Stanford graduate student named Elizabeth Newton ran a simple experiment. She divided participants into "tappers" and "listeners". The tappers were asked to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song, like "Happy Birthday", on a table, and the listeners had to guess the song. Before starting, the tappers predicted that listeners would guess correctly about half the time. In reality, listeners identified only around 1 in 40 songs. Why the huge gap? Because when the tappers tapped, they heard the melody in their heads. They simply couldn't imagine what it was like to hear only the knocking. This is what's often called the curse of knowledge: once we know something, it's extremely difficult to remember what it's like not to know it. Experts fall into this trap constantly. They skip steps, use jargon and assume background knowledge that their audience doesn't have. The cure isn't to know less. It's to test your explanations on real people — and to watch their faces, not your slides.

questions.q: How often did tappers predict listeners would guess correctly, and how often did they actually?
questions.answer: They predicted about half the time; listeners got about 1 in 40.

questions.q: What is the curse of knowledge?
questions.answer: Once we know something, it's hard to imagine not knowing it.
